scraped.title: Russell Brand sentenced to 10-and-a-half years in prison for rape and sexual assault
scraped.description: The disgraced entertainer was sentenced on Monday following a four-week trial at Southwark Crown Court.
scraped.author: https://www.facebook.com/bbcnews
scraped.h1: Russell Brand sentenced to 10-and-a-half years in prison for rape and sexual assault
scraped.body_text:
This video can not be played

Watch: Moment judge sentences Russell Brand in court

Warning - this report contains graphic content.

Russell Brand has been sentenced to 10 years and six months in prison, after being convicted of rape and sexual assault.

In his sentencing remarks, judge Joel Bennathan described Brand as a "sexual predator" and criticised his "staggering arrogance".

The 51-year-old was sentenced to nine years for rape, with an additional 18 months, nine months and eight months for three counts of sexual assault.

The disgraced entertainer was found guilty of the charges involving four women between 2004 and 2009.

Brand did not react in the dock as he was sentenced. Before being taken down to the cells, he mouthed "I love you" to his wife Laura Brand, who was in the court.

The guidelines state offenders jailed for four years or more for some serious violent or sexual offences will be released at the two thirds point. In Brand's case that would be seven years.

Once released, he is likely to spend the rest of his sentence on licence and will have to abide by specific rules such as wearing a tag. His sentence will not be included in the early release scheme. Sex offenders, along with murderers, are exempt from the scheme.

The judge also paid tribute to the bravery of the women who gave evidence during the trial.

Laura Brand was pictured as she left court following her husband's sentencing

In total, Brand was sentenced to:

Nine years' imprisonment for anally raping a 21-year-old in 2009 at his home in London

Nine months for sexually assaulting a woman whose breasts he grabbed at a bar in London in 2004 during a birthday party

Eighteen months for sexually assaulting a woman at the Choice FM studios in London in 2004 or 2005, when he grabbed her face and kissed her before touching her breasts and bottom

Eight months for sexual assault while working on a Channel 4 project in 2009, when he laid his head into the groin area of a woman working with him without her consent

In further remarks, the judge said Brand's status protected him until 2023, when journalists from the Sunday Times, the Times and Channel 4's Dispatches outlined a series of misconduct allegations, leading to women making complaints to police.

He said Brand harboured a "casual arrogant disregard to any woman's right to say no to you", while his fame meant he believed "you could act when you liked and how you liked".

The judge said the evidence in the case also showed that Brand's entourage during the peak of his celebrity had "indulged your dreadful behaviour".

Before Brand's sentencing, the court heard victim impact statements from the women he had been accused of assaulting.

One of the women, who spoke from behind a screen, said she had been in "shock and turmoil for years".

"I was extremely upset and traumatised," she said. "I didn't have any respect for myself. I was thinking I was damaged goods - scared of giving off signals that could be taken the wrong way."

She added: "I just want to say - a leopard may change its spots but it's still a leopard."

Russell Brand pictured outside court earlier this month

"Russell Brand has managed to move on," a woman, who was sexually assaulted by Brand in 2005, said in a statement read out in court. "This has had a lasting impact on my life. I recognise this now.

"However, over the years, hearing his voice on television or seeing his image has made me jump. I had a strong adverse reaction hearing his voice."

She added: "Russell Brand is a sexual predator who has no remorse... I just hope he is not allowed to hurt any more women."

A statement from the woman Brand was found to have raped was also shared in court.

"I felt anxious, humiliated and overwhelmed," she said. "I struggled to sleep and eat, I struggled to cope with my emotions, I had to take time away from my work," she said.

She continued: "I had to live with my parents, I sought help and support... I am living with trauma, something I carry every day.

"My confidence and self esteem have been badly affected. I no longer trust my instincts."

The woman said one of the worst parts of what happened was her fear that she might have contracted HIV. She also said she was in considerable pain after the assault.

A woman, who was sexually assaulted while working on a Channel 4 project with Brand in 2009, said in a statement that she was "really upset" afterwards.

"I felt I lost my trust in people, I felt my working environment wasn't safe," she said. "I felt powerless in that moment and it had a knock-on effect on my confidence."

In his sentencing remarks, Mr Justice Bennathan described Brand as a "sexual predator"

The verdicts were delivered on Thursday following a four-week trial at Southwark Crown Court in London.

Brand was found not guilty of two counts of rape and one count of attempted indecent assault.

He will automatically have to sign the Sex Offences' Register as part of his sentence because of the crimes he committed.

Laura Brand was seated just a few feet away from the former comedian in the glass-walled dock as he was being sentenced.

Earlier, as he arrived in the dock on Monday morning, Brand mouthed to his wife: "It'll be okay, I don't know how, but it will", and he was seen praying and making a cross sign with his hand as the victim statements were read out.

Brand's barrister Ian Winter KC put forward six character references, including one from Georgina Baillie, the granddaughter of the late actor Andrew Sachs.

Baillie was thrust into the spotlight in 2008 when Brand and Jonathan Ross left offensive messages about her on her grandfather's answering machine during a Radio 2 broadcast.

Winter also told the court that the former entertainer's wife Laura Brand, who gave evidence in her husband's defence during the trial, was experiencing "total devastation" at the verdicts.

He said Mr and Mrs Brand were "currently wrestling with how to exactly explain to a child who's just turned 10 what has happened here".

"It brings home the consequences of this conduct to totally innocent people who have been caught up in it," he said.

Sentencing Brand, the judge said: "I am very conscious that your imprisonment will deprive your children of the presence of their father.

"That sad loss to them, however, is caused by your serious offending."

Russell Brand on Trial

You can follow analysis and further insights on the BBC podcast Russell Brand on Trial - available on BBC Sounds, YouTube, iPlayer, or wherever you get your BBC podcasts

scraped.description: She accuses the disgraced performer of "violence, coercive control and abuse" while the two were together.

scraped.h1: Russell Brand's ex Jemima Goldsmith accuses him of violence and abuse against her
scraped.body_text:
Jemima Goldsmith (left) and Russell Brand (right) dated for about a year in the mid-2010s

Warning - this report contains graphic content.

Jemima Goldsmith, the ex-girlfriend of Russell Brand, has accused him of "violence, coercive control and abuse" while the two were together.

Goldsmith, who dated the disgraced entertainer for roughly a year around 2014, alleged that she "had to call the police to have him removed from my house in 2014 during a violent incident" but chose not to press charges.

In a lengthy statement on social media, the 52-year-old said she was "in awe of the courageous women who came forward at Brand's trial" and was "glad and relieved" he had "finally faced justice".

Brand, 51, was sentenced to 10-and-a-half years in prison earlier on Monday after being convicted of rape and sexual assault.

He was found guilty of raping a woman at his home in 2009, as well as three counts of sexual assault against three other women.

The judge at the sentencing hearing told Brand that he harboured a "casual arrogant disregard to any woman's right to say no to you", while his fame meant he believed "you could act when you liked and how you liked".

TV producer Goldsmith is also the former wife of ex-Pakistani prime minister and cricketer Imran Khan, the daughter of late billionaire entrepreneur Sir James Goldsmith and sister of ex-Conservative government minister Zac Goldsmith.

The mother-of-two said she had chosen not to pursue legal recourse against Brand over the alleged violent incident in 2014 as she was "worried about the impact of the press attention on my then teenage children".

She wrote on X on Monday evening: "Whilst my pain in relation to this pales in comparison to what the women have testified in court have suffered, this was a difficult period in my life which has had a lasting impact."

Goldsmith said she had not seen nor spoken to Brand since 2014, but claimed to have assisted the journalists who exposed the allegations against him and had been willing to testify to his "abusiveness" were they sued.

In her statement, she also addressed reports of an injunction taken out by her and Brand in October 2015 that banned a woman, Szilvia Berki, from harassing them including by making allegations of assault by Brand at Goldsmith's home the prior year.

Goldsmith said on Monday that Berki had visited her house for roughly 30 minutes on 7 June 2014 to give Brand a massage, which she said did not end up taking place once she arrived.

Jemima Goldsmith (pictured) alleged she once had to call the police on Brand

Goldsmith said that Berki later told police that Brand had pushed her in the back while she had been leaving and that she had been attacked by Goldsmith's dog. Brand's ex-girlfriend said she "did not see anything untoward" during the encounter.

She added that, after providing a statement and CCTV footage, police concluded that there was no case to answer.

Goldsmith accused Berki of then sending a series of "vicious antisemitic and threatening" messages and posting "wild and untrue allegations" about her on social media.

She said she then agreed to a suggestion from Brand's lawyer to seek an injunction to prevent harassment. She claimed on Monday that recent media reporting of the injunction had opened her up "to vile hatred and abuse online".

Sunday Times chief news correspondent Rosamund Urwin, who was involved in a media investigation into Brand in 2023, has told the BBC that Goldsmith helped her "a lot".

"I have seen the abuse she's been getting online and I did try to tell people that part of the story was much more complicated than they realise," Urwin said.

"I wish people would remember women that come forward are brave people and that is what she has done tonight – she has spoken out with immense bravery about how Russell Brand treated her," she added.

Brand's sentencing hearing heard victim impact statements from the women he had been accused of assaulting.

One of them said she was "upset and traumatised" for years after the incident, adding: "I didn't have any respect for myself. I was thinking I was damaged goods - scared of giving off signals that could be taken the wrong way."

The woman he was found guilty of raping said the trauma was something she had to "carry every day".

A van believed to be carrying Brand was seen arriving at HMP Wandsworth in London on Monday after the sentencing hearing.

items.title: France accuses Iran of cyber 'sabotage' in fridge attacks
items.summary: France says Iranian military hackers took over refrigeration controllers at around 700 different retail sites last month, turning up temperatures in the middle of the night and spoiling millions of dollars' worth of food. France says Iranian military hackers took over refrigeration controllers at around 700 different retail sites last month, turning up temperatures in the middle of the night and spoiling millions of dollars' worth of food.(Image credit: FRED TANNEAU)

scraped.title: France accuses Iran of cyber 'sabotage' in fridge attacks
scraped.description: France says Iranian military hackers took over refrigeration controllers at around 700 different retail sites last month, turning up temperatures in the middle of the night and spoiling millions of dollars' worth of food.
scraped.h1: France accuses Iran of cyber 'sabotage' in fridge attacks
scraped.body_text:
By

Jenna McLaughlin

,

Rebecca Rosman

A woman walks past empty refrigerators at an Intermarché supermarket in Névez, western France, on Oct. 12, following a cyberattack affecting the French supermarket chains Intermarché and Cooperative U that caused their refrigerators to defrost. FRED TANNEAU/AFP via Getty Images hide caption

France is accusing Iran of having launched a series of destructive cyberattacks against its critical infrastructure in October.

According to the French National Cybersecurity Agency, ANSSI, Iranian military hackers took over refrigeration controllers at around 700 different retail sites in France, from supermarkets to butcher shops, turning up the temperature in the middle of the night and spoiling millions of dollars' worth of food.

They also targeted several small hydroelectric power plants, resulting in "moderate effects," wrote ANSSI in its press release.

The hacking campaign was "unprecedented in both its scale and its level of aggression," said French Foreign Minister Jean-Noël Barrot. He said it "marks the first large-scale cyberattack aimed at sabotage on our national territory, and it constitutes a major attack on the nation's interests and the security of the French people."

The Paris Prosecutor's Office has opened its own investigation into the Iranian cyber unit, Shahid Kaveh, which the French government is linking to Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps. "The Paris Public Prosecutor's Office is requesting the issuance of international arrest warrants," the office said in a statement.

The attacks on French industrial controllers are part of a larger trend . In 2026 alone, hackers have targeted refrigeration controllers from Europe to Israel and the United States.

Grocery stores in European countries including Sweden and Ireland were hit in similar attacks last week.

In a separate incident in France, employees at a major French blood bank had to act fast to save blood samples from heating up when their refrigeration system was hit last week, prompting international calls for the health sector to protect its lifesaving products from spoiling.

In Israel in the spring, suspected Iranian hackers going by the name of "Cyber Isnaad Front" claimed responsibility for sabotaging an industrial food processing plant, including infecting its corporate computers with malware, taking over office printers to print out threatening messages and hacking office cameras for use in a propaganda video released in early October. That video included a taunt in French referencing ongoing education-related protests, and came just before the attacks on French supermarket fridges. Cyber incident response firm Profero attributed the Israel attack to a wing of Iran's Revolutionary Guard Corps .

Over the summer, commissaries on U.S. military bases also went through something similar, when food spoiled after the temperature shot up inside refrigerators and freezers overnight.

The French government is the first to formally assign blame for the wave of destructive attacks.

They were able to identify the hackers through a series of digital clues, including digital infrastructure used by the hackers, connection to a propaganda outlet, and "traces" of the use of Farsi language in the attack, according to ANSSI .

While NPR and others have reported that U.S. officials suspect Iran may have been behind the attacks on U.S. military bases in August, the Pentagon has not made any official statement, even to conclude that the disruptions were in fact the result of a cyberattack.

"Consistent with our policy and to preserve the integrity of the process, the DOD [Office of Inspector General] Criminal Investigative Service does not discuss ongoing investigations," Mollie Halpern, a spokesperson for the Department of War Office of the Inspector General wrote in an email to NPR.

If Iranian hackers are behind the attacks across Europe, the U.S. and Israel, cybersecurity experts say that would fit with what they know about Iranian hackers' strategy and goals.

"Iran's cyberattacks against refrigeration systems likely represents the IRGC attempting to reassert Iranian power abroad through both physically and psychologically disruptive operations," Alex Orleans, the head of threat intelligence at cybersecurity firm Sublime Security, told NPR. "Such activities continue to provide tangible and cost-effect results given how Iran's national resources remain tied down in the war."

"Also, Shahid Kaveh, the IRGC cyber unit that the French specifically attributed the disruptive attacks to, is repeating a pattern here," Orleans says. He referenced a series of cyberattacks on American water treatment plants in August, which most experts believe were linked to Iran, as precedent. The U.S. government has still not officially attributed those attacks.

"This unit has once again refined its tradecraft through attacks on Israeli targets before shifting their targeting to the same systems in the West," Orleans says.

For those tracking Shahid Kaveh and the other Iranian cyber units that operate alongside it, these attacks fit squarely into their modus operandi.

"Shahid Kaveh group is an offensive cyber unit responsible for some of the greatest hits of Iranian offensive cyber [operations]," says Ari Ben Am, an adjunct fellow at the Foundation for the Defense of Democracies' Center on Cyber and Technology Innovation.

One group tied to Shahid Kaveh is the Cyber Av3ngers, he explains, which the U.S. government linked to cyberattacks on Israeli-made systems in U.S. water treatment facilities in the winter between 2023 and 2024. The French government also cited other cyberattacks carried out on behalf of the IRGC against French interests, including against the satirical French magazine Charlie Hebdo and another against digital kiosks used at the Paris Olympics in 2024.

Cybersecurity experts say the attacks on refrigeration controllers have highlighted a yearslong difficulty with securing operational technology, the machines that control physical processes in the real world — from water pumps to cooling systems.

These machines are often outdated and riddled with vulnerabilities, and are very difficult to patch because operators can't afford to shut them down and disrupt critical services including healthcare and transportation. Additionally, the machines are often left exposed to the open internet — often at least in part due to contractual requirements with vendors that want to maintain those systems remotely. That combination of factors makes it a complicated problem to solve .

Iran has yet to respond to the accusations. However, Monday's accusation by the French government may lead other affected countries to take action as well.

During Monday's G7 meeting in Paris, Secretary of State Marco Rubio was asked by journalists whether the U.S. shared information with the French to help with their attribution of the Iranian hacks. Rubio said he couldn't comment, but noted that the "French are quite capable."

"What kind of sickos are these people?" he asked. "They attack refrigerators. France is not even involved in this, really," referring to the war between the U.S. and Iran, which began in February. "[These Iranians] do terrible things around the world … the news today doesn't surprise us," Rubio concluded.

Rebecca Rosman reported from Paris.

scraped.title: Supreme Court says border wall construction can continue in west Texas
scraped.description: The Trump administration filed an emergency relief request with the high court earlier in October asking for the construction to continue while a lawsuit over the plan moves forward.
scraped.h1: Supreme Court says border wall construction can continue in west Texas
scraped.body_text:
By

Carlos Morales

In September, Texas landowners filed a separate lawsuit over the federal government's border barrier plans in the Big Bend area, claiming their constitutional rights are being violated. Carlos Morales /for NPR. hide caption

The U.S. Supreme Court on Monday allowed the Trump administration to continue with its plans to construct hundreds of miles of border barrier and security infrastructure in west Texas, while a court hearing over the effort moves forward.

The federal government's plans have stirred bipartisan backlash for its inclusion of Big Bend National Park, a beloved stretch of public land known for its sweeping canyons and unspoiled desert landscape.

In a five-page decision issued Monday , the high court wrote that the federal judge who ruled on the order didn't have the authority to weigh in.

"The injunction thus impedes the Government from advancing its 'compelling interests' in border security and integrity," reads the unsigned decision. Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson was the lone dissenter in the decision.

The court wrote that federal law allows the Department of Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin to waive environmental protections and conservation laws, which they called a "clear preference for expeditious border construction over the very harms respondents assert."

In an emergency application to the high court in late October , the federal government urged the justices to intervene and allow the work to begin again, saying that a gap in "border defenses" in the Big Bend region "would act as "a dangerous magnet for cartels and other bad actors."

Along the border in Texas' Big Bend region, local residents have displayed signs protesting the Trump administration's border security plans for the area. Carlos Morales/for NPR. hide caption

A federal judge in El Paso issued the temporary injunction that halted the construction of 30-foot-tall steel barriers, patrol roads, surveillance systems and other border infrastructure.

The Center for Biological Diversity, an environmental advocacy group, brought forward the lawsuit, along with an area nonprofit working to preserve a historic church near the U.S.-Mexico border and a landowner who stands to lose his border property.

"This decision greenlights the contractors and allows the bulldozers to come roaring back into the region," said Laiken Jordahl with the Center for Biological Diversity. "It allows the dynamiting of national park canyon walls, the bulldozing of pristine desert."

The lawsuit argued that the Department of Homeland Security's plans are unconstitutional and that Big Bend residents would be "irreparably harmed" if the construction continues.

The Trump administration's plans for the beloved Big Bend region of Texas have provoked an unusual bipartisan backlash. People across the political spectrum say a wall isn't needed in the Big Bend––a region known for its sweeping canyons, tough terrain and unforgiving desert heat. They worry about the threats a wall or any other kind of infrastructure poses to the region, from the impact on the environment and Indigenous sites to the effect on the region's tourism-based economy and on wild animals .

In the Trump administration's emergency relief request to the Supreme Court , Solicitor General John Sauer called the injunction "baseless" and "unprecedented" and said any pocket of the Big Bend without a barrier would "become a funnel point for illegal alien crossings that are thwarted by barriers elsewhere."

Historically, the Big Bend area's rugged landscape has meant fewer people attempting to cross into the U.S. through this pocket of the border. And while the Big Bend Sector, a nearly 500-mile stretch covered by U.S. Customs and Border Protection, makes up over a quarter of the U.S.-Mexico border, it regularly sees the fewest number of encounters along the Texas border, according to CBP data .

In September, the group No Big Bend Wall took to a typically busy intersection in the small town of Marfa, Texas, to protest the Trump administration's border security plans for the Big Bend. Carlos Morales/for NPR. hide caption

scraped.title: Thomas Massie files articles of impeachment against Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth
scraped.description: The articles accuse Hegseth of "high crimes and misdemeanors," including for waging war against Iran in violation of the War Powers Resolution.
scraped.h1: Thomas Massie files articles of impeachment against Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth
scraped.body_text:
By

Barbara Sprunt

Rep. Thomas Massie (R-KY), seen here on September 16, 2026 at the U.S. Capitol, filed articles of impeachment against Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth on Monday. Roberto Schmidt/Getty Images hide caption

Rep. Thomas Massie has reintroduced articles of impeachment against Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, setting up a vote in the House of Representatives in the next two days.

The Kentucky Republican's resolution accuses Hegseth of high crimes and misdemeanors and lists eight specific charges against him.

The allegations include:

Pete Hegseth greets British Defense Secretary Wes Streeting at the Pentagon on Oct. 15, 2026. Hegseth says any effort to impeachment him will fail. Finn Gomez/Getty Images hide caption

Hegseth defended his record at the Pentagon in a video released last Thursday, dismissing Massie's effort as "sham articles of impeachment."

"Didn't work against President Trump and it won't work with me," Hegseth said.

Speaking to reporters during an impromptu press briefing on Monday, Trump expressed support for his embattled Defense Secretary.

"I'll stand by him," Trump said. "He won two wars. He was in charge. We all won."

Massie has long been a staunch critic of Hegseth. During the GOP primary, Hegseth campaigned on behalf of Ed Gallrein, who went on to defeat Massie.

In response to Hegseth calling him a "disgruntled defeated congressman," Massie told reporters on Monday: "Well, he's right about one thing — I'm a defeated congressman. I'm not disgruntled."

He added: "I'm being polite here. What is an impeachment? An impeachment is just firing someone, really. You don't go to prison, you don't go to jail, you don't pay a fine. When the Democrats get in charge, they are going to be very vicious."

Massie said the effort also underscores the need to litigate whether Congress has real war powers or not. The war powers resolution has largely been ignored by presidents of both parties.

"What's at heart here is the balance of power between the executive branch and Congress," he said.

Massie first sought to bring the impeachment resolution to the floor before the midterm elections , prompting Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., to call an early recess to avoid the vote. That caused the resolution to expire, which is why Massie reintroduced the resolution Monday.

Presumptive next House Speaker Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., has already signaled support for an impeachment push against Hegseth.

Even Republican members who oppose impeaching Hegseth have said the Trump administration could do a better job making the case to Congress and the public about what the plan is for the Iran war going forward.

Rep. Warren Davidson, R-Ohio., indicated to NPR that impeachment would be hypocritical given that administrations going back to the Korean War have largely ignored Congress' war powers efforts.

"I think trying to scapegoat Pete Hegseth is just the status quo politics in Washington," he said. "I think it would be a mistake to impeach."

Davidson said lawmakers who want changes are better off trying to leverage the power of the purse to withhold money from the conflict.

There could be sufficient votes to impeach Hegseth in the House, with the support of all Democrats, Massie, and a handful of Republicans. However, it is unlikely to clear the higher Senate threshold for convicting and removing Hegseth from office — which requires two-thirds of the Senate.

NPR's Eric McDaniel contributed to this report.

scraped.description: Dana White joined President Donald Trump at a White House press briefing where Trump said his suggestion to make the UFC CEO his press secretary was a joke.
scraped.author: Louis Casiano
scraped.h1: Dana White takes questions at podium during White House briefing with Trump
scraped.body_text:

President Donald Trump and UFC CEO Dana White address rumors that White was offered the White House press secretary position.

UFC CEO Dana White joined President Donald Trump at a White House press briefing on Monday, where Trump clarified that his recent suggestion to appoint the fight executive as his press secretary was merely a joke.

Trump made a surprise appearance at the briefing to address reports that he had reached out to White for the role following a difficult news cycle.

"We were having a very bad press day, and I said: 'I don't know why I thought of his name. ' He's been my friend for a long time. I said: 'You know, I think I'm going to get Dana White to be my new press secretary,'" Trump told reporters. "I said it to a group of the press and that was it. I was sort of kidding, and then they wrote the story as though I wasn't kidding."

TRUMP SAYS HE WAS ‘ONLY KIDDING’ ABOUT MAKING DANA WHITE PRESS SECRETARY

President Donald Trump welcomes Ultimate Fighting Championship (UFC) CEO Dana White to speak during a press briefing in the Brady Briefing Room of the White House in Washington, DC, on November 9, 2026. (Mandel Ngan / AFP via Getty Images)

White then took the podium to address reporters and shut down any rumors of entering government service.

"I have zero political aspirations," White said. "I was at a fight for Zuffa Boxing in London when he called me and told me that he had done this, and the last 24 hours of my life have been insane."

When asked by a reporter to break down a hypothetical UFC cage match between Trump and former President Joe Biden , White praised Trump’s toughness while dismissing the match up.

President Donald Trump and Dana White, UFC president and CEO, arrive for UFC Freedom 250 on the South Lawn of the White House in Washington on June 14, 2026. (Alex Brandon/AP)

FOLLOW US ON X

"He's the toughest, most resilient human being that I've ever met in my entire life," White said of Trump. "Many times during the last eight or 10 years, I have told him: 'Why? Why do you keep doing this? ' But as tough and as resilient as I thought he was, after he got shot, he proved he is a one-of-one unique human being."

Regarding the hypothetical fight, White added: "It would be very bad. Yeah, I think it would be very bad... I can't believe you actually have questions for me."

White added that he never explicitly told Trump "no" regarding the position.

Before stepping away, the UFC chief was also asked what advice he would give Trump regarding a potential posthumous pardon for Pete Rose , the legendary baseball player who died in 2024.

President Donald Trump speaks with Dana White (left) during UFC 309 at Madison Square Garden. (Brad Penner-Imagn Images)

Rose was banned from MLB Hall of Fame eligibility due to betting on baseball games, including those involving his own team, the Cincinnati Reds. In 2025, MLB Commissioner Rob Manfred removed Rose and 16 other deceased people from the permanently ineligible list.

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

Trump reiterated during the briefing that he favors pardoning the hit king.

scraped.author: Bonny Chu
scraped.h1: Jeffries vows Democrats won’t ‘give a dime’ to Trump’s deportation efforts
scraped.body_text:
This material may not be published, broadcast, rewritten, or redistributed. ©2026 FOX News Network, LLC. All rights reserved. Quotes displayed in real-time or delayed by at least 15 minutes. Market data provided by Factset . Powered and implemented by FactSet Digital Solutions . Legal Statement . Mutual Fund and ETF data provided by LSEG .

House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries said Democrats have pledged to withhold funding for what he calls President Donald Trump’s "violent mass deportation machine."

Rep. Hakeem Jeffries on Monday laid out an aggressive agenda for House Democrats as the party prepares to take control of the chamber following sweeping midterm election victories, declaring that Democrats will "not give a dime" toward funding the Trump administration's deportation efforts.

The House minority leader made the remarks during a press conference, one week before Democrats are set to vote on whether Jeffries should remain in his leadership position.

"The American people clearly and decisively rejected MAGA extremism on Tuesday and voted for dramatic change," Jeffries said.

"House Democrats have taken the position that we're not going to give a dime to the administration's violent mass deportation machine," he added.

DEMS PIVOT FROM ‘AFFORDABILITY’ PITCH TO DHS PROBE THREATS AFTER MIDTERM WINS

Jeffries also criticized the use of taxpayer dollars to support what he called "un-American" policies under President Donald Trump.

"Taxpayer dollars should be used to make life more affordable for the American people, not brutalize or kill American citizens, and violently target law-abiding immigrant communities and families, which is what has happened over the last two years," Jeffries said.

TRUMP TELLS DHS CHIEF TO WORK WITH DEMOCRATS ON IMMIGRATION REFORM, BUT NO AMNESTY

He added that he hopes to secure one additional signature on a discharge petition that would bypass House leadership and force a floor vote on the American Dream and Promise Act, which would provide permanent legal status and a pathway to citizenship for Dreamers and recipients of Temporary Protected Status (TPS).

"Hopefully some of our colleagues on the other side of the aisle will be willing to do that work, perhaps beginning with one additional signature that we need to force a vote on the Dream and Promise Act from a Republican," he said.

Among other priorities, Jeffries said Democrats want to pass legislation banning members of the House and Senate from trading stocks , an effort aimed at restoring public trust in government.

He also voiced support for an impeachment resolution against Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth over his handling of the war in Iran and alleged constitutional violations.

"I'm a hard yes, as I've made clear, on the impeachment resolution. Pete Hegseth has abused his power, undermined America's national security, and he's the architect of the reckless and costly failed war of choice in Iran, which has skyrocketed gas prices on everyday Americans, made the country less safe," Jeffries said.

"Iran is stronger now than they were before," he argued.

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

FILE — House Democrats will refuse funding for President Donald Trump’s deportation efforts, Hakeem Jeffries said. (Getty Images)

As the Democratic caucus leadership vote approaches next Wednesday, reporters asked Jeffries whether he was concerned about progressive members who have criticized him for not taking a more aggressive approach during his tenure as leader.

Jeffries said he plans to speak with every member of the caucus in an effort to retain his position.

"I'm going to work hard to talk to every single member about what we've been able to do together over the last two years, and what the opportunities are for us to do together in the next two years," he said.

items.summary: Erin Lee says her daughter was secretly socially transitioned at school, sparking the grassroots campaign behind Colorado's ballot measures. scraped.title: Colorado mom who said daughter was secretly transitioned helps lead effort to ban boys in girls' sports
scraped.description: Colorado ballot measures on child sex trafficking, transgender athletes in school sports and gender transition surgeries for minors passed after a grassroots campaign.
scraped.author: Rachel del Guidice
scraped.h1: Colorado mom who said daughter was secretly transitioned helps lead effort to ban boys in girls' sports
scraped.body_text:
This material may not be published, broadcast, rewritten, or redistributed. ©2026 FOX News Network, LLC. All rights reserved. Quotes displayed in real-time or delayed by at least 15 minutes. Market data provided by Factset . Powered and implemented by FactSet Digital Solutions . Legal Statement . Mutual Fund and ETF data provided by LSEG .

Protect Kids Colorado executive director Erin Lee tells Fox News Digital how her family's experience helped inspire a grassroots campaign behind Colorado ballot measures addressing girls' sports & transgender surgeries for minors.

A Colorado mother who said her daughter was secretly socially transitioned at school helped lead a grassroots campaign that delivered major midterm victories, including measures restricting boys from playing in girls' spots in the traditionally Democratic state.

Erin Lee, executive director and co-founder of Protect Kids Colorado, told Fox News Digital that the campaign's success was deeply personal, coming more than five years after an experience involving her daughter transformed her from a self-described left-leaning Democrat into a prominent parental rights advocate.

"I co-founded Protect Kids Colorado because, five-and-a-half years ago, my 12-year-old daughter was secretly transitioned in her sixth-grade classroom," Lee said.

EXCLUSIVE: RHODE ISLAND SCHOOL DISTRICT ACCUSED OF HIDING KIDS' GENDER TRANSITIONS FROM PARENTS

Erin Lee, executive director and co-founder of Protect Kids Colorado, told Fox News Digital that the Protect Kids Colorado campaign's success was deeply personal, coming more than five years after an experience involving her daughter transformed her from a self-described left-leaning Democrat into a prominent parental rights advocate. (Chelsea @ Chelsea Smith Imagery )

In 2023, Lee, her husband and another couple, who at the time had sixth-grade daughters attending Wellington Middle-High School (WMS), sued educators at the Poudre School District with the assistance of America First Policy Institute and Illumine Legal, according to a copy of the lawsuit.

Her group championed three ballot initiatives: Proposition 133, which increases penalties for child sex trafficking to life in prison without parole; Proposition 134 , which would generally require students to compete on school sports teams corresponding to their biological sex; and Proposition 135 , which would prohibit certain gender-transition surgeries for minors.

JACKSON THOMPSON: COLORADO GOV-ELECT PHIL WEISER SIGNALS POSSIBLE CHANGES TO GIRLS' SPORTS BALLOT MEASURE

A voter prepares to cast a ballot on Election Day. (PATRICK T. FALLON/AFP via Getty Images)

Proposition 133 passed with approximately 62% support , while the other two measures, proposition 134, received roughly 52% and proposition 135 also received 52%.

In the same election, Coloradans re-elected Democratic Sen. John Hickenlooper in a landslide with 60 percent of the vote.

Lee said that the results demonstrate opposition to certain transgender policies that extend beyond traditional partisan lines.

"Colorado broke ranks where they voted for Democrats," Lee said. "They also voted yes on these commonsense child protection measures."

"I think that really speaks volumes to the fact that gender ideology is not a winning issue," she added.

Lee said the campaign relied on more than 3,300 petition circulators, over 1,900 notaries and support from more than 1,000 churches. She claimed opponents spent more than $5 million , outspending her organization by more than 20 to 1.

"This really was a movement of the people," Lee said.

PORTLAND PUBLIC SCHOOLS RESCINDS BAN ON WOMAN WHO QUESTIONED CHILD'S GENDER IDENTITY ASSIGNMENT

Erin Lee and her daughter. (Chelsea @ Chelsea Smith Imagery )

She also described the personal toll of her family's experience, alleging that school officials turned against her and her husband after they questioned their daughter's change in gender identity.

"We walked through a living nightmare," Lee said.

"Prior to 2021, I was your typical left-leaning Democrat voting, politically disengaged, virtue-signaling mom," Lee said.

"And then it happened to us personally, and we were attacked by the school district when my daughter came home and declared she was suddenly a boy. We spoke up to the school and they vilified us. They sent in a well child check to check on our kids and assumed we weren't fit parents because we didn't instantly affirm. We were bullied with the suicide myth, ‘Would you rather have a living son or a dead daughter? You have to medicalize your child,’ and we're one of a few success stories," she said.

Lee said her daughter one day moved on from the gender confusion, and asked her mom to become an advocate for others who might find themselves in a similar place.

"It took almost a year to get her through this mentality," Lee said. "It included suicidal ideation and estrangement from people in our lives who didn't agree with us, not affirming her. She asked us to speak up to help other kids, and that's what launched me into sharing our story and it going viral, and really becoming this person that people could come to with their own stories of what they were going through, and I just learned how pervasive gender ideology is."

Her daughter’s request, according to Lee, helped launch the advocacy work that ultimately grew into Protect Kids Colorado's statewide campaign.

WASHINGTON STATE VOTERS APPEAR TO PASS FIRST-EVER BALLOT MEASURE SEPARATING BOYS AND GIRLS SPORTS

Coloradans sign Protect Kids Colorado measures. (Erin Lee)

Lee said she sees the election results as evidence of a broader cultural shift.

"Gender ideology is a house of cards," she said, arguing that the Colorado vote could inspire similar efforts elsewhere.

"The voters have spoken," Lee said. "We've come a long way culturally for this to have passed."

A spokesperson for Poudre School District told Fox News Digital in a statement that, "Poudre School District does not comment on individual students, consistent with federal student privacy law."

The spokesperson added that "the claims in Lee v. Poudre School District R-1 were dismissed by the U.S. District Court for the District of Colorado. That dismissal was affirmed by the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Tenth Circuit in April 2025. The plaintiffs subsequently petitioned the U.S. Supreme Court for review, and the Court denied that petition in October 2025. At no stage of this litigation was the district found liable."

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

Advocates for Protect Kids Colorado. (Erin Lee)

Fox News Digital reached out to LGBTQ advocacy organization One Colorado for comment, as well as Families Not Politics, an organization opposing the measures.

Rachel del Guidice is a culture reporter for Fox News covering the intersection of politics, faith, family, and American culture.

scraped.h1: Trump says FBI is investigating Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s relationship with alleged Chinese spy
scraped.body_text:
BREAKING: Trump says FBI is investigating Nvidia CEO’s relationship with alleged Chinese spy

For You

Settings

news Alerts

There are no new alerts at this time

President Donald Trump said that he had spoken to Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang earlier in the day Monday, after Nvidia revealed late Sunday that it had launched an investigation into his extramarital affair with an alleged Chinese spy.

Trump had called Huang, “To see if he’s feeling all right,” the president said at an impromptu press briefing.

Huang told him “he had absolutely no idea that the person in question was a spy,” Trump said.

“He said I had no idea that she was a spy, and I really, and I really believe him,” said Trump.

The president also said that the FBI was probing the events in question.

On Sunday, the Nvidia board announced it was “initiating an independent investigation in light of recent reporting that founder and CEO Jensen Huang has been the target of a foreign intelligence effort.”

At the same time, Huang announced that he had been “unfaithful to my wife,” while also apologizing to Nvidia employees.

“I was amazed because I view him as a very high quality person,” Trump told reporters at the White House. “He’s an amazing guy,” he continued, adding, “I hope there’s no problem.”

Trump indicated for the second time in as many days that he wanted Huang to remain the leader of the second largest public company in the world. “I think that he’ll be in good shape,” Trump said.

On Sunday, people familiar with the matter told NBC News that U.S. intelligence agencies had determined that Alice Huang, the woman who Jensen Huang allegedly had the affair with, was a Chinese spy. Jensen Huang and Alice Huang are not related.

Nvidia spokespeople did not immediately return a request for comment Monday following Trump’s remarks. Nvidia previously said Huang would remain CEO, despite the revelations.

Shares of Nvidia closed down 4.2% in Monday’s trading, bucking overall market momentum. The stock was the worst performing company in the Dow and Nasdaq.

The news surrounding Nvidia and Huang also drew intense congressional scrutiny.

Rep. Hakeem Jeffries, D-NY, on Monday called for “a full briefing” on the issues engulfing Nvidia. Jeffries is likely to be elected the next speaker of the House in January.

Sens. Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass., and Jim Banks, R-Ind., also said in a joint statement that Congress should “take decisive action” regarding oversight of AI-linked companies.

The disclosures by Nvidia and Huang “makes these national security concerns even more urgent and raises important questions NVIDIA must answer,” Warren and Banks wrote.

Steve Kopack is a senior reporter at NBC News covering business and the economy.

items.title: Trump admin proposes stricter unemployment work search rules
items.summary: Under a proposed federal rule, Americans seeking unemployment aid would have to conduct more job searches each week.

scraped.title: Trump administration proposes stricter work search rules to qualify for unemployment benefits
scraped.description: Under a proposed federal rule, Americans seeking unemployment aid would have to conduct more job searches each week.
scraped.h1: Trump administration proposes stricter work search rules to qualify for unemployment benefits
scraped.body_text:
Watch CBS News

Updated on: November 9, 2026 / 5:41 PM EST / CBS News

The Trump administration on Monday proposed stiffer rules for Americans seeking unemployment benefits that, if adopted, would require them to conduct more weekly job searches.

The proposed Department of Labor regulations, set to be published in the Federal Register on Tuesday, would require people applying for or collecting jobless aid to complete at least five unique work searches per week. Currently, many U.S. states require two to three qualifying work searches per week, while only four states require five. Some states require only one work search activity to qualify for unemployment benefits.

The Trump administration said the change is necessary to create consistent eligibility requirements for unemployment benefits nationwide. A national minimum weekly work search standard would "improve program integrity and strengthen labor market attachment," the Labor Department said in its proposal.

"This action is necessary to reduce inconsistencies beyond those created by local labor markets in State-level requirements for individuals to actively seek work," according to the agency. "The intended effect is to hold States accountable for administering [an unemployment compensation] program that provides temporary wage replacement to eligible individuals while they are actively seeking work through a meaningful engagement with the labor market."

The public has 60 days following publication of the proposed rule to offer comment.

Labor advocates criticized the proposed change in work search rules, saying the new threshold would be hard for unemployed people to meet and costly for states to administer.

"Not only is the proposed change devastating to claimants who may not have five search options for every week they are unemployed, but it will likely cost states hundreds of thousands of dollars," Michele Evermore, senior director of economic security and worker transitions at the National Employment Law Project, a worker advocacy group, said in a statement to CBS News. "Nearly all states will have to change their claimant intake forms, and with it, their technology — a costly fix. Many states will have to rewrite their laws to meet this rule."

Evermore also said the proposed rule would disadvantage applicants who already struggle to navigate the unemployment benefits systems. Employers "want candidates enthusiastic about their job opportunities, not ticking boxes for the work search form," she added.

The Labor Department acknowledged that the policy could temporarily raise costs as states and jobless aid applicants adapt to the new work requirement, but said the change is necessary to ensure that the eligibility rules are applied consistently across the U.S.

"These inconsistencies can create confusion for individuals, lead to uneven enforcement when allowable activities are not clearly defined, and increase the likelihood that otherwise eligible individuals may fail to meet requirements simply because expectations are unclear," the Labor Department said. "Additionally, variability in how States notify individuals of work search requirements can result in individuals engaging in activities that may not support reemployment or may not satisfy the State's rules."

Various activities would satisfy the proposed requirement that people seeking jobless aid conduct at least five work searches per week, according to the Labor Department. For example, beyond contacting a prospective employer, registering with or contacting a job placement agency or union would also count as a qualified work search.

Under the proposal, states could also designate other activities as satisfying the requirement. Additionally, states could adapt the weekly job search threshold to account for local labor market conditions through a points-based system that would allow someone applying for jobless aid to accrue multiple points for a single activity.

"Under such a system, States may assign point values to qualifying work search activities and require individuals to accumulate a minimum of five points per benefit week," the Labor Department said.

Edited by Alain Sherter

items.title: Massie introduces impeachment articles against Hegseth
items.summary: Hegseth said he's "not worried" about an impeachment effort.

scraped.title: Massie introduces impeachment articles against Hegseth
scraped.description: Hegseth said he's "not worried" about an impeachment effort.
scraped.author: ABC News
scraped.h1: Massie introduces impeachment articles against Hegseth
scraped.body_text:
Hegseth said he's "not worried" about an impeachment effort.

Republican Rep. Thomas Massie introduced articles of impeachment against Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth on the House floor Monday afternoon.

Hegseth said on Monday that he's "not worried about" efforts to impeach him over his controversial leadership at the Pentagon and role administering the Iran war, announcing a rare press conference on the topic set for Tuesday.

"We’re not worried about that,” Hegseth said when asked by a reporter about Republican support on Capitol Hill amid the impeachment effort led by outgoing Rep. Massie.

"We're going to do a press conference tomorrow morning at the Pentagon on that very topic. So I'll save my remarks there. I hope you all come loaded for bear with your questions," said Hegseth, who hasn't held a press conference since May.

Hegseth's comments came the same day Massie reintroduced a privileged resolution to impeach Hegseth. Calls to impeach Hegseth have grown as several Republicans have attributed the GOP's sweeping midterm losses to the Iran war.

Massie went through the process in mid-September only to be thwarted by Speaker Mike Johnson, who canceled the final scheduled day of legislative business before the midterm elections -- staving off a vote at the time.

"Here's the parliamentary reality of it. What Speaker Johnson has done, I believe, after talking to the parliamentarian, is I will have to refile the articles of impeachment when we get back,” Massie told ABC News on Sept. 16. "They will expire. Maybe they'll grow. Maybe he'll do something between now and the election that warrants another article, or and so I'll have to refile those when we get back."

After Massie's reintroduction of the resolution, the House must take up the measure within two legislative days -- forcing Republicans to go on the record defending Hegseth after suffering major losses in the 2026 midterm elections.

Massie, a conservative who has gained a reputation as a constitutionalist through his seven terms in the House, lost a primary earlier this summer after President Donald Trump endorsed his opponent.

It's unclear whether an impeachment effort will succeed in the House, which is still under Republican control, but Massie told ABC News’ Jon Karl that he's confident there will be enough GOP defectors for it to pass. Massie needs a simple majority for the impeachment resolution to succeed in the House, meaning that just three Republicans need to vote with all Democrats to prevail.

It doesn't appear that any Democrats will vote against the impeachment effort. House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries came out in support of impeaching Hegseth saying on ABC News' "This Week" on Sunday that he's a "hard yes."

GOP leaders could offer a motion to "table" the resolution rather than take a direct vote on the underlying measure. That would need to pass by a simple majority.

House Oversight Committee Chairman James Comer declined to back the Hegseth impeachment effort, but Massie volunteered that "there’s a lot of questions about" Hegseth, including the embattled secretary’s strategy in Iran.

"I will weigh the debate and make a decision," retiring Republican Rep. Don Bacon told ABC News' Kyra Phillips on Friday when asked if he will vote to impeach Hegseth. "I do think the secretary has made some bad mistakes."

Even if the measure passes in the House, it would still need approval by a two-thirds majority in the GOP-controlled Senate, a lofty threshold that's unlikely to be met.

Trump has maintained that he has "every intention to keep" Hegseth atop the Pentagon.

In a video posted Thursday, Hegseth proclaimed that he will not back down -- doubling down on the Iran war and his cultural agenda at the Pentagon while drawing a parallel to Trump.

"This is not about me, but of course the other side, they’re obsessed. A disgruntled, defeated congressman, along with all his Democratic allies has also dropped sham articles of impeachment against yours truly. Just like they tried against President Trump twice," Hegseth said in the video.

ABC News' Steven Beynon contributed to this report.

items.title: Trial for man accused of murdering Charlie Kirk set to begin in mid-2028, judge rules
items.summary: Defense attorneys for the suspect, Tyler Robinson, asked that the capital trial start in late 2029, while the state recommended early 2028.

scraped.title: Trial for man accused of murdering Charlie Kirk set to begin in mid-2028, judge rules
scraped.description: Defense attorneys for the suspect, Tyler Robinson, asked that the capital trial start in late 2029, while the state recommended early 2028.
scraped.author: ABC News
scraped.h1: Trial for man accused of murdering Charlie Kirk set to begin in mid-2028, judge rules
scraped.body_text:
Jury selection in Tyler Robinson's trial is scheduled to begin on June 21, 2028.

The trial for the man accused of murdering Charlie Kirk while the conservative activist was speaking on a college campus last year is set to begin in mid-2028.

Utah District Court Judge Tony Graf had been expected to set a timeline for the high-profile capital murder case , including the trial date, during a hearing last month. He ultimately scheduled a hearing on the matter for Monday afternoon, during which he announced that jury selection will start on June 21, 2028.

That timing is intended "to ensure that the constitutional rights" of the suspect, Tyler Robinson, and Kirk's widow "are upheld at every junction," Graf said.

He reserved 105 days for the trial.

Defense attorneys for the suspect in the fatal shooting asked that the capital murder trial start in late 2029, while the state recommended early 2028.

In a memo filed last month, the defense asked for the trial to start in the third quarter of 2029 -- four years after Kirk was fatally shot during a Turning Point USA event -- arguing that that timeline is consistent with other capital cases in the state.

The defense anticipated that the trial could take six to seven months and would require "substantial time" for jury selection. The defense also noted they plan to undertake a venue study and, depending on the results, may request a change of venue for the trial.

In the state's own filing, prosecutors said they anticipate the trial lasting 17 weeks and that they could be ready to start as soon as Oct. 4, 2027. However, the state recommended that the trial begin on Jan. 31, 2028, to avoid the "worst of the winter season" as well as the Thanksgiving and Christmas holidays.

Kirk's family wants the trial to start as soon as next year, according to a court filing. In response to both filings, Kirk's widow, Erika Kirk, asked the court to "enforce the right to a speedy disposition" and set the trial for as early as possible in 2027, no later than the state's anticipated readiness date of Oct. 4, 2027, to avoid "needless delay."

"Under the Defendants' proposed schedule, Mr. Kirk's two children, who were one and three at the time he was murdered, will be six and eight years old by the time the trial concludes," a motion filed on Erika Kirk's behalf stated. "They will face the uncertainty of this criminal proceeding longer than they had their father in their lives. Each hearing induces anxiety, pain, and mourning. The Kirk family deserves to have this matter resolved expeditiously."

The motion also argued that a 2029 trial start will come at a "great cost to the taxpayers of Utah."

Robinson is accused of killing Kirk with a rifle shot fired from a building's rooftop approximately 415 feet from where the co‑founder of the conservative student organization Turning Point USA was speaking at an outdoor rally at Utah Valley University in Orem, Utah, on Sept. 10, 2025.

The 23-year-old suspect was charged with aggravated murder, a capital felony, which alleges that others were knowingly endangered in the shooting. He was also charged with felony discharge of a firearm causing serious bodily injury, obstruction of justice, witness tampering and commission of a violent offense in the presence of a child.

In September, Judge Graf found probable cause for Robinson to stand trial on all charges. The judge also found that there was a reasonable known risk of death to others at the time of the shooting, allowing prosecutors to pursue the death penalty.

Robinson has pleaded not guilty to the charges.

24/7 coverage of breaking news and live events

scraped.title: Trump calls Iran war ‘effectively over’ after talks with Qatar PM
scraped.description: Iranian officials dismissed Trump’s latest remarks as ‘fake news’ after the US president suggested a close to the war.
scraped.author: Al Jazeera Staff
scraped.h1: Trump calls Iran war ‘effectively over’ after talks with Qatar PM
scraped.body_text:
Iranian officials dismissed Trump’s latest remarks as ‘fake news’ after the US president suggested a close to the war.

Save

Share

United States President Donald Trump has signalled that he considers the US-Israeli war against Iran “effectively” at an end, after meeting with mediators from Qatar.

In a surprise briefing on Monday, Trump reiterated his position that the US had destroyed Iran’s military. But his remarks suggested he faced pressure from allies in the Middle East to bring hostilities to a close.

“Iran, militarily, is effectively over. We’re just keeping it the status quo,” he said. “We’re doing that really at the behest of countries that are their neighbours.”

The US president clarified that the “status quo” would involve continuing the US naval blockade against Iranian ports, as well as the newly announced Task Force Iron Gate, which seeks to cut off trade by land and through the Caspian Sea.

“Much was discussed with respect to the Islamic Republic of Iran,” Trump said.

“Most importantly, Qatar, Saudi Arabia, UAE, Bahrain, Kuwait and others would prefer the status quo, that we remain as is — in other words, a continuation of the greatest naval blockade in the history of our country. Probably in the history of the world.”

Trump’s comments come shortly after he and Vice President JD Vance hosted Qatari Prime Minister Mohammed bin Abdulrahman bin Jassim Al Thani at the White House to discuss the Iran war.

The prime minister posted on social media that he was “grateful for the positive discussions on reaching a deal and bringing peace to the region”.

It is unclear whether Trump’s latest statements significantly change US posture in the war. Trump himself declined to commit to any long-term ceasefire.

“I don’t guarantee anything,” he told the White House briefing room. “But if we do have to go back in, we are locked and loaded and ready to go.”

Iranian officials, meanwhile, dismissed Trump’s latest remarks as a distraction. Both sides have claimed victory throughout the conflict.

“The war on Iran has already wrecked the US government. But Washington flails like a desperate gambler,” Iran’s Supreme National Security Council Secretary Mohsen Rezaei wrote in a post on social media.

“FOLD YOUR HAND. STOP manufacturing FAKE NEWS about imaginary talks.”

Separately, through Iran’s state-aligned Tasnim News Agency, Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian said that Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei had called for an end to the situation, which he described as “neither war nor peace”.

Pezeshkian added that Iran was open to further negotiations but would not be coerced. “We will not surrender to force and bullying,” he said.

This is a breaking news story. More details to come…

scraped.description: During private meetings with survivors, Pope Leo XIV pledged to reinforce safeguards and listen to victims.
scraped.h1: Pope meets with clergy abuse survivors in Argentina
scraped.body_text:
During private meetings with survivors, Pope Leo XIV pledged to reinforce safeguards and listen to victims.

Save

Share

Pope Leo XIV has met with five survivors of clerical sexual abuse on the second day of his historic visit to Argentina.

The private meetings in Buenos Aires on Monday were the first of several talks the pope is planning to hold with abuse survivors during his 12-day tour of Latin America, according to the Vatican.

“The Pope spoke individually with each of them, listened to their words and to the painful stories of their experiences, as well as to their proposals for strengthening paths towards healing within the Church,” the Vatican said in a statement.

The closed-door meetings followed a historic open-air mass that drew an estimated 2.5 million people to Avenida del Libertador, a major boulevard in the capital, at the Monumento de los Espanoles. It was the country’s first papal liturgy in nearly 40 years.

The meetings with survivors respond to the pope’s desire to “express his closeness to those who have suffered”, build paths to healing and ensure the church is a safe and “spiritually healthy” place, the Holy See Press Office said in October.

Leo, the first pope born in the United States, has consistently met with survivors during foreign visits as part of a wider outreach aiming to repair global relations and restore the Catholic Church’s credibility. Lawsuits, widespread sexual abuse and cover-ups have sullied its reputation over the last three decades.

While clergy abuse cases are difficult to track globally, a 2021 independent inquiry found there were an estimated 216,000 victims of the French Catholic Church’s clergy alone between 1950 and 2020. Earlier research found more than 10,600 people were abused by Catholic priests in the US between 1950 and 2002, while Australia counted 6,875 victims of Catholic clergy, religious and lay church workers between 1980 and 2015, according to a 2019 German study .

During the meeting, which lasted more than an hour, Leo, 71, listened to victims’ testimonies and reiterated his pledge to strengthen safeguarding in the Catholic Church. Before being named pope, Leo served as president of the Pontifical Commission for Latin America.

Argentina is the second stop on Leo’s three-country tour, which began in Uruguay and will wrap up in Peru.

His visit was the first by a pontiff since Pope John Paul II’s trip in 1987.

scraped.author: Al Jazeera Staff
scraped.h1: Hungarian police reportedly detain brother of ex-PM Viktor Orban
scraped.body_text:
Save

Share

Former Hungarian Prime Minister Viktor Orban has accused the country’s new government of “political persecution” after the reported arrest of his younger brother.

Hungarian police arrested Aron Orban on Monday on suspicion of people smuggling, among other offences, according to a press report shared by Prime Minister Peter Magyar. Viktor Orban’s staunch opposition to immigration defined his 16 years in power that ended in defeat at elections in April.

News of the arrest was first reported by Kontroll, a news site owned by Magyar’s brother, Marton. Police carried out raids involving Aron Orban’s business associates but did not confirm whether he was among those detained, local media reported.

Viktor Orban accused the government of arresting his brother as a way to “divert attention” from other issues.

“I am the real target. My younger brother is simply being used to get to me,” he wrote on X.

Like other members of the Orban family, Aron built several successful businesses during his brother’s rule.

Last year, an investigation by news site Telex linked Aron Orban and his business associates to an alleged scheme involving visas for foreign guest workers.

Authorities said they had detained four people suspected of people smuggling.

Pro-EU conservative Magyar won a landslide election victory in April, ending 16 years of Orban’s rule, after promising to investigate his predecessor’s alleged corruption and abuse of power while in office.

scraped.title: Skydance replaces James Gunn and Peter Safran as DC Studios chiefs following Warner Bros. takeover
scraped.description: In another major shake-up for the DC Studios, Skydance is replacing Hollywood director James Gunn and producer Peter Safran with a former Marvel executive.
scraped.h1: James Gunn, producer Peter Safran out as DC Studios heads
scraped.body_text:
In another major shake-up for the DC Studios, Skydance is replacing Hollywood director James Gunn and producer Peter Safran with a former Marvel executive.

James Gunn and Peter Safran are stepping down as co-heads of DC Studios after four years, Skydance Motion Picture Group announced on Monday.

Their departure marks another major shake-up for the superhero franchise following Skydance 's takeover of Warner Bros , just a year after Gunn's "Superman" reached cinemas.

Skydance chairman and CEO David Ellison has chosen Jeremy Latchman, a former Marvel Studios executive, to lead DC Studios. He is set to become president and chief creative officer of DC Studios on December 1.

Latchman will oversee the next phase of DC's film and television business, which includes characters such as Superman, Batman and Wonder Woman.

He was involved in major Marvel productions including "Iron Man" and "The Avengers," and previously worked with Gunn and Safran on Marvel's "Guardians of the Galaxy" movie.

Gunn and Safran took charge of DC Studios in 2022, tasked with rebuilding the franchise and creating a more unified cinematic universe.

Their first film, "Superman," earned nearly $619 million (€553 million) worldwide in 2025.

But their second release, "Supergirl," flopped in June 2026, taking around $126 million worldwide against a reported production budget of $170 million. The horror-inspired "Clayface" followed in October.

Overall, DC has struggled to match immense profits and cultural impact made by Marvel in the early years of its own cinematic universe.

"James and Peter launched a new era for DC Studios and led it through a period of real transformation, resetting the foundation and building a slate we're incredibly proud of," Ellison said in a statement.

"We're grateful for their passion, contributions and commitment to this legendary brand."

Gunn is currently completing "Man of Tomorrow," a sequel to "Superman." Other DC projects in development include "The Batman: Part II" and the television series "The People v. Gorilla Grodd."

Although Gunn and Safran will no longer oversee DC Studios' long-term plans, several projects developed under their leadership remain in production.

Gunn's "Superman" sparked a political controversy in 2025 after the director described the superhero as an immigrant and emphasized themes of human kindness.

Conservative commentators accused the film of being "woke."

Skydance CEO Ellison has cultivated close ties with US President Donald Trump. Ellison has acknowledged having a good relationship with the administration but denied politicizing the company.

There is no evidence that the controversy surrounding "Superman" played a role in Gunn and Safran's replacement.

items.title: Republican Thomas Massie seeks to force House vote on impeaching Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth over Iran war
items.summary: Trump critic Thomas Massie is calling for a vote to impeach Pentagon chief Pete Hegseth, accusing Hegseth of waging war without congressional approval.

scraped.title: US: Hegseth faces impeachment push from Massie over Iran war
scraped.description: Trump critic Thomas Massie is calling for a vote to impeach Pentagon chief Pete Hegseth, accusing Hegseth of waging war without congressional approval.
scraped.h1: US: Hegseth faces impeachment push from Massie over Iran war
scraped.body_text:
Trump critic Thomas Massie is calling for a vote to impeach Pentagon chief Pete Hegseth, accusing Hegseth of waging war without congressional approval.

Republican lawmaker Thomas Massie, an outspoken critic of President Donald Trump , introduced eight articles of impeachment against US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth on Monday as pressure builds on the Trump administration over the Iran war .

The resolution proposed by the Kentucky congressman accuses Hegseth of conducting the war illegally without congressional authorization. Massie also claims Hegseth has abused his powers as the head of the Pentagon.

Massie is using a special procedure that could see the US House of Representatives vote on the resolution within two days, with the legislative chamber still dominated by Republicans.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Trump defended Hegseth in a telephone interview with the Reuters news agency after the articles were filed.

"Well, he won two wars. I don't know how you can impeach him," Trump said.

Earlier on Monday, Hegseth sought to downplay rumors about the push against him.

"My team, we’re not worried about the noise," he told reporters.

Hegseth said he would hold a press conference Tuesday — his first in more than 180 days — and defended the war as necessary, even if unpopular.

Democratic House leader Hakeem Jeffries backed the effort Sunday.

"I'm a hard yes on the Hegseth resolution," he told ABC News. "Pete Hegseth has got to go."

Some Republicans have signaled they might support the charges. Arkansas congressman French Hill said he wanted to hear the debate before deciding.

The push follows Democrats' victories in both chambers of Congress in last week's midterm elections amid anger over the Iran war and soaring fuel prices. Republicans retain control until January 3.

Impeachment requires a simple majority in the House and amounts to bringing formal charges. Removal would require a Senate trial and conviction by two-thirds of senators present.

Even with their enlarged majority next year, Democrats would need substantial Republican backing to reach that threshold.

items.title: Pope Leo draws 2.5 million in Buenos Aires, renews warning over Milei's austerity
items.summary: Some 2.5 million people have attended Pope Leo's mass in Buenos Aires, his largest gathering yet. The pontiff once again called for protecting the vulnerable as President Milei cuts disability care and social services.

scraped.title: Pope Leo draws 2.5 million in Buenos Aires, renews warning over Milei's austerity
scraped.description: Some 2.5 million people have attended Pope Leo's mass in Buenos Aires, his largest gathering yet. The pontiff once again called for protecting the vulnerable as President Milei cuts disability care and social services.
scraped.h1: Pope Leo draws 2.5 million to Argentina mass, warns against austerity
scraped.body_text:
Some 2.5 million people have attended Pope Leo's mass in Buenos Aires, his largest gathering yet. The pontiff once again called for protecting the vulnerable as President Milei cuts disability care and social services.

An estimated 2.5 million people attended Pope Leo XIV 's open-air mass in Buenos Aires on Monday, according to local authorities, making the event the largest gathering of his papacy so far.

Crowds stretched for miles along Avenida del Libertador in Argentina's capital, with the faithful waving Vatican flags and chanting "Long live Pope Leo!" as the US-born pope passed in an open-top popemobile.

"It fills my heart with joy to celebrate... with you," Leo said in his sermon.

The pope also reinforced an appeal to President Javier Milei to protect vulnerable Argentines, visiting a disability care home struggling with the government's cuts to health care and social services.

Before the mass, Leo visited the Cottolengo Don Orione care center in Claypole, south of Buenos Aires, which houses more than 400 people with disabilities.

He told residents their lives were a blessing rather than a burden, and challenged the idea that economic success alone measures a country's achievements.

"A nation's progress is also measured by how it welcomes all people with disabilities and particular needs," he said.

The remarks followed his appeal Sunday, at a reception attended by Milei, for economic growth to benefit people facing the greatest difficulties. He also urged leaders to choose their words carefully and recognize the limits of their power.

Milei became the president of Argentina some three years ago, Since then, his government has cut disability services and resisted implementing a law increasing funding for care, despite Congress overriding Milei's veto in 2025. The Senate is due to consider next year's disability funding in the coming days.

Some worshippers camped overnight to secure a place near the Monumento a los Espanoles, where Pope John Paul II celebrated Argentina's last papal mass in 1987.

Monday was declared a national holiday to allow people to attend. President Milei and his sister Karina were among those present.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

In his sermon, Leo spoke of families facing unstable employment, violence and addiction, while describing them as a pillar of society.

The visit is Argentina's first by a pope in nearly four decades. Leo's predecessor Francis , despite being born in Argentina, never returned to his homeland during his papacy.

Leo, 71, visited Uruguay before arriving in Argentina on Sunday. He is due to travel to Peru on Wednesday and return to Rome on November 17.

The first US-born pope spent decades in Peru as a missionary and bishop. The Vatican has described his South American tour as a "homecoming."

The demanding trip comes less than a month after surgery to remove a cancerous tumor from his lung.
