items.title: U.S. House Republican moves to force vote on impeaching Pete Hegseth
items.summary: Republican Rep. Thomas Massie moved Monday to force a vote to impeach Secretary of War Pete Hegseth, putting pressure on his fellow Republicans to decide whether to remove one of the Trump administration's most prominent figures following sweeping election losses.

scraped.title: U.S. House Republican moves to force vote on impeaching Pete Hegseth | CBC News
scraped.description: Republican Rep. Thomas Massie moved Monday to force a vote to impeach Secretary of War Pete Hegseth, putting pressure on his fellow Republicans to decide whether to remove one of the Trump administration's most prominent figures following sweeping election losses.
scraped.h1: U.S. House Republican moves to force vote on impeaching Pete Hegseth
scraped.body_text:
Republican Rep. Thomas Massie moved Monday to force a vote to impeach Secretary of War Pete Hegseth, putting pressure on his fellow Republicans to decide whether to remove one of the Trump administration's most prominent figures following sweeping election losses.

The impeachment resolution largely focuses on the war in Iran. It also includes references to Hegseth's role in carrying out military actions in Yemen and Venezuela.

Massie said the secretary's actions amount to "high crimes and misdemeanours" and his leadership at the Pentagon "thus warrants impeachment."

A vote in the House could come by mid-week, putting pressure on Republicans — many of whom blamed their election wipeout on the Iran war — but next steps are highly uncertain.

House Speaker Mike Johnson had tried to prevent this outcome, and warned lawmakers against impeaching Hegseth while the U.S. is engaged in military actions in the Middle East.

"Impeaching a cabinet secretary right now, especially the Department of War in the middle of hostilities abroad would be a terrible, terrible look, a terrible thing for our allies and our enemies to see that," Johnson, a Republican, said as he opened the chamber.

"We don't impeach cabinet secretaries for political gain or for cheap tricks, and I think that's what this is and I think everybody knows it."

Speaking to reporters Monday afternoon, Massie said Hegseth has violated international norms and the U.S.'s own conventions of war in Iran.

"It's to the disadvantage and the dishonour of our country, and to the danger of our soldiers in future conflict," he said.

Hegseth said earlier Monday he's eager to litigate the military actions that he and U.S. President Donald Trump have taken against Iran, Yemen's Iranian-backed Houthi rebels and Venezuela's previous leaders.

"If you want to take issue with what we did in Epic Fury or Rough Rider or nabbing Nicolás Maduro, you're taking issue with the troops and what they accomplished, which is historic," Hegseth told reporters Monday, using the military code names for the Iran war and campaign of strikes to halt the Houthis' attacks on shipping in the Middle East.

Hegseth defends record as Pentagon chief, slams 'sham' push for his impeachment

Hegseth also announced that he would hold a rare news conference on Tuesday — his first in more than 180 days — on the impeachment threat. His last briefing was in May, and he has not held one on the Iran war, strikes on alleged drug-trafficking boats or other U.S. military actions since then.

The Pentagon chief is bearing the brunt of anger and calls for his ouster after the Iran war and its economic impact contributed to severe Republican losses in the midterm elections that cost the party control of Congress. Massie pushed forward an impeachment resolution over the objections of House Republican leadership as momentum grows to hold Hegseth accountable for the conflict.

Hegseth gave a State of the Force address at Marine Corps Base Quantico, Sept. 30, but has not held a media availablity since May. (Alex Wong/Pool/The Associated Press)

Hegseth, after giving a speech at the Naval War College in Rhode Island, brushed aside the possible impeachment push.

"There's a lot of politically motivated people who may have substantial policy disagreements, but their disagreements are with success," he told reporters. He added that "if we want to litigate" the military actions that the Trump administration has taken, "I'm happy to do it all day long."

"My team, we're not worried about the noise — it's what I told the troops, too — don't worry about the noise," he said.

Asked about U.S. Vice-President JD Vance blaming the Iran war for the massive Republican losses in the election, Hegseth noted that Trump said he would do it again, and "I agree."

He largely repeated a line that Secretary of State Marco Rubio said to reporters a day earlier: "It doesn't have to be necessarily popular, but it can be necessary."

Hegseth argued that the war was necessary because "someone had to confront the Iranian regime's pursuit of a nuclear weapon" and said "the choice was don't act and wish it away or take a bold move."

Iran has long maintained that its nuclear program is peaceful. According to the International Atomic Energy Agency, Iran has 440.9 kilograms of uranium that is enriched up to 60 per cent purity, a short, technical step from weapons-grade levels of 90 per cent.

Trump defended Hegseth to reporters on Sunday night.

"He's guilty of two things, basically winning two wars," Trump said. "I believe we saved the Middle East and Israel combined. And it's awfully hard to say let's impeach somebody who did that."

On Monday, he told reporters he would stand by Hegseth even if he is impeached.

Trump defends Hegseth as Democrats prepare for political war

Hegseth reiterated that "Iran is devastated," even though the Islamic Republic has been able to keep striking military bases in the Middle East that are used by the United States, causing billions of dollars in damage, as well as commercial ships in the Strait of Hormuz.

Disruptions to shipping in the waterway, where one-fifth of the world's oil passed before the war, have led to higher energy prices that hit voters' pocketbooks.

He said the next steps on the war are up to Trump, including telling Iran: "Hey, we're done, and we're going to watch your nuclear material. You better not move it."

With anger in Congress rising, Hegseth has been on a social media blitz, posting a video last week acknowledging the threat of impeachment. He said it would be "all about the politics of personal destruction" and insisted that "won't work with me. You can rest assured of that."

Since then, scores of political appointees within the Pentagon have posted images of Hegseth emblazoned with the words, "Stand. Fight. Defend the Republic." The White House also posted a video to social media that featured praise from Trump.

items.title: Tyler Robinson, man accused of shooting Charlie Kirk, to face trial in 2028
items.summary: A ​Utah judge on Monday set a June 2028 trial date for Tyler Robinson, the man accused of murdering prominent right-wing activist Charlie Kirk last year.

scraped.title: Tyler Robinson, man accused of shooting Charlie Kirk, to face trial in 2028 | CBC News
scraped.description: A ​Utah judge on Monday set a June 2028 trial date for Tyler Robinson, the man accused of murdering prominent right-wing activist Charlie Kirk last year.
scraped.h1: Tyler Robinson, man accused of shooting Charlie Kirk, to face trial in 2028
scraped.body_text:
A ​Utah judge on Monday set a June 2028 trial date for Tyler Robinson, the man accused of murdering prominent right-wing activist Charlie Kirk last year.

Robinson, 23, has pleaded not ‌guilty to seven counts, including aggravated murder, in the shooting of Kirk as the conservative held one of his trademark debates at Utah Valley University in Orem, Utah.

Utah District Court Judge ​Tony Graf set jury selection for the ​trial for June 21, 2028, after Robinson's attorneys requested a late 2029 date to give them time to challenge ​Utah's request for the death penalty, gather additional evidence ⁠and seek a change ⁠of venue. Robinson's lawyers expect ‌a six-to-seven-month trial.

Prosecutors had sought a date of January 31, 2028 to start what they expect to be a 17-week trial for the shooting death of Kirk, an ally of U.S. President ⁠Donald Trump.

In a separate filing, Erika Kirk, Kirk's widow, requested the trial to start in 2027 to speed what she described as a painful ‌legal process.

Trump last month slammed Graf's handling of the case, saying the trial should start within a month and the judge was asking "questions that people already know the answer to."

Charlie Kirk is seen in a file photo taken March 17, 2025, when he was speaking at a town hall in Oconomowoc, Wis. (Jeffrey Phelps/The Associated Press)

Kirk was ​a polarizing figure in U.S. politics. He was admired by conservatives for mobilizing young voters ⁠around his Christian and right-wing views. Civil rights advocates criticized Kirk for ⁠rhetoric they called racist, anti-immigrant, transphobic and misogynist, citing his public remarks denigrating ⁠Black ⁠Americans, LGBTQ communities, ​Muslims and immigrants.

Prosecutors allege Robinson targeted Kirk for his opposition to same-sex marriage and ​transgender rights. Defence ⁠attorney Richard Novak has said in court that Kirk spoke "hatefully" about people who did not have traditional gender identities or were not heterosexual, but Robinson's defence say there was no evidence Robinson opposed those views.

Topic: State and Territory Elections

Victorians will head to the polls on November 28 to decide who will hold the balance of power in the state for the next four years, with party leaders ramping up their campaigns.

The Big Build royal commission will also continue in its first block of hearings, with the first witnesses to be called today.

Follow our live coverage below:

Choose what information you see below by using filters

All

3

Greens

1

Key Event

By Judd Boaz

The Greens have pledged to make major concerts and events more affordable in Victoria, promising to launch a new lottery scheme for $50 tickets.

The party has dubbed its policy the Affordable Ticket Scheme , which would mandate that major events receiving state government funding or using state government-funded venues make a portion of tickets available through a lottery.

Only open to Victorian residents, the scheme would make $50 the maximum price of event tickets.

The Greens say it lottery would include events such as the Australian Open , major international concerts and sporting events like the NFL , with the Greens committing an initial $2 million to establish the scheme.

The party said it modelled the scheme partially on a similar one run in New York City by Mayor Zohran Mamdani during the FIFA World Cup.

Greens leader Ellen Sandell said the scheme would open up events to Victorians who might otherwise not be able to afford them.

"Melbourne prides itself on being the sporting and live music capital of Australia, but more and more Victorians are being priced out of the very events that make our city great," Ms Sandell said.

"These events often receive enormous amounts of taxpayer funding, and many are held in venues built and maintained with public money. If organisers are benefiting from public funding, the public should get something back."

By Judd Boaz

We want to know what's shaping your vote in this election and why.

Whether it's cost of living, housing affordability, crime, regional roads, healthcare or jobs, let us know in our form below.

You can also ask the election questions you want answered from candidates, parties or the ABC.

All submissions will be reviewed by a journalist and we may be in touch if we need more information.

By Judd Boaz

Good morning and welcome to our live coverage on the Victorian state election campaign.

Labor's big red bus is on the road again, while the Coalition and One Nation are fronting the media and the Greens have a new policy announcement.

Plus, the Big Build royal commission will call its first witnesses as the first block of public hearings continue.

We'll bring you all that here in our blog today.

items.title: Defence site in Darwin's suburbs pitched as location of potential new hospital
items.summary: The Northern Territory Labor Opposition says it will build a new Royal Darwin Hospital if it wins the 2028 NT election. Chansey Paech says NT Labor will deliver a new Royal Darwin Hospital if the party wins the next election.

scraped.title: Defence site in Darwin's suburbs pitched as location of potential new hospital
scraped.description: The Northern Territory Labor Opposition says it will build a new Royal Darwin Hospital if it wins the 2028 NT election.
scraped.author: https://www.abc.net.au/news/matt-garrick/10492138
scraped.h1: NT Labor pledges to build new Royal Darwin Hospital if it wins 2028 election
scraped.body_text:
Emergency

Backstory

Newsletters

中文新闻

BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

TOK PISIN

By Matt Garrick

Topic: Health

Chansey Paech says NT Labor will deliver a new Royal Darwin Hospital if the party wins the next election. ( ABC News: Pete Garnish )

NT Labor has committed to building a new Royal Darwin Hospital if it wins the next territory election in 2028.

The Australian Medical Association NT (AMA NT) has welcomed the promise, saying a replacement for Darwin hospital is sorely needed.

Labor has conceded it doesn’t have a firm commitment from the Commonwealth for funding.

The Northern Territory Labor Opposition has promised to build a new Royal Darwin Hospital (RDH) if it wins government in 2028, revealing new details about how and where it could be built.

The current RDH, the NT's biggest and busiest hospital, is deteriorating and in a near perpetual state of crisis, with rolling code yellows , overcrowded wards and stretched staff.

Shadow Health Minister Chansey Paech said Labor was "committed to delivering a new Royal Darwin Hospital here, for everyone".

"We're starting the work now," he said.

Chansey Paech says NT Labor is doing the work now to prepare for a new RDH so they are ready if they are elected. ( ABC News: Pete Garnish )

"We're working with our medical professionals, we're working with architects, we're working with Territorians to understand what a future hospital needs to look like here in Darwin.

"So that when we do come into government we don't have to wait around … we can get to the business of getting a hospital built."

While NT Labor has been alluding to this promise over recent weeks, today marks the first time the party has publicly outlined the extent of its planning.

The Northern Territory's largest hospital is "literally creaking at the seams" after Cyclone Fina, prompting NT Health to call for more federal funding.

The pledge also marks the first major election pitch from NT Labor since it lost government in a landslide to the Country Liberal Party (CLP) in 2024 .

The promise has been welcomed by the Australian Medical Association NT (AMA NT).

AMA NT vice president Dayna Duncan said the current RDH "is ageing to a point where it can't be patched up anymore".

"We do need a brand new hospital from scratch," she said.

While no exact cost has been cited, health officials have previously floated that a new RDH would likely exceed $1 billion.

Dayna Duncan says RDH is in a poor state and a new hospital needs to be built. ( ABC News: Pete Garnish )

Mr Paech said NT Labor was currently looking at two possible locations: the site of the current hospital in Tiwi or on Defence land earmarked for divestment in Berrimah.

"We believe … the Berrimah barracks presents the greatest opportunity to build a new premiere tertiary hospital for the Territory, one that is close to the airport for aerial retrieval services, it's in between Palmerston and Darwin," he said.

Berrimah Defence Establishment has been suggested by NT Labor as a site for a new RDH. ( ABC News: Pete Garnish )

Dr Duncan said while a future hospital location was still to be negotiated, "the Berrimah site certainly has benefits".

The current eight-storey RDH opened in 1980 in the wake of Cyclone Tracy from existing plans for Canberra's identical Woden Hospital .

Mr Paech said under Labor, a new construction would likely look very different.

"We're hearing from people that it shouldn't be a multi-storey tower, that it should be something that takes in the tropical climate," Mr Paech said.

The design of Royal Darwin Hospital was modelled off the existing plans for Canberra's Woden Hospital in 1980. ( ABC News: Pete Garnish )

CLP government Health Minister Steve Edgington criticised NT Labor's track record on spending in government and questioned why it hadn't made the promise in its last term.

He also said the CLP was "not ruling in or ruling out" building a new RDH, but that his government had embarked on planning for new health infrastructure across the NT.

Steve Edgington says his government has not ruled out the possibility of a new Royal Darwin Hospital. ( ABC News: Marcus Kennedy )

"We're looking at the needs of the future and that includes the Royal Darwin Hospital," he said.

"We're not here to make political headlines.

"We want to do the responsible thing for Territorians, and that's to do the proper planning … look at the clinical needs right across the territory so that we can plan for the future."

The Commonwealth has never publicly committed to helping fund a future RDH, with Prime Minister Anthony Albanese recently watering down the prospect .

But Mr Paech said he believed they would come onboard.

"We have had a very welcoming reception with our federal colleagues to begin the conversation about the future health care needs of Territorians," he said.

Anthony Albanese has dashed hopes of federal funding for a new hospital in Darwin, while announcing $10 million to improve maternity services at RDH.

"We are … going to remain committed to this, and we're going to keep talking to the federal government about this important need for a new hospital here in the Top End."

In a statement, an Albanese government spokesperson put the onus on the NT government as the entity "responsible for the planning, funding and delivery of capital" for a new RDH.

The spokesperson said "any decision to provide funding to support progression of a new tertiary hospital would need to be contemplated" in context of current funding arrangements between the NT and the Commonwealth.

When asked if a future NT Labor government would go it alone without federal support, Mr Paech said "the Territory Labor Opposition is going to work through that" possibility.

Royal Darwin Hospital is located in Tiwi in Darwin's northern suburbs. ( ABC News: Pete Garnish )

Independent economist Saul Eslake said building a new hospital would be "incredibly expensive for the territory government especially considering its current financial position".

scraped.body_text:
Emergency

Backstory

BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

TOK PISIN

By Kenji Sato

612 ABC Brisbane

Topic: Cats

Lisa Roberts-Daintree with her rescue cat Jesse. ( 612 ABC Brisbane: Kenji Sato )

Animal welfare campaigner Lisa Roberts-Daintree has been dobbed into council for exceeding the city's cat limit.

Redland City Council allows only two cats per household in its local by-laws.

The council has given her until November 23 to surrender the cats.

A Queensland animal welfare campaigner has been threatened with fines for owning five rescue cats.

Lisa Roberts-Daintree received a compliance notice from Redland City Council after a neighbour reported her for exceeding Redland's two cat maximum rule.

Council documents obtained by 612 ABC show there were no other concerns about welfare, hygiene or containment following an inspection of the property.

However, the council told her via letter that owning more than two cats was a violation of its by-laws.

"While I recognise that this situation has arisen from compassionate action, Council must also ensure that Local Law No. 2 (Animal Management) 2015 is applied consistently and fairly across the community," the letter said.

"The prescribed limits on the number of animals permitted on a property are in place to protect animal welfare, maintain community amenity and ensure fairness and equity for all residents."

The letter said if she did not comply by November 23, the council could issue a fine, enter her house and seize her cats.

Ms Roberts-Daintree is the spokesperson for Cats Assistance to Sterilise (CATS), a charity which desexes cats to control feral populations.

She said four of her cats had been rescued from a "traumatic" home, and they had medical and socialisation issues which made them difficult to rehome.

The Russell Island resident said it was therefore highly likely they would eventually be euthanised if they were impounded by the council.

The net prevents the cats from escaping the backyard. ( 612 ABC Brisbane: Kenji Sato )

She said she had only been trying to keep the animals off the street where they would breed and kill native wildlife.

Ms Roberts-Daintree said all five cats were now desexed.

The council said she could get a special permit to keep a third cat, but no more.

Ms Roberts-Daintree said she did not know how to choose which cats would get to stay, and which two would be surrendered.

"That's not fair to the cats," Ms Roberts-Daintree said.

Juergen Holscher says the cats are like family. ( 612 ABC Brisbane: Kenji Sato )

Her partner, Juergen Holscher, said he had sent dozens of letters to local, state and federal politicians pleading with them for help.

The traffic controller said he had installed cat netting around the entire house and backyard to make sure the cats did not leave the property.

Mr Holscher said he felt the council was being rigid and uncompromising in enforcing the rules, even though the cats were well looked after and not harming anyone else.

He said he felt as though they were effectively being asked to kill the cats in order to protect their welfare.

"They've got no compassion, no sympathy, no critical thinking skills," Mr Holscher said.

"I'm a traffic controller and fair dinkum, I think I'm brighter than these people."

A Redland City Council spokesperson said the matter was ongoing.

"Redland City Council is unable to comment on an active investigation," the spokesperson said.

"Under Council's Subordinate Local Law No. 2 (Animal Management) 2015, residents can keep up to two cats over the age of three months without an approval, and may apply for an approval to keep three cats."

One of the best upgrades you can make to your PC gaming setup is an OLED monitor. Fortunately, MSI’s factory-reconditioned Mag 272QP X24 is on sale at Woot through November 18th with a 180-day manufacturer warranty for $290.99, which is more than $100 cheaper than the full MSRP of $399.99.

MSI’s 27-inch screen is well-featured for the price, with 1440p resolution, a 240Hz refresh rate, and both G-Sync and FreeSync compatibility, which help reduce screen tearing when your FPS is below the max refresh rate. PC games are particularly well-suited to take advantage of the deep black levels OLED panels produce, too, giving every game you play a deeper, more immersive feel. MSI’s budget OLED also features quantum dots for fuller, more vivid colors. It doesn’t cut corners on ports either, with two HDMI 2.1, one DisplayPort 1.4a, and one USB Type-C DP Alt input.

A pledge to make AI less of an environmental disaster is floating around United Nations climate negotiations this month, but it’s just lip service.

A pledge to make AI less of an environmental disaster is floating around United Nations climate negotiations this month, but it’s just lip service.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

See All by Justine Calma

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

See All by Justine Calma

At this point, reading through the latest splashy pledge to use AI for the good of the environment feels like downing a nonalcoholic beer. Admittedly, I’m suspicious from the onset. How can this be good? But I love beer and our planet enough to give it a whirl — and hey, why not try a little harm reduction ?

Negotiators from more than 190 countries around the world are in Antalya, Turkey, this month for the annual United Nations climate summit, called COP31 (the 31st “Conference of the Parties” that ratified the UN Framework Convention on Climate Change). Turkey previewed its Antalya Artificial Intelligence Pledge ahead of the convening, inviting delegates from other countries to endorse the pledge before its official launch on November 16th.

Like that nonalcoholic beer, it’s deeply unsatisfying

The pledge actually includes some common sense measures that could curb planet-heating pollution from energy-hungry AI data centers . Unfortunately, like that nonalcoholic beer, it’s deeply unsatisfying.

At first glance, many of the ingredients you’d expect from a real commitment on AI’s environmental impact are here. It sets out to ensure that data centers are increasingly powered by clean energy, calling for internationally recognized standards for responsible AI development. Similarly, it pushes for reporting requirements so that there’s greater transparency into the impact data centers — which run primarily on fossil fuels — already have on the environment. It even acknowledges the need to manage the tons of e-waste created by the generative AI boom .

And yet, there is no there there because, as the text states clearly, “these objectives of the pledge are voluntary and non-prescriptive, create no new obligations, and are to be implemented in accordance with national circumstances.” In other words, these are voluntary commitments that countries can choose to follow or not follow based on their whims.

There’s also no way this pledge will garner the support of the most influential player in this game (at least for now). The US has way more data centers than any other country, but Donald Trump has pulled the nation out of the global climate accord and has no official delegates at the summit in Turkey.

The last point in the pledge is to ensure that advances in generative AI can be used to create more renewable energy and reduce greenhouse gas emissions, particularly in economically developing countries. To that end, research published in a Nature journal in August found that AI causes more carbon emissions by boosting fossil fuel production than it would help avoid through gains in renewable energy.

When it comes down to it, this pledge offers a placebo effect at best. In the face of data centers demanding tremendous amounts of electricity and spurring the development of more fossil fuel infrastructure , negotiators can’t be seen as doing nothing about the issue. And with global average temperatures still on the rise, we could all use an emotional support beverage.

After publishing a support article in early September outlining usage limits for some Apple Intelligence features, the company has updated Logic Pro with an option to “Buy More Usage” for a one-time purchase price of $49.99, as spotted by 9to5Mac . It has a built-in AI assistant to do things like “start a new song, set up a vocal track from a single prompt, or refine an active project.”

These Intelligence Usage Packs, as Apple calls them, will allow users to continue accessing certain Apple Intelligence features that have usage limits because they rely on cloud-based AI models from OpenAI or Google Gemini. The Usage Packs can only be used by the Apple Account that purchased them (Family Sharing isn’t supported) and, as Apple explains on its website , any unused additional usage will roll over from month to month, but will expire 12 months after it was purchased.

For Logic Pro, Apple says the usage limit is “impacted by the complexity of conversations you have with the assistant.” Users finding themselves running out of access can find the option to buy an Intelligence Usage Pack in the Intelligence Features > Show Usage section of the app’s main menu. Currently, only Logic Pro has the option to buy more usage, but it’s expected to be added to other Apple Creator Studio apps this month, including Pixelmator Pro, Final Cut Pro, Motion, plus Pages, Keynote, and Numbers that are getting access to Apple’s AI chatbot .

scraped.title: DCU shake-up: James Gunn and Peter Safran out post-merger
scraped.description: Producer and former Kevin Feige protege Jeremy Latcham will replace Gunn and Safran.
scraped.h1: DCU shake-up: James Gunn and Peter Safran out post-merger
scraped.body_text:
Producer and former Kevin Feige protege Jeremy Latcham will replace Gunn and Safran.

It’s barely been two months since the controversial Paramount and Warner Bros. merger, and we’ve already got a shockingly unexpected ouster : Co-CEOs of the rebooted DC Universe, James Gunn and Peter Safran, are stepping down from that role despite the Hollywood rumor mill assuming that the duo would be safe.

It’s unclear whether the pair chose to resign or were forced out, or what will happen to their planned slate of projects beyond 2028’s Superman: Man of Tomorrow , which is in post-production. Producer Jeremy Latcham—a protege of Marvel’s Kevin Feige who worked with Gunn on Guardians of the Galaxy among other MCU films—will replace them. Per Gunn and Safran’s joint statement :

Four years ago, we set out to unite DC under one creative vision. In that time, we helped restore Superman to the heart of DC, while opening new doors and telling new stories in film and television with Peacemaker , Creature Commandos, Lanterns and Clayface. We’re immensely proud of the team that turned that ambition into something real, including the actors, crews and executives we had the opportunity to collaborate with. We’ve shared a creative history with Jeremy going back to Marvel, and we’re eager to see the perspective he brings to DC’s next chapter. We’re excited to return to what drew us to this job in the first place, which is telling the stories we love, including the next chapter of Clark and Lex’s journey in Man of Tomorrow .

DCU fans are mourning the news and what it could mean for the franchise. My feelings are mixed. On the one hand, I’m on record that I’ve found the rebooted DC Universe films released thus far to be enjoyable but rather forgettable, even when the positives outweigh the negatives . (I have yet to see Clayface , which debuted to good reviews and a solid box office showing.) But HBO has done right by the DCU: I loved both seasons of Peacemaker; Lanterns is a shining beacon of what is possible when someone is allowed to get really creative within the genre; and I’m very much looking forward to next year’s Jimmy Olsen (Skylar Gisondo) series The People v. Gorilla Grodd —described as a “mockumentary crime comedy superhero series.”

I also love Gunn’s more irreverent sensibility with superhero fare and his rapport with fans. At least now he will get to focus on what he does best—and Gunn seems to feel the same way, per his personal Instagram post . Gunn says he had mixed feelings about taking the job at first but “couldn’t pass up the unique opportunity,” adding that he has no regrets and is glad he took it.

A post shared by James Gunn (@jamesgunn)

But Gunn also noted that he sometimes found the job trying, with very little time to recharge between projects; that his ADHD made it challenging to juggle so many projects at once; and that he disliked “the at-times corporate nature of the job,” thanking Safran for “taking the brunt of that.” He concluded, “I will miss being the co-caretaker of these great characters, but I’m also incredibly relieved and excited to get back to pure filmmaking.”

While Gunn and Safran reported directly to Warner Bros. Discovery CEO David Zaslav—unusual for the industry—Latcham will report to Dana Goldberg and Josh Greenstein, co-chairs of the Skydance Motion Picture Group. “Jeremy brings a deep reverence for DC and its passionate fanbase, recognizing that they are the very foundation of this storied, multigenerational brand,” Goldberg and Greenstein said in a statement . “Under his leadership, every film and television show will be ushered from start to finish through the prism of the legions of fans who love and champion it. Jeremy’s track record exemplifies the excellence he will bring to building out DC and the many beloved characters within it.”

Latcham issued his own statement:

DC’s pantheon of characters is among the most iconic in American popular culture. I’ve had the privilege to help bring some of the most celebrated superhero stories to life on the big screen, and I’m excited and honored for the opportunity to now lead DC Studios into its next era. The chance to steward the incredible cast of DC characters to the screen in a way that excites lifelong fans while introducing their timeless stories to the next generation is a massive responsibility that I do not take lightly. I am grateful to Dana and Josh for putting their trust in me. I can’t wait to work night and day alongside filmmakers, comic book creators, artists and storytellers of every kind, across film, television and animation, to build something ambitious for longtime DC fans and newcomers alike.

Latcham has the superhero bona fides, having been a producer on some of Marvel’s biggest hits: Guardians , Iron Man, Iron Man 2, The Avengers, Age of Ultron , and 2017’s Spider-Man: Homecoming . He left to create his own production company, which spearheaded 2023’s Dungeons and Dragons: Honor Among Thieves and 2018’s Bad Times at the El Royale .

The DCU should be in capable hands, even if the overall vision changes. I’d like to see the DCU move away from the connected universe model and back to standalone films where the storytelling and character development aren’t beholden to setting up the next three films. But I’m not the head of a major studio.

Ars Technica has been separating the signal from the noise for over 25 years. With our unique combination of technical savvy and wide-ranging interest in the technological arts and sciences, Ars is the trusted source in a sea of information. After all, you don’t need to know everything, only what’s important.

scraped.title: Man who lost $308,000 on sports bets sues Kalshi for offering illegal gambling
scraped.description: Lawsuit demands Kalshi return losses because online betting is illegal in Washington.
scraped.h1: Man who lost $308,000 on sports bets sues Kalshi for offering illegal gambling
scraped.body_text:
Lawsuit demands Kalshi return losses because online betting is illegal in Washington.

A man who lost over $308,000 making sports wagers on Kalshi is suing the prediction market for violating the state of Washington’s ban on online gambling. He’s trying to turn those losses into an overall victory with a lawsuit seeking a payment of over $580,000.

Bellevue, Washington, resident Scott Bright’s “wagering occurred at a time when it was unlawful in Washington and when the Washington Attorney General had already sued KalshiEX LLC in this Court alleging precisely that,” said the gambler’s lawsuit filed on September 24 in King County Superior Court. Kalshi has since filed a motion to dismiss the lawsuit.

While state attorneys general throughout the US are trying to shut down Kalshi for allegedly violating state gambling laws, Bright’s case tests whether unsuccessful gamblers can obtain restitution from the company through individual lawsuits.

“Washington has prohibited Internet gambling since 2006. Washington has also provided, since long before that, a statutory cause of action permitting any person who loses money at illegal gambling to recover it from the proprietor for whose benefit the game was conducted,” Bright’s lawsuit said.

Even if Bright’s lawsuit fails, gamblers who lost on Kalshi could get money back through the lawsuits filed by state governments. For example, Washington’s lawsuit against the company said the attorney general “is entitled to recover all money Washingtonians have lost through Defendant Kalshi’s illegal gambling operation” under the state’s Recovery of Money Lost at Gambling Act. Washington already won a court order restricting the kinds of wagers Kalshi can offer in the state, but it took effect after Bright’s losses.

Kalshi wants Bright’s lawsuit to be moved to US District Court for the Western District of Washington, saying it must be tried in a federal court instead of a state one. In an October 30 motion to dismiss Bright’s case, Kalshi argued that he did not lose any money on “gambling.” Kalshi said he lost money on “event contracts,” which Kalshi says can only be regulated by the federal government.

“The contracts which Plaintiff mischaracterizes as gambling are event contracts offered on the Platform subject to the CEA [Commodity Exchange Act], in conformance with the rules and regulations of the CFTC [Commodity Futures Trading Commission], the federal agency which has statutory authority to oversee the CEA,” Kalshi said.

We contacted Bright’s attorney, Michael Daudt, about Kalshi’s court filings and will update this article if we get a response.

“Plaintiff alleges that his activity on the platform was gambling and that he ‘lost,’” Kalshi wrote. “He does not allege that anyone misled him about how the platform worked, what it charged, or the risk that any position might lose. Yet, he now sues KalshiEX and its parent, Kalshi Inc., to recover nearly double his own alleged net realized loss under Washington’s gambling loss-recovery statute, and a theory of unjust enrichment.”

Between June 17 and August 14, 2026, Bright transferred $315,353.94 to Kalshi in 253 separate debits from his checking account, his lawsuit said. Kalshi allegedly collected $5,589.05 in funding fees on those transfers.

Bright made numerous wagers on sporting events including professional baseball games and tennis matches. He apparently put any winnings into new bets, and alleges that “Kalshi’s platform cycled Plaintiff’s deposits through $14,396,457.30 in transactions and assessed and retained $84,062.71 in trading fees on them, equal to 26.7 percent of everything Plaintiff deposited.”

After all his bets, Bright suffered a net loss of $308,781.62, and his account was left with a balance of $983.27. Kalshi said that Bright’s “alleged losses went to counterparties rather than” to Kalshi itself and that Bright’s “positions were matched with counterparties and resolved according to the outcomes of the underlying events.”

“The Complaint does not allege that KalshiEX or Kalshi Inc. was the counterparty to any of Plaintiff’s positions,” Kalshi said.

Kalshi calls itself “a neutral exchange platform” with no financial stake in the outcome of any event. It makes revenue by collecting fees on transactions. But while Kalshi describes itself as a neutral operator and collector of transaction fees, its business model also includes a trading affiliate that places wagers on the platform.

Kalshi’s rulebook says its trading affiliate “participates on the Platform and provides liquidity to the Platform by placing orders on either (or both) sides of a market at competitive price levels.” Kalshi says its affiliate only has access to the same public information that other traders on the platform have.

Bright’s lawsuit alleges that Kalshi’s affiliate “took the opposite side of a substantial portion of Plaintiff’s positions,” meaning that “Kalshi and the enterprise under common ownership with it were not a neutral venue but the dealer or player winning within the meaning of [state law], in addition to being the proprietor for whose benefit the wagering was conducted.”

Bright doesn’t know for sure whether Kalshi’s affiliate was on the other side of any of his bets. “The identity of the participant on the opposite side of each of Plaintiff’s positions, and the profit each such participant realized, is information exclusively within Kalshi’s possession,” Bright’s lawsuit said.

The US Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit ruled in August that Nevada can regulate Kalshi under gambling laws. Although that case involved Nevada, the Ninth Circuit’s jurisdiction includes the state of Washington. Bright’s lawsuit quoted the ruling’s finding that “placing sports bets, even when called by another name, is still gambling.”

Although Bright’s lawsuit said his net loss was $308,781.62, he asked for $580,544.98 based on an “event-by-event” calculation derived from a 1950 ruling issued by the Washington Supreme Court. “Computed on the event-by-event basis required by Heitfeld , under which winnings in separate and distinct events may not be offset against losses, the sums Plaintiff lost total $580,544.98,” the lawsuit said.

Bright’s lawsuit said that if the court declines to order $580,544.98 in restitution, it should instead award “all funds Plaintiff transferred to Kalshi and the $89,651.76 in funding and trading fees Kalshi collected.” That would amount to over $405,000.

In addition to its motion to dismiss the case, Kalshi filed a motion to stay the proceedings at least until the US Supreme Court decides whether to take up a separate case on whether state gambling laws apply to prediction markets. “The orderly course of justice favors a stay because Supreme Court review will settle or simplify every claim and ensure uniform treatment of like suits,” Kalshi told the US district court.

Kalshi has suffered some notable losses in US appeals courts, which found that states can regulate the platform’s event contracts under gambling laws. But federal courts have not unanimously sided with states, and New Jersey asked the Supreme Court to settle the question of whether states can regulate Kalshi under gambling laws.

Kalshi’s motion for a stay in the Bright case noted that Washington government officials are “pursuing overlapping claims” against Kalshi. “The State of Washington is pursuing the same theory, and seeks the same recovery for Mr. Bright, in a case pending before the Superior Court of Washington for King County,” Kalshi wrote.

Kalshi tried to get the state’s case moved to a federal court, but it was sent back to King County Superior Court in May. Washington won a preliminary injunction against Kalshi in August, when a King County judge ordered Kalshi to implement geofencing and stop allowing many types of wagers in the state.

The county court’s order required Kalshi to stop offering or accepting event contracts “related to sports, elections, politics, entertainment, culture, tech and science, or mentions” in the state. The injunction did not affect wagers in the commodities, climate, economics, and finance categories.

Bright transferred his funds to Kalshi before the geofencing order took effect. His lawsuit claims that on September 15, he tried to access the app but received a notice that “using this app in your current location is prohibited.”

This article was updated to correct the date the lawsuit was filed .

scraped.title: A Sam Altman parody offers an amusing lesson in memory management
scraped.description: We verified the RAM numbers are real without sending any emails to OpenAI.
scraped.h1: A Sam Altman parody offers an amusing lesson in memory management
scraped.body_text:
We verified the RAM numbers are real without sending any emails to OpenAI.

Sam Altman’s recent comments on the Cheeky Pint podcast inspired developer Iain Kay to create a satirical script that allows users to email the OpenAI CEO once per day if more than 10 percent of their system RAM is reported as available. Ram-Altman is described by its creator as a “parody project” launched in response to Altman’s viral remarks about RAM in your personal PC.

As reported by The Verge , on the October 29 episode recorded with Stripe President John Collison, Altman said, “A lot of people want local inference. And somehow, they assume that the problem is solved now because we are going to have open source models, we’re going to be able to run them on our computers, and so we’re not going to need all the stuff in the data center. But from a global allocation perspective, actually, it’s quite terrible to have everybody have a bunch of the world’s limited supply of DRAM sitting in their own computer and being used 5 percent of the time.”

Altman has since explained that his comments were taken out of context and briefly changed his display name to “RAM Altman” on X, which Kay calls on the project GitHub, “objectively excellent and where the project gets its name.”

In an email to Ars, Kay said, “Ram-Altman is a bash script that takes MemTotal minus MemAvailable from /proc/meminfo, so the figure includes page cache and reclaimable slab but leaves out tmpfs and shared memory.”

If the script only showed what Linux reports as “free” RAM, it would paint an incomplete picture. Linux often reports a surprisingly small amount of “free” RAM, as it doesn’t count memory that is currently claimable for use. Linux will fill available RAM caches with file data for quick access, but the kernel can reclaim that usage at a moment’s notice when needed. The MemAvailable figure is the kernel’s own estimate of how much memory it could hand over without swapping.

Users can schedule the script to ask the kernel for a status update every five minutes, and if more than 10 percent of RAM is available, it triggers a joke email from one of several joke templates. The script limits outgoing emails to one per day.

The GitHub page for the RAM-Altman project includes a dry-run option that any Linux user with a Bash terminal should be able to paste and run without the need for email trolling. When the threshold is exceeded, each dry run output features one generated joke email, so repeated runs produce different amusing examples.

A test run of the script on my Fedora 44 KDE machine confirmed the author’s measurements. Inside the System – Info Center of my Fedora desktop, the system reports 14.9 GiB of total usable system RAM after the kernel and firmware take their needed slices of the 16 GiB of physical memory. This reflects the total amount of capacity the system has to work with, not the amount available at any given time. The Ram-Altman script shows that of that 14.9 GiB total pool, 10 GiB is used, with 4.9 GiB available (33.1 percent). That figure isn’t the simple sum of the “free” and “cache” lines that the script displays, but a kernel-calculated figure that accounts for the full amount of memory that can be reclaimed.

The project concedes the nuance that Altman was referring to how much time memory spends being utilized, while the script measures how much capacity is free at the time of measurement. While the script might tell Altman that 33 percent of your system RAM is available, it doesn’t outline how often that’s the case. The concession steps on the joke slightly, but it keeps everyone honest.

The GitHub is wise to point out that “ --dry-run is the best way to enjoy this. It costs nothing and all the jokes are there.” Used irresponsibly, this cheeky joke could morph into a harassment tool, and Kay quickly points out that the script does not include anyone’s email, including Altman’s. Users who deploy their own operating version are encouraged to only use their own real email addresses and honor any requests to stop, as is outlined at the bottom of the script-generated output.

If you’re interested in taking a look at some of the emails generated without having to spin up a Linux machine that reports the system status every five minutes, the ram-altman.lol project website rotates through sample emails generated by the script. Kay writes on the website that, “In fairness, he says the remarks were taken out of context , posted ‘i want you to have so much ram’ , and briefly went by Ram Altman on X. That makes this script a daily progress report.”

Six months before the Nvidia spy scandal emerged , the New York-based short seller firm Culper Research had already raised questions about Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s unusually close relationship with Alice Huang, an executive at Megaspeed, a Singapore-based company that buys Nvidia chips. She is now suspected to be a Chinese spy.

The Nvidia CEO admitted to an extramarital affair over the weekend, and the company has now opened a formal investigation into his relationship with Alice Huang (who shares his last name but is not related). U.S. intelligence officials believe she was recruited by the Chinese government to collect intelligence on Jensen Huang and influence his position regarding U.S. export controls on advanced AI chips.

Culper’s May 13 report is resurfacing because it picked up on the connection between Jensen Huang and Alice Huang while investigating Megaspeed’s ties to Nvidia.

NEW: We are short Nvidia $NVDA . We believe Nvidia has a significant China problem. Please see our full report and disclosures now available on our website, link in bio. pic.twitter.com/oTaJyL7S2R

In particular, the report called the relationship between the two executives “uncomfortably close,” noting that the Nvidia CEO was spotted partying and socializing with Alice Huang on multiple occasions. The report even claimed that some Nvidia employees wondered whether they had a “special relationship.”

Culper Research also theorized the China business that Nvidia lost to export controls had been rerouted through Southeast Asia, and that Megaspeed, a major chip buyer in the region, was secretly financed by Chinese tech giant Alibaba through shell companies. It pointed to financial records that showed Megaspeed’s total liabilities and equity had grown from $33 million at the end of 2023 to around $3 billion by the end of 2024, much of it in the form of refundable deposits from an unidentified source.

The Financial Times reported Monday that documents show Alibaba lent money to Megaspeed through subsidiaries.

Culper is a short seller, so it stood to financially benefit from making these allegations, and those about possible illegal chip diversion have not been independently verified. Its report is available on the web and was posted to X back in May .

Nvidia’s stock slid more than 4% on Monday, the first trading day after its board said it would investigate CEO Jensen Huang over his relationship with Alice Huang, an executive U.S. intelligence believes was spying for China.

Securities lawyers were already moving. Schall, Brown & Schwartz, a Los Angeles shareholder-rights firm, was among the first to plant a flag, announcing Monday morning that it’s investigating whether Nvidia made false or misleading statements, or failed to disclose information pertinent to investors. Robert Bartlett, a Stanford Law professor and securities law expert, expects it to have plenty of company.

“I would definitely wager that there’ll be a filing,” Bartlett said in an interview, adding that he wouldn’t be surprised if a case had been filed by the end of day Monday. Plaintiffs’ lawyers have good reasons to be first in line; under federal securities law, the first complaint triggers a public notice, and investors then have 60 days to ask the court to be named lead plaintiff. A firm that files early gets a head start on signing up investors with large losses, as well as on shaping the story of the case. Nvidia is headquartered in Santa Clara, so it’s likely we’ll see this in the Northern District of California. (It’s very possible a case has already been filed; newly filed cases can take up to 24 hours to be discoverable online.)

While much remains unknown, the legal theory here doesn’t depend on anything the board’s investigation turns up about Huang’s private life. When The New York Times first reported on Huang’s ties to Alice Huang last month, the executive at the Singapore data center company Megaspeed, an Nvidia spokesperson described the relationship to another outlet, The Hill, as “ not unusual or unexpected .” The company representative added, “Megaspeed has been no different than many other regional cloud customers. Meetings with customers are part of a CEO’s job; Jensen talks with thousands of customer executives every year.”

Since then, Huang has acknowledged to the board that the relationship was intimate. Meanwhile, The Times reports that U.S. intelligence had been monitoring Alice Huang for more than a year.

From a securities perspective, Bartlett said, the company’s earlier statement was “clearly a misleading statement.” And because Huang is CEO, Bartlett said, “his knowledge gets imputed to the company.” In other words, Nvidia is treated as having known what its chief executive knew.

Bartlett says the likely vehicle is a “classic fraud on the market” claim, in which investors argue they paid prices that reflected false or incomplete public information, and lost money when the truth emerged. Monday’s drop gives them a lot to work with. Damages in such cases are tied to the stock’s decline, and Nvidia is one of the most valuable companies in the world, so you can imagine a settlement could prove exceedingly expensive.

The usual path is that the case is litigated for a long time and then settles, Bartlett notes. That means a large payment from the company and its directors-and-officers insurers, but typically no personal consequences for the CEO or the board. It is also a civil matter, so Huang isn’t facing prison over it. The irony, as Bartlett noted, is that the suit is brought in the name of Nvidia’s shareholders, and shareholders ultimately pay for the settlement, directly or through insurance premiums.

Bartlett sorted Nvidia’s wider exposure into buckets. The first is the securities fraud claim, which is the clearest immediate problem for the company and potentially for Huang. The second is governance: what the board knew and when. It’s possible directors were kept in the dark, but the board also has oversight duties, and once the Times began reporting on the Megaspeed connection, the company should have had reporting lines to bring a critical risk like this to directors. If it didn’t, or if directors didn’t act, board-level liability is possible.

A third category, one that would change everything, would arise only if the board’s investigation finds Huang knew about the intelligence connection. That would be “a whole other ball game,” as Bartlett said. (The board said in a statement to the public Sunday that it has no reason to believe national security or Nvidia secrets were compromised.)

There’s also the question of government action. The SEC can seek an officer-and-director bar for intentional securities-fraud violations, which Bartlett said is technically on the table. But he doubted the current SEC under Chairman Paul Atkins would have the appetite, given President Trump’s support for Huang. A roughly two-year clock after discovery of the facts would leave room for a future administration to act, though the window would be tight, and Bartlett posited that’s pretty unlikely when asked about it.

It’s worth underscoring that an announcement like Schall, Brown & Schwartz’s is not on its own a sign of a strong case. SBS files a lot of “investigation” notices. A notice shows a plaintiffs’ firm sees an opportunity. Which firm winds up leading the case is decided later by the court, and that decision usually depends on which investor has the largest loss.

Other firms that are lining up against Nvidia include Rosen Law Firm, Levi & Korsinsky, Bronstein, Gewirtz & Grossman and the Law Offices of Frank R. Cruz. Each announced their own investigations Monday, and Rosen said it is preparing a class action lawsuit.

Geothermal company Fervo couldn’t have picked a better time to deliver its first power plants.

In its third-quarter earnings report, released Monday, the company said it now has $11.9 billion worth of contracted revenue on the books, up from $7.2 billion last quarter.

Fervo has been hitting its deadlines recently, which undoubtedly has helped to drive orders.

As hyperscalers scour the earth for electricity to power their AI data centers, Fervo is on track to complete a 396 megawatt power plant for Google by the end of 2028. The geothermal company connected its first 100 megawatt power plant to the grid earlier this year.

Both projects are built at Cape Station in Utah, a resource that could generate 8.4 gigawatts of electricity. Previously, experts told Fervo the site could only produce about 4 gigawatts .

The Google project, now called Cape Google 400, will be grid connected, co-founder and CEO Tim Latimer said in an earnings call Monday. The arrangement means that Google can draw power from the deal and sell it to other customers if it’s not ready to use it.

“We built Cape Station on our schedule. Google can develop a potential data center on their schedule, and neither party is waiting on the other,” he said.

Latimer’s statement also underlines an advantage that geothermal has over competing generating sources like large nuclear or natural gas power plants — the phased nature of its construction.

Fervo’s newer wells are deeper and hotter, each capable of generating 15 megawatts gross power, and several are linked together into what the company calls a GeoBlock. The first completed GeoBlock generated 33 megawatts, while recent ones hit 50 megawatts. They’re sized to match the demand of a typical data center hall, so hyperscalers can bring them online as they’re completed.

As a business, Fervo is still in the early stages. It ended the quarter with an operating loss of $43.7 million, though it holds cash and cash equivalents of $1.9 billion and long-term debt of $301.6 million, which should give it plenty of runway.

Much will depend on the company bringing down the cost of its power plants. While hyperscalers are hungry for power today, they may not always be as price-indiscriminate.

Yet if Fervo can deliver on its promises, it could end up winning on price. The first phase of its Cape Station project cost $7,000 per kilowatt of capacity, the company said. The cost for its Google project is $5,500 per kilowatt, a significant drop that suggests Fervo is on the right path. With subsidies, that’s about equivalent to a new natural gas power plant running on fuel that costs $6 per million BTUs. Still about twice what natural gas costs today, but trending closer to where it needs to be.

But if Fervo can hit its long-term target of $3,000 per kilowatt, it could significantly undercut natural gas power, even at today’s prices. That’s a pretty ambitious target, but the company has made significant strides in just a few years. No wonder Google is getting in early.

scraped.title: Jensen Huang affair puts Nvidia's future at risk, with no clear successor to the renowned CEO
scraped.description: Jensen Huang is practically synonymous with Nvidia, the chipmaker he co-founded in 1993 and turned into one of the most valuable companies on the planet.
scraped.author: Annie Palmer,Lora Kolodny
scraped.h1: Jensen Huang affair puts Nvidia's future at risk, with no clear successor to the renowned CEO
scraped.body_text:
In this article

Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang 's admission of an affair with a purported Chinese spy has raised questions about his future at the company, and what happens if the 63-year-old co-founder, who built the chipmaker into one of the most valuable businesses on the planet, is forced out.

Shares of Nvidia sank more than 4% on Monday, even as the broader market rallied sharply, after Huang acknowledged the affair in a message to staff on Sunday, and said that the board was launching an investigation into whether he was targeted by a foreign intelligence agency. The board said it has "confidence in Jensen," and that it has "no reason to believe that either national security or Nvidia secrets were compromised."

The New York Times first reported that the Chinese businesswoman was a spy for China's Ministry of State Security, according to people briefed on the intelligence circulated in a memo among the Trump administration in the spring. China has called the allegation a smear.

While Nvidia says Huang will continue to lead the company during the probe, pressure is rapidly mounting on the chipmaker, whose technology has powered the first four years of the generative artificial intelligence boom. Leaders from both parties are calling for briefings, and Democrats poised to take control of both houses of Congress are calling for investigations and new legislation "to stop advanced AI chips from fueling China's military," Sen. Elizabeth Warren of Massachusetts wrote in a post on X on Monday.

Huang has outsized influence over Nvidia, and is the sole face of the company with no clear second-in-command. He's also among the loudest champions of AI in the country, is critical to the financing of the broader infrastructure buildout and has a close relationship with President Donald Trump , giving Nvidia a front-row seat when it comes to discussions on AI policy, safety and regulation.

"The issue at Nvidia is that there is no clear successor to Jensen, and we had expected him to stay in this role for at least 10 more years," analysts at Melius Research said in a Monday research note.

Stacy Rasgon, an analyst at Bernstein, told CNBC's "Squawk on the Street" on Monday that, "Jensen is Nvidia. Nvidia is Jensen." He added that Huang "runs the thing pretty much top down," and "sort of pulls all the strings."

Nvidia didn't immediately respond to a request for comment.

Nvidia has long maintained a flat, non-hierarchical organizational structure. Huang has deep involvement in the company's day-to-day operations and frequently serves as its spokesperson in front of world leaders and at industry conferences. In addition to being co-founder and CEO, Huang is also Nvidia's president.

In September of 2025, Huang told CNBC's Becky Quick that he had as many as 60 direct reports. Internal records reviewed by CNBC reveal that, as of this week, he had 33 direct reports, including CFO Colette Kress, influential Chief Scientist Bill Dally, senior vice president of software engineering Dwight Diercks, and Ian Buck, best known as the inventor of Nvidia's CUDA software.

However, relative to some of his founder peers in tech like Meta's Mark Zuckerberg and Elon Musk at SpaceX , Huang has minimal actual control. He owns just over 3% of the outstanding shares and is one of 11 members on a board that has no official chair.

And in the risk factors of Nvidia's financial filings , Huang isn't specifically identified as a key person. Rather, the company says, "we are highly dependent on the services of our longstanding executive team."

"Failure to ensure effective succession planning, transfer of knowledge, and smooth transitions involving executives and key employees could hinder our strategic planning, execution, and long-term success," Nvidia says.

Still, Huang's influence is undeniable, so much so that the question of succession is one that's hardly broached among analysts and investors.

Timm Schulze-Melander, an analyst at Rothschild & Co. Redburn, wrote in a Monday note that Huang could be forced to step back from the CEO role if the board's investigation reveals "something materially more serious" than an undisclosed relationship.

But Schulze-Melander said Huang's potential resignation isn't a foregone conclusion of the investigation, pointing to the importance of his leadership at the company.

Nvidia's board "needs to demonstrate independence and protect shareholders without destabilizing a company whose success is unusually dependent on its founder," Schulze-Melander wrote. "Its initial statement suggests it is attempting to achieve both."

Several analysts said the investigation could lead to governance changes at Nvidia, including putting a transition contingency plan in place.

The Melius analysts wrote that Nvidia has a "strong bench" of executive talent across its networking, hyperscale and high-performance computing businesses, along with "technical expertise" stemming from Chief Technology Officer Michael Kagan as well as Dally, the chief scientist.

"While these folks can keep the engine running, Jensen is one of a kind, and his energy will be needed to maintain confidence in the AI trade," the analysts wrote.

— CNBC's Kif Leswing, Kristina Partsinevelos and Michael Bloom contributed to this report.

items.title: Hegseth impeachment articles introduced by Rep. Massie
items.summary: The House is likely to vote this week on articles of impeachment against Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth filed by Republican Rep. Thomas Masie.

scraped.title: Hegseth impeachment articles introduced by Rep. Massie
scraped.description: The House is likely to vote this week on articles of impeachment against Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth filed by Republican Rep. Thomas Masie.
scraped.author: Garrett Downs
scraped.h1: Hegseth impeachment articles introduced by Rep. Massie
scraped.body_text:
Rep. Thomas Massie , R-Ky., on Monday introduced articles of impeachment against Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth , triggering a vote in the House of Representatives as early as this week.

The unusual impeachment push against Hegseth by a member of his own party comes after Democrats swept to majorities in both the House and Senate during last week's midterm elections . Many Republicans, including Vice President JD Vance , have cited the Iran war Hegseth has led as a reason for the electoral bludgeoning.

Massie, who lost his reelection bid in a Republican primary in May, introduced eight articles of impeachment against Hegseth. They include waging war in contravention of war powers resolutions Congress passed to limit war, extrajudicial killings tied to boat strikes in the Caribbean that purported to target drug smugglers and suppressing free speech by targeting Sen. Mark Kelly, D-Ariz., a veteran.

"Wherefore, Secretary of Defense Peter Hegseth, by such conduct, has demonstrated that he will remain a threat to the Constitution if allowed to remain in office, and has acted in a manner grossly incompatible with his duties and the rule of law," the articles, which Massie read from the House floor, read. "Peter Brian Hegseth thus warrants impeachment and trial, removal from office, and disqualification to hold and enjoy any office of honor, trust, or profit under the United States."

Massie's resolution will force House Republican leaders to put the measure up for a vote by the end of this week. Impeachment resolutions are privileged, meaning the House must act on them, table them or vote to refer them to committee within two legislative days.

President Donald Trump once again defended Hegseth later Monday, telling reporters at the White House he will stand by the secretary even if he is impeached.

"He won two wars. He was in charge," said Trump, who was impeached twice in his first presidential term.

Trump also credited Hegseth with boosting military recruitment, claiming there are "waiting lists of people trying to get in."

"He's done a very good job," Trump said.

Congress has the authority to impeach Cabinet secretaries, though it is a highly unusual move. Republican leadership in the House has not yet laid out how they plan to deal with the Hegseth impeachment, and it is unclear whether they have the votes to dispose of Massie's measure following the election.

The last Cabinet Secretary to be impeached was Homeland Security Secretary Alejandro Mayorkas in 2024 over his handling of the U.S.-Mexico border. Before Mayorkas, a Cabinet secretary had not been impeached since Secretary of War William Belknap in 1876. Neither was convicted by the Senate.

If the House votes to impeach Hegseth, the Senate would be tasked with holding a trial and voting on removing the secretary from office. If convicted by a two-thirds majority of the Senate, Hegseth would be removed from office.

Republicans hold a razor-thin 218-214 majority in the House, meaning only a handful of Republican defections could result in Hegseth's impeachment.

House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries , D-N.Y., reiterated his support for impeaching Hegseth on Monday at his first press conference at the Capitol since last Tuesday's elections. "Pete Hegseth has abused his power, undermined America's national security, and he's the architect of the reckless and costly failed war of choice in Iran," Jeffries said.

Hegseth has appeared to be preparing for an impeachment fight. The secretary put out a video last week defending his actions atop the Pentagon, and the department has led a media campaign to "Stand. Fight. Defend the Republic."

Hegseth on Monday announced he would hold a press conference Tuesday morning at the Pentagon. His most recent press conference way May 5, just over two months after the Iran war began.

items.title: A key report for where inflation stood in October comes out Tuesday. Here's what to expect
items.summary: The CPI headline reading is expected to show an increase of 0.3% while the core is forecast to increase 0.2%.

scraped.title: A key report for where inflation stood in October comes out Tuesday. Here's what to expect
scraped.description: The CPI headline reading is expected to show an increase of 0.3% while the core is forecast to increase 0.2%.
scraped.author: Jeff Cox
scraped.h1: A key report for where inflation stood in October comes out Tuesday. Here's what to expect
scraped.body_text:
Falling gasoline prices provided some relief to consumers in October, but Federal Reserve officials are increasingly concerned that inflation pressures elsewhere in the economy are proving harder to contain.

Prices at the pump declined by more than 4%, according to the Energy Information Administration, providing a respite from a surge that had added more than a dollar a gallon over the past year.

However, the consumer price index for the month, which the Bureau of Labor Statistics will release Tuesday at 8:30 a.m., is expected to show only a slight let-up.

Meanwhile, Fed officials say they are worried that inflation initially driven higher by President Donald Trump 's tariffs and the Iran war is proving more persistent than expected, with price pressures emerging in sectors beyond those directly affected by the shocks.

At a time when the central bank is increasingly confident about the state of the labor market, concerns over the cost of living are what are top of mind for the Fed.

"We've been moving up to what historically we'd consider full employment, and the big problem has all been on the inflation side. We go around, we talk to people everywhere in this district, all we hear about is affordability on the business side, the cost," Chicago Fed President Austan Goolsbee said Monday during an event in his home district. "So we've got to come to terms with this cost-side and inflation-side failure."

The CPI reading for all items is expected to show an increase of 0.3%. Core inflation, which excludes volatile food and energy costs, is forecast to increase 0.2%, according to the Dow Jones consensus forecast. While both would be slower than the respective September monthly gains of 0.6% and 0.3%, they still represent further price pressures.

There will be no annual reading for October because of the government shutdown a year ago, which prevented the BLS from collecting some data and compiling a full index level. Because of the data issue, there isn't a comparable figure for the index.

Bank of America, using an assumed baseline interpolating data for the period last year, estimated the annual growth rates at 3.8% for headline and 2.7% for core, both 0.1 percentage point higher than September and well above the Fed's 2% goal.

Goolsbee said the current run on inflation is defying what normally could be expected from supply shocks and tariffs, with the current situation intensified by the hyperscaler build-out related to artificial intelligence.

"It was supposed to have gone away by now, and we're now starting to see the inflation kicking up in areas that probably weren't from oil prices and tariffs, like a bunch of services. Now this stuff with the AI data center build-out is, to my eyes, starting to look more just like old-fashioned demand overheating," he said.

The massive investment in data centers is creating demand for construction workers, electricity and equipment, potentially adding to price pressures even as AI promises longer-term productivity gains, he added.

Though the Fed in October voted to hold its benchmark interest rate in place, markets are pricing in a better than 80% probability that the central bank will raise rates by a quarter percentage point at its next meeting in December, according to CME FedWatch data.

Goolsbee, who doesn't vote on the rate-setting Federal Open Market Committee this year but will in 2027, didn't commit to which way he was leaning on additional rate hikes, though he said current conditions could warrant action.

"The conventional wisdom there is: Be aggressive up front, to never let the economy overheat, because once it gets overheated, it's extremely painful to get rid of that kind of overheating," he said. "So I think we've got to watch out in that space."

The CPI release comes with economic growth strong — 3.4% in the third quarter for gross domestic product and tracking at 3.5% for the final three months of the year, according to the Atlanta Fed — and the labor market seemingly in solid shape as well. Nonfarm payrolls expanded by a much better-than-expected 165,000 in October, while the unemployment rate edged lower to 4.1%, though inflation-adjusted wage growth has been negative.

That puts the inflation reading squarely in focus.

Bank of America said it sees tariff impacts fading but that goods prices could be pushed higher because of AI demand. Further, the firm is cautious about "sticky" services prices as well as pressures from health insurance and autos.

The bank has been hawkish in terms of Fed expectations and sees a December hike as likely so long as there isn't an escalated stock market sell-off that might dissuade the central bank.

"This will be the final inflation report before the Fed's December 8-9 meeting. If our forecast is correct, we think it would effectively lock in another 25bp hike, all else equal," BofA economist Stephen Juneau said in a client note. "Absent an indisputably soft 0.1% [month-over-month] print, we doubt the inflation data will dissuade the Fed from hiking in December. The bigger risk to our call comes from financial markets."

scraped.h1: What’s going on with the Russia IIHF World Juniors controversy?
scraped.body_text:
