What’s going on with the Russia IIHF World Juniors controversy? WHO GIVES A F / K ???

The decision by the International Ice Hockey Federation to allow Russia back into the World Juniors Hockey Championship next month continued to stir backlash on Monday with Norway saying its team was being bumped to make room for Russia and Sweden vowing not to play against Russia .

In a statement to Global News on Monday, a spokesperson for the Prime Minister’s Office reiterated Ottawa’s stance saying, “athletes from Russia and Belarus will not be able to compete for their countries in Canada so long as the unjustified war against Ukraine continues. That position has not changed.”

It is not yet clear whether Russian and Belarussian players will be allowed to compete for a neutral team rather than for their national teams.

The first puck drops on Dec. 26., with the tournament taking place in Edmonton and Red Deer, Alta.

“For better or for worse, athletes that are participating and representing their country do get involved, whether they like it or not, in the political implications of international sports,” says Simon Darnell professor of kinesiology and Sport for Development & Peace at the University of Toronto.

“Allowing the Russians to play at the World Juniors, unfortunately, would be a tacit acceptance of the war in Ukraine, and I don’t think that’s what the international sports community should be doing.”

Here’s what to know about how this came to be and everything we know so far.

Russia has been waging an ongoing unprovoked war on Ukraine since early 2022, and various international sports groups banned Russia from participating in response, including the International Olympic Committee (IOC) and the International Ice Hockey Federation (IIHF), which conducts the World Juniors Hockey Championship.

The IIHF ban on Russia’s participation was squashed last month after the Court of Arbitration for Sport ruled on Oct. 30 that the federation must allow Russia to compete in its sanctioned events, including the upcoming tournament.

Norway’s hockey federation said Sunday the IIHF had informed it that Russia would be added to the men’s under-20 tournament in Edmonton and Red Deer next month at Norway’s expense .

The IIHF has not formally announced the change, and its website still lists Norway among the 10 teams in the tournament.

Global News sent a request for comment to the IIHF on Monday asking if Russia has been added to the upcoming tournament and replaced Norway. A response was not received as of publication.

Shortly after the court ruling last month, Prime Minister Mark Carney announced a ban on Russian athletes , in addition to those from Belarus, from participating in the tournament while in Canada because of the war with Ukraine.

“This is a decision we take on our own, which is we will deny, while Russia and Belarus are supporting this illegal unjustified horrific war in Ukraine — as long as that’s going on, there will be none of those athletes competing for their countries in Canada,” Carney said last week.

That decision by Carney was also supported publicly by Wayne Gretzky.

Ukrainian Canadian leaders say the court ruling allowing Russia to participate was “unjustified, ridiculous and egregious.”

“The court decision to allow Russia back into international hockey is a disgrace and has brought shame onto that court,” says Orest Zakydalsky, senior policy advisor with the Ukrainian Canadian Congress.

“Norway and the Norwegian people have been strong supporters of Ukraine and continue to be. We are immensely grateful for all that they have done for Ukraine and I think that the Hockey Federation should take a look at the logic of this ruling and reverse it.”

Norway acknowledged that the IIHF has been handcuffed by the court’s ruling. As the 10th-ranked team entering the tournament, Norway said it was relegated to the 1A Division to open the spot for Russia.

“The situation is still unclear,” Norway’s ice hockey secretary general Peter Salsten said in a statement posted on the association’s website and translated from Norwegian to English. “This makes us hope that the last word has not been said about our participation in Canada.”

“We are aware of the status and the measures the IIHF feels compelled to take, and will await further information from the IIHF in the coming days,” Salsten said. “This also clearly shows all the practical challenges and immediate consequences for everyone involved when countries are reinstated immediately.”

The Russians haven’t competed in the tournament since a fourth-place finish in 2021, with their ban beginning after the nation invaded Ukraine in February 2022.

“I suspect that Norway’s probably trying to figure out how they’re going to deal with this situation and they know that they have allies,” says Darnell.

“It reminds us that sports and politics are always connected, and I think we can all agree that this is much more about politics than it is about sports at this point.”

Since the announcement from the Norwegian Hockey Association, the Swedish Ice Hockey Association says it will refuse to play Russia if the teams meet at the world juniors and stood in solidarity with Team Norway.

Adam van Koeverden, Secretary of State for Sport of Canada, spoke Monday and reaffirmed Ottawa’s stance on Russia’s involvement in the tournament, although few specifics were given regarding any exceptions.

“The prime minister was as clear as day last week. Russia will not be competing at the World Juniors in Alberta,” said van Koeverden to reporters when asked about Norway reportedly being bumped to allow Russia to participate.

He also suggested that Russian players could, in theory, participate in the tournament provided that they don’t represent Russia by wearing a neutral jersey.

“If they’re not competing with a neutral status as an AIN, that’s, en français, Athlètes Individuels Neutres, then they would not be permitted to compete, and that AIN designation has not been tested in a team format,” said van Koeverden.

“Working with Hockey Canada, working with the IIHF, with respect to Norway’s inclusion in this tournament. I spoke with the Minister of Sport from Norway last week and had a great conversation. We’re very, very aligned and we hope to see Norwegian athletes competing in Alberta December and January.”

When asked to clarify if he meant that Russian players could participate provided they wear a neutral jersey on the ice, van Koeverden said, “I want to be just as clear as the prime minister was last week. The Russians will not be represented at the World Juniors in Alberta.”

– with files from The Canadian Press

The CEO of tech giant Nvidia is under scrutiny by both his own company and politicians amid reports he was the target of an alleged Chinese spy.

As a result of the allegations and investigation, Nvidia’s stock fell four per cent on Monday.

The New York Times reported on Oct. 29 that Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang had been involved in a relationship with Alice Huang , a former executive of Nvidia Cloud partner Megaspeed. Eight days later on Nov. 6, the New York Times reported U.S. intelligence had alleged she was a spy for Beijing.

Huang acknowledged his affair in a letter to his family and the company this weekend.

Here’s what is known so far about Huang, his relationship with the Megaspeed former executive and what this means for the Nvidia going forward.

Jensen Huang is the president and CEO of Nvidia and co-founded the multi-national technology company in 1993 with Chris Malachowsky and Curtis Priem.

The 63-year-old was born in Taiwan then moved to Thailand with his family as a child before being sent by his parents to live in the U.S. at age nine. He graduated from Oregon State University as an electrical engineer and received a master’s degree in the same field from Stanford University.

Ranked the eighth richest man in the world by Forbes and sometimes known as “Daddy Huang,” he’s been also recognized for his trademark leather jackets and high-profile launches.

Huang also has a close relationship with President Donald Trump, having travelled to China in May as part of a state visit. He’s also pushed Trump to ease export restrictions on Nvidia chips.

He’s been married to his wife Lori Huang since 1985 and has two children. Their daughter Madison is a senior director of product and technical marketing for physical AI platforms at Nvidia, while son Spencer manages robotics software products.

The Nvidia CEO apologized to both his wife and children in a letter the company posted Sunday, admitting he was unfaithful.

“My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did. I am deeply sorry,” Huang wrote. “My family bears no responsibility for my choices. I do. Please give them privacy.

According to the New York Times, Alice Huang was recruited by China to collect intelligence on Nvidia’s CEO in an effort by Beijing to learn more about American AI chips. There was also the potential for influencing Nvidia to push for its most advanced chips to be made available to China, which is rapidly pursuing advance AI development and seen as a key rival to the U.S. in the industry.

Global News has not independently verified the New York Times reporting.

China criticized the reporting on Monday.

“The so-called claims of Chinese spy narrative are purely a groundless accusation, slander, and a smear,” said Gua Jiakun, spokesperson for China’s foreign ministry.

But Beijing has been interested in AI microchips from Nvidia for several years.

Its most advanced chips are barred from sale in China, but the Trump administration gave permission for Nvidia to sell its H200 chips to 10 approved Chinese firms last year.

China has imposed its own restrictions over concerns of dependence on U.S. technology, with Reuters reporting about 600,000 of the company’s chips are stored in Hong Kong awaiting shipment.

“We know for a fact that China has engaged in espionage particularly in those areas it has identified as strategic and one of those areas right now is going to be frontier AI,” said Stephanie Carvin, a former national security analyst and associate professor at Carleton University.

“It absolutely needs and wants the chips that are produced by Nvidia and other companies to further its ambitions in this kind of geopolitical race.”

Alice Huang is a Chinese citizen and former executive of Megaspeed, an AI company that calls itself a specialized Cloud provider and a partner of Nvidia in the Asia-Pacific region.

Huang is a common surname in China.

The company has been under investigation by the U.S. government over suspicions it helped Beijing gain access to the U.S. tech giant’s advanced AI chips that are currently barred.

In December 2025, Megaspeed posted a message that its company had undergone multiple inspections by U.S. government departments, as well as Nvidia.

“These thorough investigations have confirmed that there has been no evidence of any violations concerning the illicit transfer of chips or any illegal activities, and this demonstrates that we are a compliant and legitimate company,” the statement reads.

Global News has requested comment on the latest investigation involving its former executive.

It is not known at this time when the pair started their relationship, but Reuters reported the two were previously pictured at a bar together in Taipei in 2025 during a technology conference.

The affair appears to have hallmarks of what security experts call a “honey pot.”

“They could be convincing you to try and give up information that you have or to make certain decisions and try to persuade you in some way,” she said. “But even just the affair itself can be harmful, right, because it can be used as blackmail.”

Chinese industrial espionage has been a significant concern for officials over recent decades in both Canada and the U.S.

Last year in Canada, a former researcher with Hydro Quebec was put on trial for allegedly spying for China. He’s accused of sharing confidential research with Beijing for the commercialization of battery technologies. A verdict has not yet been delivered.

The U.S. FBI calls the counterintelligence and espionage efforts by China a “grave threat” to the country’s economic well-being and democratic values.

“The counterintelligence and economic espionage efforts emanating from the government of China and the Chinese Communist Party are a grave threat to the economic well-being and democratic values of the United States,” the FBI says.

“Confronting this threat is the FBI’s top counterintelligence priority.”

According to the Center for Strategic and International Studies, there have been at least 224 reported instances of Chinese espionage up to 2023 starting in 2000.

The listed incidents primarily involved the illicit acquisition of information by Chinese intelligence officers or their agents and over the years have targeted NASA, General Motors, Ford Motor Company, Coca Cola, Google as well as oil companies, the U.S. Department of Defense, and multiple technology firms, among others including political campaigns and military research.

“It should be noted that the incidents of Chinese espionage far outnumber those by any other country, even Russia,” the Center for Strategic and International Studies noted in its assessment.

“The long-term cost to the American economy and national security cannot be precisely measured, but estimates run into the billions of dollars for commercial and technological espionage.”

Following Huang’s apology, Nvidia announced Sunday it was launching an investigation led by a committee of independent directors and assisted by outside counsel.

The company said it prioritizes national and economic security, though adds it has “no reason to believe” either national security or Nvidia secrets were compromised. The board said it has confidence in Huang and his leadership team.

Nvidia appears to be backing its CEO for now, but Jeffrey Sonnenfeld at Yale University’s School of Management said while Huang has no successor at this time and has been praised for his work with the company, his future is “50-50.”

“It’s 50-50 whether or not he can hold onto his position,” Sonnenfeld told Global News. “There’s a blow to his credibility though already that he would put the company at risk … Even if exonerated, he certainly has a permanent black eye for the recklessness.”

U.S. lawmakers have launched their own investigation, with three Republican House committee chairs requesting Huang appear before them for a joint, closed-door briefing on his interactions with Alice Huang.

They’ve asked him to appear on Nov. 18 or to provide an alternative date by Nov. 11.

The U.S. president commented on the allegations against Huang on Sunday, calling him an “honourable guy,” but said he hasn’t spoken with the CEO about the allegations.

“I think he probably has an excuse for it. You have to hear it,” Trump said, adding he’d take Huang with him to Asia on his planned trip next week.

scraped.title: Man unanimously acquitted of raping female friend at HK campsite
scraped.description: A 24-year-old man has been acquitted of raping a female friend at a Sai Kung campsite three years ago, with the jury unanimously finding him not guilty.
scraped.author: Hillary Leung
scraped.h1: Hong Kong man unanimously acquitted of raping female friend at Sai Kung campsite
scraped.body_text:
Hong Kong Free Press HKFP

Hong Kong news, breaking updates – 100% Independent, impartial, non-profit

A 24-year-old man has been acquitted of raping a female friend at a Sai Kung campsite three years ago, with the jury unanimously finding him not guilty.

Fung Cheuk-kei appeared at the High Court on Monday morning following an eight-day trial for two counts of rape before a seven-member jury – including four women and three men.

He was accused of raping a woman, known to the court as X, when they went to Sai Kung on November 10, 2023.

According to the prosecution, the pair were camping at Wan Tsai South Campsite that day, when Fung entered the tent twice while she was asleep and raped her despite her protests.

X testified on the first day of the trial last month that the camping trip started off normally, with the two of them cooking and then drinking soju at night, according to local media.

She said that after they went to bed, Fung entered the tent twice and assaulted her despite her protests. He wore a condom only the first time.

The two slept in the same tent that night. X testified that when she woke up, she found she was bleeding, and that when she showed Fung the bloodied tissues and said she was in pain, he apologised.

After she went home, she messaged Fung on Instagram and said his behaviour was akin to rape. She told her brother what had happened, and the two met Fung at a shopping mall, where he admitted to raping her, X testified.

She added that the pair met as colleagues in 2019 and reconnected in 2023. He expressed romantic interest in her and tried to kiss her on one occasion when they went cycling in Cheung Chau, but X rejected him and said she only wanted to be friends.

Judge William Tam said on Monday that X’s testimony was dishonest. He said she admitted that when she, her brother, and Fung met at the shopping mall, her brother had hit Fung.

Tam said Fung’s apology was perhaps only because he had caused her pain. In contrast, Fung’s conduct did not warrant suspicion, he added.

Under Hong Kong law, rape is punishable by up to life imprisonment .

scraped.title: Who is Alice Huang, Chinese exec accused of spying on Nvidia CEO?
scraped.description: Tech executive Alice Huang is the woman accused of spying for China during an affair with Jensen Huang, head of US artificial intelligence chip titan Nvidia, according to media reports.
scraped.author: AFP
scraped.h1: Who is Alice Huang, the Chinese tech executive accused of spying on Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang?
scraped.body_text:
Hong Kong Free Press HKFP

Hong Kong news, breaking updates – 100% Independent, impartial, non-profit

Tech executive Alice Huang is the woman accused of spying for China during an affair with Jensen Huang, head of US artificial intelligence chip titan Nvidia, according to media reports.

Public details are sparse about the woman, also known as Huang Le, who had reportedly been a top figure at a Singapore-based data centre company called Megaspeed International.

Here is what we know about her and the company:

Alice Huang is a Chinese citizen recruited by Beijing to collect intelligence on the Nvidia boss, according to the New York Times, which first reported that Jensen Huang was the alleged target of a spy plot.

Despite their shared surname, Alice Huang is no relation to the 63-year-old Taiwanese-born head of the world’s most valuable company.

The Times, citing people briefed on the surveillance, said that Alice Huang speaks good English and is well connected at the highest level of the global AI chip industry.

The sector is highly sensitive as the United States and China race to develop advanced AI systems with potential military applications.

An online search brought up a short profile for Alice Huang, with her photo, on a Chinese fund database. It listed previous jobs including at HSBC bank, and as a reporter for Chinese media outlets CCTV and Hunan TV.

AFP was unable to verify the contents of the profile, or who had written it, but has attempted to contact the companies cited.

Media reports last week said they had a close relationship, and Jensen Huang told Nvidia employees on Sunday he was “deeply sorry” for being “unfaithful to my wife”.

One photo from an industry party in 2024, posted on LinkedIn, appears to show the leather jacket-clad Nvidia boss sitting next to a long-haired woman in glitzy jewellery believed to be Alice Huang.

The following year, they both attended a dinner hosted by Jensen Huang at a Chinese restaurant in Taipei during Computex, the island’s top tech expo.

Journalists stood outside the restaurant filming through glass windows and doors as Jensen Huang and a woman identified as Alice Huang, who was wearing a pink dress, mingled with other attendees.

At one point, Jensen Huang can be seen putting his arm around Alice Huang as she kisses him on the right cheek, press livestreams show.

Alice Huang is also seen following the Nvidia chief as he re-enters the restaurant after talking to journalists outside, running her fingers down his lower back.

They later leave the restaurant in the same car.

US officials concluded last year that Alice Huang was targeting Jensen Huang as a spy, according to the New York Times and the Wall Street Journal.

At the time, Alice Huang was said to be a top executive at data centre firm Megaspeed International, which rents out computing power to other companies to train and run AI.

Megaspeed’s website says it is “a core business partner of Nvidia’s computing power cloud business in the Asia-Pacific region”.

On LinkedIn, it says it has offices in Singapore, Malaysia and Indonesia, with around two to 10 employees and 25 “associated members”.

When AFP called the number listed on Megaspeed’s website, the person who answered said they were unfamiliar with the company and that the number was a residential line.

The firm was previously called 7Road International, according to the Singapore government’s website, suggesting links to Chinese gaming company 7Road.

Washington restricts the export to China of Nvidia’s most cutting-edge silicon chips, citing national security concerns but also seen as a measure to stay ahead in AI.

The New York Times said the US government had been probing Megaspeed since 2024 over its potential steering of Nvidia chips to China.

The company has also reportedly been under investigation by Singapore authorities, who the Times says questioned Alice Huang in 2025.

AFP has contacted Singapore’s police and the home affairs ministry for comment.

Last year Bloomberg News also reported on the Singaporean probe into Megaspeed over the alleged smuggling of Nvidia chips to China.

In December 2025, Megaspeed said Bloomberg’s reporting “contains misleading information and incorrect insinuations, including suggestions that we may have been involved in illegal chip transfers”.

scraped.title: HK must reform ticketing and venue rules to attract int'l acts - think tank
scraped.description: Hong Kong must step up its ticketing systems and ensure promoters can secure venues to attract touring artists, a think tank has said, after finding that most Western artists' tours skipped the city in recent years.
scraped.author: James Lee
scraped.h1: Hong Kong must reform ticketing and venue rules to attract touring mega-acts, think tank says
scraped.body_text:
Hong Kong Free Press HKFP

Hong Kong news, breaking updates – 100% Independent, impartial, non-profit

Hong Kong must step up its ticketing systems and ensure promoters can secure venues to attract touring artists, a think tank has said, after finding that most Western artists’ tours skipped the city in recent years.

Out of 95 Western artists’ concert tours between 2023 and 2026 analysed in a report published on Monday by the Hong Kong Future Economy Institute, just 21.1 per cent included Hong Kong.

Almost half of the tours included Singapore, at 49.5 per cent, while Tokyo was on almost three-quarters of the tours, at 74.7 per cent.

“Ed Sheeran played sixteen Asian cities on one tour without a Hong Kong date; Dua Lipa played eight. In total, 75 of the 95 Western tours did not include Hong Kong,” it said.

The report also stated that “the data shows no clear improvement in Hong Kong’s position” since the opening of Kai Tak Stadium, noting that Coldplay was the sole Western act to have played the venue as of September 2026.

Canadian singer The Weeknd had not yet performed at the stadium when the report was compiled. He went on to play four sold-out shows at the venue last month, with his new track “Hong Kong” — which samples a 1993 song by Cantopop icon Faye Wong — topping local charts.

Rising ticketing fraud and short venue booking windows are “weaknesses” that have contributed to the lag behind the city’s regional rivals, the report said.

“Hong Kong has the assets of an events capital: strong policy backing, international connectivity and major new venues. Yet these strengths have not translated into a comparable share of international Western tours,” it said.

“Audiences need to be able to buy tickets with confidence, and promoters need to secure suitable venues while coordinating dates across cities. Our review identifies weaknesses on both fronts.”

See also: Hong Kong striving to bring in large-scale int’l events, says culture chief amid word that Singapore to host Lady Gaga

The report cited a 62 per cent rise in concert ticket fraud cases between 2024 and 2025, alongside a 202 per cent surge in Consumer Council complaints regarding public performances, rising from 626 to 1,889 over the same period.

Bot purchases and scalping — as well as weak controls and enforcement against those practices — may also have undermined “the reliability and transparency that fans and organisers need,” the report said.

The institute also said that booking rules at government-run venues such as the Hong Kong Coliseum in Hung Hom were “poorly suited” for international tours, pointing to the 12-month window for booking concerts and the lack of a provisional holding system.

The institute recommended that the government modernise ticketing and consumer protection arrangements by raising scalping fines, publishing ticket allocation data, and upgrading platform infrastructure.

It also urged the introduction of a two-year booking window with clear evaluation criteria for international applications, alongside cost-free provisional holds, and called for the publication of approval timelines and booking outcomes.

Published - November 10, 2026 03:53 am IST - LONDON

M. John Harrison, author of "The End of Everything" holds the trophy for winning the Booker Prize during the Booker Prize 2026 ceremony at Old Billingsgate in London, November 10, 2026. | Photo Credit: AP

U.K. author M. John Harrison won the Booker Prize on Monday (November 9, 2026) for his enigmatic novel "The End of Everything", which echoes concerns about artificial intelligence in a darkly satirical depiction of post-apocalyptic Britain.

Mr. Harrison, 81, became the oldest winner of the award, which comes with a £50,000 ($67,000) prize and a boost in sales and profile for the winner.

Review | ‘The End of Everything’ by M. John Harrison: the aliens are here

A veteran of the British science fiction literary scene, it was Mr. Harrison’s first time being shortlisted for the coveted prize, which critics have said was long overdue.

He beat shortlisted authors Marlon James, Douglas Stuart, Elizabeth Strout, Luke Kennard and Rebecca Perry, whose entries ranged from a queer epic unfolding in 1980s Kingston to a campus satire set in modern-day London.

"The End of Everything" came out "ahead in terms of both its extraordinary expert writing, but also huge ambition," chair of the judges Mary Beard told a press conference.

Mr. Harrison's 13th novel follows the beachcomber Phillip Tennent and his dementia-stricken, free-spirited aunt Marnie, set in the near-future on the windswept English coast invaded by mysterious objects known as the iGhetti.

An unnamed catastrophe plunges the characters into a murky post-apocalyptic world where the European continent seems to have disappeared and the arrival of the iGhetti, which can imitate humans, evoke interactions with artificial intelligence.

"One main point of the book is that if, or when, such an apocalypse comes it will be incomprehensible," Ms. Beard said, adding the book spoke to the present "moment".

"This is the politics of now seen through the lens of the future," Ms. Beard said in a statement.

In dream-like episodes this tight, 198-page novel alludes to Brexit, the COVID-19 pandemic and the invasion of technology into daily life.

As is often the case with Mr. Harrison's writing, which has been described as genre-bending and singular, the plot counts less than the atmosphere, and the author's elliptical and poetic style heightens the feeling of gradual collapse.

"Current affairs provided the themes and the satire," Mr. Harrison said of his book. "What happens when all of our expectations and explanations of the world become an ongoing disaster, but we still have to make a life?"

The author previously said he was inspired by the 2008 financial crisis, and wanted to write a novel about the "failure of explanation in society".

Born in Rugby, England, in 1945, Mr. Harrison is the author of numerous science fiction books, including the Viriconium saga (1971-1984) and "Light" (2002), the first volume of a trilogy known as The Kefahuchi Tract, renowned as major works of the genre.

Little known to the general public beyond circles of science fiction enthusiasts, when he was shortlisted, The Telegraph newspaper wrote: "Finally, he's getting his due."

The theme of artificial intelligence has been on the judges' minds through the year-long selection process, which saw them whittle down 163 entries to a shortlist of six novels.

Ms. Beard pointed out concerns surrounding AI were "pretty high on this book".

"Phillip has got this object, this artefact, and it's not clear how sentient it is. It's not clear what it is," Ms. Beard said in a press conference to announce the winner.

In an earlier interview with AFP , Ms. Beard said the prize-awarding panel would have to think about the role of AI in publishing and writing in the coming years.

"I think for the future it's inevitable that that will be on the agenda. You can't bury your head in the sand about that," she said.

The other judges have talked about wanting to create a shortlist of books that were distinctly human, and could not be replicated by AI.

The prize, which celebrates the best work of long-form fiction by writers of any nationality, written in English and published in the last year, was awarded on Monday (November 9, 2026) at a London ceremony.

Last year, British-Hungarian author David Szalay won the prize for "Flesh", his tortured tale of a Hungarian emigre in London.

The Directorate of Enforcement (ED) on Monday (November 9, 2026) attached the immovable properties worth ₹10.63 crore under the Prevention of Money Laundering Act (PMLA) in alleged misuse of the Prime Minister Employment Generation Programme (PMEGP) case.

An ED spokesman said there was misappropriation of PMEGP Scheme’s loans in criminal conspiracy with the PMEGP borrowers, bank officials of Sumbal Branch and Gamud Gadkhud Branch of J&K Bank and other unknown persons.

“The accused have cheated the bank and misappropriated bank funds and caused wrongful loss to the bank and corresponding wrongful gain to themselves. Investigation revealed PMEGP Loans amounts availed by projecting dummy PMEGP borrowers by using fake invoices of non-exist firm/companies and in criminal conspiracy with bank officials branches Sumbal and Gamud Gadkhud of J&K Bank by private persons-cum-brokers,” said the spokesman.

The CBI and J&K’s anti-corruption bureau (ACB) has also registered a case in the matter in June 2026.

The ED said the suspected proceeds derived from the scheduled offences were diverted through bank accounts in multiple transactions and part of it was utilised for construction and renovation of assets and personal enrichment. “Investigation conducted so far, was able to trace the generation of Proceeds of Crime to the tune of Rs. 11.37 crore. Further investigation is under progress,” said the ED.

items.summary: Heavy snow, freezing temperatures and strong winds are threatening transportation across Hokkaido on Tuesday, November 10, with Japan Airlines and All Nippon Airways warning of possible flight disruptions at several airports and JR Hokkaido reporting train cancellations and delays across parts of its northern network as of 6 a.m. (News On Japan)

scraped.description: Heavy snow, freezing temperatures and strong winds are threatening transportation across Hokkaido on Tuesday, November 10, with Japan Airlines and All Nippon Airways warning of possible flight disruptions at several airports and JR Hokkaido reporting train cancellations and delays across parts of its northern network as of 6 a.m.

scraped.h1: Hokkaido Travel Alert: Flight Disruptions, Train Cancellations and Icy Highways
scraped.body_text:
HOKKAIDO - Heavy snow, freezing temperatures and strong winds are threatening transportation across Hokkaido on Tuesday, November 10, with Japan Airlines and All Nippon Airways warning of possible flight disruptions at several airports and JR Hokkaido reporting train cancellations and delays across parts of its northern network as of 6 a.m.

Road authorities were also enforcing restrictions on major expressways as freezing conditions increased the danger of accidents. The disruptions come as midwinter-like cold air moves across northern Japan, bringing heavy snow to areas along the Sea of Japan coast. Snowfall could reach 30 centimeters in parts of northern and central Hokkaido over the 24 hours through Tuesday evening, with around 20 centimeters possible in northern districts of Sapporo. Air travel is among the services facing immediate uncertainty. Japan Airlines identified Sapporo's Okadama Airport as vulnerable to disruption on November 10 because of snow, warning that affected flights could be delayed, canceled, diverted to another airport or forced to return to their departure point. All Nippon Airways separately identified Wakkanai Airport in northern Hokkaido as facing similar risks because of snowfall. The airline warned that actual flight operations would depend on weather conditions, aircraft type and departure time. At New Chitose Airport, Hokkaido's principal aviation gateway, snow had accumulated to 3 centimeters by 5 p.m. on November 9 following periods of intense snowfall. Further snow was forecast overnight and into Tuesday morning, creating the possibility of delays caused by runway conditions, aircraft deicing and reduced visibility. New Chitose was not specifically identified in the airline-wide weather disruption notices examined for November 10, and widespread weather-related cancellations there had not been confirmed as of early Tuesday. Some flights from New Chitose experienced delays on November 9. ANA Flight 82 from Sapporo to Tokyo's Haneda Airport, originally scheduled to arrive at 10:10 p.m., was reported arriving at 11:50 p.m. Air Do Flight 32, also operating as ANA Flight 4732, arrived at Haneda at 8:38 p.m. instead of its scheduled 7:35 p.m. arrival. However, the causes of those individual delays were not confirmed as snow-related. Rail transportation is also facing operational problems, although not all are directly associated with the winter weather. JR Hokkaido reported at 5:06 a.m. on November 10 that the discovery of rail damage exceeding permitted safety limits had resulted in cancellations or delays affecting services in northern Hokkaido, with disruption notices also covering the Sapporo metropolitan and central Hokkaido operating areas. The railway had previously reported disruptions on the Soya Line after a local train traveling from Otoineppu toward Wakkanai struck a deer between Osashima and Saku stations on the evening of November 9. Further cancellations or delays were reported after midnight. In eastern Hokkaido, a separate deer collision on the Hanasaki Line between Bettoga and Ochiishi disrupted services between Kushiro and Nemuro on November 9. JR Hokkaido warned that the incident would also cause some train cancellations on November 10 because of operational arrangements. The incidents have complicated railway operations as the region enters another period of heavy snowfall. However, the cancellations linked to rail damage and animal collisions should be distinguished from disruptions caused directly by snow. Early railway service reports indicated that many principal routes, including the Hakodate Main Line, Chitose Line and Gakuen-Toshi Line, had no general disruption notices, although individual services remained subject to change. Road transportation faces a more widespread threat from frozen surfaces and reduced visibility. As of 5:15 a.m. on November 10, winter tire requirements and speed restrictions were in effect across extensive sections of the Do-O Expressway, Hokkaido's principal north-south highway. Between Shibetsu-Kenbuchi and Sapporo, motorists were subject to a 50-kilometer-per-hour speed limit because of freezing conditions, with winter tires required. Similar restrictions applied on sections between Eniwa and Chitose, as well as between Noboribetsu-Muroran and Yakumo. Other sections of the expressway were operating under 80-kilometer-per-hour restrictions, including stretches between Kitahiroshima and Eniwa and between Chitose and Tomakomai-Higashi. Winter tire requirements were also reported on the Sasson Expressway linking Sapporo and Otaru, the Shiribeshi Expressway, the Doto Expressway serving eastern Hokkaido, and the Fukagawa-Rumoi Expressway. These were restrictions rather than confirmed blanket closures of the expressway network, but further snowfall could force authorities to introduce additional controls if visibility or road conditions deteriorate. Bus services are also vulnerable to the worsening road conditions, particularly on routes linking Sapporo with Otaru, Iwamizawa, Rumoi, Asahikawa and other communities along the Sea of Japan side of Hokkaido. Hokkaido Chuo Bus was monitoring local, intercity and airport bus services, although a comprehensive list of snow-related cancellations for November 10 was not available in the early-morning information examined. Hokto Kotsu reported normal operations on its principal airport bus routes between central Sapporo and New Chitose Airport, as well as services connecting Okadama Airport with the city. However, its Soen and Jozankei airport routes were listed as fully suspended, without confirmation that the suspensions were caused by Tuesday's snowfall. Ferry transportation also faces possible disruption as strong winds and high waves affect waters surrounding northern Hokkaido. Heartland Ferry, which operates services between Wakkanai and the islands of Rishiri and Rebun, said decisions on November 10 sailings would be made at around 5:30 a.m. The operator had also scheduled services between Esashi and Okushiri Island, but the early information available did not confirm whether individual crossings would proceed. The Japan Coast Guard reported strong wind and wave advisories affecting the Soya region and the islands of Rishiri and Rebun as of 4:20 a.m. Gale-force conditions were also a concern in waters west of Hokkaido and around the Soya Strait, increasing the possibility of ferry delays or cancellations. In Sapporo, subway operations were not confirmed to be affected by the snowfall. However, the city's public transportation information system experienced a separate disruption on November 9 after unauthorized access led to false notices claiming subway suspensions and network-wide delays. Municipal officials said subway services had actually been operating normally, and the affected information service was temporarily shut down. The most difficult travel conditions on November 10 are expected across northern and western Hokkaido, particularly in Kamikawa, Rumoi, Sorachi and parts of the Ishikari region. Bifuka, Horokanai, Iwamizawa, Ebetsu and Kutchan are among the communities forecast to receive significant snowfall, increasing the risk of delays on local roads and regional transportation networks. Visibility remains a particular concern following severe blizzard conditions in Bifuka on November 9, when blowing snow temporarily reduced visibility to almost zero. Sapporo is forecast to reach a high of just 2 degrees Celsius on November 10, with morning snow giving way to more settled conditions later in the day. Temperatures near or below freezing could nevertheless leave roads slippery even after snowfall eases. Although transportation services may face additional disruption through Tuesday morning, the early reports do not establish a widespread shutdown of Hokkaido's railway, aviation or highway networks. The confirmed problems include individual railway cancellations, flight delays carried over from November 9, and extensive highway restrictions, while further weather-related cancellations remain possible. Conditions are expected to improve gradually from November 11, but authorities are urging motorists and travelers to check the latest operating information before departure, allow additional travel time and remain alert to rapidly changing weather, particularly in northern Hokkaido and along the Sea of Japan coast.

scraped.h1: More Snow and Freezing Temperatures Blast Hokkaido
scraped.body_text:
HOKKAIDO - Hokkaido is facing another day of heavy snow, freezing temperatures and strong winds on Tuesday, November 10, as midwinter-like cold air sweeps across northern Japan, with snowfall of up to 30 centimeters forecast in some areas and blizzard conditions threatening to disrupt transportation. As of 6 a.m. on November 10, snow advisories remained in effect for parts of Hokkaido, including Sapporo, where a heavy snow advisory was scheduled to remain in place until 9 a.m.

Snowfall is expected to be concentrated along the Sea of Japan coast, while strong winds could produce further whiteout conditions in exposed areas. The severe weather began on November 9, when widespread snowfall accompanied by powerful winds struck Hokkaido. In Bifuka, in the Kamikawa region, a blizzard temporarily reduced visibility to almost zero, creating dangerous conditions for motorists. Forecasts issued on November 9 indicated that northern and central Hokkaido could receive as much as 30 centimeters of snow over the 24 hours through the evening of November 10. Particularly heavy accumulations were expected around Bifuka and Horokanai in northern Hokkaido, Rumoi along the western coast, and inland areas around Iwamizawa, Ebetsu and Kutchan. Parts of Sapporo, particularly northern districts away from the city center, could receive around 20 centimeters of snow. The combination of wet snow and strong winds has raised concerns about slippery roads, reduced visibility and disruptions to public transportation. Tuesday is also expected to bring some of the coldest weather of the season across Hokkaido. Sapporo is forecast to reach a high of just 2 degrees Celsius after an overnight low of minus 3 degrees, with snow showers possible during the morning before conditions gradually improve in the afternoon. In Asahikawa, temperatures are expected to range from minus 4 degrees to a high of 1 degree, with snow continuing into the early morning and a chance of thunderstorms. Rumoi is forecast to experience more persistent snow and blizzard conditions, with temperatures ranging from minus 2 degrees to 2 degrees and snowfall continuing intermittently throughout the day. Further north, Wakkanai is expected to see occasional snow and a high of around 1 degree, while Kutchan in the mountainous Shiribeshi region is forecast to remain particularly cold, with a low of minus 5 degrees and a high of zero. Snowfall is expected to ease across parts of central Hokkaido by late Tuesday morning, although western coastal districts, including Rumoi, could continue to experience intermittent snow into the afternoon and evening. The unsettled conditions are being driven by a series of low-pressure systems and a mass of cold air comparable to that normally experienced in midwinter. The resulting unstable atmosphere has also raised the possibility of thunderstorms, while strong northwesterly winds are expected to affect coastal areas. Weather advisories have highlighted the risk of heavy snow, strong winds, lightning, snow accumulating on power lines and avalanches in some mountainous districts. Wet snow could also weigh down trees and electrical infrastructure, potentially causing localized damage. Drivers are being urged to exercise caution as accumulating snow and freezing temperatures increase the risk of icy roads, while rail and other transportation services could face delays or cancellations. Conditions are expected to improve gradually from November 11, when Sapporo's temperature is forecast to rise to around 6 degrees, although occasional snow or rain remains possible. A more substantial warming trend is forecast later in the week, with daytime temperatures in Sapporo potentially reaching 14 degrees on November 12.

Hokkaido is facing another day of heavy snow, freezing temperatures and strong winds on Tuesday, November 10, as midwinter-like cold air sweeps across northern Japan, with snowfall of up to 30 centimeters forecast in some areas and blizzard conditions threatening to disrupt transportation. As of 6 a.m. on November 10, snow advisories remained in effect for parts of Hokkaido, including Sapporo, where a heavy snow advisory was scheduled to remain in place until 9 a.m.

As of 3 a.m. on November 10, Typhoon No. 32 was moving northeast over waters south of Japan, with the powerful storm expected to approach the Ogasawara Islands late Tuesday through Wednesday morning, November 11, bringing strong winds, heavy rain and waves exceeding 6 meters in some areas.

A male bear weighing approximately 270 kilograms was killed by hunters in Iwamizawa, Hokkaido, on November 8th after being caught in a box trap, with local hunters suspecting it was responsible for a series of attacks on a nearby poultry farm that left more than 100 chickens and ducks dead since August.

A magnitude 5.7 earthquake struck central Japan early on November 8th, registering an upper 5 on Japan's seismic intensity scale in Aichi Prefecture and injuring at least 21 people, while damaging buildings and disrupting Shinkansen and conventional railway services across the region.

The Tokaido Shinkansen resumed normal-speed operations across its entire route at 8:57 a.m. on November 8th after a magnitude 5.7 earthquake disrupted rail services across central Japan, with JR Central reporting delays to 29 bullet trains affecting approximately 17,000 passengers, while Meitetsu restored services across its entire network by 9:15 a.m. following widespread morning suspensions.

Heavy snow, freezing temperatures and strong winds are threatening transportation across Hokkaido on Tuesday, November 10, with Japan Airlines and All Nippon Airways warning of possible flight disruptions at several airports and JR Hokkaido reporting train cancellations and delays across parts of its northern network as of 6 a.m.

Japan's younger generation is increasingly turning away from driving and car ownership, with the number of driver's license holders aged 24 and under falling by approximately 590,000 over the past decade to around 5.15 million in 2025, reflecting changing attitudes toward transportation, spending and the traditional appeal of owning a car.

A field of approximately 20,000 cosmos flowers has reached peak bloom at Nagai Botanical Garden in Osaka's Higashisumiyoshi Ward, where a limited-time installation by art collective teamLab is transforming the autumn landscape into a glowing display of light and sound after dark.

East Japan Railway (JR East) opened its Haneda Airport Access Line construction site to the media on November 6, offering a glimpse of a major underground railway project that will connect Haneda Airport directly with central Tokyo, with services scheduled to begin in fiscal 2031.

Residents of Awaji Island, one of the Kansai region's most popular resort destinations, are facing growing disruption from vacation rentals, with complaints involving late-night drinking, outdoor barbecues, fireworks, illegal parking and garbage disposal violations, while one property operator has been accused of destroying a warning sign installed by neighbors.

A bear cub charged toward a family standing outside their home in Ome, western Tokyo, on November 3rd, rushing straight toward the front door moments after a high-pitched cry was heard from nearby bushes, in an encounter that left the resident shaken.

scraped.title: We Know Where Our Food and Clothes Are Made. Why Not Our Prescriptions?
scraped.description: ProPublica spent 14 months investigating how the Food and Drug Administration regulates foreign drugmakers. We found a system that gives manufacturers a special pass to continue sending generic drugs from substandard factories to the U.S.
scraped.author: Katie Nixdorf, Debbie Cenziper, Megan Rose, and Brandon Roberts
scraped.h1: Watch: Where Do Our Generic Drugs Come From? We Dug to Find Out.
scraped.body_text:
Investigative Journalism in the Public Interest

Investigative Journalism in the Public Interest

Investigative Journalism in the Public Interest

ProPublica is a nonprofit, investigative newsroom that exposes corruption. We report in all 50 states and partner with local newsrooms . Our work spurs real-world impact and has received numerous awards, including nine Pulitzer Prizes.

How Abortion Bans Lead to Preventable Deaths

How Recent Arrivals at the Border Have Changed the Country and Its Attitudes

SCOTUS Justices’ Beneficial Relationships With Billionaire Donors

Rx Roulette

ProPublica is a nonprofit newsroom that investigates abuses of power. Sign up to receive our biggest stories as soon as they’re published.

These days, we know where almost everything comes from. Everyday items like food, clothes and pens all carry labels listing where things are grown, manufactured or even designed.

So why is it so hard to find where prescription drugs are made?

That question set off a 14-month investigation into where our medications are made, how the FDA polices drug manufacturers and what happens when inspectors report issues inside factories. The vast majority of prescriptions filled in the United States are for generic drugs, which are often far cheaper than brand-name alternatives.

For years, Congress, doctors and watchdog groups have questioned the quality of generic drugs made overseas. India produces about half of all generics used in the U.S., but the labels on pill bottles often don’t list where a drug is manufactured. Inspection reports describe unsafe manufacturing conditions at generic drug factories, but the Food and Drug Administration redacts the names of the medications made in those factories. That means if drugs made in errant factories wind up in your medicine cabinet, you’d have no way of knowing.

To better understand how the FDA regulates the generic drug industry, Debbie Cenziper and Megan Rose interviewed current and former factory inspectors, tested medications in a lab and sued the federal government for critical documents.

Here’s what they found:

In a response to ProPublica, a spokesperson for the FDA said in a statement that the exemptions given to banned factories are “thoroughly evaluated through a multi-disciplinary approach” but declined to say exactly what those evaluations entailed. The agency also said it requires manufacturers to conduct additional quality checks with third-party oversight before sending drugs to the U.S. The agency did not respond to questions about how it can know that generics are safe without a more robust testing program.

In statements to ProPublica, drug companies said that they take patient safety seriously, adhere to quality standards and are committed to working with the FDA on any regulatory issues. ProPublica’s investigation , which went on to be a finalist for the Pulitzer Prize for investigative reporting , published in 2025.

ProPublica’s Brandon Roberts and a team of data journalists made a tool called Rx Inspector that will show you the facility that manufactured your generic prescription drugs and any inspection reports, warning letters and import bans we have from the FDA. The data isn’t perfect; it’s possible the FDA hasn’t published everything it knows about a given facility, for example. Also, one company may have acquired another or moved the factory somewhere else. This tool also isn’t meant to provide you with medical advice: If you find something troubling, it doesn’t necessarily mean that your drug is compromised. Doctors and pharmacists advise that you not stop taking your medications. Instead, you should talk to your healthcare provider about any concerns.

Step 1: Enter the name of your prescription drug, as well as the company name found on your pill bottle or drug label.

Step 2: If there are multiple matches in our database, you can narrow your search using the markings found on a pill, for example.

Step 3: When you click on a drug, we’ll show you any manufacturing facilities we’ve been able to connect to it. Click on a facility to see any information we have from the FDA.

FDA inspections come with compliance outcomes, such as import alerts or warning letters. The best possible outcome of an inspection is “acceptable state,” which means the FDA took no compliance action and ProPublica found no issues documented by inspectors. Search your prescription here.

ProPublica described Rx Inspector and the methodology used to build it to the FDA, which did not comment. The agency previously told ProPublica that it doesn’t reveal where drugs are made on inspection reports to protect what it deemed to be confidential commercial information.

Read more of Cenziper, Rose and Roberts’ reporting from their series Rx Roulette or watch their video explainer .

I adapt our investigations into midlength videos for YouTube.

I write about national issues, from housing to healthcare, and the agencies most responsible for the welfare of Americans.

I welcome tips from anyone familiar with the FDA and issues involving drug safety, medical device safety and health care.

I cover national security, the U.S. military and how the armed forces are deployed here and abroad.

Tell me about changes being made to how the military operates and where, who is in charge, and how decisions are determined. I’m interested in how norms and safeguards are transforming on paper, through personnel and in the field.

I’m a journalist using data and code to hold power to account.

If you have a tip about a dataset, a use of technology or a complicated government process, reach out.

scraped.title: Firm Tied to Trump Sons Won Nearly $40 Million in Federal Funds to Screen for Ebola, Other Diseases
scraped.description: XpresTest has years of experience conducting disease screening in U.S. airports but has never worked with Ebola or provided biosecurity services abroad. It’s “a new thing for us,” the company’s CEO said.
scraped.author: Sharon Lerner, Anna Maria Barry-Jester, and Robert Faturechi
scraped.h1: Firm Linked to Trump’s Sons Got Nearly $40 Million in Federal Contracts to Screen for Ebola and Other Diseases
scraped.body_text:
Investigative Journalism in the Public Interest

ProPublica is a nonprofit, investigative newsroom that exposes corruption. We report in all 50 states and partner with local newsrooms . Our work spurs real-world impact and has received numerous awards, including nine Pulitzer Prizes.

How Abortion Bans Lead to Preventable Deaths

How Recent Arrivals at the Border Have Changed the Country and Its Attitudes

SCOTUS Justices’ Beneficial Relationships With Billionaire Donors

ProPublica is a nonprofit newsroom that investigates abuses of power. Sign up to receive our biggest stories as soon as they’re published.

The Trump administration awarded a small biosecurity company nearly $40 million to screen for Ebola and other infectious diseases just months after a firm linked to President Donald Trump’s elder sons invested in its parent company, according to records and interviews.

The contracts, one to screen for Ebola in several U.S. airports and the other to respond to disease outbreaks in the Democratic Republic of Congo, are seven times the total value of government contracts the company had directly received before.

The company, XpresTest, has years of experience monitoring for COVID-19 and other diseases for the government at U.S. airports. That makes its parent, XWELL, an unusual hybrid, selling both spa treatments and biosecurity services. Last year, it made most of its money from waxing salons and airport spas that offer manicures, massages and “ chakra beds. ”

The contracts are the latest example of the president’s family benefiting financially from his administration’s actions. And the stakes for these deals are particularly high. In the Democratic Republic of Congo, an Ebola outbreak has killed more than 5,000 people this year, and the federal government is trying to stop the pathogen from coming to the U.S.

XpresTest has never worked with Ebola or provided biosecurity services abroad, let alone in the kind of volatile locales it’s now expected to work in. The CEO of its parent company, Ezra Ernst, said XpresTest won both contracts in a competitive bidding process and pointed to its years of experience doing screening for COVID-19 and other pathogens at American airports. But even he acknowledged that working internationally is “a new thing for us” and expressed uncertainty about being able to complete the work in the Democratic Republic of Congo.

“This is a risky contract. I’m not sure we can do it,” Ernst said in an interview.

Jeremy Konyndyk, who helped oversee the U.S. government’s response to a 2014 Ebola outbreak in West Africa, said there are some parallels between monitoring for COVID-19 and Ebola at airports, but he said it’s concerning that the government would award such a lucrative contract to a company that has no experience in Africa.

“There are countless organizations in the world that have decades of experience doing this work,” Konyndyk said. “I have to wonder why the hell they’re not going with someone who has actually done this before.”

Under previous administrations, the U.S. government addressed international disease outbreaks in partnership with the World Health Organization. But Trump withdrew from the group last year, dismantled the U.S. Agency for International Development , which handled much of this work, and dramatically scaled back the global presence of the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.

At the same time, the State Department launched the America First Global Health Strategy , which calls for the U.S. to use aid to foreign countries to “promote American companies and American innovations abroad.” This March, the State Department announced it would be giving up to $4.5 billion in funding for various purposes, including responding to infectious disease outbreaks.

Under that program, XPresTest was awarded $20 million. Other funding went to better-known global aid nonprofits, including International Medical Corps, Save the Children and the International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies, whose awards ranged from $25 million to $35 million.

The CDC also awarded XPresTest a contract, for $18.8 million.

In response to questions from ProPublica about XPresTest and its parent company, XWELL, the State Department noted the firm’s previous work screening for diseases at airports under a contract with the CDC and said its own award was made “through a competitive process that builds on this successful model.”

The CDC did not respond to a request for comment.

A spokesperson for the president’s sons Donald Jr. and Eric Trump said that they are “merely passive, minority investors in a fund that invested in this company,” and that they had no “involvement in or knowledge regarding the negotiation or procurement of any of its contracts, including any government contracts.”

“Both are private citizens who hold no government positions, broken no laws and who have every right to pursue lawful business and investment opportunities,” the spokesperson said.

The Trump sons’ connection to XWELL was established in February, when a fund called American Ventures invested in the company. The fund was launched by Dominari Holdings, a small financial firm with offices inside Trump Tower in New York. The leaders of Dominari hired the Trump sons as advisers after their father was elected to a second term and granted them a stake of more than 10% in Dominari.

Anthony Hayes, the CEO of Dominari Holdings, told ProPublica, “We have never seen or even heard of Don or Eric using their family name to influence the granting of a government contract.”

American Ventures has taken stakes in other companies that have benefited from Trump administration actions. The Florida-based drone company Powerus got a contract worth up to $90 million from the U.S. Air Force five months after the Trumps’ involvement was announced. Through American Ventures, Donald Jr. and Eric Trump also are acquiring a stake in a critical minerals group that has received U.S. government support to mine for tungsten in Kazakhstan. The Trumps have described themselves as passive investors who do not advocate for the companies they have stakes in before their father’s government.

XWELL was founded in 2006 as a line of airport-based spas that provided massages and facials. During the pandemic, the company, then known as XpresSpa Group, got $5.5 million from the CDC to offer travelers COVID-19 testing. It also collected waste from airplane toilets to check for new viral strains. It has done similar work for at least one other company that has received government contracts.

In January, XWELL announced that it was hiring a former senior adviser at the CDC who created and led the agency’s traveler surveillance program. The firm said the move was part of a plan to expand “its traveler-based pathogen surveillance capabilities to support international travel hubs and large-scale mass gathering events worldwide.”

The following month, American Ventures invested about $30 million in XWELL. The company had lost money the previous year. “We were so cash-strapped, close to bankrupt,” its CEO said.

Its valuation before the cash infusion was just $3 million. In exchange, American Ventures got a roughly 10% stake in the company to start, with an option to essentially print and sell millions of shares in the future.

Why American Ventures would invest so much in XWELL is unclear. In other cases, when the fund has invested in similar tiny publicly traded companies, some of those firms have moved into hot new sectors and drawn publicity for their connection to the Trumps, then Dominari has offloaded shares. In this case, there is no indication it has sold any of its stake yet.

In June, XpresTest was awarded the CDC contract for what a public notice about the grant said was “Ebola entry screening services.”

XpresTest then received the State Department grant for “rapid, effective, and coordinated outbreak response” to infectious disease threats in the Democratic Republic of Congo, which began in September, according to a government database . The company is also planning to work in Kenya and Morocco. XWELL’s website shows it is now hiring specialists in Ebola response training and biosecurity in the U.S.

In July, after XpresTest was awarded the CDC contract, XWELL announced plans to sell the subsidiary along with its line of spas to a private facial spa company. Ernst, the CEO, said the government contracts played a role in the $13 million sale price and will follow XpresTest to the new company.

That means XWELL, the company that the Trump-linked investment fund took a stake in, will benefit financially from the Trump administration contracts if the sale closes, even though it won’t be involved in doing the work for the government.

XWELL said in a public filing that the sale was part of an effort “to pursue a new direction in the national security sector.” Ernst said he didn’t know the exact plans but thought the parent company might be looking to work with the Department of Defense.

XWELL did not announce either of XpresTest’s biosecurity contracts, which recently became public in federal contracting disclosures. Public companies like XWELL are required to report so-called material events, developments that could affect their share price, such as a large government contract. XWELL has publicized previous work for the federal government, including a $2 million, eight-week pilot program for testing COVID-19 in 2021 .

When asked why his firm didn’t announce the awards, Ernst gave various reasons, including the possibility that XPresTest might wind up not being able to do the work — either because of its own inexperience working internationally or because the Trump administration might suddenly shift priorities and only pay for a fraction of the contract.

“None of these contracts are guaranteed,” he said.

The biosecurity awards add to the questions about the Trump family’s enrichment during his second term. The Trump family’s business activities extend far beyond Dominari and American Ventures. The president himself has made more than $1 billion from cryptocurrency ventures whose value has ballooned as his administration has taken a friendly stance to the industry. And other companies backed by his sons Donald Jr. and Eric have received billions of dollars in federal deals. Earlier this year, ProPublica reported that the Pentagon granted a small North Carolina startup linked to Trump Jr. a $620 million loan after a top aide to the president intervened on the company’s behalf. The Pentagon denied preferential treatment, and a spokesperson for Trump Jr. said he played no role.

The Trumps’ financial ties to government deals and actions are expected to be a primary focus of Congress in the coming months after Democrats won control of both the Senate and the House in last week’s midterm elections.

“When the government is corrupted for personal gain over the public interest, Americans lose trust and taxpayer dollars are wasted,” Robert Garcia, the top Democrat on the House Oversight Committee, wrote in a letter to colleagues last week.

I cover health, the environment, foreign aid and the agencies that govern them.

I write about health in the U.S. and abroad as well as human rights, the environment and foreign aid. I’d like to speak with government workers and anyone who has an important story to tell. I take confidentiality seriously.

I report on global public health and the agencies that govern it, including the NIH, IHS, USAID and CDC.

I welcome tips from people with knowledge of public health at the local, state, federal and international level, including scientists, government officials and advocates, and anyone who knows about issues that affect the public’s health.

I am a Pulitzer Prize-winning reporter at ProPublica.

Contact me, by email or securely on Signal, with tips about the federal government and Trump’s businesses.

How Abortion Bans Lead to Preventable Deaths

How Recent Arrivals at the Border Have Changed the Country and Its Attitudes

SCOTUS Justices’ Beneficial Relationships With Billionaire Donors

A Closer Look

Co-published with The Philadelphia Inquirer

This article was produced for ProPublica’s Local Reporting Network in partnership with The Philadelphia Inquirer . Sign up for Dispatches to get our stories in your inbox every week.

One morning in July 2025, I was the lone spectator in Judge Frank Palumbo’s courtroom in Philadelphia, watching prosecutors and public defenders haggle over the fates of defendants.

Palumbo paused the proceedings to talk to a lawyer he’d appointed to help a prisoner who had ineptly challenged his conviction. The lawyer profusely thanked the judge for the job. Then, Palumbo offered a bit of guidance: “I think I know where this is going to go. I don’t want to make it overly complicated. It’s real simple.”

The judge said he’d pass along a brief that a different lawyer had filed arguing that there was no merit to the man’s claims in a related case. “I’m not saying plagiarize,” the judge said.

The attorney told the judge he got the message. “So it’s called a Finley letter,” he said, using the common legal term for that no-merit brief, in which an attorney can argue against the client’s claims and ask to withdraw from the case.

“It’s looking like it’s going to be a Finley dismissal,” the judge agreed after a bit more discussion, “but every option is open.”

I’ve spent years covering criminal justice in Pennsylvania, including the post-conviction system that allows people to argue that their lawyer had mishandled their case or to raise newly discovered evidence. That day, I left the courtroom wondering how what I’d observed squared with the state’s promise of effective legal representation in cases like this.

That question sent me on a yearlong reporting odyssey, during which I read hundreds of Finley letters, tracked down court financial records from all 67 Pennsylvania counties, interviewed dozens of lawyers and analyzed thousands of court dockets. What I wanted to know was: Why has it become the norm for Pennsylvania’s lawyers to argue against their own clients? And who is this system serving?

I found that lax rules, low pay and heavy caseloads have compromised legal representation under the state’s Post Conviction Relief Act. Over the past year, I’ve reported on how lawyers, working under fee structures banned in other states, fell years behind on their cases. I spoke with prisoners who’d waited nearly a decade for their lawyers to file anything and others whose lawyers filed Finley letters despite compelling evidence of innocence . I also looked at three years’ worth of invoices and found that, three quarters of the time, Philly lawyers who wrote Finley letters had never spoken with their clients, contacted the trial lawyer or obtained available police files before deciding their claims had no merit.

None of those seemingly basic steps, I was surprised to learn, is required under the law. In fact, dozens of lawyers I spoke to expressed sharply divided opinions about the extent of their obligations to these clients.

But court-appointed lawyers are not working unsupervised. Judges are largely in charge of appointing them to cases, and those same judges are supposed to make sure they’re doing a timely and diligent job.

I noticed that judges continued to assign lawyers more cases even after appeals courts flagged serious issues with their work. And when it came to Finley letters, judges accepted almost all of them over the three years of cases I reviewed, despite the lawyers’ minimal investigative efforts. Some of the letters they approved contained obvious factual errors or even named the wrong client.

Last fall, after Palumbo gave the lawyer a copy of a Finley letter, the lawyer followed the template. His no-merit brief said that his client’s claim could not be considered because he’d missed his filing deadline. The bulk of the document was, in fact, identical to the other lawyer’s brief.

Palumbo, who didn’t respond to my requests for comment, accepted the Finley letter anyway, let the lawyer drop the client and dismissed the claim.

I thought a fair way to evaluate judges would be to look at the rulings of the Pennsylvania’s Superior Court, the state’s appeals court that hears hundreds of challenges to judges’ rulings on post-conviction matters each year.

And boy, did the Superior Court have thoughts on how judges are handling post-conviction cases.

In one withering opinion, a judge bemoaned an “embarrassing saga” of deficient lawyering that a Berks County judge had tolerated. Another derided a Philly judge and the five attorneys she’d appointed who all missed appeals deadlines, writing, “As Hall of Fame manager Casey Stengel said of the hapless 1962 New York Mets, ‘Can’t anybody here play this game?’”

After logging hundreds of rebukes laid out in Superior Court opinions by hand, I asked some colleagues with data skills to help identify as many of these cases as possible across the last 14 years, the time frame for which opinions were reliably posted online.

We found that the appeals court flagged more than 250 cases in which judges didn’t intervene as lawyers provided what the court labeled ineffective representation: “sandbagging” a client at a hearing, stonewalling a petitioner who’d mailed two dozen letters to the lawyer’s office or filing boilerplate appeals so vague that they doomed their clients’ cases. In hundreds more cases, judges failed to appoint a lawyer at all, held hearings where petitioners went unrepresented or allowed a lawyer to drop a case, leaving the client stranded on appeal. More than 200 times, they oversaw lawyers who abandoned clients, tanking their appeals or stalling their cases for years.

“Judges are in a terrific position to be able to prevent these kinds of injustices,” said Marissa Boyers Bluestine, a longtime post-conviction lawyer who now works at the University of Pennsylvania’s law school.

The scathing reversals aside, the Superior Court affirms about 80% of lower-court rulings. That’s expected given the strict deadlines and complicated rules about how appeals must be filed. The appeals court is also required to defer to the lower court’s factual decisions. And when it reverses due to an error, the recourse is generally limited to ordering a do-over or, on rare occasions, instructing the lower court to explore sanctions. In one opinion, the court resorted to using boldface to call out an egregious failure: “The PCRA court did nothing in this case for 20 years.” Then, it told the lower court to try again.

Judges do have the authority — and, in fact, an obligation under state rules — to make disciplinary referrals. Because complaints are confidential, there is no way to know how often they do so. But only six lawyers in the last decade have been publicly sanctioned for work on court-appointed post-conviction cases.

Judicial discipline is even rarer. No lower-court judge in at least a decade has been publicly disciplined for mishandling a post-trial matter. Judges who, according to the Superior Court, exhibited biases, imposed vindictive sentences or improperly denied recusal requests remained on the bench.

Even after the Superior Court raised alarms, more than 100 cases ricocheted between the appeals court and county judges two, three, four or more times, as judges repeated errors or reappointed lawyers to cases they’d already mishandled .

One such case played out after Jefferson County’s only judge, John Foradora, sentenced a woman to up to 22 years in prison for passing two narcotics pills in prison. Her lawyer failed to object to or appeal the lengthy sentence. After she filed a PCRA, the Superior Court found that her lawyers’ inaction enabled the “ unduly harsh and clearly unreasonable ” punishment to stand. But each time the Superior Court reversed, Foradora again imposed a lengthy term. After three such reversals, the woman wound up serving more than eight years. Foradora said through a court spokesperson that he was unable to comment.

Shannon McDonald, an attorney in the Philly suburbs, said that “some judges don’t consider PCRA a priority.”

She described waiting as a petition languished on a Delaware County judge’s desk for two years, until her client had finished his sentence and been released from prison. Then, the judge finally ruled, dismissing the claim.

Like lawyers, judges I’ve spoken with seem to be divided on their obligations, especially when it comes to the no-merit letters known as Finley letters. The state Supreme Court says that when a lawyer submits a Finley letter, the judge needs to conduct a review of the merits of the case.

Attorney Rob Perkins, who leads the nonprofit Allegheny Lawyers Initiative for Justice, told me that while he’s encountered some judges who take post-conviction matters seriously, others seem to view them as a nuisance. He said several lawyers told him that they were afraid that if they litigated cases too aggressively, judges would withhold future assignments. The no-merit letter becomes the simplest path forward: “When a judge is handed a no-merit letter that sounds good, I think their inclination is to accept that the attorney did their job.”

Superior Court opinions reflect this pattern as well. In my review, I found hundreds of cases overruling lower-court judges who accepted flawed Finley letters. The appeals court noted that lawyers claimed, incorrectly, that their clients had missed filing deadlines, rejected legitimate claims as meritless or failed to notice that their clients were serving illegal sentences.

In dozens of cases, judges approved defective Finley letters that did not fulfill basic rules, such as including a notification to the client or addressing all the claims the client wanted to raise.

Several judges told me that Finley letters serve an important purpose, in shutting down frivolous challenges that waste resources.

“Not all [claims] have merit,” Judge John J. Mead of Erie said. “A lot of them initially you could look at and make a determination [as to] whether or not it’s going to require a hearing.”

I’ve noticed that the system makes accepting Finley letters the simplest choice for judges. A judge who rejects a Finley letter must either find a new lawyer willing to take the case, or force the same lawyer to pursue a matter they previously deemed meritless.

Judges who take that path risk pitting a lawyer against his own client, the Superior Court wrote in one recent case, finding the judge’s actions resulted in the denial of a man’s right to counsel. His lawyer, forced to handle a hearing after writing a Finley letter, treated it “ more like a cross-examination of a witness that [he] does not believe than a direct examination of his client.”

Jon Auritt, who retired after more than 50 years as a lawyer in Delaware County, said that these failures stem from a common cause: Instead of working independently, lawyers are beholden to the local judges who appoint them.

Even if judges are not as explicit as Palumbo was with their instructions, Auritt said, their message is often clear: “The judges are never incentivized to appoint a lawyer who might earnestly find a reason to overturn the conviction.”

To identify cases in which Pennsylvania appeals court judges reversed or vacated lower court rulings on Post Conviction Relief Act cases, we compiled about 19,000 opinions from 2011 through July 2026 published on the Pennsylvania’s Superior Court website. The documents were identified by a keyword search for “PCRA.”

We used artificial intelligence to identify cases in which the appeals court took issue with judges’ errors and lawyers’ failings in lower-court proceedings. To make the AI classifications as accurate as possible, we first read and classified about 500 of the 19,000 opinions. We then tested the classifications of multiple AI prompts against these 500 classifications, to make sure they were giving us accurate results. Finally, we ran the prompt with the best results against the rest of the documents.

Every AI classification was checked against an AI-written summary of the opinion, or against the opinion itself. Finally, we manually checked a random sample of 50 AI summaries to confirm that AI accurately summarized the corresponding opinions.

Aaron Brezel of ProPublica contributed reporting.
