scraped.title: What happens after a midterm tsunami? Lessons from 1974 and 1994
scraped.description: Surprising midterm elections that create new majorities on Capitol Hill look to be revolutions in the days after they occur. Years later, they often appear to be more complex – and less significant.
scraped.author: Robert A. Strong
scraped.h1: What happens after a midterm tsunami? Lessons from 1974 and 1994
scraped.body_text:
Share article

Print article

There were lots of surprises on the evening of Nov. 3 when the picture of the Democratic midterm success began to be painted on network news touch screens.

The maps kept getting bluer. Eventually, it was clear that this was not an ordinary midterm cycle when the party out of power slaps the wrist of the sitting president and his administration.

It was much bigger than that, something on a scale the U.S. has seen only two times in the past half-century.

One was the Newt Gingrich “revolution” in 1994 that put Republicans in control of the House of Representatives for the first time in 40 years.

The other was the election of 1974 that flooded Capitol Hill with “Watergate babies” – new members elected just after the Nixon-era scandals.

In both cases there were high hopes that big changes would take place in the aftermath of remarkable midterm elections. The actual results were more modest than the victors expected.

The 1994 midterm elections gave the Republican Party a dramatic victory. The Democrats lost their majority in the Senate, and 54 seats were flipped in the House of Representatives, making Gingrich the first Republican speaker of the House since Eisenhower lived in the White House.

It was a wipeout election that had not been expected, and it changed the dynamics of Democrat Bill Clinton’s presidency .

The combative Gingrich emerged as a political celebrity; partisanship intensified and gridlock became the new norm. Confrontations over spending led to controversial government shutdowns and the first modern threat to default on America’s debt obligations .

Because the new Republican congressional majorities appeared to overreach in their efforts to cut taxes and spending, Clinton was able to recover sufficient popularity to win a second term.

In the run-up to his bid for reelection, Clinton took the electoral rebuke of 1994 to heart and followed a centrist strategy that represented a move to the right of longtime Democratic positions on welfare, crime and immigration. He continued to oppose many Republican policy proposals but worked with Republicans to craft welfare reform legislation and new bills dealing with crime and immigration . Budget confrontation eventually gave way to compromise, and for a few years in the late 1990s the United States had a balanced budget .

Partisanship became more personal in Clinton’s second term when Gingrich pushed for impeachment following the revelations of the president’s affair with Monica Lewinsky.

Clinton, with a tarnished reputation, survived his Senate trial . Ironically, it was Gingrich who resigned after failing to remove the president at the ballot box or in the impeachment process.

Gingrich, the biggest winner in the 1994 midterms, left office with a promised revolution largely unrealized.

Going back even further in American political history, the midterm elections following President Richard Nixon’s resignation after the Watergate scandal produced a Democratic Party victory.

That victory was not a surprise; the scale of it was.

Democrats, who already had majorities in the House and Senate, won a huge margin in the congressional popular vote and brought new members to both chambers who were younger, more liberal and reform-minded .

They wanted to prevent future Watergates. New laws would make the government more open, more honest and more accountable . New and more staff would allow Congress to be less reliant on executive branch information and better able to act in foreign policy and budget management. Special prosecutors would be appointed to investigate abuses of power and violations of law.

A Democrat, Jimmy Carter, would be elected president two years after the massive 1974 midterm victory, and more reform legislation would be passed.

The post-Watergate congressional agenda was long and bold – the war powers resolution, a freedom of information act, the creation of inspectors general, campaign finance reform, a presidential records act and new legislation to regulate foreign intelligence surveillance and the bribing of foreign officials.

These new laws were supposed to stop, or uncover, the kind of wrongdoing that made Nixon an imperial president .

The new laws and institutions certainly made a difference – but not without creating their own problems .

All the post-Watergate presidents thought the war powers resolution was unconstitutional , objecting to its restrictions on the president’s authority as commander in chief, and U.S. military interventions overseas continued to occur . Special prosecutors conducted many investigations , but often at great expense and without adequate supervision or meaningful results.

Carter, narrowly elected president in 1976, served only one term and lost reelection to Ronald Reagan , who fully restored the Republican Party’s dominance in presidential politics.

Over time, many presidents, especially Donald Trump , dismantled or ignored important elements of the post-Watergate reforms.

The large and enthusiastic congressional majorities that took power after the 1974 midterms were energetic but produced a political legacy with complicated and controversial results .

What is the country likely to see in the next few months and the next two years?

Will it be chaos, conflict and occasional compromise, like the politics that followed the midterms in 1994? Or will it be earnest and sometimes heavy-handed congressional efforts to investigate and prevent presidential wrongdoing, like those that swept through Washington after 1974?

Surprising midterm elections that create new majorities on Capitol Hill look to be revolutions in the days after they occur. Years later, they often appear to be more complex – and less significant.

Senior Fellow, Miller Center, University of Virginia

A number of my links to outside sources are links to the Miller Center website. I am currently a senior fellow at the Miller Center.

scraped.title: New blood test claims to detect 50-plus cancers before symptoms – but there’s no evidence it can reduce your risk of dying from cancer
scraped.description: A physician who devises screening guidelines for the American Cancer Society explains the pros and cons of the Galleri multicancer early detection test.
scraped.author: Andrew Wolf
scraped.h1: New blood test claims to detect 50‑plus cancers before symptoms – but there’s no evidence it can reduce your risk of dying from cancer
scraped.body_text:
Share article

Print article

Cancer isn’t the leading cause of death in the United States ; heart disease ranks first in that regard. But it’s cancer that strikes fear into the hearts of many Americans.

Cancer can take an excruciating toll on its millions of victims and their family members. Cancer treatments are often highly toxic, and the disease is increasingly striking people at younger ages , which is why it accounts for more years of potential life lost than heart disease.

So when a blood test comes along that claims to be able to screen for over 50 cancers at once in a single blood draw before symptoms appear – as is the case for the Galleri test , by the biotech company GRAIL – it might seem like society has a Holy Grail of modern medicine at their fingertips.

But a closer look at the evidence suggests that the Galleri test is not yet the universal screening breakthrough patients and doctors hope for.

As a physician who studies early cancer detection , and as chair of the American Cancer Society’s screening guideline development group , I have been following this test’s development with interest.

While the Galleri test certainly shows great promise, clinical trial data indicates that it struggles with early-stage cancer detection and has not yet been shown to lower the risk of death from cancer or prevent advanced cancer. Across all cancer stages, the test missed over two-thirds of cancer cases.

On Sept. 23, 2026, an advisory panel to the U.S. Food and Drug Administration voted to recommend approval of the Galleri test. While a recommendation from the FDA’s advisory panel is not the same as full approval from the agency, it marks a critical first step in the process of potentially making the test widely available to the American public. The FDA has not yet announced when it will make a decision on the test.

But even as the advisory panel approved the test, panelists recommended that the word “early” be removed from “early cancer detection test” in product labeling. Panel members were not convinced the test can find cancers at their earliest and most curable stages, and they expressed uncertainty about the test’s benefit to patients at this time.

Given this uncertainty, careful scrutiny of the data behind the test can help doctors and patients make informed decisions about whether to use it.

Galleri is part of an emerging class of multicancer early detection tests . These tests do not diagnose cancer: If a test is positive, further evaluation is necessary to determine whether cancer is present, and, if so, what type of cancer. It is offered as a screening test, similar to mammography for breast cancer screening or PSA testing for prostate cancer screening, but with the potential advantage of screening for many cancers at once, including many for which no screening test currently exists.

The Galleri test looks for DNA fragments in blood that are associated with cancer. When something goes wrong with your DNA, whether because you inherited a mutation or something in your environment triggered that mutation, the processes that regulate cell division can go awry. Uncontrolled cell division can trigger the growth of cancer cells.

Galleri and other multicancer early detection tests in development look for differences that distinguish the DNA produced by tumor cells from normal cells. Galleri identifies unique tags on cancer DNA called methylation markers and uses machine learning algorithms to generate a positive or negative test result.

The Galleri test looks for DNA signals from over 50 cancers , including the 12 that account for almost two-thirds of cancer deaths in the U.S , such as lung and pancreas cancer. Importantly, it provides information on which organ the possible tumor likely originated from. Currently recommended cancer screenings are largely limited to four types of cancer.

Many of the cancers the Galleri test looks for are not currently included in routine screening. Moreover, the test has a very low false positive rate: Only about 0.5% of people who get the test are incorrectly identified as having cancer, or one person out of every 200 tests. A false positive rate is the percentage of people who are told they have cancer but actually don’t. This requires that patients get more testing, which can be costly, sometimes risky and often worrisome.

In comparison, many currently recommended screening tests, such as the Cologuard stool test for colorectal cancer, have false positive rates in the 10% range .

This very low false positive rate also translates into another strength – a very high positive predictive value, or PPV , which is the probability that a positive test result actually means cancer is present. The PPV of the Galleri test was 52% across three annual screens , meaning over half the positive results actually led to a cancer diagnosis. This is good because it gives people confidence that the test is more than 50% correct.

For context, the PPVs of most recommended screening tests – such as stool tests for colorectal cancer, mammography for breast cancer, or the HPV test for cervical cancer – are typically below 10%, meaning most positive results don’t lead to a cancer diagnosis.

The Galleri test also can predict with high accuracy where a cancer originated in the body. In one study of 32,000 U.S. adults age 50 and older who received a Galleri blood test, cancer was diagnosed in about 0.5% of them – 173 patients . Of these patients, the test correctly predicted the cancer type in 91%. This specificity could help clinicians select more targeted evaluations rather than looking for cancer anywhere in the body.

Despite these impressive results, the Galleri test has several major shortcomings.

For one, the test is not as good at detecting cancer in its earliest stages as currently recommended screening tests, which is the main point of a cancer screening test. The test’s ability to detect cancer at all stages was less than 31% over three annual rounds of screening, meaning the test missed 69% of cases . Of the cancers detected in the study, comparing outcomes from getting the Galleri test three years in a row to routine cancer screening, 60% of the cancers detected in the people who got the Galleri test were early stage, which was almost identical to those who didn’t get it.

In addition, the Galleri test did not perform any better than standard screening tests at detecting cancer early. The detection rate for early-stage cancers was only 21% over three years of screening , meaning almost 80% were missed. Cancer is most curable in its early stages , so this shortcoming is a major one. Such a low detection rate can lead to false reassurance from an incorrectly negative test result.

Perhaps the most important shortcoming of the Galleri test is that it hasn’t yet proved that it can save lives or even reduce the risk of being diagnosed with late-stage cancer. The main goal of the trial was to show that the test could reduce the incidence of late-stage cancers over three years of screening – and it failed to do so . In other words, one of the hopes was that the test could reduce the risk of being diagnosed with advanced cancer by finding and treating cancer early – but as of now, there is no evidence to support this.

There was a hint that the incidence of Stage 4 cancer was trending lower by the third year of screening. But more time is needed to determine whether this is a true finding and, if so, whether it leads to a lower risk of dying from cancer.

Requests for comment from GRAIL were not returned.

The FDA advisory panel took three votes . While one of of these votes followed the evidence, two of them were surprisingly counterintuitive.

First, the panel voted 10-0 to recommend that the Galleri test is safe. While undergoing a blood test doesn’t typically involve any substantive risk, a positive result may prompt further testing, such as biopsies, that are riskier than a blood test and can incur additional costs.

These harms can be particularly hard to swallow if the test turns out to be a false alarm, as it will in about half of cases. One study evaluating Galleri’s safety found that 0.6% of those who had the test ended up undergoing an invasive diagnostic procedure , but none experienced serious complications. Hence, the safety vote appears to have been warranted.

Second, the panel voted 6-4 to recommend that the test is effective, though a number of the panelists cast their yes vote on the condition that the company remove the term “early” from the label “multi-cancer early detection” test.

This outcome, however, does not have the evidence to back it up. Available studies indicate the Galleri test does not reduce the incidence of late-stage cancer and performs poorly in detecting early-stage cancer. Additionally, there is no evidence that it lowers the risk of dying from cancer.

Finally, the panel voted 7-2 with one abstention to recommend that the benefits of the Galleri test outweigh the risk. But if there is no proven benefit to the test, how can the benefits outweigh the risks, even if the risk is low?

While the advisory panel acknowledged the test’s serious limitations, it still went ahead and recommended approval. One of the panel members stated that the ability to find more early-stage cancers in a broader population is a benefit, even though that hasn’t been proved yet. “So perhaps my ‘yes’ is a hopeful (vote) rather than an accurate one,” said the panel member.

The problem is that “hope” does not reduce death and disability from cancer.

If the FDA agrees with its advisory panel’s recommendation and approves the Galleri test, it will likely be more widely marketed to the American public. Regardless, there remain many caveats, and I believe patients will want to be cautious.

First, FDA approval does not guarantee insurance coverage. The Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services has a separate coverage determination process , and it is not required to grant coverage to FDA-approved tests. The out-of-pocket cost of the Galleri test is currently US$949 .

It remains unclear whether the test can reduce your risk of dying from cancer or being diagnosed with advanced cancer. However, if you’re willing to pay the annual cost of the test, are willing to undergo further testing despite a high rate of false alarms, and are not overly reassured by a falsely negative test result, you can ask your doctor for more information about the test.

What doctors and researchers are certain about is the importance of staying up to date with currently recommended cancer screening tests for colon, breast, cervical and lung cancers, even if you decide to get the Galleri test. These tests are proven to detect early-stage cancer and lower your risk of dying from cancer. That’s the bottom line.

Professor Emeritus of Medicine, University of Virginia

scraped.title: Paraguay’s bank collapse brought down a president – and exposed as myth the nation’s status as a ‘Dubai of South America’
scraped.description: The collapse raises troubling questions about who benefits from financial modernization, who controls it and who bears the risks when it fails.
scraped.author: Joel E. Correia
scraped.h1: Paraguay’s bank collapse brought down a president – and exposed as myth the nation’s status as a ‘Dubai of South America’
scraped.body_text:
Share article

Print article

It started on Nov. 3, 2026, when millions of Paraguayans trying to access the Ueno banking app found they could no longer get their money . In a matter of days, the financial situation escalated into political crisis, in which the country’s president was ousted, placed under house arrest and charged with several corruption-related crimes.

The political and financial crisis exposes a central contradiction in Paraguay’s recent economic development . Ueno, a bank celebrated for expanding financial access to ordinary Paraguayans, grew through unusually close relationships with political elites and public institutions. And while the Ueno crisis came as a shock, there were clear warning signs.

As scholars with expertise in various aspects of Paraguay’s contemporary political , economic and environment development , we believe the collapse raises troubling questions about who benefits from financial modernization, who controls it and who bears the risks when it fails. The political relationships through which financial institutions grow, regulators exercise authority and public resources are entrusted to private companies are crucial national concerns, especially in a country that has presented itself internationally as a model of economic stability.

Founded as a digital lender in 2021, Ueno attracted customers with mobile banking and cash-back offers. Its expansion brought useful services to people underserved by conventional banks, including rural customers. Ueno also expanded the credit card market to low-income customers , an unprecedented move compared to previously restricted banking practices.

As Ueno expanded, Paraguay increasingly attracted investors drawn by its low taxes, economic stability and business-friendly policies. Promoted by some as a “ Dubai of South America ,” the country also became a magnet for conservative influencers , particularly from Brazil, who contrasted Paraguay’s economic model with the purported mismanagement of left-wing governments elsewhere in the region. Indeed, under President Santiago Peña, Paraguay has been one of Latin America’s most enthusiastic allies of the Trump administration and its expansive regional vision.

But beneath the financial stability, Ueno stood at the precipice of a much deeper problem.

The central bank finally acted after accounting adjustments left Ueno’s solvency ratio below half the legal minimum. But problems had surfaced earlier. That included a supervisory report put out by the bank regulators in June 2026 that described roughly US$146 million in loans to three companies linked to Grupo Vázquez, Ueno’s controlling shareholder. Some companies had been transferred to group employees; supervisors questioned the collateral and ultimate use of the funds.

That these warning signs went unheeded raises a related question of why regulators didn’t have a better handle on the situation and were not better able to contain the exposure.

In any case, Ueno’s problems were exposed in dramatic fashion on Nov. 2, when the central bank placed Ueno into resolution, a process similar to bankruptcy but managed directly by Paraguay’s central bank. The lender, which says it has nearly 3 million customers – about half of the country’s population – halted transactions.

The crisis quickly ensnared the governing party. Peña, an economist by training who was elected president in 2023 and had close ties to the bank, resigned on Nov. 5. The Senate then voted unanimously to remove him from office, thereby stripping Peña of his parliamentary immunity. He was swiftly put under house arrest, charged with corruption and succeeded by his Vice President Pedro Alliana, who was sworn in to serve until 2028.

Meanwhile, the crisis has led to widespread protests, including outside Congress, with citizens accusing Peña and the ruling Colorado Party of “ stealing” their savings .

Part of the story of Ueno is a tale of the closeness between political and financial elites in Paraguay.

Carlos Carvallo chaired Ueno’s predecessor bank before Peña appointed him Paraguay’s central bank president in 2023. Carvallo resigned on Nov. 3 and has since been charged with the same corruption crimes as Peña. For its part, the Paraguayan central bank says Carvallo recused himself from any Ueno decisions.

Yet the potential conflicts of interest ran much deeper. Peña previously directed Banco Basa, linked to Colorado Party leader and former President Horacio Cartes, who retains considerable influence and was instrumental in helping push Peña out of office. Finance Minister Carlos Fernández Valdovinos also served on Basa’s board. Local reporters had documented these revolving-door relationships early in Peña’s term.

Peña reportedly held a 1.58% stake in Ueno Holding , which shared its principal shareholder, Grupo Vázquez, with Ueno bank. His brother Francisco held shares in Luxembourg-based U Holdings , an indirect shareholder in the bank. Another shareholder was Juan Carlos López Moreira, Cartes’ former chief of staff. Both brothers exited in 2025.

Peña has denied any wrongdoing , while prosecutors are examining allegations concerning his former business interests and his administration’s financial supervision.

The inclusion of significant reserves of public funds made these connections especially consequential. Ueno held approximately $850 million in public funds , including $355 million from the country’s social security system , IPS, including health and retirement funds. It amounted to roughly 9% of IPS’s investment portfolio.

Under Peña-appointed chairman Jorge Brítez, IPS relaxed eligibility requirements for bank deposits in 2023 and removed a capital-based exposure limit in 2024. Over the same period, its deposits at Ueno rose sharply. Grupo Vázquez’s technology firm ITTI won at least $2.3 million in state contracts after Peña took office, versus $675,000 before. ITTI attributed the increase to business expansion and denied a conflict of interest.

Together these ties and regulatory changes raise important questions about regulatory capture and other potential conflicts of interest.

Paraguay’s economic gains are real. In August, the International Monetary Fund projected 4.4% growth in 2026 following 6.6% in 2025. Moody’s granted the country’s debt investment-grade status in 2024, and S&P followed in 2025. Hydroelectric power exports, agriculture and new infrastructure continue to underpin the economy.

Washington is also drawing Paraguay more firmly into its regional economic strategy. On Oct. 23, the country became the 26th signatory to the Pax Silica Declaration , an initiative involving critical minerals, hydropower and advanced computing infrastructure. While the announcement did not specify financing commitments, it shows how Paraguay’s resources and perceived political predictability are being positioned as strategic assets.

But growth figures and credit ratings say little about who shapes financial oversight or bears the costs of banking failures. Paraguay’s legacies of political patronage make it necessary to examine political and corporate connections and changes to public-fund investment rules .

Paraguay has been here before. Between 1995 and 1998, 13 banks and 35 financial firms closed , with direct costs estimated by the IMF at 10% to 13% of the country’s GDP. This preceded a smaller bank crisis in the early 2000s. Both ordeals exposed weak supervision and connected lending .

Paraguay’s deposit guarantee, which covers balances up to about $38,000 , is meant to limit depositor losses, and the Paraguayan Central Bank insists that failure is isolated in the latest case. Yet account transfers have already strained the system , producing outages at several banking institutions.

Yet for most Paraguayans, the crisis was experienced not through technical financial or macroeconomic indicators but at the stark level of seeing from their phones that they couldn’t access their money. Wages, pensions and savings froze simultaneously . Young Ueno employees burned their company cards outside the Labor Ministry, demanding unpaid wages.

Riot police used pepper spray and rubber bullets against depositors marching on Congress. For small businesses that banked and paid staff through Ueno, the real economy stopped.

This widespread anger challenges the ruling party’s claims to the economic vision they cite as the engine for future growth. Whether it leads to institutional change or a reshuffle within the Colorado Party remains an open question. The test is how Paraguayan legislators and regulators will move forward and whether they separate banking supervision and public deposits from partisan and business networks.

In any case, the myth of the “Dubai of South America” has come under serious scrutiny. While the protests were noteworthy, the Colorado Party has for now managed to resolve its own internal crisis by quickly sacrificing key political elites, including the president.

Marco Castillo Ph.D., Paraguayan sociologist, recent graduate and former director of research at the Center for Latin American, Latino and Caribbean Studies at Graduate Center CUNY, and Sheyla Rios Galeano, a Ph.D. Student in human dimensions of natural resources, Colorado State University, contributed to this article.

Associate Professor in Human Dimensions of Natural Resources, Colorado State University

scraped.title: Fallout From the Flames - Inside Climate News
scraped.description: Inside Climate heads to the Pacific to discuss the impacts of deadly and damaging wildfires in Maui and Los Angeles.
scraped.author: By Kiley Price, Keerti Gopal, Nina Dietz
scraped.h1: Fallout From the Flames
scraped.body_text:
An inside look at top climate news, delivered every two weeks.

Welcome to Inside Climate, a podcast from the staff of Inside Climate News. Powerful wildfires upended life for residents in Maui, Hawaiʻi , in 2023. In early 2025, the Eaton and Palisades fires caused similar devastation in greater Los Angeles. Years have passed since the fires were contained but researchers are still trying to understand the lasting effects of these disasters. Co-host Kiley Price discusses those efforts with Inside Climate News reporter Keerti Gopal, who has chronicled the recovery in Maui, and contributor Nina Dietz, who has covered the health impacts of the fires in Los Angeles .

Listen and subscribe on YouTube , Spotify , Apple Podcasts , Amazon Music , and iHeart .

KILEY PRICE

It’s been three years since high winds spread multiple wildfires across Maui and eviscerated the town of Lahaina.

KEERTI GOPAL: The Maui wildfires were the deadliest fires that the U.S. has seen in more than a century.

Since then, researchers have been closely following thousands of survivors, trying to understand the fire’s lingering effects on human health.

KEERTI GOPAL: They’re finding elevated levels of these metals in survivors’ urine months after the fires.

MEDICAL WORKER: You’re gonna take a huge inhale.

KEERTI GOPAL: Some of these metals are linked to elevated cancer risks.

Meanwhile, Los Angeles is on a similar recovery path to Maui, due to the deadly Palisades and Eaton fires that covered portions of Los Angeles in ash almost two years ago.

NINA DIETZ: There’s this huge issue of contaminated homes. They have things like lead and cadmium, and in some cases, even cyanide and arsenic in crawl spaces.

As large, urban wildfires burn more synthetic materials, researchers are racing to better understand health impacts.

NINA DIETZ: A few scientists have actually brought up 9/11. There’s this real concern that we’re going to see this major cancer cohort that we do not have the capabilities to deal with and that could have been prevented.

That’s coming up on Inside Climate.

Welcome to Inside Climate. I’m your host, Kiley Price.

On Aug. 8, 2023 a red flag alert was issued by the National Weather Service in Honolulu, warning of “high fire danger with rapid spread.” That same day, fires tore across parts of Maui and leveled thousands of structures on the island’s western shore.

The flames have been extinguished, but the fire continues to leave its mark on thousands of survivors who have struggled to rebuild their lives. Many battle insurance companies over homes and hospital bills. Others endure lingering health issues, but can’t afford to seek medical care.

A multi-year research project spearheaded by the University of Hawaiʻi aims to chronicle the health impacts of the fire. Its early findings indicate that urban wildfires could have far more damaging impacts than previously known.

Meanwhile, a couple of scientists who studied the Maui aftermath have since relocated to California to conduct similar analyses following the Los Angeles wildfires of 2025. Both places have struggled to maintain funding for research as the Trump administration reshapes FEMA and other agencies that have historically supported disaster recovery and response.

We’ll speak to ICN reporter Keerti Gopal, who traveled to Maui earlier this year to follow the researchers studying and addressing survivor health and raising funds to expand the study.

And then we’ll talk to contributor Nina Dietz, who has been reporting on the health risks of the LA wildfires as part of ICN’s “After the Fires” series, supported by the Pulitzer Center.

KILEY PRICE

Keerti, thanks so much for coming on the show today.

KEERTI GOPAL

Thank you for having me.

KILEY PRICE

Keerti covers the intersections of climate change, public health and environmental justice at Inside Climate News. She’s a National Geographic Explorer and has received several fellowships from Fulbright, the Solutions Journalism Network and the National Press Foundation.

So you traveled to Hawaiʻi a few months ago to report on the aftermath of the devastating Maui wildfires, which broke out in August 2023. That wildfire killed more than 100 people and destroyed more than 2,200 buildings, costing around $5.5 billion in damages. How are things looking three years later?

KEERTI GOPAL

Recovery is definitely moving forward, but there’s still a lot of work to be done and it’s going pretty slowly in some ways. As of October, according to the county, there are about 300 single-family homes that have been completed and another 300 homes in multifamily units. And that’s part of only about 30 structures. Overall, that’s about 330 buildings out of 2,200 that were destroyed, like you said. And more than 12,000 people were also displaced in these fires. So there’s a lot of people that are still living in temporary housing.

KILEY PRICE

So how have the wildfires and this recovery process itself affected people’s health?

KEERTI GOPAL

Yeah, so I went to Maui to write about the Maui Wildfire Exposure Study, which is a multi-year research effort from the University of Hawaiʻi, and they’re really looking to chronicle both the short- and long-term health impacts of the fires. In the past three years, they’ve had more than 2,500 participants in the study, and they’re looking at a range of kind of dimensions of health. So they’re looking at lung function, metabolic health, mental health. They’re looking at cancer risks and environmental exposures, things like heavy metals in survivors’ urine.

They’ve found so far that the health impacts are ongoing. So there have been widespread mental health impacts, including high levels of depression, anxiety and PTSD. And they’ve also found that those are really closely related to things like housing instability and lack of employment. And they’ve also found things like breathing troubles with survivors and links between elevated levels of heavy metals, some metals that were found in the burn zone ash as well, and links between that and impaired lung function in survivors.

So food insecurity and declining levels of social support are also two things that are persistent issues three years on. And they’ve found that in children there are some pretty concerning results with ongoing emotional stress and trauma and some issues with blood pressure and lung health that you wouldn’t be expecting to see in young kids.

KILEY PRICE

Yeah, and you kind of touched on this, but this is an interesting place for a fire to happen because it’s partially urban. How is that different from a forest wildfire? And can you explain to me how and why Maui wildfire victims were exposed to those heavy metals that you mentioned?

KEERTI GOPAL

Yeah, so the Maui wildfires were the deadliest fires that the U.S. has seen in more than a century. And when a wildfire burns through an urban environment where people are living, it’s burning up all of the chemicals that are part of our daily lives. So things like cars, homes, electronics, other synthetic materials that we have in our homes, and that brings a lot of unique health concerns that you might not see in a forest fire that’s burning through organic materials, so like a forest, trees, things like that, not the kind of man-made synthetic types of things that we have in our urban environments, which can contain chemicals, contain toxins. And in urban environments, fires can also kind of dislodge some of the contamination that might be existing in a soil from another era of a place. So on Maui, they’re continuing to research this, and it’s actually really difficult to pinpoint the source of some of the heavy metals that you’re mentioning. So they’re finding these elevated levels of these metals in survivor’s urine months after the fires. And right now they’re trying to understand better, like, where those could be coming from. Some of those sources might predate the fires. They’re looking into, kind of, the history of agriculture and industry and plantations on Maui to try to see what connections there might be there.

KILEY PRICE

And what health impacts might those specifically have?

KEERTI GOPAL

So some of these metals are linked to elevated cancer risks and widespread health risks. And specifically in this study, they found an association—so they’re not necessarily able to say causal yet—but they found an association between elevated levels of some of these metals and lower lung function, so trouble breathing. And that’s months after the fires happen. So it’s really kind of underscoring the need for continued monitoring and the fact that these fires can have an impact on people’s bodies long after the smoke is gone.

KILEY PRICE

Right. ’Cause in the context of fire and recovery, three years is not that long, right?

KEERTI GOPAL

Absolutely. Something this study has really underscored that is broadly applicable to disasters is how long the aftermath is, both for people’s like literal recovery, rebuilding, getting home and also health and mental health and ongoing trauma. So, yeah, the researchers are hoping to keep this study going for several more years. And it’s something that’s a conversation in the post-disaster research space, is that we need to be doing these kind of longitudinal studies looking long term at these health impacts, because you can’t know right after the fires what the long-term health impacts are gonna be.

KILEY PRICE

It makes sense that researchers would want to study survivors and understand these health impacts, but how does this project differ from other response efforts?

KEERTI GOPAL

This is a really unique study. It’s called the Maui Wildfire Exposure Study. It’s also known as MauiWES for short. And it’s kind of unique because they’re combining research with interventions. And they’re working to kind of get participants connected with things like therapy, food assistance, in some cases, like cash support, healthcare providers, in some cases even health insurance, and so they’re really hoping that this could potentially become the new norm for post-disaster research. And I’ve spoken with a lot of post-disaster researchers in other parts of the country about this study. And there’s a broad consensus, it seems like, that this is a really unique and kind of remarkable study. Some participants even said that the study saved their lives.

KILEY PRICE

Wow, can you tell me more about that?

KEERTI GOPAL

There’s one participant who I met, her name is Amy Jackson, and she came into MauiWES about a year after the fires. And she had such a low hemoglobin count that it wasn’t even registering on MauiWES’s system. And so the team immediately was like, “You need to go see your doctor.” She went to urgent care, they sent her to the hospital, and at the hospital she had to get a blood transfusion because her hemoglobin was so low, and the doctors told her that, you know, she was in critical condition. So she really sees MauiWES as having saved her life. And she actually was a trauma nurse, and she said that she, like, never really goes in to get medical care typically, and she had only signed up for the study because she wanted to get the $100 cash incentive that they were giving out to give her daughter for her birthday. So she herself was like, “I would never have gone in to see a doctor if it wasn’t for this study.” And that was something that I heard a lot because, you know, there is a provider shortage on Maui and it is kind of difficult to see specialists. It can also be difficult to see primary care providers. And so when MauiWES did their kind of first round of testing, about six to 12 months after the fires, that was a lot of people’s first time ever seeing a health care provider since the fires, which is pretty intense considering what people had been going through.

KILEY PRICE

Can you tell me more about this provider shortage?

KEERTI GOPAL

Yeah, so that’s something that affects across the state of Hawaiʻi, and it’s particularly severe on Maui. Maui is a relatively rural island, so they have kind of like a more rural healthcare infrastructure, and it’s been a challenge to get physicians to come to and stay in Hawaiʻi. So that’s something the state is dealing with. There’s a shortage in primary care providers across the board, and then there’s also a real shortage in specialists.

KILEY PRICE

I think this is probably at odds with how a lot of people who are not from Hawaiʻi might understand what Maui looks like. Can you talk to me about what the full time population is on Maui?

KEERTI GOPAL

Maui overall is really diverse, and Lahaina in particular, which is where the fires hit hardest, is a really diverse community. So before the fires, from census data, about a third of Lahaina residents are immigrants, and Maui also has a really strong Filipino population, partially because of the plantation history of the island.

And something that the researchers mentioned was that for some of the immigrant population, and particularly undocumented immigrants, that kind of access to healthcare was even more of a challenge and even more of a concern. There was one participant who I met who is undocumented and she came into the study with kind of persistent symptoms of, like, bronchitis and pneumonia. She’d had them for months, she hadn’t seen a doctor. And she was showing kind of signs of a potentially serious lung infection. And some of the physicians who were volunteering with MauiWES were really concerned and they said she needed medical attention. But she didn’t have insurance and she was also one of the 10 percent of study participants who had lost their jobs in the fire, so she didn’t really have options. And this was a pretty unique situation where the study actually was able to partner up with this local community organization called Roots Reborn that works with immigrants on Maui. And they worked with Kaiser Permanente, a private insurance company, to get her charitable insurance and then she was actually able to get surgery that she needed. And that has happened through MauiWES and their partnership with Roots Reborn. They’ve done that for hundreds of people, getting them get connected with health insurance.

KILEY PRICE

There’s been a lot of reporting about challenges to post disaster recovery and funding under the Trump administration as it aims to reshape FEMA and other related agencies. Has that impacted MauiWES at all or the broader wildfire recovery?

KEERTI GOPAL

Yeah, it’s definitely a big conversation in the wildfire recovery and post disaster recovery space. Something that has been an ongoing challenge for MauiWES is funding and keeping the study funded. Partially because they are trying to do this as a long-term effort, and it’s expensive to keep that up. So when they first started, they kind of like hit the ground running after the fires, trying to get testing up as quickly as they could, and they did that with kind of early charitable funding from some organizations and companies on Maui. And then they got some funding from the state. And then about a year after the fires, they got funding from the NIH, National Institutes of Health. But that support kind of came into question after Donald Trump took office because he was slashing a lot of the programs focused on diversity and health outcomes, and their funding was from the Minority Health Disparities Program. And so they weren’t really sure what that was going to look like going forward.

KILEY PRICE

Where do things stand now? Is this study going to continue?

KEERTI GOPAL

Yes, so it’s a happy ending. They actually ended up getting their federal funding through. And that came through this summer and in the fall. And they also got another $2 million from the county, Maui County, and that one’s really focused on kind of expanding the initiative to other more remote corners of the island and kind of places that are impacted by those healthcare shortages we were talking about.

KILEY PRICE

When you’ve spoken to the researchers, how are they talking about some of the lessons learned from their experiences and passing it on to other communities, places like California, which is no stranger to fires, and other places around the country?

KEERTI GOPAL

Yeah, that’s been really striking. Something that’s been coming up a lot is that climate change is bringing more of these intense and severe disasters with more frequency. I mean, Hawaiʻi this summer alone has been kind of hit with back to back storms. There’s been a lot of damages and just a lot of kind of like very little time to recover in between these storms.

Building that resilience and trying to figure out how do we respond to disasters better and more quickly and more holistically is super important right now. And so they’ve been talking to researchers in Utah after the fires there. They were talking to researchers across the country and in particular, in Los Angeles and Southern California. There’s a big health study effort that’s happening right now following the fires there in 2025. And they’ve been partnering really closely with MauiWES and kind of talking about how do we incorporate a lot of the same kind of holistic structures and things like that into that study there.

KILEY PRICE

Keerti, I think this is the perfect place to pause because we’re going to speak with Nina Dietz, who has been doing related reporting on the Palisades and Altadena wildfires that happened in 2025. Thank you so much for sharing about your reporting.

KEERTI GOPAL

Awesome. Thank you for having me.

Our nonprofit newsroom provides award-winning climate coverage free of charge and advertising. We rely on donations from readers like you to keep going. Please donate now to support our work.

KILEY PRICE

Nina, it’s great to have you join the show given all the extensive reporting you’ve done at Inside Climate News on the series “After the Fires,” which examines the health risks following the LA wildfires. Welcome.

NINA DIETZ

Thanks. And thanks for having me here to talk about this series.

KILEY PRICE

Yeah, Nina is a contributor at Inside Climate News and frequently writes about climate, environmental health and accessibility in the environmental context as a freelance journalist. Her work has appeared in Sierra Magazine, Wired and Science Friday, among others.

Nina, we just heard from Keerti Gopal about the health impacts victims of the Maui wildfires are experiencing, but they are in year three of their recovery. You’ve been documenting the health impacts of the wildfires in Los Angeles, which took place in January 2025. The Eaton and Palisades fires burned through more than 38,000 acres, destroyed more than 16,000 structures and killed 31 people. They also displaced 205,000 people.

Where do things currently stand with recovery efforts in the Palisades and Altadena?

NINA DIETZ

So the recovery’s been pretty slow. More than 70 percent of survivors are still displaced and there’s this huge issue of contaminated homes. A lot of the homes that were left standing were at first assumed to be safe, but we’ve learned that they are pretty toxic. They have things like lead and cadmium and in some cases, even cyanide and arsenic in crawl spaces, just soaked into the paint. And the cleanup itself has had a number of issues because the Army Corps of Engineers and EPA declined to do post-remediation soil testing. So though it had been cleaned up, it’s not really clear to what standard.

KILEY PRICE

Yeah, and as I mentioned, we just spoke about the Maui wildfires. You’ve been following researchers studying fire impacts in the spring of 2025 in LA. Have any of their efforts mirrored what happened in Maui or diverged?

NINA DIETZ

One of the saving graces in the case of the LA wildfires, if such a thing can be said to exist, is that this occurred in a state that has a very robust university system where there are a lot of interlinked universities, where as soon as it became clear that the government was not going to be stepping in to do the testing, the UC system and individual scientists just sort of jumped in, as well as the Harvard T.H. Chan School, who’s also done a lot of work in Maui. So I think some of the same scientists who actually spent several months out in Maui afterward were ones I interviewed for my initial story.

KILEY PRICE

Yeah, you, you mentioned some federal involvement right after the fires, but why isn’t the Army Corps collecting soil samples? And have the cleanup efforts been satisfactory in LA?

NINA DIETZ

It comes down to some rather bureaucratic bid issues. They couldn’t get a contract or bid that was within their budget. Part of that has to do with the scale of the wildfires, and another part of that has to do with how underfunded the post-disaster branch of these major agencies is. So I would not be surprised if this is not the last time we see this happening.

KILEY PRICE

Yeah, we heard from Keerti that Maui victims had elevated levels of heavy metals in their samplings. Did researchers discover similar findings with LA victims of the fire?

NINA DIETZ

They found a lot of high levels of lead. There was, some of that testing is still ongoing, and some of it has yet to be released. Of what’s been released, some of it has to do with the firefighters themselves, where they actually took samples before the fire season and samples again right after the LA fires, and they found really elevated levels of inflammation proteins in the blood and inflammatory markers.

KILEY PRICE

And what might that indicate?

NINA DIETZ

It can indicate a variety of things, but in this instance it indicates probably that something has done some damage somewhere in the body, or that the immune system is noticing something that it does not like in the body. The immune system is sort of the bouncers of the body. And that works really well if you’ve got a virus or bacterial infection, but if you have tiny particles that are really embedded in your cells, it can actually become a problem because the body’s attempts to get it out can actually cause more damage.

KILEY PRICE

Was there anything else the researchers discovered with exposures to heavy metals?

NINA DIETZ

So the toxic metals actually showed up in these really ultrafine particles known as nanoparticles that are under one micron. They’re small enough to reach the heart, the lungs, and like I said, really embed themselves in your cells. UCLA’s Candace Tsai says there’s no safe exposure level for these particles. They really just embed themselves all over your body. And they can end up in your brain, which is particularly terrifying to me.

KILEY PRICE

Are researchers finding that various air, water or soil tests and results for certain hazards are within the range that the EPA deems safe?

NINA DIETZ

So the academic community has known for a long time that the EPA limits are too high. A lot of them are based on OSHA limits, which are set based on occupational exposure, which assumes either a certain level of PPE or eight hours a day of exposure, and it’s not at all expected for kids. So there’s particular compounds, especially lead, lithium and barium, that people are particularly concerned about in this instance. But the rulemaking is very slow, and the Trump administration is actually currently walking things back instead of making things stricter. So while on paper things might look OK—which isn’t the rule across the board, but in some instances things do look OK on paper—that doesn’t mean that they’re safe for human health.

KILEY PRICE

We heard of funding issues that threaten to end Maui’s health impact study. Have LA researchers faced similar issues in regards to funding or any setbacks to their research due to state or the federal government?

NINA DIETZ

So the fires happened at a really bad moment in terms of funding. It was just before Trump’s inauguration. There sort of seemed to be a very big show being made of trying to do the clean cleanup quickly without really funding the studies to make sure it was done thoroughly. That got even worse when the Trump administration and UCLA were at loggerheads, and the administration decided to freeze all federal funding. It really disrupted a lot of studies. I know that one lab actually tried to buy the equipment that they would need and the reagents that they would need for the year, and tried to plan ahead before their funding was frozen.

KILEY PRICE

People have said that the LA fires burn materials that have stark similarities to substances that caught fire in the aftermath of 9/11. What have researchers said about concerns they have comparing those two events?

NINA DIETZ

So a few scientists have actually brought up 9/11, especially from the fine particulate asbestos standpoint. But one scientist in particular pointed to research suggesting that the exposure might be similar to what we saw after the World Trade Center collapse. People living nearby during cleanup later had elevated cancer mortality due to the exposures of the burning urban structures that released heavy metals, asbestos and synthetic carcinogens. There’s a very similar concern for the workers who were doing the cleanup and the people who were working on the pile after 9/11, and there’s this real concern that we’re going to see maybe 10 years out, this major cancer cohort and this major COPD cohort that we do not have the capabilities to deal with it, and that could have been prevented.

KILEY PRICE

LA is obviously a big place, but research has shown that the impacts of a wildfire can expand far beyond the burn zone and can sometimes be invisible to the eye. Do you feel like people understand the risks that they’ve been exposed to across LA?

NINA DIETZ

I feel like that varies. The Palisades actually were relatively, I mean it’s hard to say lucky, but the people around that area weren’t exposed nearly as badly because the Santa Anas were blowing the debris and the dust straight out over the Pacific. But the Eaton fire was on the eastern edge of the city, so it had a whole city to blow over before it reached the Pacific. We’re not quite sure how far away this damage extends, or what the long-term outcomes will be, but we can definitely say that it is probably not just within the burn scar. That being said, people who were instructed, like right after the fires, that all they needed to do was go back to their homes if they were still standing and vacuum up and wipe down walls and things like that, we now know that that was not the correct thing to do. Things were really driven into the homes by 100 mile per hour winds in such a way that they were really heavily contaminated. And that it’s very hard to actually get all of that unless you’re taking a house apart and down to the studs or you have some experienced professional remediation.

KILEY PRICE

So people might have thought that their homes were clean and they weren’t. You mentioned that some LA researchers have previously studied the Maui wildfires. What can California learn from Hawaiʻi, which is further along in its process in some ways?

NINA DIETZ

I will say that there’s a same sort of toxic fingerprints in certain areas. And the need to approach it with care and clean things correctly has become clear that it’s running parallel in both places. I will also say that much like in Maui, in LA, there are also undocumented immigrants and children that are at higher risk of health issues and a lack of medical care and funding is impacting both. Scientists sampling in the field have also noted that many of the workers on the cleanup did not speak English in LA. I believe the same was noted in Maui in some areas and that they often didn’t have PPE. And even when they did, they did not necessarily know what the dangers they were trying to protect themselves from were. It was not explained to them in their language. So there is a significant concern for their health in the long term.

KILEY PRICE

Nina, thank you so much for all of this in-depth reporting. We’ll look for more of it as the second anniversary of the fires approaches this January.

NINA DIETZ

Sounds good. Thank you for having me.

As people look to repair and rebuild after a disaster, a number of scams have further complicated those efforts. Dozens of individuals who lost their homes in the 2023 Maui wildfire have contacted state and local officials reporting serious problems with contractors. No criminal charges have been filed against contractors, for now.

To avoid becoming a victim of construction scams, experts recommend hiring licensed contractors, consulting a lawyer before signing a contract and withholding payment until any outstanding issues are resolved.

California has several laws that protect consumers from contractor and home improvement fraud. But in the wake of the Eaton fire that destroyed the community of Altadena, many residents have encountered predatory developers that are buying up property and making it harder for locals to rebuild.

To prevent further expansion by developers, this fall California Gov. Gavin Newsom signed the “Keep Altadena Land in Altadena Hands Act.” The law will limit the number of controversial high-density developments in two Altadena ZIP codes.

While the law will help limit future developments, it won’t have much impact on the 60 new housing proposals that have already been approved and represent between 200 and 300 new structures in Altadena.

scraped.title: Chesapeake Bay’s Osprey Population Is Falling. Is Its Food Supply a Factor? - Inside Climate News
scraped.description: Scientists and industrial fishermen are locked in finger-pointing over the causes.
scraped.author: By Aman Azhar, Johnny Sturgeon
scraped.h1: Chesapeake Bay’s Osprey Population Is Falling. Is Its Food Supply a Factor?
scraped.body_text:
For 20 years, Roberta Kellam, a retired lawyer and longtime birder, has watched ospreys return to their nests and raise chicks from her home on Nassawadox Creek, on Virginia’s Eastern Shore.

She’s been monitoring around two dozen nests near her house. Kellam has also surveyed osprey populations with Bryan Watts, a longtime researcher at William & Mary’s Center for Conservation Biology and logs her observations on Osprey Watch , a citizen-science project the center runs.

Nassawadox Creek drains into the Chesapeake Bay, the nation’s largest estuary and home to the world’s largest breeding population of ospreys. The birds typically return from their wintering grounds in late February and early March to rebuild nests and raise chicks.

But about eight years ago, the situation turned from joy to dread.

“Once they hatched, they were disappearing,” Kellam recalled. By mid-to-late May, according to Kellam, the creek could shift from active osprey nests to “just silence” in recent years, with adults no longer feeding the young, signaling a worrying decline. The disturbing observations prompted her to report the situation to Watts, who she’d known for nearly two decades.

Early on, they considered possibilities such as predation. But nothing seemed to explain the losses. Watts, who’s studied Chesapeake Bay ospreys for about 40 years, said they decided to ramp up nest monitoring after residents and watermen raised concerns about poor osprey reproduction.

The first comprehensive survey of Kellam’s local osprey colony began in 2024, which she described as “very grim.” That was the first time she could “look inside the nest and see the dead chicks and the abandoned eggs.” Sometimes chicks were still alive, she said, but many did not survive.

The center’s 2026 osprey breeding performance survey found the bay’s osprey population in steep decline, especially in saltier regions of the estuary. The study linked the decline to severe food stress tied to the low availability of Atlantic menhaden for nesting ospreys.

Menhaden for decades have been considered a “keystone prey species for the osprey population” due to their abundance, high energy density and schooling behavior, the survey said. Nesting ospreys “require high fish abundance during April, May and June to successfully raise broods” and are not able to adjust when menhaden do not arrive in large numbers until late June or July.

The study described the 2026 breeding season as “the worst productivity year ever recorded for ospreys in the Chesapeake Bay,” raising fears that breeding rates are too low to sustain the population.

Watts said that on the lower Patuxent River, where ospreys depend more heavily on menhaden, pairs are raising too few young to replace the adults that die. Upriver, where birds have access to a different mix of fish, pairs are doing better.

The food shortage is visible in the nests, he said, and chicks were starving at older ages than historically observed. Watts estimated an 80 percent decline in menhaden deliveries and a 50 percent decline in food quality compared with the 1980s.

More than 30 percent of osprey females in some study areas were not laying eggs, Watts noted, compared with about 2 percent in the 1980s. Current productivity was about 0.26 chicks per pair, below the minimum break-even estimate of 0.8.

Watts said ospreys show strong fidelity to their nesting sites, but in saltier bay regions, where menhaden is the birds’ primary food source, many pairs now cannot bring home enough food to raise their young. “They need [menhaden] in mid-May to about mid-June. That’s a critical period, and they’re not available.”

Researchers have a much firmer grasp on what is happening in the nests than on why fewer menhaden are reaching ospreys. According to Watts, climate change is a contributing factor, shifting the fish’s distribution and arrival times. And while state and regional fisheries councils emphasize that localized menhaden depletion has not been empirically linked to commercial harvest, conservationists and researchers like Watts have field observations to raise questions about that.

Watts said researchers lack fisheries monitoring data, and industry-held commercial data is not available to the public, leading to data gaps about menhaden availability and older age classes of ospreys.

The American Small Pelagics Network, a group representing fishermen and processors tied to the menhaden industry, have pushed back on the Center for Conservation Biology’s research.

“A struggling predator does not by itself prove a menhaden harvest problem,” the group said in a recent statement . “The 2025 Atlantic menhaden assessment found the stock is not overfished and overfishing is not occurring.”

A spokesperson for a leading menhaden fishing firm, Ocean Harvesters, stated the “suggestion that the fishery’s catch is hidden from scientists and regulators is wrong,” pointing instead to federal catch records and a daily logbook database —though both have access restrictions.

From the chilled estuaries of Nova Scotia to the brackish bays of northern Florida, massive schools of metallic menhaden form the ecological and economic foundation of the Atlantic shoreline. Following blooms of phytoplankton, menhaden migrate north in the spring and return south in the fall, offering a concentrated calorific meal for dozens of predators.

The largest commercial fishery, by volume, along the East Coast— second nationally only to Alaskan pollock—menhaden are a primary target of striped bass, predatory birds, marine mammals and fishermen alike.

In 2024, an estimated 410 million pounds of Atlantic menhaden was caught coastwide.

But menhaden isn’t the kind of fish you can easily buy at the supermarket.

Instead, roughly 20 percent of the U.S. catch is used as commercial bait for lobster and blue crab fisheries. The other 80 percent is reduced into fertilizer, livestock feed or dietary supplements, according to New Jersey Fish and Wildlife .

Rich in nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium, menhaden is a key ingredient in agricultural products, used to fertilize crops across the country. Originally developed by Indigenous communities , “reduction factories” today cook, press and dry the silvery species into micronutrient-filled scraps to spread across fields.

Since the mid-1980s, the explosion of aquaculture has also made the omega-3 and fatty acid-filled menhaden a prime commodity in the production of fishmeal, a protein-rich, dark-yellow powder used to feed farmed fish.

Using spotter planes and small aluminium chase boats, fishing fleets are able to rapidly deploy large purse seines that encircle dense schools of menhaden with a vertical wall of netting, including in the lower Chesapeake Bay’s vital menhaden nursery .

Though researchers have not proven these industrial fleets are the cause of osprey food depletion, some conservationists point to them as a possible factor.

The largest players in the menhaden reduction industry are Ocean Harvesters, an American fishing firm, and Omega Protein, a processor owned by Canadian aquaculture giant Cooke Seafood. As part of a long-standing partnership, Omega Protein processes roughly 70 percent of the coast’s menhaden catch, according to the Chesapeake Bay Foundation.

From their three menhaden plants in Virginia, Mississippi and Louisiana, Omega Protein produces fishmeal that’s shipped from Mexico to Greece. While 70 percent of Omega Protein’s 2025 sales remained in the U.S., much went to feeding the ever-growing $313 billion global aquaculture industry.

A spokesperson for Ocean Harvesters told Inside Climate News that “poor osprey breeding in parts of the Chesapeake Bay does not establish that commercial menhaden fishing caused the food stress or that further restricting the fishery would solve it.”

The spokesperson added that U.S. Geological Survey “scientists identified a range of factors that can affect osprey reproduction, including food availability, competition, disease, weather and environmental contaminants,” and highlighted similar osprey population trends in states without menhaden fisheries.

While Atlantic menhaden are “not overfished,” according to the Atlantic States Marine Fisheries Commission’s 2025 stock assessment, local anglers have reported an “alarming absence of menhaden” off New Jersey and New York.

Last month, a collection of recreational fishers and charter captains filed a petition to Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, calling for the prohibition of industrial menhaden “reduction fishing”—when catch is processed into fishmeal or fish oil rather than for direct human consumption—in the New York-New Jersey Bight. They warned in a press release that “the region’s fall fishing season and coastal economy are at risk,” and demanded permanent protections from May to December annually.

“Healthy fisheries are the backbone of our coastal economy, and those fisheries depend on [menhaden],” said Phil Sciortino of Tackle Box Fishing Co. in a press statement. “When industrial vessels remove massive quantities of these fish, the consequences ripple through our communities.”

Though Virginia is the only East Coast state that permits menhaden reduction fishing within its three-mile state waters, anglers in New York and New Jersey are far from the only mid-Atlantic residents calling for a change to fishing in federal waters, where menhaden fishing is currently allowed from three to 200 miles offshore.

Two Maryland Democrats, U.S. Sen. Chris Van Hollen and U.S. Rep. Sarah Elfreth, called last month for the regional fisheries commission to prioritize an ecosystem-based management approach to protect menhaden populations.

“Worrisome signs in the Chesapeake Bay — from dwindling osprey populations to reduced bait fishery landings — indicate that Atlantic Menhaden populations may be declining,” said the letter , signed by eight fellow House and Senate Democrats. “Atlantic menhaden are a public resource that benefit Atlantic coast communities in many ways, and so managing this species for long-term sustainability is key.”

A similar letter signed by 29 Maryland state lawmakers—22 Democrats and seven Republicans—in September noted: “Osprey chicks are starving at unprecedented levels in parts of the Bay where the birds depend heavily on menhaden.”

A spokesperson for Omega Protein told Inside Climate News that “fishermen and their families want healthy osprey populations, just as they want a healthy menhaden population. They also want decisions that affect their livelihoods to be based on evidence that identifies a problem, establishes its causes and demonstrates that a proposed restriction will help.”

Both Omega Protein and Ocean Harvesters said any reduction to quota allowances might result in facility closures and job losses, noting the Southern Christian Leadership Conference had urged Maryland Gov. Wes Moore to consider the benefits menhaden fishing provides African American working families.

Greg Kearns is a senior park naturalist at Patuxent River Park in Maryland.

For more than 40 years, he monitored ospreys along the Patuxent River and frequently partnered with Watts, including in 2024 on a bay-wide study comparing the river’s lower, saltier reaches with its upper, fresher waters. In one lower-river study area, he said, the number of osprey chicks that fledged fell from about 201 in 2019 to 11 this year.

“That’s a 95 percent decline in seven years,” he said.

Lower-river ospreys depend heavily on menhaden, Kearns said, whereas birds upriver feed more on gizzard shad and catfish. The upper-river population has also struggled, he noted, but “the freshwater birds are doing much better.” The difference made him question if changing weather patterns alone can explain the decline.

Cold, wet springs can delay fish movements, leaving returning ospreys short of food. But over the years, Kearns has increasingly come to see commercial menhaden fishing as a central driver, arguing that industrial harvests reduce the supply of larger, energy-rich fish the birds need.

“I am now convinced it is the menhaden,” he said.

Kearns questioned how fleets equipped with powerful boats, sonar and industrial equipment are managed amid uncertainty over fish population estimates, arguing that commercial interests wield too much influence over fishing decisions.

He acknowledged, however, that the causes of the decline have not been conclusively established and that more data is needed.

After decades of building and monitoring nest platforms, Kearns described the observed osprey decline as “stunning” and “shocking.” Speaking for himself rather than his employer, he warned that commercial fishing pressure could be pushing the bay’s ecosystem toward collapse.

For Will Poston, forage campaign manager at the Chesapeake Bay Foundation, some of the information needed to understand menhaden in the estuary remains out of public reach.

He said there was a single operator in the reduction fishery and confidentiality rules shield key catch records from public scrutiny, although some scientists and managers have had access to them. Menhaden are “a public resource that benefits the entirety of the commonwealth,” he noted.

The Chesapeake Bay Foundation and its partners have repeatedly sought funding for menhaden research in Virginia through legislation and budget amendments. But industry opposition delayed or defeated those efforts, Poston said, until a budget amendment from Gov. Abigail Spanberger in June secured $2 million for the Virginia Institute of Marine Science to carry out comprehensive bay-wide menhaden research in partnership with the Virginia Marine Resources Commission. Though the institute is now developing population studies, he said, getting any answers could take years.

Poston sees warning signs with osprey pairs producing fewer young, smaller menhaden catches among bait fishermen and an industrial reduction fishery falling short of its coastwide quota because there are already too few menhaden in the bay. Conservationists believe this is mainly due to heavy harvesting, but the industry challenges a causal link. Those signals, he argued, warrant reducing harvests even without a precise estimate of how much fish predators need.

“The recourse is the same,” he said. “Remove less menhaden” so more remain in the estuary.

Poston explained that the Chesapeake Bay Reduction Fishery Cap was intended as a precaution against the industry’s expansion within the estuary. First implemented in 2006, the cap was lowered several times in its early years, but has remained at 51,000 metric tons since 2018, despite coastwide limits fluctuating. The commission is now considering another reduction.

While coastwide catch limits draw on stock assessments and ecosystem-based science, he noted, comparable research for the bay remains limited.

He said technical committee projections called for a 39 percent reduction to stay within ecosystem-based management targets.

Just as advocates and researchers ponder if the regulators will heed the signs of an ecosystem in crisis because of the menhaden scarcity, Roberta Kellam plans to drive to Rhode Island to attend the Atlantic States Marine Fisheries Commission’s 2026 annual meeting, set for Nov. 9-12.

The commission will vote on whether to cut the Chesapeake Bay cap on the reduction fishery by up to half, and whether to spread that harvest across the season.

Kellam said she’s particularly concerned about this year’s decisions in view of the dwindling osprey population. She’s already sent comments calling for maximum limits to be placed on the menhaden catch coastwide.

According to the Chesapeake Bay Foundation, which supports the largest possible reduction, the commission received 42,000 comments on its proposal.

Dozens of groups partnering with the foundation and “tens of thousands of stakeholders from the public” provided comments supporting stronger measures, Poston said.

Omega Protein told Inside Climate News that it supported “management based on sound science,” but that it did not support further Chesapeake Bay restrictions until more research to inform such decisions had been produced.

The Atlantic states commission will also decide the coastwide menhaden catch limit for 2027 through 2029. The 2026 limit was set at 186,840 metric tons.

In modeled scenarios, the commission’s scientists tested a cut of 50 percent and found it led to a good chance of hitting the fishing target meant to leave enough menhaden for predators.
