scraped.title: Britain’s Data Center Boom Meets Growing Resistance - Inside Climate News
scraped.description: As Britain follows the United States in its bid to build for the AI future, its government is grappling with mounting resistance from those who find the industry moving in next door.
scraped.author: By Leana Carbonez
scraped.h1: Britain’s Data Center Boom Meets Growing Resistance
scraped.body_text:
Ambily Banerjee moved to Langley, in the borough of Slough, 18 miles west of London, for its good schools and green spaces.

Now, Microsoft is planning to move in nearby. Its proposed 140-megawatt data center, the company promises, will be a good neighbor.

It is the latest operator drawn to Slough for its fast fiber-optic connections to London and to major transatlantic subsea cables farther west, as well as its proximity to, but geographic separation from, the capital, offering security should London’s data infrastructure be compromised.

The borough is home to 40-plus data centers, with more in the pipeline, earning it a reputation as Europe’s data-center capital and placing its cluster among the largest in the world.

We deliver climate news to your inbox like nobody else. Every day or once a week, our original stories and digest of the web’s top headlines deliver the full story, for free.

Our #1 newsletter delivers the week’s climate and energy news – our original stories and top headlines from around the web.

Dan Gearino’s habit-forming weekly take on how to understand the energy transformation reshaping our world.

A once-a-week digest of the most pressing climate-related news, written by Kate Waxman and released every Tuesday.

Don’t miss a beat. Get a daily email of our original, groundbreaking stories written by our national network of award-winning reporters.

An inside look at top climate news, delivered every two weeks.

A digest of stories on the inequalities that worsen the impacts of climate change on vulnerable communities.

Recently, residents like Banerjee have begun to push back, questioning not only what the data-center boom has brought to the borough, but what its longer-term costs might be.

“Where is this supposed investment? Slough has not become Silicon Valley,” said Banerjee, a scientist and mother. “Residents shoulder all the risk, while developers sit in their ivory towers.”

Those questions are being asked far beyond Slough, and have increasingly found their way into electoral politics. In the 2026 U.S. midterms, opposition to the facilities helped Democrats make massive gains. Some 56 percent of voters said data centers were a major or crucial factor in their congressional choices, according to polling by The Wall Street Journal, even as the industry poured mammoth sums into defending its interests.

The British government has played a more direct coordinating role in data center development than its U.S. federal counterpart, giving projects greater weight in the planning system, incentivizing development in designated areas and accelerating planning decisions and grid access for developers that demonstrate specific public benefits.

It remains to be seen what electoral consequences the incumbent Labour Party’s approach will carry. The party, characterized as center-left and sharing similarities with the Democrats, has set out to triple its data center capacity by the decade’s end, dismissing the Green Party’s proposed moratorium, warning it “would be a disaster for jobs and national security.”

Its efforts to manage the industry’s expansion have also been accompanied by significant gaps in oversight, particularly around energy demand and environmental issues.

An investigation by Spotlight on Corruption, a nonprofit that advocates for government transparency, found that ministers and officials had consulted 137 businesses on data center expansion, but just two community groups and no environmental organizations. Government estimates of the sector’s energy demands have also differed by as much as tenfold, according to The Guardian .

Public confidence in how that expansion will be managed appears fragile. With 84 percent of Britons believing the government will “prioritize its partnerships with large technology companies over the public interest” when regulating AI, and sizable campaigns opposing development emerging in Devon, Scotland, Essex and London’s Brick Lane, the prospect of opposition derailing the industry’s expansion is not merely theoretical.

A report by the Sovereign AI Leadership (SAIL) taskforce, drawing on input from the likes of Nvidia, Microsoft and Cisco, warned that organized local opposition in the U.S. has already halted fully permitted data center projects, prompting moratoriums even in states otherwise supportive of development.

“Britain has a window—we think of roughly 12 months—to build a compact that earns public consent before that pattern takes hold,” the report said.

The U.K. is the third-largest AI market in the world after the U.S. and China. There are around 500 data centers across the U.K. Up to the end of 2025, around 90 percent were sited in England, with London alone accounting for nearly two-thirds of the national total.

The question of who benefits and who bears the cost took on new significance in Chancellor John Healey’s Oct. 28 budget, which announced a new British Data Centre Covenant . For developers, it set out a clear offer: faster, more certain access to grid connection in exchange for a “credible” commitment that they will not over-reserve, but will use and pay for the grid capacity they request, invest in clean power and net zero, deliver benefits for local residents and businesses and adhere to the “highest” environmental standards.

This comes amid Britain’s growing grid-connectivity problems, which have left some developers waiting years for access, and others forced to abandon projects altogether.

The connections queue, historically operated on a first-come, first-served basis, has become choked with speculative or unviable projects. Microsoft recently withdrew from a flagship data center project in Essex, developed by British startup Nscale, after it became clear it would not be connected to the grid until the 2030s.

There are 315 hyperscale data center projects awaiting access to the national grid, accounting for 73 GW of Britain’s demand connection queue, according to Ofgem, the U.K.’s energy regulator. Peak national demand in 2025 was around 45 GW.

The government is also trying to steer where facilities are built through its AI Growth Zones program, designed to attract investment to locations where data centers can more readily access power. In the past year, five such zones have been announced.

At times, regions generate more power than the grid can transmit elsewhere. Scotland, for example, can produce more wind power than its transmission lines can carry south. The government argues that locating data centers in such areas would allow them to absorb this otherwise-wasted generation, reducing costs across the electricity system. To encourage developers, the government is proposing discounts on electricity costs, expected to take effect in April 2027. For a 500-megawatt facility, the savings could reach around $32 per megawatt-hour in Scotland, $21 in Cumbria and $18 in the North East.

For local authorities, there is also a financial incentive: those in England’s AI Growth Zones will be able to retain 100 percent of additional tax revenue generated by new data center development for the next 25 years, providing a long-term source of funding for community projects and public services.

The government also plans to help developers build their own power infrastructure and give ministers greater control, taking planning decisions on “nationally significant” data center projects away from local councils.

The push reflects the scale of the market Britain hopes to capture. BloombergNEF expects installed data center capacity across Europe, the Middle East and Africa to reach 53.1 gigawatts by 2035, up from an estimated 19.2 gigawatts in the first quarter of 2026. The U.K. is projected to account for around 14.5 percent of that.

“There’s a massive gulf between where communities are at, and the discussions they want about data centers, and where political leaders are currently at. Local councils are opposing data centers, and elected councilors are turning down proposals, only for them to be approved at the national level,” said Owen Espley, campaigns manager at the environmental charity Global Action Plan.

On the government’s new Data Centre Covenant, he said: “Local groups don’t think it’s worth very much. They want the normal rules to apply to data centers.”

A recent investigation by Spotlight on Corruption found that environmental groups had been largely excluded from the government’s policymaking on data centers and AI Growth Zones.

It found that, alongside the lack of environmental organizations involved in shaping policy, the government’s Sustainability Working Group, established in January 2025 to examine the environmental impacts of artificial intelligence and related technology policy, met just once in its first 17 months, with no environmental organizations represented.

Donald Campbell, director of advocacy at Foxglove, a U.K. nonprofit that campaigns for greater accountability from technology companies and governments, argued that the government lacked the assessments and information needed to make decisions in the environment’s interest.

“There is a serious information gap around the impacts of hyperscale facilities, particularly how much energy they will consume, and the resulting emissions,” he said.

The government itself has struggled to establish the emissions data centers will produce. In April 2026, it revised its estimate to as much as 123 million tons of carbon dioxide over the next decade, or 12.3 million tons annually, up from a previous estimate of no more than 142,000 tons in a single year, according to The Guardian .

Research by Foxglove, using developers’ own estimates, found that the 10 largest data centers planned in the U.K. in 2025 could produce as much annual carbon emissions as the combined savings from Britain’s transition to electric vehicles.

Meanwhile, a new report commissioned by Global Action Plan and written by economist James Meadway estimates that data center expansion could add $3.48 billion to household electricity bills across the U.K. by 2035. The projection is based on the National Energy System Operator’s highest-growth scenario for the industry.

The increase could push 77,000 more households across England, Wales and Scotland into fuel poverty.

“With communities across the world questioning the value of these digital behemoths, the figures in this report raise urgent questions for government about their wholehearted support for U.S. Big Tech’s data center frenzy,” said Meadway.

Resistance to data center development is bringing people together across Britain. Concerns range from electricity costs and water shortages to noise, potential health impacts and anxieties about artificial intelligence. Campaign groups are increasingly sharing information, coordinating their efforts and looking to one another for examples of successful challenges. The campaigns vary in their demands, from tighter planning controls and greater transparency to outright moratoriums.

In the U.K., an additional concern is that the country could bear the environmental costs of an industry whose economic rewards flow disproportionately to the U.S.

“People are protesting because the U.K. is on course to build digital infrastructure that uses up our power and water while the economic benefits are extracted to Silicon Valley,” said Taylor Gese, U.K. lead at the Future of Tech Institute, a European think tank focused on technology policy and digital sovereignty, in a statement. “We cannot let U.S. hyperscalers monopolize this market—we must find ways to ensure the economic value from this infrastructure stays in the U.K.”

The race to build AI infrastructure is global; its consequences are local. Britain’s new Data Centre Covenant is an attempt to bridge that divide. Whether it will be enough to convince communities that they have a stake in the AI boom remains an open question.

scraped.body_text:

Δ

A nonprofit, independent media organization dedicated to telling stories of climate solutions and a just future.

Δ

A monster is growing in the Pacific — not the kraken, but something far scarier and deadlier. El Niño is a natural phenomenon in which a band of warm water forms every three to five years off the coast of South America. It raises ocean water temperatures by just a few extra degrees for typically nine to 12 months and ends up injecting an extraordinary amount of energy into the sky. It’s already the strongest El Niño on record , and it might not even peak for about another month or two.

“Those are actually really big changes for the ocean,” Art Miller, a climate scientist at the Scripps Institution of Oceanography, told Grist in September. “The ocean has a lot of heat content — 1,000 times more ability to hold heat than the atmosphere — so slight changes in the ocean surface temperatures can actually do a lot for the atmosphere.”

While scientists are still trying to figure out how climate change might be influencing El Niño, some research suggests that rising temperatures have led to stronger El Niño events. At the very least, we can use this event’s temporary warming to imagine what the climate will look like by default in two decades, as planetary temperatures continue to rise.

The effects of the current El Niño will be global, and they will be severe. Scientists have estimated that the additional heat alone could kill around 450,000 people worldwide. Drought is gripping some places, like the Amazon rainforest , while extreme rainfall hits others, like the Greater Horn of Africa . And the polar vortex — another phenomenon that periodically blasts the eastern and central United States with frigid air — interacts with El Niño in ways that can scramble weather even further . El Niño, then, won’t just fire heat into the atmosphere — it will fundamentally shift weather patterns the world over.

The atmospheric changes are so complex that different parts of the U.S. will endure vastly different impacts from El Niño. (There’s also a lot of uncertainty here: Models can predict general changes across regions, but no one can tell you what the weather will be in a given spot a month from now.) California, for example, typically sees increased rainfall and flooding. The Midwest might be relatively better off with a milder, drier winter, whereas the Southeast could get colder and wetter.

Which is all to say: Things are going to get very weird, and often very dangerous, across the U.S. To break it all down by region, Grist spoke to state climatologists and meteorologists. Here’s what they expect in the months ahead.

The National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration’s outlook for December through February predicts a warm North and a wet South. Darker shading means higher confidence in the forecast. Click a region to learn more.

Source: NOAA Climate Prediction Center seasonal outlook for December 2026 through February 2027. “Slightly favors” means a 33–50 percent chance, “favors” means 50 percent or more, and “equal chances” means no category is favored. Hawaiʻi is shaded from CPC’s Hawaiian Islands outlook. Puerto Rico and the Virgin Islands are unshaded; NOAA’s outlook suggests warmer temperatures in this region but publishes no corresponding probability.

Clayton Aldern / Grist

Alaska is America’s largest state and home to all of its Arctic territory. That makes it uniquely vulnerable to the effects of climate change, which is warming the region several times faster than the rest of the planet. El Niño years add a blast of heat on top of that warming, intensifying local effects in the short term.

A strong El Niño, like the current one, tends to strengthen the Aleutian Low, a broad area of low pressure over the North Pacific that helps shape Alaska’s winter weather. But El Niño is only one of many factors influencing the Low’s strength and location. Depending on how these conditions line up in any given year, the state could experience vastly different outcomes. That makes the effects of El Niño especially difficult to predict in Alaska, said Martin Stuefer, the state climatologist and director of the Alaska Climate Research Center at the University of Alaska Fairbanks.

“We have to be on the lookout for more intense events, that’s for sure,” Stuefer said. “But we should be cautious about making conclusions based on what we know now.”

Evidence from previous El Niño events indicates that populated regions along the Gulf of Alaska and the state’s southeast might experience warmer winter temperatures, and precipitation may fall as rain instead of snow, Stuefer said. According to the National Weather Service , most strong El Niño years have resulted in below-average snowfall in Alaska.

Anything that intensifies warming in the state isn’t welcome news. Climate change is already melting away sea ice, leaving Alaska’s vast shorelines exposed to erosion during storms. It’s also thawing permafrost — the frozen ground found across much of Alaska — to collapse. Meanwhile, warmer waters are setting the stage for harmful algae blooms and changing the distribution of fish species that Native Alaskans have depended on for generations. A strong El Niño in the coming months could add to these pressures.

— Sachi Mulkey

Hawaiʻi and the Pacific have had a tough year already, and El Niño threatens to cause even more disruption. Low-pressure storms known as Kona lows and hurricanes have hit Hawaiʻi throughout the summer and fall, leading to severe flooding and power outages. Elsewhere in the region, super-typhoons like Sinlaku made landfall, causing 17 deaths in the western Pacific.

In the coming months, Pacific islands are broadly expected to face drier conditions and stronger storms. According to the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration, for example, Guam and the Commonwealth of the Northern Mariana Islands are facing an above-normal typhoon season, which will build on an already destructive summer and fall period. The threat is in addition to the rising probability of storms, fueled by warming ocean waters due to climate change.

“It only takes one storm to come over the island to cause crazy rainfall and devastation,” said Ryan Longman, who is the consortium program director at the University of Hawaiʻi at Mānoa for the Pacific Islands Climate Adaptation Science Center.

The Pacific islands are also bracing for a drier winter and spring. In Hawaiʻi, a strong El Niño can lead to a drier wet season, which typically lasts from October to March. That could mean less water available for residential, agricultural, and commercial uses and elevated wildfire risk.

The landscape is currently thick with grass and other vegetation from a historically wet summer. As the climate shifts toward drier conditions, those fuels on the landscape will dry up, increasing the chances of wildfires. Longman suggested that residents clear dry grasses and other fuels from their properties to reduce their risk.

For some Pacific islands, historic patterns suggest that the worst drought effects come the year following El Niño’s onset, meaning the most severe impacts could arrive in early to mid-2027.

— Joseph Lee

The Midwest may catch a break when El Niño peaks this winter.

The cyclical climate pattern is mostly associated with milder, drier winters in the Midwest. El Niño shifts the polar jet stream — the band of fast-moving Arctic air high in the atmosphere — farther north, making it less likely that cold winds will dip into the region, resulting in warmer temperatures.

That doesn’t rule out snow and winter storms, though. It only means that average temperatures between December and February tend to be somewhat warmer. During recent strong El Niño events, winter temperatures ranged from 3 degrees Fahrenheit to more than 8 degrees F warmer than the 20th-century average, according to the U.S. Geological Survey .

The Midwest has already experienced a warmer fall this year, said Daria Kluver, a professor in the Department of Earth and Atmospheric Sciences at Central Michigan University. Average September temperatures across the region were the highest in the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration’s 132-year record. Illinois and Missouri had their warmest September on record; Wisconsin, Minnesota, Iowa, Indiana, and Michigan also saw above-average temperatures.

That warmth will continue into the winter. And reduced ice cover on the Great Lakes could contribute to the warmer temperatures, Kluver said. Without as much ice, warmth stored in the lakes over the summer is likely to slowly dissipate into the surrounding air. The changes in ice cover could impact Great Lakes economies, recreation , and the ecosystems that depend on it.

Fall has been dry so far, but winter might not be. Kluver said precipitation levels will depend on other dynamics like Arctic sea-ice levels and Atlantic Ocean currents. But the El Niño typically tilts the odds toward less snowfall and more rain or ice.

“Whether you find that good or bad maybe depends on what you do for winter recreation,” Kluver said.

El Niño could also mean a reprieve from the Midwest’s record-setting tornadoes next year, according to Chris Callahan, a climate scientist and assistant professor at Indiana University Bloomington.

“We are likely to have a relatively quiet tornado season in the spring, because those tornadoes are shifted south into [states] like Arkansas, Georgia, and so they might have a more active tornado season,” Callahan said.

— Vivian La and Juanpablo Ramirez-Franco

The Northeast has so far avoided El Niño’s impacts — but that’s about to change.

Brad Pugh, a meteorologist with the National Weather Service’s extended prediction division, said the unusually strong El Niño this year gives the Northeast more than a 50 percent chance of a milder-than-normal winter. There could also be more precipitation, he added, though those odds will vary within the region. While areas farther east are generally more likely to be wet, he said, “it’s hard to tell how much is going to be rain or snow.”

Government outlooks don’t include snow totals because snow is difficult to predict far ahead. But the winter outlook from AccuWeather , a private forecasting company, projects fewer flakes for the Northeast. That, however, doesn’t mean the region won’t see snow, Pugh added.

“The forecast leaning on the wetter side does raise the prospects that there could be some high-impact winter storms,” he said, pointing to the I-95 corridor between New York and Boston as one area that could be hit. He suggested keeping an eye on the NWS’ eight- to 14-day forecasts to get a more accurate and timely sense of what weather may be on the way.

Even water that falls as rain could be concerning, said Auroop Ganguly, a hydrologist and co-director of Northeastern University’s Global Resilience Institute. “If I were an urban planner, I’d plan more for the possibility of flooding in urban areas,” he said. A mix of rain, snow, and ice on the roads could also make driving dangerous. “I’d prepare for somewhat more hazardous conditions on the roads.”

Still, many in the region may welcome El Niño’s arrival, especially after last winter, which was the coldest in a decade . Milder temperatures this year could, for example, lower heating needs at a time when heating oil and electricity prices are spiking.

As for the prospect of a warmer winter in the Northeast, said Ganguly, “Most people would say, ‘I’ll take it.'”

— Tik Root

There is less certainty about the total El Niño impacts for the Northern Great Plains compared to the rest of the country. Nebraska, Montana, and the Dakotas are expecting a warmer-than-average winter, but rain and snowfall forecasts across these states are less conclusive.

In Nebraska, some of those effects may already be emerging. Earlier this fall, the eastern part of the state experienced milder temperatures and heavy rain, leading to flash flooding. Wetter-than-normal conditions are likely to continue in eastern Nebraska through winter, increasing the risk of additional floods, said Eric Hunt, a University of Nebraska-Lincoln agriculture meteorology and climate resilience extension educator. The state could still see intense winter storms, and western Nebraska could experience a wetter winter, though those forecasts are less certain.

Farther north in the Dakotas, the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration has forecasted a 40 percent to 60 percent chance of higher average temperatures from December to February. For North Dakota, that still means average temperatures below freezing. Winter also tends to be dry in both states, and forecasts for precipitation are variable, according to both states’ climatologists.

In South Dakota, a snowy winter could alleviate drought, replenish surface water, and reduce fire risk in the Black Hills, said state climatologist Laura Edwards. A dry winter in the state could be a tipping point for drought conditions next spring.

In North Dakota, it’s not clear if any precipitation this winter would improve drought conditions, said Daryl Ritchison, North Dakota state climatologist and director of the North Dakota Agricultural Weather Network. One winter storm could push seasonal totals above average for precipitation for the season, but if the winter remains dry and spring rains are slow to arrive, fire risk might increase.

Montana faces much of the same uncertainty. In the Northern Rockies, the odds favor a below-average snow year — but only slightly, said Kyle Bocinsky, the director of climate extension with the Montana Climate Office. Montana has experienced four strong El Niño events in the past 40 years; three saw below-normal precipitation and snowpack, but one saw above-normal snowpack. “It’s a small sample size,” Bocinsky said, which makes it hard to definitively say what the impacts will be. “It’s still a fifty-fifty chance,” he said.

Bocinsky said warmer temperatures could make for a rainy winter similar to last year, particularly at lower elevations. Like much of the Great Plains, eastern Montana is still in drought carried over from last year’s mild winter. Farmers and ranchers are hoping snow settles on the landscape this year, but it’s just too soon to tell, he said.

— Ellis Juhlin and Anila Yoganathan

The Pacific Northwest typically sits in the center lane of a storm highway. Every winter, ocean storms travel across this familiar route, delivering a steady supply of the cool, drizzly weather that gives the region its gloomy charm. But El Niño is likely to reroute this storm track to the south, dumping rain onto sunny California instead. This often leaves the Northwest warmer, and sometimes drier, than usual.

That combination could be a double whammy for mountain snow, which is the main source of water for much of the Northwest, since snow can’t form if it’s too warm or too dry. “If we were to get both of those this year — both the warmer temperatures and less precipitation — that could spell trouble for our snowpack,” said Jacob Genuise, an engagement climatologist at the Washington State Climate Office.

Climate change is also slowly chipping away at snow levels. Since the mid-20th century, snow levels in Washington’s Cascades have been steadily decreasing in both El Niño and La Niña years alike. These factors could lead to less snow stored in the mountains for next spring and summer, driving up the risk of drought or wildfires, and leaving less water available for irrigation, drinking water, or hydropower.

On the coast, El Niño can also lead to more tidal flooding. As ocean and wind patterns shift across the Pacific, seawater can get pushed toward the West Coast, raising high tide levels by several inches. This extra tidal boost could also combine with sea level rise, storm surges, or winter king tides to drive up the flood risk in Washington’s and Oregon’s coastal communities. “It’s not a huge effect,” said Genuise. “But that can mean the difference between a property getting flooded or not during these El Niño years.”

— Jesse Nichols

El Niño often delivers rain and snow to the Southwest and could bring a glimmer of hope to a region suffering historic drought. Jon Meyer, assistant state climatologist at the Utah Climate Center, expects the weather pattern to bring “favorable storm activity” to the desert Southwest, including Arizona and New Mexico, with effects bleeding into Nevada and parts of southern Utah and southern Colorado.

But northern Utah, which is home to most of the state’s population, “is right in the bull’s-eye of being very unpredictable,” he said. Colorado’s outlook is also mixed. El Niño tends to bring more precipitation in spring and fall, but it also typically creates drier conditions for the Northern Rockies, said Peter Goble, assistant state climatologist at the Colorado Climate Center.

“The strong El Niño, as interesting a story as it’s been,” he said, “doesn’t guarantee us anything.”

The region is in dire need of snowpack in the winter months ahead. Utah’s Great Salt Lake hovers just a few inches above eclipsing the record-low elevation it set in 2022, and its vast exposed lake bed is drying into a dust source impacting the health of the roughly 2.5 million residents living in cities near its shores. Meanwhile, Lake Mead and Lake Powell, the nation’s largest reservoirs, saw a fraction of their normal inflows from the Colorado River and set their own record lows over the fall. Around 40 million people in the West depend on water supplies delivered by the Colorado River system.

The early autumn run-up to the super El Niño has already brought downpours, sending torrents through city streets and arroyos across the region. Arizona is already facing flash flooding and could now see tornadoes and other extreme weather, according to meteorologists at AccuWeather.

More moisture would boost desiccated reservoirs and reduce sleepless nights for farmers, but experts are already repeating an all-too-familiar warning: One good year won’t solve the region’s water woes. Western states saw record-breaking snow in 2023. Today, that moisture is gone, and both the Rio Grande and Colorado River basins look more stressed than ever. Climatologists say those extreme oscillations will become more common as climate change heats up the region.

— Austin Corona and Leia Larsen

For the notoriously hot and humid Southeastern U.S., El Niño typically has two main effects: It gets wetter and it can bring bouts of cold weather. In general, climate change is making the Southeast warmer and more susceptible to both drought and heavy rainfall events, and winter temperatures drop below freezing far less often. But that long-term warming trend doesn’t rule out frigid winter days and nights this year.

The wet weather comes down to the same forces that inundate the Southwest during an El Niño cycle, according to Chuck Watson, a Georgia-based disaster researcher who tracks weather impacts worldwide.

“That jet of air that’s coming across California continues on across the Gulf of Mexico and drags moisture from the Gulf and whatever was left over after it rained all over California,” he said. “It drags that across the Southeast.”

The National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration is predicting enough rainfall between mid-October and the end of January to improve or eliminate drought conditions in several parts of the region, which has grappled with an unusual level of drought over the last year. The period from September 2025 through April 2026 was the driest in Georgia history, fueling wildfires in the spring that destroyed homes and forced evacuations; other states in the region also saw precipitation levels at or near record lows over the same period. As a result, the U.S. Department of Agriculture declared disasters due to drought in more than 200 counties in the spring.

El Niño might also bring ice storms. The wet air moving east from California typically interacts with a flow of Arctic air high in the atmosphere, Watson said, creating the potential for colder weather. For a region that doesn’t deal with sustained temperatures too far below freezing most winters, the combination often means ice storms that people and infrastructure aren’t accustomed to.

“That’s really just a recipe that’s ripe for disaster,” Watson said. “That tends to be just bad news all around for tree limbs falling and slick roads and particularly extended power outages.”

One piece of good news for much of the Southeast is that El Niño typically suppresses hurricane formation in the Atlantic . So while Hurricane Isaias wreaked havoc when it hit the region in early October, it was also the first Atlantic hurricane this year — an incredibly rare occurrence .

But the reprieve from tropical systems doesn’t apply equally, Watson said. El Niño’s effect on the complex upper air currents that steer hurricanes actually makes the band across South Florida and the Bahamas more likely to be hit by a hurricane, he said.

— Emily Jones

When it rains, it pours. El Niño is expected to bring much-needed relief to the drought-stricken Southern Great Plains. The upcoming event is significant enough that the Texas Railroad Commission, a state agency that oversees oil and gas production, recently issued a notice warning operators that “this event may be outside the historical envelope” and that “past El Niño events may not be a good guide to this event.”

But unless this winter is exceptionally wet, it is unlikely to eliminate drought conditions entirely.

That’s because a wet winter won’t ease every impact at once, and different sectors may see varying effects, said Andrew Hoell, a research meteorologist with the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration. Depleted aquifers, for instance, may take years to return to normal levels, whereas agriculture might rebound quickly depending on when and where the rain falls.

In Texas, El Niño tends to increase seasonal snowfall totals in the north and west, but not for the rest of the state, said state climatologist John Nielsen-Gammon.

“Over the longer term, the warming trend in place over the past several decades is expected to continue,” said Nielsen-Gammon, referring to climate change. A 2024 report that he authored concluded that “extreme rainfall is strongly affected by increased temperatures.”

Meanwhile, El Niño’s effects in Kansas are less certain because of the state’s central U.S. location. Hoell described Kansas as a “toss-up” in a “transition zone” and emphasized that regional impacts in northern Kansas may be more pronounced.

If the past is any indication, though, Kansas too might be in for a wetter winter. The National Weather Service in Wichita examined 11 strong to very strong El Niños since 1950 and concluded the event produced above-average precipitation across Kansas from fall through early to mid-spring.

— Celeste Guajardo

Like a camel stumbling into a desert oasis, California could soon get more water than it can possibly use all at once. El Niño can bestow the Golden State with increased rainfall — so much extra water, in fact, that Governor Gavin Newsom has declared a state of emergency to prepare the state to fight coastal flooding and erosion (partly due to an oceanic “Kelvin wave” slamming into California ) and monster storms.

The built environment wasn’t made for this. For centuries, the mantra has been to funnel rainwater into sewers and rivers as quickly as possible to keep it from flooding cities. Climate change is already making it rain harder , pushing wastewater systems to their limits. Now comes El Niño, supercharging rainfall even further. Worst case, this winter the state gets successions of the punishing storms known as atmospheric rivers, saturating soils and overwhelming sewers. That could overwhelm crops in the state’s bountiful Central Valley and dump dangerous amounts of snow in its Sierra Nevada mountains to the east.

California has been preparing for this moment , though. Los Angeles, for example, is deploying “sponge” infrastructure like roadside gardens, which allow rainwater to soak into the ground instead of pooling on streets. (Over just a few rainy days in 2024, the city captured enough stormwater to supply 106,000 households for a year .) The state has also been working with farmers to divert rain into open spaces, where it can seep into the dirt and recharge underlying aquifers . “Essentially, the top line is: flood-safe and recharge-ready,” said Steven Springhorn, supervising engineering geologist in the California Department of Water Resources’ sustainable groundwater management office. “Flood safety and flood response is our number one priority going into a year like this.”

Counterintuitively, extreme rainfall could also prime the California landscape to burn catastrophically. More water means more plant growth, which desiccates through the summer — and this one could be extra hot if El Niño remains strong — turning into tinder. The wildfire danger could be particularly acute next fall, when intense seasonal winds can turn a spark into an inescapable blaze . With the state already cycling between extra-dry and extra-wet periods thanks to climate change , El Niño could literally add more fuel to the fire.

— Matt Simon

scraped.body_text:

You may have heard about El Niño — the natural, recurring phenomenon that releases heat from the ocean into the atmosphere, influencing temperature and precipitation around the world. Its effects will differ this fall and winter depending on where you live, but heavy rainfall, flooding, and snowfall are some of the most likely impacts.

There’s a lot of information available on navigating extreme weather, so we came up with five things you can do to prepare right now, from packing an emergency kit and bookmarking your local National Weather Service page to knowing how to stay safe around floodwaters.

Your city or county has an emergency management department, which is part of the local government. Emergency managers are responsible for communicating with the public about disasters, managing rescue and response efforts, and coordinating among various agencies. They usually have an SMS-based emergency alert system, so sign up for those texts now. Some also have an app you can download.

If you’re having trouble finding your local department, you can search for your state or territory here — but it’s easier to type your city or county name followed by “emergency management” into Google to quickly find the closest agency in your area. In larger cities, emergency management is often a standalone agency; in smaller communities, fire chiefs or sheriffs may manage emergency response and alerts.

To support our nonprofit environmental journalism, please consider disabling your ad-blocker to allow ads on Grist. Here's How

If you’re not signed up for alerts from your utility company about power outages in your area, now is the time to do that, too. Your utility company likely has an app or dedicated website for reporting outages and tracking when power will return. For example, the Nebraska Public Power District, the power company that serves Nebraska, has an outage map here , as well as a mobile app .

Many people find out about disasters in their area via social media, so it’s important to make sure the information you’re receiving is correct. Below is a list of reliable sources to check and our guide to spotting misinformation about extreme weather.

This agency, called NWS, is part of the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration, or NOAA, and offers information and updates on everything from wildfires to hurricanes to air quality. You can enter your ZIP code on weather.gov and customize your homepage to get the most up-to-date information and receive alerts for a variety of weather conditions. The NWS also has regional and local branches where you can sign up for SMS alerts . Local alerts in multiple languages are available in some areas.

If you’re in a rural area or somewhere that isn’t highlighted on the agency’s maps, keep an eye out for local alerts and evacuation orders. NWS may not have as much information ahead of time in these areas because there often aren’t as many weather monitoring stations.

Grist thanks its sponsors. Become one .

To support our nonprofit environmental journalism, please consider disabling your ad-blocker to allow ads on Grist. Here's How

“Watch” versus “warning”: You’ll often see meteorologists refer to storm watches or warnings. If a “watch” is issued, that means the conditions are ripe for extreme weather. A warning, however, means the threat is more imminent, and you should be prepared to take shelter or evacuate if told to.

You can track extreme weather via these websites:

The local television news and social media accounts from verified news sources will have live updates during and after a storm. Meteorologists on your local news station use NWS weather data. Follow your local newspaper, radio station, and television station on Facebook or other social media, or check their websites regularly. If you don’t have cable, these stations often livestream online for free during severe weather. Your local news may also have a live blog that is updated regularly.

The Weather Channel, AccuWeather, Apple Weather, and Google, which all rely on NWS weather data, will have information on major storms. That may not be the case for smaller-scale weather events, and you shouldn’t rely on these apps to tell you if you need to evacuate or move to higher ground. Instead, check your local news broadcast on television or radio, or check NWS.

Trying to fact-check during a crisis is stressful, and extreme weather makes you feel like there’s a lot to figure out in a short period of time. That’s why it’s important to know ahead of time who you can trust, how to vet information, and how to talk to your friends and family about it. Here’s a guide from Grist about how to spot misinformation.

It’s important to have an emergency kit ready in case you lose power or need to leave your home. Review this checklist from the Federal Emergency Management Agency for what to pack so you can stay safe, hydrated, and healthy. (FEMA has these resources available in multiple languages here .)

These can often be expensive to create, so contact your local disaster aid organizations, houses of worship, or charities to see if there are free or affordable kits available — or buy one or two items every time you’re at the grocery store. Ideally, this will be packed well in advance of hurricane or fire season, so gather as much as you can ahead of time in case shelves are empty when a storm is on the way. If you’re facing possible heavy snow, it’s a good idea to have an emergency kit in your vehicle as well.

FEMA has activities for kids to make this process more fun; the American Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals also has useful guidelines for people with pets.

Here are some of the most important things to have in your kit:

Wirecutter , Wired , Popular Mechanics , and some other news outlets have “best of” lists for many of these items, where you can find different price points and features. You can also find reviews on Consumer Reports .

One of the most important things to have in your emergency kit is documents you may need to prove your residence, demonstrate the extent of damage, and vote . FEMA often requires you to provide these documents in order to receive financial assistance after a disaster. Keep these items in a water- and fire-proof folder or container. You can find more details about why you may need these documents here .

Disabled people have a right to all disaster alerts in a format that is accessible. The Partnership for Inclusive Disaster Strategies, a disability-led nonprofit focused on disasters, has a list of these rights. The organization also runs a hotline for any questions: (800) 626-4959 or [email protected] . FEMA has a list of specific planning steps for people with disabilities. Some of these recommendations include:

It’s impossible to know what might happen to your home during a disaster, but there are many best practices to keep your belongings and property as safe as possible.

Here are some ways to protect your home and valuables from flooding, based on tips from the National Flood Insurance Program and local government sources:

The list below contains tips from several sources, including FEMA and the U.S. Energy Department, on protecting your home from frigid temperatures:

Here are some best practices if your power goes out, or you come into contact with downed power lines:

Here are some best practices when coming into contact with heavy rains or floodwaters:

If you’re facing heavy snowfall, ice storms, or freezing temperatures, here are some important things to know:

For more information about our work around disaster resources, check out Disaster 101 . Contact us if you’d like to collaborate on distributing this information in your community: [email protected] . ​

scraped.title: What to expect as world leaders gather for COP31
scraped.description: With few sweeping commitments expected, negotiators will tackle unfinished business on climate finance, fossil fuels, and the future of COP.
scraped.author: Joseph Winters
scraped.h1: What to expect as world leaders gather for COP31
scraped.body_text:
We hand-package the week’s best Grist stories . Delivered free every Saturday morning.

We hand-package the week’s best Grist stories . Delivered free every Saturday morning.

Δ

A nonprofit, independent media organization dedicated to telling stories of climate solutions and a just future.

Δ

World leaders convene in Antalya, Turkey, on Monday for the United Nations’ 31st Conference of the Parties, or COP31 , after another year of deadly climate disasters. Forest fires in Canada , Indonesia , and Brazil impacted millions of people. Heat waves contributed to more than 50,000 deaths in Europe. Floods prompted by the collapse of a melting glacier killed more than 1,500 people in Nepal and caused nearly $5 billion in damages.

And things may only get worse. This will be the first COP since the U.N.’s sobering report on the inevitability of breaching 1.5 degrees Celsius (2.7 degrees Fahrenheit) of global warming. That temperature target was a focal point for climate ambition even before the landmark 2015 Paris Agreement , with scientists warning that exceeding that benchmark could push the planet past dangerous tipping points , triggering climatic changes that may be impossible to reverse.

Despite the urgent need for action, few expect COP31, co-hosted by Turkey and Australia, to produce another breakthrough like the Paris Agreement or COP28’s call to transition away from fossil fuels .

“There’s a whole bunch of decisions that have to be taken, but none of them on their own is going to make headlines,” said Kaveh Guilanpour, vice president of international strategies for the nonprofit Center for Climate and Energy Solutions.

Grist thanks its sponsors. Become one .

To support our nonprofit environmental journalism, please consider disabling your ad-blocker to allow ads on Grist. Here's How

This is in part due to the nature of the negotiations. This year’s event is being referred to as an “implementation” COP, where countries will focus on fleshing out existing commitments under the Paris Agreement rather than making sweeping new ones. The bulk of the official agenda aims to chip away at workstreams that began last year or at previous meetings.

But it’s also related to the state of the world. Although the historic “blue wave” in the midterm election means Democrats could curb the Trump administration’s rollback of federal climate policy, the global outlook remains bleak. Wars and economic turmoil continue to strain multilateral negotiations, and many wealthy countries have limited international aid. “In the current geopolitics, just delivering on housekeeping is news in itself,” Guilanpour said.

Here’s what to watch for.

The ‘housekeeping’ COP

Grist thanks its sponsors. Become one .

To support our nonprofit environmental journalism, please consider disabling your ad-blocker to allow ads on Grist. Here's How

Much of the agenda involves the less visible work of assessing where things stand and putting previous agreements into practice. Countries are set to discuss, for example, the beginning of the next “ global stocktake ,” the assessment of climate progress that takes place every five years under the Paris Agreement.

They’ll also talk about ways of measuring progress toward the “ global goal on adaptation ” that delegates agreed to last year in Brazil, and they’ll consider whether to extend a “ mitigation work programme ” that kicked off in 2022 to encourage faster and more extensive emissions reductions in line with international climate targets.

Countries are also expected to formally create the “ just transition mechanism ” discussed last year. Broadly, it will aim to boost international coordination and support for a transition away from fossil fuels — for example, by providing job retraining for those employed in the oil and gas industry, or transferring carbon-free technologies from rich countries to poor ones.

“This is a sort of roll-up-your-sleeves-and-get-work-done COP,” said David Waskow, International Climate Initiative director for the World Resources Institute.

Where’s the money?

Climate finance has been a “perennial” discussion, said Jennifer Allan, a senior lecturer in international relations at Cardiff University, and this year wealthy countries will face renewed questions about funding they’ve pledged but failed to deliver .

August’s catastrophic flooding in Nepal illustrates the scale of the problem. Last month, the disaster triggered the first allocation from the U.N. Fund for Responding to Loss and Damage. Yet the $21.6 million payout was not even 1 percent of the damages the country sustained.

The fund itself has little more to offer. About $826 million has been pledged to underwrite it, but only some $450 million has been delivered.

Developing countries successfully lobbied for a “work stream” on climate finance in the COP31 agenda. This could give delegates an opportunity to discuss aligning existing financial flows with climate action and to flesh out a vague promise they made last year to triple adaptation financing by 2035.

But many of the world’s richest countries have curtailed international aid in response to growing energy insecurity, high inflation, global conflict, and other factors. The Trump administration has effectively cut all international climate finance , and Guilanpour said the remaining donor nations “unfortunately just wouldn’t support an increase in climate finance.” A memo circulated among European Union members made clear that there is “ no appetite ” for committing more money.

Fossil fuels in a post-1.5 future

It took nearly 30 years, until COP28 in 2023, for the conferences to even mention “fossil fuels,” let alone commit to transitioning away from them. But at last year’s meeting in Brazil, delegates failed to make any new commitments on how they’d do it.

Observers hope COP31 will address that unfinished business and the new post-1.5 degree climate reality. Waskow said countries should “reaffirm the need to reduce emissions dramatically, but also ramp up what we’re doing on carbon removal from the atmosphere.”

Still, these issues — especially anything about fossil fuels — are unlikely to appear in the formal negotiating agenda. Turkey and Australia remain heavily invested in coal, oil, and gas, and Axel Michaelowa, an economist at the University of Zurich, said they lack the credibility needed for strong leadership. Turkey has instead promoted, as part of an “action agenda” that is also not on the negotiating schedule, a goal of electrifying 35 percent of the world’s energy consumption by 2035, up from 23 percent today. That is more palatable, Miachaelowa said, because it doesn’t specify that the electricity come from renewable sources.

Any of those high-level goals and statements could appear on the COP’s “cover decision,” a statement reached by consensus at the end of each conference. These texts often don’t represent legally binding treaty commitments but have political value, Waskow said, because they can serve as signposts for later negotiations. Battles over the decision’s final wording have in previous COPs led to dramatic, late-night battles over a single word .

Fixing the COPs

An outsize focus on headline-making decisions, however, may be part of the COPs’ broader problem. “We seem to be trapped in this one-year cycle of expecting a historic outcome … every year,” Guilanpour said.

“What we should be thinking about is a so-called ‘big COP’ every five years,” he added, referring to the cycle of stocktakes when countries are supposed to ratchet up their emissions-reduction commitments. Seen this way, COP31 is a prelude to COP33, when the next stocktake is scheduled to conclude.

Erika Lennon, a senior attorney for the nonprofit Center for International Environmental Law, said she often worries that the conferences are a sort of a “circus,” where countries emphasize flashy pledges over implementing their commitments. Still, she added, the U.N. process is the best we have, and there are several ways of making it more effective, including better decision-making protocols and stricter conflict-of-interest policies.

Rachel Cleetus, climate program director for the nonprofit Union of Concerned Scientists, said it’s “unfair” to place the blame for stagnation solely on the U.N. climate regime. Ultimately, she said, countries must carry out the emissions reductions that science says are needed.

“These kinds of large multilateral negotiations are just one part of what it will take,” Cleetus said. “Then countries have to go home and act on what they’ve promised.”

Elaine Chen

Elaine’s stories explore the boom in new obesity treatments, new drug payment models, the ways companies are affected by FDA changes, and the emerging psychedelics drug sector. She co-writes The Readout newsletter , and co-hosts STAT’s weekly biotech podcast, The Readout Loud . You can reach Elaine on Signal at elaineywchen.70.

Elizabeth Cooney

Liz covers cardiovascular and metabolic disease, asking why we’re not doing better or even losing ground against the world’s leading killer. Send tips on Signal at LizC.22.

The Food and Drug Administration on Monday approved Bayer’s drug to reduce recurrence of stroke, making available the first in a novel class of medications that hold the promise of preventing blood clots more safely.

Many blood thinners aren’t used in this setting due to their increased risk of bleeding. But Bayer’s drug, which will be sold under the brand name Sunharbo, inhibits a protein called XIa, utilizing a mechanism that’s thought to stop the formation of bad clots without increasing the risk of bleeding.

Advertisement

In a Phase 3 trial that enrolled people who had already had a stroke and were taking common stroke treatments, 8.4% of participants who took placebo experienced a secondary stroke, while 6.2% of patients who took Sunharbo experienced one, translating into a 26% risk reduction. Another way to look at the data is that in one year, 53 patients need to be treated for one recurrent stroke to be prevented.

After months of skirmishing, the Trump administration removed WuXi AppTec, a key contract developer and manufacturer for the pharmaceutical industry, from its list of “Chinese military companies” operating in the U.S.

The Department of Defense took this step to comply with a court ruling last August, according to a notice with the Federal Register. At the time, a U.S. District Court judge temporarily blocked the administration from pursuing the designation after WuXi filed a lawsuit arguing it was arbitrary and capricious under the Administrative Procedure Act.

Advertisement

Two months earlier, the administration had placed WuXi AppTec on the list over concerns that the company has ties to the Chinese government and military, and that U.S. biotech leadership is at risk due to growing competition from Chinese companies. WuXi is seen by China hawks in Washington as a rising threat to national security.

scraped.title: Chinese AI firms want Silicon Valley’s top minds. Poaching them won’t be easy
scraped.description: As MiniMax, Moonshot, and ByteDance open U.S. offices to recruit elite AI researchers, they face massive salary gaps, fierce competition, and potential national security scrutiny.
scraped.h1: Chinese AI firms want Silicon Valley’s top minds. Poaching them won’t be easy
scraped.body_text:
Innovation

Startups like MiniMax and Moonshot are setting up U.S. outposts, but massive pay gaps, weaker prestige, and national security tensions make luring talent away from OpenAI and Anthropic an uphill climb.

Chinese AI companies are hiring Silicon Valley-based engineers to work on their models, potentially tapping into the talent at American labs like OpenAI and Anthropic.

MiniMax, the Hong Kong-listed Chinese AI startup, currently has around 16 San Francisco-based job openings listed on its website, including for a research lead focused on developing its core AI model . The company is also recruiting specialists in finance, law, life sciences, and cybersecurity, as well as a lead recruiter to attract top AI talent in Silicon Valley and Seattle.

Moonshot AI, the Chinese company behind the Kimi AI model, is looking for U.S.-based “ solutions architects ,” who will “help enterprise customers integrate its AI models into their businesses.”

American AI companies, with their deep pockets, have attracted global talent, including many Chinese engineers, by offering high compensation and opportunities to work on the world’s best models. In comparison, Chinese companies have so far largely relied on homegrown talent. Hiring in the U.S. reflects a strategic shift by Chinese companies as they look to compete and stay close to one of their most lucrative markets, experts said.

“Wanting to establish research teams in Silicon Valley makes perfect sense for Chinese AI companies seeking access to talent and the latest developments in the industry,” Cheryl Wu, a researcher in the economics of AI at Yale University and global think tank GovAI, told Rest of World .

More than half of the world’s top AI researchers complete their undergraduate studies in China, a September study by research center Carnegie China said, based on the educational backgrounds of people who published papers at NeurIPS, one of the world’s leading AI conferences.

Yet the U.S. remains a global magnet for AI talent, the study concluded.

In 2025, the U.S. saw a net gain of 2,145 researchers while China recorded a net loss of 1,729, according to the analysis.

China’s AI companies have been trying to lure top Chinese researchers at American AI labs to return home. One high-profile example is Tencent, which recruited former OpenAI researcher Yao Shunyu to lead its AI research.

Chinese companies are seeking “little geniuses” who have worked at companies like OpenAI and Anthropic, a headhunter recruiting for Chinese labs in the Bay Area told Rest of World , requesting anonymity as she is not authorized to speak to the media.

These attempts, however, have not had much success because Chinese companies often struggle to match the salaries paid by their Silicon Valley peers.

“It’s money. Chinese companies simply don’t have enough of it to offer competitive wages for talent,” said Wu, who published a report examining Chinese AI companies’ financing with research institute Epoch AI. “They have only recently begun raising more substantial funding and still lag far behind their U.S. competitors.”

There is a stark gap between what Chinese and American AI companies pay employees.

MiniMax spent $84.3 million on employee remuneration in 2025, equivalent to roughly $203,000 per person, based on its year-end head count of 415, according to its financial filings . The annualized remuneration costs of Z.AI, another Hong Kong-listed Chinese AI lab, in the first half of 2026 amounted to $140,000 per employee. Neither company disclosed a breakdown of pay for engineers or researchers, and both figures include share-based compensation and staff across all departments.

In comparison, OpenAI advertises annual base salaries of $250,000 to $445,000 for research engineers in San Francisco, before equity awards. Three Chinese researchers working in Silicon Valley say it’s common for their peers to get an annual compensation package worth more than $1 million.

As of September, China’s six leading AI firms collectively generated only about 10% of the combined AI-related revenue of OpenAI and Anthropic, according to Wu’s research.

“Career prospects are another factor. Even senior Meta engineers might accept a lower-ranking position to join Anthropic because of its work on frontier AI,” Wu said. “That makes it even harder to persuade top talent to join a lab whose models are just not at the cutting edge.”

Chinese tech companies are now ramping up their salary game. If an AI researcher had offers from OpenAI or Anthropic, ByteDance’s frontier model division Seed would try to lure them with a competing offer that’s 1.5 times higher, according to a person familiar with the team.

Wu Yonghui, a veteran AI researcher who worked at Google for 17 years, joined Seed as the head of research in early 2025. Seed currently lists 71 positions in San Jose, San Diego, and Seattle.

But even with matching pay, three Chinese researchers working in the U.S. told Rest of World they preferred American companies for better work-life balance and the chance to work on frontier models.

“I think most of the top Chinese talent would feel pretty comfortable in Silicon Valley; it’s the only other place where “ 996 ” isn’t really frowned upon,” Damien Ma, director of Carnegie China, told Rest of World , referring to the demanding work culture common in China’s tech industry, where employees work from 9 a.m. to 9 p.m., six days a week.

Washington has spent years restricting Chinese companies’ access to advanced Nvidia chips, and is scrutinizing their use of overseas data centers and cloud services. But no comparable restrictions prevent Chinese AI companies from establishing U.S. operations and hiring engineers there.

Both Washington and Beijing are increasingly seeking to protect their most advanced AI technologies from each other.

The Chinese government proposed export controls on some of the country’s most advanced AI models, particularly those trained using the country’s “important data,” despite specifications.

U.S. officials and American AI companies, meanwhile, have accused Chinese AI labs of using unauthorized distillation techniques to replicate their models’ capabilities. On other sensitive tech fronts, like the semiconductor industry, the U.S. has already restricted some American engineers from working in Chinese facilities without a license.

While neither country has imposed a blanket ban on AI companies hiring researchers across borders, the growing competition over advanced technology could make talent recruitment another flashpoint.

“Given it is already so competitive, it doesn’t take much to imagine U.S. companies at some point capitalizing on U.S.-China competition and making national security arguments that will make it more difficult for Chinese labs to operate or to attract the best talent. Conversely, it’d be a similar dynamic if U.S. labs were operating in China,” Ma said. “This elite talent is by definition scarce; we are talking [about] like the top 5%–10% of people. Who wouldn’t want to hoard the best and the brightest for themselves?”

Chinese tech companies have previously faced U.S. restrictions that disrupted their American research operations. In 2019, telecom giant Huawei cut more than 600 jobs at its U.S. research arm, Futurewei, after Washington placed the company on a trade blacklist.

Not all Chinese AI companies want to hire in the U.S. China’s AI poster child, DeepSeek, continues to advertise research and engineering positions in China. It recently announced about 150 positions for engineers who would expand AI agentic and back-end infrastructure. In a 2024 interview, DeepSeek founder Liang Wenfeng said he hired mostly Chinese-educated people and believed the company itself could cultivate elite AI researchers.

Yale researcher Wu is skeptical that Chinese startups could attract enough top researchers to compete with America’s leading AI labs. “They may have plans to hire, but that doesn’t necessarily mean they’ll be able to find the people,” she said.

It may be some time before AI agents can fully navigate the complexities and cultural nuances of developing nations.

Africa must develop AI systems with local control to protect critical infrastructure such as mobile money networks from growing AI-powered cyberthreats.

Some languages require far more tokens for AI models to process, raising costs and reducing context for the people who use them.

scraped.title: The backlash about data centers might really just be about electricity
scraped.description: Big Tech sees a culture war over progress. But the real fault line is electricity: drawing it from the grid and generating it onsite provoke different kinds of backlash, neither easily solved by public relations.
scraped.h1: The backlash about data centers might really just be about electricity
scraped.body_text:
Big Tech sees a culture war over progress. But the real fault line is electricity: drawing it from the grid and generating it onsite provoke different kinds of backlash, neither easily solved by public relations.

This story originally appeared in The Algorithm, our weekly newsletter on AI. To get stories like this in your inbox first, sign up here .

As voters went to the polls across the US last week, I was in Ashburn, Virginia, part of what’s known as Data Center Alley—the world’s largest data center hub. It’s also where the backlash now sweeping the country arguably first began taking shape.

Driving through it is surreal. Concrete monolithic buildings loom along every major road, with names like Skybox and CloudHQ.

It’s accepted wisdom in Big Tech that the war against data centers must be about something bigger than just data centers themselves. Two days after the midterms, OpenAI’s chief global affairs officer, Chris Lehane, wrote that data centers “have become a proxy for public unease about affordability, corporate power, and people losing control over their futures.” It’s a culture war, in other words.

But spending a few days in Data Center Alley left me wondering if it’s really the proxy that Lehane describes. I came away convinced that the data center backlash is more about electricity than Big Tech admits. The industry can improve its image, but it can’t escape the physical consequences of its enormous appetite for electricity.

Here’s why. There are two ways to power the sort of data center that AI companies want: connecting to the grid, or generating electricity onsite. In Virginia’s Loudoun County, where data centers are ubiquitous but have been built at a steadier pace than the breakneck expansion now underway elsewhere in the country, most are connected to the existing grid.

One facility I went inside, operated by Equinix, has massive diesel generators onsite for backup but gets its power from the local utility, Dominion Energy. Much of Dominion’s electricity is generated by natural gas (which is cleaner than coal or oil, but worse than renewables).

The average data center operating in this part of Virginia today has a power capacity of 54 megawatts. That’s more than the power draw of the Denver International Airport .

Elena Schlossberg, a prominent activist against data centers in Virginia, told me she’s “always banging my head against the wall” when the industry paints the fight as a culture war. “It was always about power,” she says—that is, electricity.

Some Virginia protesters appear more animated by a broader anti-tech populism than Schlossberg, to be fair. But it’s the particular consequences of drawing so much power from the grid that have done the most to shape how the backlash has played out.

Recent protests have led to new rules from the state that data centers must pay fully for the cost of new transmission lines to the grid and make sure they’re not spread among everyone else. Data center developers told me they’re preparing for new rules that would cut them off from grid power during peak demand. Schlossberg also worries about the downstream effects of a strained grid—for example, that data centers will run more diesel generators or that Dominion Energy will expand fossil fuel inputs rather than renewables to meet demand.

The overwhelming majority of AI data centers being built elsewhere in the country are not designed this way. The scale desired is so massive that companies are setting up in rural areas where there is virtually no grid infrastructure to connect to. Building there means bringing your own power (so-called “behind the meter” power), in the form of natural-gas-powered turbines. Companies also build diesel generators for backup. Anthropic, for example, has reportedly agreed to pay $3.4 billion for gas turbines in what’s described as the largest power generation purchase by an AI company.

Even if grids were nearby, they’d be unlikely to serve the amount of power demanded. The smallest data centers attractive for AI training are 300 megawatts. It’s a lot of power for one industrial site, but not unprecedented: One data center developer told me he’s eyeing a former steel mill already equipped to draw that much electricity from the grid.

But the ideal facilities are more like 6,000 megawatts. That’s the estimated draw of the city of Chicago, which is powered by more than 20 power plants within the city alone (and dozens farther out).

The notion of data center companies’ bringing their own power might seem attractive at first, because they wouldn’t be straining the grid. But generating electricity at this scale inevitably affects surrounding communities, and when public utilities build infrastructure of this magnitude, communities have traditionally expected a say in where it goes. Now, private companies are undertaking projects on a similar scale.

Natural-gas turbines of any scale release air pollutants. When diesel generators are used, it’s even worse. And in the unprecedented rush to get these facilities operating, companies have become horrible neighbors (recall that Elon Musk violated air quality laws when he set up dozens of turbines to power a data center in Memphis, according to the Environmental Protection Agency).

Big Tech’s tendency to chalk the backlash up to a culture war obfuscates one simple fact: There’s only so pleasant you can make a small city of computers to live around. Sure, companies can pursue better deals that raise tax revenues, hire local workers, and get more community involvement, as the protests are leading them to do . But if a small town is asked to welcome a Walt Disney World, an international airport, a steel plant, and the power plants to run them all, should we be surprised by its trepidation?

Again, that’s not to say this is the sole reason for opposition to data centers. Fears of job losses, existential risks, and concentrated corporate power all fuel the backlash, as does misinformation (most facilities use far less water than many people think). Nor is consuming enormous amounts of electricity inherently bad: Many of the advances that have improved modern life have required just that.

But as one developer recently told me, industry insiders see their ambitions as constrained less by public opposition than by a lack of electricity. That should tell us something.

So what happens next? It’s possible that newly elected politicians’ actual stances on data centers won’t be as negative as the ones they campaigned on. But what seems true regardless is that if new data centers need their own power generated onsite, they’ll go where there are the fewest people able to resist them. That might mean the Permian Basin , where a network of natural-gas lines can be easy for developers to connect to and populations are sparse. Companies might also try their chances abroad; Google, in fact, announced the day after the elections that it will spend $15 billion on data center projects in Malaysia.

But there’s one place where Big Tech may find virtually no limits at all, as Elon Musk posted just hours after the midterms results came rolling in: “Data centers in space looking pretty appealing right now.”

Ten years after AlphaGo’s match against Go champion Lee Sedol, today’s AI still isn’t tapping into the machinery that made that win possible.

scraped.h1: Nancy Pelosi’s replacement is ready to regulate AI
scraped.body_text:
Scott Wiener has made AI regulation a cornerstone of his political career. Now he’s headed to Congress.

As a California state senator, Scott Wiener authored legislation aimed at curbing the risks of advanced AI. Now, after winning a tight congressional race for former Speaker of the House Nancy Pelosi’s open San Francisco seat, he could play a key role in setting federal AI policy.

I spoke with Wiener on Friday, only a few hours after he had been declared the victor. But he was already thinking about AI risk. The previous day, the AI nonprofit METR had released a report that had been widely interpreted as evidence that Anthropic had achieved recursive self-improvement, a phenomenon in which AI meaningfully contributes to its own advancement and AI progress potentially spins out of control.

“It’s very concerning,” Wiener said, citing the report as evidence that we are quickly running out of time to regulate AI. “It was my hope that Congress would take decisive action before [the end of] this year,” he said. “That does not appear to be happening.”

Wiener has been increasingly focused on AI in recent years, and he’s made many of the AI safety movement’s concerns his own: During our 20-minute conversation, he used the phrase “recursive self-improvement” half a dozen times, for example.“We need to slow this down,” he says. “Because it’s moving very quickly, and we could sleepwalk into a disaster.”

Wiener has already had real influence on AI policy. SB 1047, a bill that he authored in 2024, was set to become the first real piece of frontier AI legislation in the country before it was vetoed by California governor Gavin Newsom; he then sponsored SB 53, a lighter-touch bill that Newsom signed. Both bills have inspired proposed federal legislation.

Wiener’s congressional campaign received over $3 million from Public First Action, a nonprofit in favor of AI regulation that receives substantial funding from Anthropic. That contribution led opponents to criticize him for being too close to the AI industry , but Wiener says that couldn’t be further from the truth.

“Public First supported me because I was the first lawmaker in the country to introduce AI regulation and the first to pass it and get it implemented,” he wrote in a message after our interview. “The attacks on me for [Public First’s] support were shockingly cynical—literally attacking a candidate who actually regulated AI over Big Tech’s objection and falsely claiming the candidate is somehow too close to Big Tech.”

Wiener says that if Congress forms a select committee on artificial intelligence—something that Democrats have discussed since September—he’d be eager to serve. And he’s enthusiastic about many of the policy ideas floating around Congress. “I think it’s really important to have a strong, empowered, nimble federal regulator,” he says, noting that Representative Ro Khanna, a fellow Democrat from California, has proposed legislation to establish such a regulator.

He also highlights the importance of whistleblower protections, testing and auditing requirements, and a kill switch requirement, and he wants to see Congress leverage its oversight powers to hold the AI labs to account. “This is about the future of humanity, and we want to make sure that the public has a say and that the public knows what's going on,” he says.

And as a longtime state legislator, he is opposed to broad federal preemption of state AI laws, which some of the proposed federal legislation would require. “States are, as Brandeis says , laboratories,” he notes. “You want the states to be able to continue to be nimble in ways that Congress sometimes is not.”

Above all, Wiener says, he wants Congress to pass policies with real teeth. “It’s critically important that when Congress acts, that we do so in a way that is truly meaningful and that meets the moment,” he says. That means taking seriously the possibility of AI catastrophe, something he discusses in the sort of language typically used by AI safety experts. “We’re in a moment that is very dangerous in terms of the risk of loss of control over AI,” he told me. “We need to deal with recursive self-improvement. Once you’re in that realm, that really is potentially a recipe for total loss of control.”

He’ll have some allies in the fight against catastrophic AI risk. Senator Bernie Sanders, for instance, has met with many of the AI safety movement’s most influential figures and has spoken repeatedly about AI and existential risk. But there’s still a large gap between Wiener’s Bay Area, AGI-pilled perspective and the national mood on AI, which is anchored by opposition to data centers. The fact that voters approved 40 out of 41 anti-data-center ballot measures on Tuesday might seem to be a good sign for Wiener and others who support AI regulation, but Wiener says he sees this movement as far more tied to local concerns than to bigger questions about AI risk.

“Peoople who are really opposed to where AI is going—this is an area where they can actually do something about it,” he says. “But the data center revolt—to me, I think it’s more so that people are upset that there could be something like this in their community, with all the impacts near people’s homes, driving up electric bills and using water. I think that’s the bigger issue for most people, from what I can tell.”

Wiener describes himself as only “cautiously optimistic” about Congress’s ability to rein in AI, given its poor track record on regulating the tech industry. He also has concerns about the ability to get legislation past President Donald Trump, who called concerns about catastrophic AI risk a “hoax” in September and has demonstrated a stark unwillingness to collaborate with China, something that Wiener sees as essential to preventing the worst consequences of AI.

But he says Trump’s unpredictability provides some measure of hope, though it’s a fraught kind of hope. “So far what we’ve seen are some problematic things, but not complete disasters,” Wiener says. “I hope that it doesn’t take a disaster to spur the president into acting. And I hope if that’s what it does take—which, like I said, I hope it doesn’t—but if it does, I hope it’s as small as possible.”
