scraped.h1: The Download: empty AI climate claims, and an Nvidia investigation
scraped.body_text:
Plus: Democrats are planning a blitz of investigations into Big Tech.

This is today's edition of The Download , our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what's going on in the world of technology.

—By Mary Nichols, distinguished counsel at the UCLA School of Law and the former chair of the California Air Resources Board, and Jeremy Tamanini, the founder of Dual Citizen, a sustainability research and advisory firm

This week, as countries meet in Antalya, Turkey for the United Nations climate conference, one topic is likely to dominate the conversation: artificial intelligence. The host has already called on countries to commit to ensuring that AI is designed, powered, and deployed in ways that support climate action.

But so far, industries around the world aren’t doing nearly enough to harness the technology to actually drive down the greenhouse-gas emissions heating up the planet. AI companies like to make very optimistic claims about AI’s potential to help address climate change. The reality is far less promising. Read the full story .

Tropical forests are our planet’s biggest terrestrial carbon sink, accounting for around 40% of carbon stored on land. Forest ecologist Daisy Dent, a senior scientist at ETH Zurich, is part of an international network of researchers working to decipher the networks of animal and plant interactions that enable some forests to recover after destruction.

The goal is a low-cost, high-impact alternative to typical carbon-­crediting schemes, which plant huge areas with a single species of tree. For over a decade, her research has helped show that these large “monocrop” programs could be expensive mistakes—and that more resilient forests can rebound naturally in just a few decades, re-creating ecosystems that suck up vast quantities of carbon dioxide.

Learn more about Dent, her work, and her impact on how we understand the role rainforests play in regulating our climate.

—Matthew Ponsford

The must-reads

I’ve combed the internet to find you today’s most fun/important/scary/fascinating stories about technology.

1 Nvidia is investigating its own boss Jensen Huang has admitted to intimacy with a suspected Chinese spy. ( NYT $) + Shares in Nvidia were down 5% in pre-market trading. ( CNBC ) + Huang’s children are also employed by Nvidia. ( WSJ $)

2 Democrats are planning a blitz of investigations into Big Tech Reportedly starting with Apple, Meta, and Musk’s companies. ( WP $) + They’re hoping to harness the data center backlash to rein in the AI sector. ( Vox $) + Here’s why the midterms sparked an AI stock selloff. ( BBC ) 3 The UN annual climate meeting starts today It’s the first to be held after confirmation the planet will exceed 1.5 °C warming. ( Nature ) + How to study a swiftly melting climate disaster. ( MIT Technology Review ) 4 Connecting fridges to the internet looks like a bad move now We still don’t know who is behind recent hacks, or even if they’re connected. ( The Atlantic $) + Experts say they should be a “wake up call” for the industry. ( NPR ) + Are we in the foothills of a hacking epidemic? ( The Guardian ) + AI is already making online crimes easier. It could get much worse. ( MIT Technology Review ) 5 Tesla is axing the Cybertruck RIP, we hardly knew ye. ( Wired $) + The Cybertruck was on our “worst tech flops of 2025” list. ( MIT Technology Review ) 6 Iran might attack subsea cables if the US escalates again That’s the message it’s sending via several loitering tankers. ( FT $) 7 Chinese AI labs are struggling to poach Silicon Valley workers Startups like MiniMax and Moonshot have an uphill battle as they try to fill new US offices. ( Rest of World ) + China’s AI models have Trump’s AI world at war with itself. ( MIT Technology Review )

8 Online piracy is back 🏴‍☠️ But this time, archivist zeal is at least as big a draw as accessing content for free. ( The Verge ) + Inside the race to save our online lives from a digital dark age. ( MIT Technology Review ) 9 How do you land on a moon with almost no gravity? It’s a huge challenge to land on Martian moon Phobos—here’s how Japan’s going to attempt it. ( IEEE Spectrum )

10 Meet Philadelphia's delivery robot saboteur Carolyn Marvin is going to court for blocking them, and it’s turning her into a local hero. ( The Guardian )

Quote of the day

—Jensen Huang apologizes to Nvidia employees for his affair with a suspected Chinese spy in a mass email sent yesterday, the Washington Post reports.

One more thing

AI models are marching into a creative field that is uniquely vulnerable to disruption: music.

AI-generated creative works—from orchestra performances to heavy metal—are poised to suffuse our lives more thoroughly than any other product of AI has done yet.

The songs are likely to blend into our streaming platforms, party and wedding playlists, soundtracks, and more, whether or not we notice who (or what) made them.

Here’s why AI is set to forever change how we make music.

—James O’Donnell

We can still have nice things

A place for comfort, fun, and distraction to brighten up your day. (Got any ideas? Drop me a line .)

+ French bardcore band Corseval has given ABBA a medieval makeover . + A stunning collection of prehistoric engravings has been found in a Spanish cave. + This browser game flips a retro classic on its head: you control the asteroids, not the spaceship. + From a caiman in a wig to a leopard doing a handstand, the Comedy Wildlife Awards shortlist is a delight.

scraped.body_text:
Sign up for Democracy Now!'s Daily Digest to get our latest headlines and stories delivered to your inbox every day.

Lina Attalah, editor-in-chief of Egypt’s leading independent news outlet Mada Masr , faces a criminal trial this week on charges of “spreading false information,” just two weeks after being convicted of operating an unlicensed website and fined more than $50,000. A judge also ordered the publication to be shut down. The cases are part of a broader crackdown on independent Egyptian media under the government of President Abdel Fattah el-Sisi, including the arrest of the entire newsroom of another outlet, Matsadaash . More than 100 organizations, including Amnesty International, Human Rights Watch and the Committee to Protect Journalists, have condemned the arrests and prosecutions and called on Egyptian authorities to drop the charges.

“Putting us in jail is not going to solve the country’s problems,” Attalah told Democracy Now! in an interview Friday. “We need to be operating as journalists in our newsrooms as opposed to being defendants in courtrooms.”

Attalah says she and Mada Masr will appeal the ruling to shut them down, hoping to “use this crisis” as a way to fight censorship in Egypt and expand the space for independent reporting.

AMY GOODMAN : This is Democracy Now! , democracynow.org, The War and Peace Report . I’m Amy Goodman.

We turn now to the escalating crackdown on press freedom in Egypt. Lina Attalah, the editor-in-chief of Egypt’s leading independent media outlet Mada Masr , faces a criminal trial Wednesday on charges of, quote-unquote, “spreading false information.” Depending on the outcome, she could be imprisoned for a year. The criminal trial comes just two weeks after an Egyptian court convicted Attalah of managing an unlicensed website. She was detained for several hours, fined $50,000, Mada Masr ordered closed.

Mada Masr was founded in June 2013, a year before a military coup led to President Abdel Fattah el-Sisi taking office. Mada publishes in Arabic and English, is internationally recognized for its investigative reporting and editorial independence. It’s continued working over the past 13 years despite repeated website blocking, office raids, staff arrests and judicial harassment.

The attack on Mada Masr follows a crackdown on another independent Egyptian media outlet, Matsadaash , where authorities arrested the entire newsroom, accused them of belonging to the banned Muslim Brotherhood, and forced them to record false confessions under torture.

Over a hundred groups, including Amnesty International, Human Rights Watch and the Committee to Protect Journalists and Reporters Without Borders, have condemned the crackdown on press freedom and called on Egyptian authorities to drop the charges against Lina Attalah, release the Matsadaash journalists and allow independent media to operate freely.

On Friday, Democracy Now! ’s Anjali Kamat and I spoke to Lina Attalah. We asked her about the charges she faces and her upcoming trial Wednesday.

LINA ATTALAH : Two weeks ago, I was summoned by the prosecutor for interrogations on accusations of running a website without a license. It is not unusual to be faced with this allegation, even though we’ve been going through the bureaucratic motions of trying to apply for a license and have simply been not getting any response from the licensing authorities.

The new thing that happened two weeks ago is that our case was swiftly referred to trial, and last week we had the first and the very quick verdict already pronounced in this first session. So, Mada Masr was ordered closed. We were fined over $50,000. And I was briefly detained until the fine was collected, which is, again, unusual practice.

The entire trial saw a lot of violations that we’ve been talking about, including the judge refusing all our defense team’s demands. The trial ended with the judge even appointing a lawyer on my behalf. And upon my objection, he already proceeded to pronouncing the verdict that basically closes Mada and charges us a fine of over $50,000, all while I was pulled violently by the cops to a detention spot until the fine was collected.

Upon my release that day, after a very long day, after everybody showed up in solidarity to help us pay the fine, I learned that I’m facing another — a trial, where there could be a charge of one year in prison. So, it does feel like the most violent legal campaign against us in the last years, where we faced other forms of challenges, legal challenges to our work, but we’ve never really reached that level before.

ANJALI KAMAT : And, Lina, are you going to have to shut down Mada Masr ? How are you fighting these charges against you and this publication that you co-founded in 2013?

LINA ATTALAH : We are doing everything possible to challenge this verdict. I do not think it’s fair for a media that has served this country for over 13 years, doing what has become very scarce in the country, reporting bravely and independently about everything that’s been happening, not only in Egypt, but also in the region. I do not believe it can be shut down through a court verdict that did not last over an hour, or a court session that did not last over an hour.

So, our plan is to appeal. Our plan is to also try to apply for a license again. And our plan is to use this crisis, as has been our habit, to open up the conversation about how licensing cannot be a tool for censorship and control. Licensing can be a regulating mechanism, but it can be — it cannot be used to shut down independent media in the country. And this should be resolved not only for us, but also for all other media outlets that are trying to work independently in the country.

AMY GOODMAN : Can you tell us about what’s happened with Matsadaash , with the journalists there? Where are they right now? The entire newsroom was arrested?

LINA ATTALAH : An entire newsroom was arrested right before our own ordeal began, which, you know, easily signals how this is a crackdown on all independent voices. And that’s why the sentiment right now is that we’re not just fighting for Mada , but we’re fighting for that very space in Egypt today.

Matsadaash is a fact-checking platform. The newsroom is made up for six brilliant young journalists. I’ve worked personally with four of them as they were starting in their careers. The youngest of them is 21 years old. They are all young, promising journalists who dared to do this work with bravery, courage and curiosity.

They have been arrested over about a month ago, and they remain in remand detention. They are facing terror charges for doing their work. We are still hoping that their ordeal ends, as ours, too. We are hoping for them to be released from detention. They are in detention facilities in Egypt, again, like I said, remand detention. So, we are hoping for this crackdown to stop here and for the authorities to wake up to the fact that the young men of Matsadaash are not their problems, Mada Masr is not their problems. Putting us in jail is not going to solve the country’s problems. And the wise thing to do is to drop the charges against us and against them, and to release them right away.

ANJALI KAMAT : And, Lina, can you talk about the timing of this escalating crackdown on the press? This is coming as, you know, in the middle of this crackdown, we saw a surprise announcement from the Egyptian President Abdel Fattah el-Sisi that he would be stepping down in 2030, at the end of his third and current term. Never in Egypt’s modern history has the head of state chosen to hand over power voluntarily. What does this mean for the future of Egypt and the space for dissent?

LINA ATTALAH : It is a very charged moment in the country, politically and economically. Politically, we’re not just talking about what’s happening on the local level; we’re also talking about regional challenges with surrounding conflicts, the Red Sea conflict, the war in Iran, and Egypt is not isolated from that. It is — it is a pressuring situation on the country and on the authorities here.

At the same time, the announcements that you mentioned point to a certain shift that might be happening, that, unfortunately, we couldn’t get a chance to report on properly because we’ve been having to face all these legal ordeals ever since the announcements were made. But we do have the sense that something in the mode of rule is shifting. And that’s why we need to be operating as journalists in our newsrooms, as opposed to being defendants in courtrooms, to understand what is happening.

And then, you know, the other context in which this crackdown is happening is a major economic challenge. You know, Egypt has been heavily integrated in the global economy, especially after 2016. So it’s been heavily affected with global shifts, market shifts, having become, having turned into so-called an emerging market and being quite dependent on hot money. We have major debt service to commit to. We have a gas bill to pay. So the country is also going through an important economic challenge that is getting more and more pronounced on a day-to-day level. So, I would say this is the political and economic context under which these decisions against us are being made, and it’s important to note them.

AMY GOODMAN : I wanted to ask you, Lina, about the amount of money from the United States — I think it’s second only after Israel, U.S. sending Egypt one-and-a-half billion dollars in military aid each year — and the significance of the timing of U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio waiving this restriction on $320 million in military aid to Egypt that was previously withheld over human rights concerns. In the past month, he has waived this, the State Department citing Egypt’s, quote, “helpful role” in the war with Iran, and, said Rubio, signed off on the waiver in the interest of U.S. national security. Do you think this timing of your trial — as you said, you want to be reporting, not fighting in court — is related to your trial and the charges brought against you, to keep you quiet and a message to all the press in Egypt: “This is what you could face if human rights concerns are raised”?

LINA ATTALAH : So, Amy, we cannot, obviously, establish direct causalities. Again, we haven’t had the chance to report properly on this.

But also, it is not unprecedented that the U.S. administration does this, applies this mechanism of the waiver, you know, in previous cycles of the military aid of $1.3 billion. In recent years, it has always been pegged to the fact that Egypt is playing an important role, be it in negotiating a ceasefire in Gaza. Currently, it’s been pegged to its role in negotiations on the Iran front.

But all of this, if it’s signaling something, it’s signaling this rising belief amongst Western powers that have alliances and key alliances in Egypt that its — the stability of the country in the midst of so many regional wars and regional turmoils rests solely on the authority of those who are ruling. It’s a political calculus that has proven wrong in previous times, meaning that stability does not rest on how those in power rule alone, but also it rests on the political and economic health of the people. And we have a lot of issues there.

And we always say that the work of independent media is an important, actually, stabilizing factor, because instead of people having no outlets to ask questions, understand what’s happening, now all these spaces are being shut, and people are left alone to implode. So, I do believe that it continues to be the wrong political calculation, even though it has been prevalent in recent years.

ANJALI KAMAT : Lina, can you, you know, for our audience, that doesn’t — might not be so familiar with Mada Masr , can you talk a little bit about the history of Mada and how and why you founded it in 2013, and how you’ve managed to keep it alive despite so many attempts to shut it down? And talk also a little bit about the kind of investigative stories that Mada is known for.

LINA ATTALAH : So, we started publishing in the summer of 2013. We are a group of journalists. We had just been fired from another media, again because of political disagreements and economic restraints. And at the same time, it was a summer of major political transformation in the country. So, we had a Muslim Brotherhood elected leader to the presidency who was arrested or who was ousted from power by the military authorities. We had a military takeover. A year after, we have President Abdel Fattah el-Sisi taking over, and he was here to stay until today.

So, back then, we felt that this is going to be the beginning of a new era in terms of the mode of rule, in terms of the mode of authority that we are being subjected to. And we also saw that — or, foresaw that there won’t be any independent media out there who could report about that. So we thought maybe we should begin instituting an experiment that can house this kind of journalism, that can create a record on the goal of what is happening, what’s going on, to basically provide this companionship for the people in trying to understand what this transformation is looking like.

What kept us staying, up until today, is none other than the journalism itself. You create valued journalism — and this is something that we learned from Democracy Now! and other important independent media — and, you know, it provides you with the force and the power to stay even in the hardest of circumstances. I do believe that it is our journalism that kept us safe. The credibility of it is what kept us protected, because it also builds support around it, and it created this necessity.

Authorities rule with the understanding that people don’t need to know, and this is — this is not right. People do need to know. People who read Mada and other independent media, people who follow Matsadaash , are are not necessarily people who are aligned with us politically or people who know us. They are people who need to understand what’s happening at a moment where there are lesser and lesser spaces for independent media practice.

Our investigative work spans, you know, many areas and topics. We have started, for example, the investigation into Senator Menendez’s practices by reporting about the halal meat certification that he provided support for to an Egyptian businessman who is tied to the Egyptian authorities here. So, it was an investigation that we started in our Cairo newsroom, and then, you know, it sprang out into something much bigger, which you have followed very closely, amongst other American media. We’ve published investigations about, you know, how authorities have engineered different parliamentary elections since 2013 up until now, investigations into the current genocide in Gaza. So, yeah, the work we’ve done and the investigative work we’ve done spans different topics and areas.

ANJALI KAMAT : How can our audience do more to support independent media in Egypt and support you and Mada Masr ?

LINA ATTALAH : We’ve been saying that whoever has any tools, they need to find them and use them. So, if you still live in a context where a democratic practice remains — and this is something that we have seen in the U.S. in the past days — then let’s use these tools. Let’s speak to representatives. Let’s make them aware. Let’s ask — let’s ask for statements. Let’s ask for support. Let’s write about these independent media.

And let’s write about and talk about these issues, not from the vantage point that these are distant newsrooms in the Third World, in Egypt, but this is a shared struggle for our right to independent media, which isn’t also something that’s far from democratic contexts. Independent media is struggling everywhere. And by choosing to support us and Matsadaash and other independent media in the region, one chooses also to support this kind of practice back at home.

AMY GOODMAN : And finally, Lina, Zazu Goodpup, one of the leading news hounds in the United States, wanted to express her support. She demanded to come into our studio, because she knows how much you care about little critters like her and that you have news hounds yourself at Mada Masr . I’m wondering, personally, how you’re preparing for this, you and your family.

LINA ATTALAH : First of all, all my love to Zazu and to our animals and our pets, friends who have been a massive source of affective support to us in this difficult time. My team and myself, we are busy with defense strategy, with support campaigns, with doing interviews. And in the evenings, we just spend time with our families to sort of calm them down and tell them that even though we are a little bit scared, but also we’re a little bit hopeful.

AMY GOODMAN : Lina Attalah, editor-in-chief of Egypt’s leading independent media outlet Mada Masr , which the government has ordered closed. She spoke to us from Cairo. She faces a criminal trial Wednesday on charges of, quote-unquote, “spreading false information.” If found guilty, she faces up to a year in prison.

And that does it for today’s show. Happy birthday to Diana Parra! Oh, and Steal This Story, Please! , the documentary about Democracy Now! , is now available on many streaming platforms in the U.S. and Canada, from Amazon Prime to YouTube to Apple TV and Google Play. Go to StealThisStory.org to see where you can watch it. And Democracy Now! — the film about Democracy Now! , Steal This Story, Please! , will be at the IFC in New York , 4:30 on November 11th, Wednesday. I’ll be speaking after in the Q&A with the film’s Oscar-nominated directors Tia Lessin and Carl Deal. I’m Amy Goodman. Thanks for joining us.

Special guests Angela Davis, Bruce Springsteen, Patti Smith, Michael Stipe and more came together to celebrate 30 years of Democracy Now! at a sold out Riverside Church event in NYC on March 23, 2026.

scraped.body_text:
Sign up for Democracy Now!'s Daily Digest to get our latest headlines and stories delivered to your inbox every day.

The next Congress will include about 100 new lawmakers in the House of Representatives, the largest freshman wave in decades. That also includes six newly elected members of the Democratic Socialists of America, bringing the total number of DSA members in Congress to eight. One of the incoming DSA congressmembers will be California’s Angela Gonzales-Torres, who worked two other jobs while campaigning and was massively outspent by her opponent, incumbent Democratic Congressmember Jimmy Gomez.

In her first national TV interview, Gonzales-Torres tells Democracy Now! she will prioritize immigrant justice, Medicare for All and fighting corruption, when she is sworn in. She also explains why she has not yet committed to supporting Hakeem Jeffries for House speaker.

“As of right now, my vote is no,” she says. “Over 100,000 Angelenos voted for courage. They voted for change.”

AMY GOODMAN : This is Democracy Now! , democracynow.org. I’m Amy Goodman.

Newly elected members of Congress are in Washington, D.C., this week for orientation. The new class of Democrats will include the largest-ever incoming class of progressives, including six newly elected members of DSA , the Democratic Socialists of America. This will bring the total number of DSA members in Congress to eight, joining Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez and Rashida Tlaib.

On Tuesday, our next guest, Angela Gonzales-Torres of Los Angeles, defeated the sitting Democratic Congressmember Jimmy Gomez, who’s under investigation by the House Ethics Committee over sexual misconduct allegations, which he denies. Gonzales-Torres grew up in the district she’ll represent, in Highland Park. She was raised by a single mom after her father was deported, and her family relied on Section 8, SNAP and Medicaid. She ran a campaign focused on affordable housing, abolishing ICE , rooting out corruption in Congress. This is Angela Gonzales-Torres speaking after her election.

REP .- ELECT ANGELA GONZALES - TORRES : We took on corporate donors and corruption, and this apparent culture in Congress in which men appear to abuse their positions of power and abuse women. And I am sick of it. And so I’m ready for change, because Los Angeles doesn’t belong to AIPAC , right? Los Angeles doesn’t belong to crypto or big AI lobbies. And Los Angeles certainly doesn’t belong to corporate real estate developers. And so, it belongs to us.

AMY GOODMAN : During the primary, Gonzales-Torres was working two jobs — in education, supporting formerly incarcerated students; as an affordable housing advocate — also served as president of the Highland Park neighborhood.

For more, we go to Washington, D.C., where we’re joined by Congressmember-elect Angela Gonzales-Torres.

Thank you so much for being with us. It’s great to have you. You’re in D.C. right now for the incoming congressmembers’ orientation. Can you talk about what you plan to bring to Congress? What are your demands, Congressmember-elect?

REP .- ELECT ANGELA GONZALES - TORRES : Sure. I’m so happy to be here.

Yes, we are in D.C. now. They threw me right in here. Our election was Tuesday, and here we are, ready to hit the ground running and take this information back home and fight for working families like my own.

I am really focused on why I got into this race in the first place, which is that I grew up in this district that has some of the highest costs of incarceration. One of the largest jail systems on the face of the planet is actually in the middle of California’s 34th Congressional District. And we have some of the dirtiest air in all of L.A. County, some of the largest eviction notices issued in the entire city. And I am so proud to be now, hopefully soon, representing one of the largest immigrant populations in the country.

I am really hoping to bring this urgency. I really feel the urgency of this moment, and I’m looking forward to representing Los Angeles with the respect that we deserve.

AMY GOODMAN : And tell us more about your district. You’re right next to where Stephen Miller —

REP .- ELECT ANGELA GONZALES - TORRES : Yeah.

AMY GOODMAN : — grew up. As you are there in Washington for your first days for orientation, he has started —

REP .- ELECT ANGELA GONZALES - TORRES : Yes.

AMY GOODMAN : — his first day, the architect of the immigration crackdown, as the chief of staff of President Trump.

REP .- ELECT ANGELA GONZALES - TORRES : Yeah. First of all, Stephen Miller is a fearmonger. He is a fool. And we definitely saw this coming. I think the Trump administration knew that they were going to lose big this midterm, and I think that this is proof that they’re trying to double down on their cruel and corrupt agenda.

And the reason I got into this race as the daughter of a deportee, as someone that proudly works with formerly incarcerated and undocumented students, is because we are going to need to fight back. And so, while they are trying to lean in on fear, we are going to lean in on love and courage in this time of extreme cowardice. And I’m ready to get to work.

AMY GOODMAN : Can you talk about the race for the House leader, for the House speaker? I mean, you have —

REP .- ELECT ANGELA GONZALES - TORRES : Yeah.

AMY GOODMAN : — a real controversy brewing. In the Senate, it’s around Chuck Schumer, now the Democratic minority leader. In the House, it’s Hakeem Jeffries. And will you be endorsing him for House speaker? In our headlines just now, we talked about progressives demanding new leadership. An online petition urging Democratic Congressmember Hakeem Jeffries to remove himself from the running to become next House speaker has surpassed 1 million signatures, facing mounting opposition over his pro-Israel interests, continued acceptance of corporate PAC money, including from AIPAC , the American Israel Public Affairs Committee. Your thoughts?

REP .- ELECT ANGELA GONZALES - TORRES : As of right now, my vote is no. I know for sure that over 100,000 Angelenos voted for courage. They voted for change. And I think that what I don’t know is what Representative Hakeem Jeffries is offering my community and constituents of California’s 34th Congressional District for their vote. I think I know for sure that the incumbent would have rolled over and handed over the vote without keeping our community in mind, without one community conversation, and that is not the case anymore. Those days are behind us.

And so, respectfully, Representative Hakeem Jeffries will have to work for our vote. And again, we have not spoken yet. I just got here. This is my second day in D.C., and I’m really looking forward to the rest of orientation, learning as much as possible. But I’m really looking forward to getting back home and making sure my community feels heard.

AMY GOODMAN : Can you talk about your father being deported when you were a teenager? And talk about your own district more. You can talk about the critical issues one of the poorest districts in this country face, and the fact that you had, what, at least two jobs while you were running for Congress in order to support yourself.

REP .- ELECT ANGELA GONZALES - TORRES : Right. That is proof alone that anything is possible. We won the primary election while I was working two jobs, but also we had to stretch, you know, $200,000, which might sound like a lot to my neighbors and I, but in this political world, that was proof that anything is possible, and it’s possible not to sell out your community to corporate PACs and corporate donors.

And I think that, for me, the reason why I got into this race, again, is because I, for generations, have seen the same issues over and over and over again — largest eviction notices in the heart of Los Angeles, some of the dirtiest air in all of L.A. County. I mean, kids in East L.A. have lead found in their teeth, while we’re also trying to recover from the Lineage warehouse fire and an oil spill and ICE raids and the warmest year on record with no ACs in our public schools. It’s unacceptable.

And I think that being the — one of the poorest districts in the country, yet part of the fourth-largest economy in the world, I know that Angelenos are some of the hardest-working people you will ever meet. And I am here to represent them in the way that they deserve to be represented. So, we are looking forward to finally having in-person town halls to make sure that, you know, people know that even now in this transition period, they can go to Angela4Congress.com and leave a comment, especially for constituents of CA-34, to make sure that our office is prepared to meet people where they’re at.

AMY GOODMAN : And how do you fight for Medicare for All and abolishing ICE , two of the issues you ran on, as we wrap up this discussion?

REP .- ELECT ANGELA GONZALES - TORRES : Sure. I mean, fortunately, and I have to tell you, the energy here in D.C. is electric. I mean, the Progressive Caucus had a press conference yesterday alone, and you can feel that we are ready to actually fight for these bare minimum things that people should be guaranteed across the country. Medicare for All is bare minimum.

And I think that there’s certainly a difference between former elected officials, that would just co-sponsor or sign on to these bills, and those of us moving into Congress this January, that will actually fight for it and make sure that we’re doing everything that we can to let people know what abolish ICE even means, holding accountable those masked agents that are terrorizing our communities, redirecting those funds back into our districts. And really, it’s an energy that you can feel, and I’m really looking forward to carrying that through this transition, and certainly after we’re all sworn in.

AMY GOODMAN : And as you go off to your next meeting, I’m wondering how you feel in this first national TV broadcast to be standing in the Capitol Rotunda as an incoming congressmember from Los Angeles.

REP .- ELECT ANGELA GONZALES - TORRES : It’s incredible, honestly. Yeah, it’s really — I think, for me, this is exactly where we need to be, because that was a really hard past year and a half, and our community asked us to step up and throw our name in this race because they know I am in these fights already, this fight to get AIPAC and crypto and big AI funding out of our politics, certainly out of California’s Democratic Party. And it’s possible. We just proved that. And I’m really excited and proud that over 100,000 Angelenos made their voices very clear.

AMY GOODMAN : Well, I don’t want you to be late for one of your first meetings —

REP .- ELECT ANGELA GONZALES - TORRES : Thank you so much. Yeah.

AMY GOODMAN : — as congressmember-elect, Angela Gonzales-Torres, democratic socialist, elected to represent California’s 34th Congressional District in Los Angeles.

REP .- ELECT ANGELA GONZALES - TORRES : Yes.

AMY GOODMAN : I want to thank you so much for being with us, in her first national TV broadcast.

This is Democracy Now! Coming up, we look at the crackdown on press freedom in Egypt. We’ll speak with the editor-in-chief of the largest independent newspaper in Egypt, Mada Masr . She faces a criminal trial this week and possible prison. Stay with us.

scraped.body_text:
Sign up for Democracy Now!'s Daily Digest to get our latest headlines and stories delivered to your inbox every day.

Stephen Miller, the architect of the Trump administration’s mass deportation policies, has replaced Susie Wiles as White House chief of staff. In a recent 60 Minutes interview, President Donald Trump acknowledged that his immigration policies may be “too tough” and contributed to his party’s steep losses in the midterm elections, but in elevating Miller, he is “choosing to double down,” says journalist Jean Guerrero. “Stephen Miller enables [Trump] in this instinct to choose cruelty over everything else,” she says.

Guerrero is a New York Times contributing opinion writer, USC journalism professor and author of Hatemonger: Stephen Miller, Donald Trump, and the White Nationalist Agenda .

AMY GOODMAN : White House adviser Stephen Miller starts his new job today as President Trump’s chief of staff, replacing Susie Wiles, following sweeping Republican losses in last week’s historic midterm elections. Miller is the chief architect of Trump’s zero-tolerance immigration crackdown. Trump’s decision to promote Miller is widely seen as a signal the president will double down on his agenda despite the rebuke from voters. Trump praised Miller Friday.

PRESIDENT DONALD TRUMP : Stephen has been with me from the beginning. He gets it, very good politically, and he’s a very good man. He’ll do a great job, great manager. … I wanted to make a change. I think Susie’s done a very good job, great job, but I just wanted to make it. Stephen’s been great. And we’ve got to make — we’ve got to make moves.

AMY GOODMAN : Democratic Congressmember Robert Garcia, the ranking member on the House Oversight Committee, who will lead that committee next term, spoke to CNN over the weekend.

REP . ROBERT GARCIA : Stephen Miller is the architect of this horrific, unjust policy happening across the country in the way that we are treating folks. Stephen Miller called Alex Pretti, as we know, an assassin. The way that he is going around creating immigration policy that separates families, that is causing people harm, that’s creating a detention process where a few large companies are profiting, the unconstitutional detention of people, the way that folks are losing their due process rights, that has to be investigated. And we know that Stephen Miller has been an architect of that. And so, what’s happening there, what’s happening in Iran, Stephen Miller is at the center of the major policy decisions that are happening in the administration, and so it does deserve oversight and investigation.

AMY GOODMAN : Congressmember Garcia also said in a statement, “Stephen Miller should lawyer up,” to which Todd Blanche, the attorney general, said he is his lawyer.

According to The New York Times , just one day after the election, Stephen Miller called national security officials to push forward with the immigration crackdown.

For more, we go now to Los Angeles, where we’re joined by Jean Guerrero, author of Hatemonger: Stephen Miller, Donald Trump, and the White Nationalist Agenda . She’s also a contributing opinion writer at The New York Times and an associate professor at the USC , the University of Southern California, Annenberg School for Communication and Journalism.

Jean Guerrero, welcome back to Democracy Now! Can you share your response when you heard that after the massive Republican midterm defeat, the response of the president, even though he has said over the weekend he didn’t think it was the Iran war, but his crackdown on immigrants, that he has chosen Stephen Miller, who symbolized that crackdown on immigrants?

JEAN GUERRERO : Yes. Thanks for having me, Amy.

This decision is not at all surprising to me, given that Stephen Miller, as we all know, is the most effective sycophant in the Trump administration. As Trump himself said, he’s one of his longest-lasting advisers, one of his most trusted advisers. But it is a deeply disturbing decision, because Miller is one of the most troubled and one of the most dangerous individuals in this White House. He is responsible for federal agents being unleashed in communities across the United States to target people based on their race and based on their language. He had federal agents go into workplaces, into construction sites, into Home Depots, into farms, which devastated communities economically, as well as psychologically and spiritually.

But to me, this is indicative of the fact that Trump is choosing to double down, which is an instinct that he shares with Stephen Miller and which Stephen Miller enables him in, this instinct to choose cruelty over everything else and and to just — I think Trump hopes that Miller is going to get him out of this mess, because in the past when he has gone with Miller’s decisions to use the scapegoating of immigrants to rally the base, it has worked. But this war on immigrants has reached a level that has horrified the American public, and I really don’t believe it’s going to work this time. Stephen Miller is not going to get Trump out of this mess.

AMY GOODMAN : So, if you can start off — I mean, you wrote a whole book, Jean, on Stephen Miller, called Hatemonger — why you decided to do that? I mean, yes, and the subtitle, it’s Stephen Miller and Donald Trump. But give us a short history of who he is.

JEAN GUERRERO : Yeah. Stephen Miller grew up in Santa Monica, California, which is known as a liberal progressive community. And he is, in many ways, a product of liberal hypocrisy. He saw the hypocrisy of Democratic leaders in California and how often their support for immigrant rights and social justice was often performative, and he decided to exploit that to rise in political power. And he was mentored by individuals who believe that war needs — that politics needs to be a form of warfare.

And I chose to write this book and to investigate Stephen Miller because I was an immigration reporter and I was seeing the impact of the first Trump administration’s policies on families at the border. The administration kept saying that they were going after criminals, that if you didn’t want to be targeted by the family separations, you just had to follow the law. But I was talking to people who were having 1-year-old babies ripped out of their arms after having presented at ports of entry legally. So I wanted to understand: If this wasn’t about the law, if this wasn’t about law and order, which the administration was claiming that it was, and it clearly wasn’t, then what was it about? And to me, I felt that I had to understand Stephen Miller.

And what I understood is that, at the end of the day, this was about reengineering the racial demographics of this country. That is why Stephen Miller, during the first administration, focused on strangling legal pathways into this country, whether it was gutting the asylum system, the refugee system, restricting green card access for the poor. This was never about going after criminals. It was about changing what America is and who is allowed to come here. And that is why, during this administration, they have focused on invading American cities to pursue operations that amount to ethnic cleansing.

And these operations, he has told federal agents they can act with immunity, which is why you saw the killings across the United States of citizens and noncitizens alike. And I think this was deliberate. I mean, Stephen Miller — one thing that people need to understand about Stephen Miller is that he is, above all, a sadist, and there is one group of people that he despises more than immigrants, and that is the allies, the citizen allies, of immigrants, people who choose compassion and who choose to stand up for their neighbors. He was shaped by this book called The Camp of the Saints , which basically the heroes of this book are people who call for genocide of Brown immigrants, who are cast as a threat to civilization. And the worst villains are not the immigrants, but the citizen allies who stand up for their neighbors.

And so, I think Miller has this profound hostility for immigrants of color, and we’ve seen that, but he also — and I think this is what we’re going to see in the coming two years — has a deep, deep loathing for the people who use their privilege and who use their power to stand up for those who are being persecuted. He despises that. And he is going to use the powers that he now has to target and to terrorize and to torture not only immigrant communities, but their allies, people who are citizens who are — who believe in welcoming the stranger.

AMY GOODMAN : You said the book is The Camp of the Saints . I wanted to ask you about President Trump, who sat down for an interview on CBS’s 60 Minutes following the widespread Republican defeat in the midterm elections. Trump made these remarks about his immigration raids and deportations.

ROSS DOUTHAT : So, you think your deportation policy —

PRESIDENT DONALD TRUMP : I think it was too tough.

ROSS DOUTHAT : — went too far. It was too tough.

PRESIDENT DONALD TRUMP : I think it might be too tough, yeah. And a lot of people would say that it’s great, but a lot of people think it’s too tough.

ROSS DOUTHAT : What would happen —

PRESIDENT DONALD TRUMP : And I think, ultimate —

ROSS DOUTHAT : What does the deal look like with the Democrats?

PRESIDENT DONALD TRUMP : I think, ultimately, that hurt me. … But there’s a group of people that, I would say on the sort of pretty far right, that would like everybody taken out.

ROSS DOUTHAT : Do some of them —

PRESIDENT DONALD TRUMP : And there’s a group of people on the —

ROSS DOUTHAT : Do any of those people work in your administration?

PRESIDENT DONALD TRUMP : Yes.

ROSS DOUTHAT : Are they in the building with us right now?

PRESIDENT DONALD TRUMP : No, no. Well, there are a lot of those people.

ROSS DOUTHAT : Yeah.

AMY GOODMAN : So, this is very interesting, Jean Guerrero. On the one hand, you have Vice President Vance putting out a statement after the midterm saying the war did the Republicans in. Trump has refuted this, but then went on to say it was the immigration crackdown, and appoints Stephen Miller, the symbol and architect of that, as his chief of staff. Can you explain?

JEAN GUERRERO : Trump is trying to play both sides. He’s trying to exploit the echo chambers. He’s hoping one group of people will receive one piece of information and the others will receive the other. But this is clearly contradictory. He has chosen to elevate Stephen Miller, who for his entire life has expressed deep antagonism for immigrants who are here, whether they’re legally here, whether they came here and don’t have status.

One thing that I included in my book that I want to talk about is that Stephen Miller, from the time he was in high school and throughout college, he would disparage custodial staff, and he would throw his food on the ground. He would leave his trash out, and he would say, “Why do I have to pick up my trash when there are people here to do it for me?”

And so, what’s really interesting is that Stephen Miller is somebody who, I think, during the first administration, was primarily motivated by his restrictionist beliefs and his desire to racially reengineer this country, as I mentioned. But during this administration, we’re seeing something else. I mean, you’re pointing out a really interesting contradiction, Amy. There’s another really interesting contradiction, which is that while they are deporting longtime undocumented immigrants who’ve been contributing to this country and who’ve accumulated some level of power in the form of U.S. citizen children, in the form of jobs, in the form of neighbors who care about them, they are pursuing a foreign policy that is displacing masses of people across Latin America, across the Middle East. And Stephen Miller has been one of the most vocal proponents of Trump’s foreign interventions and invasions.

And what I think is happening here, it sounds contradictory, but at the end of the day, it boils down to who Miller was as a teenager, which is somebody who didn’t mind immigrants being around so long as they served, they were serving him without complaint, so long as he could subjugate them. They are eliminating people who have deep roots here, and what they are doing is displacing people who have no roots here, who are ultimately going to come here.

And so, I think, at the end of the day, Stephen Miller and Trump are exactly who they’ve been criticizing all along. They are transnational. They are in alliance with transnational corporate elites who are displacing people across the country. And I think people need — are starting to understand that. This is one of the reasons that we saw this blue wave in the midterms.

AMY GOODMAN : Jean Guerrero, you just finished leading a program at USC Annenberg that’s geared to change the immigration debate by the next presidential election in 2028. Can you talk about this program, Our Unsilencing? The sons of Lorenzo Salgado Araujo participated, the man, 52-year-old father, Mexican father, who was shot to death by an immigration agent in Houston July 7th?

JEAN GUERRERO : Yes. So, I have been using my knowledge of Miller’s playbook and the impact that he had on the immigration debate to build a countermovement, and this is what the boot camp is about. We are empowering individuals who have been overlooked and who have not been at the center of the immigration debate to be at the center of the immigration debate. We’re training them how to tell their own stories on their own terms, and how to do so in a way that’s well researched, that’s grounded in tying their experiences to specific calls to action, that’s grounded in knowledge of the history of how personal testimony has transformed social movements in the United States, and also in a way that’s strategic in the immigration debate.

And so, we have people who have different levels of experience. The sons of Lorenzo Salgado came with more experience. They’ve been doing an amazing job. But everybody left knowing that they’re going to be central in changing the course of U.S. history.

And I think everybody listening has a role to play. We all need to be talking about the war on immigrants as a war on people power, because that is what it is. And I think people are starting to realize that. The war on immigrants, which is pouring billions of taxpayer dollars into jailing and displacing valued community members, and, ultimately, it is a war on labor. It is a war on civil and constitutional rights. And we need to demand the Democrats, with their new majorities — yes, it’s important that they hold the Trump administration accountable, but if they are not also prioritizing legislation on this issue, on the war on immigrants, then they’re going to come off as completely disingenuous. They need to pursue legislation to abolish ICE , and we need to demand that they do that.

We need ICE out of our cities. And we need also to prioritize legislation for the longtime undocumented population. You cannot have a sector of the working population that is criminalized and subjugated, because when you have that, then you are able to exploit the entire working class. And that is what this has always been about. And that is what this boot camp is determined to infuse into the public imagination, that the war on immigrants is a war on you. It is a war on everybody in this country, and we are going to expose it for what it is.

AMY GOODMAN : Jean Guerrero, I want to thank you for being with us, author of Hatemonger: Stephen Miller, Donald Trump, and the White Nationalist Agenda .

Coming up, meet Los Angeles’s new DSA Congressmember-elect Angela Gonzales-Torres. Her father was deported to Mexico when she was a teenager. Stay with us.

Special guests Angela Davis, Bruce Springsteen, Patti Smith, Michael Stipe and more came together to celebrate 30 years of Democracy Now! at a sold out Riverside Church event in NYC on March 23, 2026.

scraped.description: “I think there’s a high chance that it will be successful,” a member of Congress told The Intercept.
scraped.author: Nick Turse
scraped.h1: Impeachment Vote Looms for Hegseth
scraped.body_text:
© THE INTERCEPT

ALL RIGHTS RESERVED

“I think there’s a high chance that it will be successful,” a member of Congress told The Intercept.

Calls for self-styled War Secretary Pete Hegseth’s ouster have grown louder on Capitol Hill as a possible impeachment vote looms this week. At the same time, Hegseth has shored up support at the White House and among MAGA faithful, according to dismayed Pentagon officials.

Rep. Thomas Massie, R-Ky., introduced articles of impeachment on the House floor Monday afternoon, charging Hegseth with “high crimes and misdemeanors.” Top Democrats have indicated a desire to join Massie’s effort since their midterm election landslide . “I am a hard yes on the Hegseth resolution,” Rep. Hakeem Jeffries of New York, who is poised to be the next House speaker, told ABC’s “This Week” on Sunday. Rep. James Comer, R-Ky., the current House Oversight Committee chair, told Newsmax on Friday it is “very possible” the votes exist to impeach Hegseth.

Rep. Yassamin Ansari, D-Ariz., one of the leading voices for Hegseth’s impeachment, agreed. “I think there’s a high chance that it will be successful,” she told The Intercept of Massie’s effort. In April, Ansari filed six articles of impeachment against Hegseth, including violations of the law of armed conflict and targeting of civilians, abuse of power, and obstructing congressional oversight. She called for a floor vote on his ouster this week.

“Hegseth has demonstrated that he is wholly incompetent. He’s committed what I believe to be war crimes in Iran and the Caribbean and he is ill-equipped for the job,” said Ansari. “My reason for introducing the articles of impeachment back in April had a lot to do with his conduct and the war crimes in Iran, including the bombing of the children’s school. But it’s refreshing to see that since then, more and more Republicans are also recognizing that his leadership has failed and that he’s putting all of us in danger.”

Most Read “Dead Man Walking”: Officials Say Hegseth Has to Go Nick Turse Haley Stevens Destroyed Her Political Career for Absolutely Nothing Eoin Higgins Pentagon Officials Float Names of Hegseth’s Replacement Nick Turse

In the wake of a devastating election rout of the GOP that handed Democrats firm control of the House and the Senate, Congress begins a five-week lame-duck session on Monday. With dozens of Republican lawmakers ending their tenure in the House, it’s unclear how many will even show up for votes. Such absences, as well as outright defections in the GOP ranks, make it increasingly likely that Massie’s measure will pass, staffers on Capitol Hill told The Intercept.

On Sunday, GOP Rep. French Hill of Arkansas left open the possibility of backing the measure. “I want to hear the debate on it to see if it merits impeachment versus some other disciplinary action or action by the president,” he said on CBS News’s “Face the Nation.” Outgoing House speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., did not answer when asked by Politico if GOP leaders would whip the Hegseth impeachment vote. House leaders must take up the matter within two legislative days; opponents could table the resolution or refer it to committee instead of voting directly on impeachment.

After narrowly being confirmed by the Senate, which required Vice President JD Vance to break a 50-50 tie, Hegseth’s tenure has been marked by fiascos and failures beginning with Signal-gate , the sharing of secret war plans in a chat group with a journalist. In that case, according to the Pentagon’s own inspector general, “Hegseth violated security protocols and endangered U.S. troops and objectives.” Since then, Hegseth has been under perpetual fire for the unsuccessful Iran war in 2026, specifically a strike on an elementary school in Minab, Iran, that killed more than 150 civilians, most of them children . He faces pressure over his campaign of extrajudicial killings in attacks on so-called drug boats in the waters off Latin America. And questions continue to mount about his purge of top military leaders — many of them women and minorities .

“The fact that many career officials from the department have left citing his leadership, I think, is very telling,” said Ansari. Last week, The Intercept published an exposé quoting six current and former defense officials who currently serve or served under Hegseth and called for his ouster. “He is conducting state terrorism. He is 100 percent a war criminal. He needs to be prosecuted,” said Wes J. Bryant, one of those officials and, until last year, a senior targeting adviser and policy analyst at the Pentagon who was pushed out of his job for blowing the whistle on Hegseth’s efforts to undermine protections for civilians .

As calls for his ouster have grown louder, Hegseth launched a desperate bid to whip up support at the White House, including a nakedly obsequious video seeking Trump’s support that he posted on X . It was accompanied by a coordinated campaign of social media posts by Pentagon underlings tying Hegseth’s fortunes to the president with the text “ STAND. FIGHT. DEFEND THE REPUBLIC .”

Hegseth’s hand was strengthened on Friday when Trump’s chief of staff Susie Wiles stepped down and was replaced by his hard-line domestic policy adviser, raging xenophobe, and illegal boat strike proponent Stephen Miller, according to two Pentagon officials. The embattled war chief was quick to offer “ Huge CONGRATS ” to Miller on X, and posted a photo of himself alongside Trump’s new consigliere. The same coterie of Hegseth devotees at the Pentagon followed with similar posts featuring Miller .

Wiles had reportedly soured on Hegseth, blaming his woeful management of the Iran war for flagging Republican fortunes. A senior Trump administration official also told MS Now that Miller and Hegseth “have been extremely close since the beginning of the administration.”

If the House impeaches Hegseth, removing him from office would require a two-thirds vote in the Senate — a high bar, even when Democrats take control of the chamber in January. Neither of the two Cabinet secretaries impeached by the House — William Belknap, the secretary of war, in 1876; and Alejandro Mayorkas, the secretary of homeland security, in 2024 — were convicted by the Senate.

An Armed Services Committee staffer who spoke with The Intercept was skeptical that Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., would bring the measure to a vote. Ansari held out hope. “Thune is very much aligned in terms of his view that Hegseth is not fit for the job,” she said, adding, “I do think that the resounding victories on Tuesday night will impact the way Republicans operate moving forward.”

Sen. Thom Tillis, R-N.C., who is retiring at the end of the year, has said for months that he regrets his vote to confirm Hegseth and rebuked the war chief for his desperate video address aimed at Trump. “[C]abinet secretaries shouldn’t be wasting taxpayer dollars on campaign style videos. Kristi Noem learned that the hard way,” he wrote on X on Friday, also laying into Hegseth for “the incompetence you’ve displayed, the bad advice you’ve given to president, and your shameful and embarrassing episodes from firing our top generals to texting war plans to reporters.” Tillis had also previously said Hegseth “ needs to go .”

Massie suggested his impeachment resolution is the legislative equivalent of a mercy killing, calling it “ a much gentler version ” of what Democrats will do when they take control of Congress in January. Congressional committees have broad investigative powers, and Ansari said that if Hegseth survives this year’s impeachment push, there were “many ways” for Democrats to hold him accountable in the next session, specifically compelling him to testify before the American people. “I would be surprised to see him last the next two years in this administration,” she told The Intercept. “I think that he is not only one of the most incompetent members of the administration, but also the most unpopular — and it’s on a bipartisan basis. So the pressure will continue to grow for there to be some change at the Pentagon.”

Trump expressed mild “confidence” in Hegseth in a “60 Minutes” interview taped on Friday, touting the U.S. victory over Venezuela, but stopped short of praising his Pentagon chief for it. Asked if he credited Hegseth for what he considers a major victory, Trump replied: “No, but he was a part of it.” On Saturday, Trump wrote on Truth Social that calls for impeachment of administration officials amounted to “ extortion at the highest level ” and ordered the Justice Department to investigate those making the push.

Attorney General Todd Blanche, himself a potential target of impeachment, said on Sunday that the Justice Department would represent Hegseth during any impeachment proceedings. He added that he “would be very worried” if he were a Democrat threatening to investigate administration officials. Asked if he considered those threats to be a crime, Blanche said, “It depends on what’s said. So yes, there could be.”

The White House did not respond to questions about Trump’s support for Hegseth.

Update: November 9, 2026, 2:50 p.m. ET The article has been updated to note that Rep. Thomas Massie, R-Ky., introduced articles of impeachment against War Secretary Pete Hegseth on Monday afternoon.

IT’S EVEN WORSE THAN WE THOUGHT.

What we’re seeing right now from Donald Trump is a full-on authoritarian takeover of the U.S. government.

This is not hyperbole.

Court orders are being ignored. MAGA loyalists have been put in charge of the military and federal law enforcement agencies. The Department of Government Efficiency has stripped Congress of its power of the purse. News outlets that challenge Trump have been banished or put under investigation.

Yet far too many are still covering Trump’s assault on democracy like politics as usual, with flattering headlines describing Trump as “unconventional,” “testing the boundaries,” and “aggressively flexing power.”

The Intercept has long covered authoritarian governments, billionaire oligarchs, and backsliding democracies around the world. We understand the challenge we face in Trump and the vital importance of press freedom in defending democracy.

IT’S BEEN A DEVASTATING year for journalism — the worst in modern U.S. history.

We have a president with utter contempt for truth aggressively using the government’s full powers to dismantle the free press. Corporate news outlets have cowered, becoming accessories in Trump’s project to create a post-truth America. Right-wing billionaires have pounced, buying up media organizations and rebuilding the information environment to their liking.

In this most perilous moment for democracy, The Intercept is fighting back. But to do so effectively, we need to grow.

That’s where you come in. Will you help us expand our reporting capacity in time to hit the ground running in 2026?

scraped.author: Noah Hurowitz
scraped.h1: Tons of “Bunker-Buster” Bomb Parts for Israel Go Through JFK Airport
scraped.body_text:
© THE INTERCEPT

ALL RIGHTS RESERVED

At the height of the Iran war, parts for destructive “bunker-buster” bombs moved through JFK airport on their way to the Israeli military.

An Israeli airline shipped thousands of pounds worth of parts for controversial “bunker-buster” bombs through John F. Kennedy International Airport in New York during the height of the Israeli–U.S. war against Iran, according to a new investigation by a left-wing research group.

Challenge Airlines, a cargo hauler based in Israel, made three flights this spring carrying the bomb casings for BLU-109s — a 2,000-pound munition that has been tied to numerous mass-casualty attacks on civilian neighborhoods in the Gaza Strip, Lebanon, and Iran in recent years — according to open-source data obtained by the Movement Research Unit and reviewed by The Intercept.

The airline also made more than 100 shipments of guidance kits known as joint direct attack munitions, or JDAMs — which are used to convert so-called “dumb bombs” into GPS-guided munitions capable of striking a specific target — according to data shared with The Intercept. Many of the guidance kits were marked for use on the MK-84, another 2,000-pound bomb Israel used in its campaign to level Gaza, where fragments of JDAMs have repeatedly been found at the site of airstrikes .

The 2,000-pound bombs present a serious risk of civilian casualties, according to Josh Paul, a former State Department official who resigned at the outset of the war in Gaza to protest the Biden administration’s sale of weapons to Israel .

“If you look at historic U.S. use of 2,000-pound bombs, in the entire counter-ISIS campaign, there were just two that were dropped in the vicinity of the city of Mosul precisely because there is no way to use a 2,000-pound bomb discriminately in an urban environment,” Paul said, referring to an American air war during the final years of the Obama administration to end the Islamic State’s control of the Iraqi city of Mosul.

Israel hasn’t shared the United States’s reservations. The country made extensive use of the weapons to attack targets in Gaza and Lebanon, including a deadly strike on Gaza’s Jabaliya refugee camp that killed dozens of civilians, according to an analysis by the New York Times.

“If you look at a picture of Gaza right now, I would say Israel’s use of these weapons is functionally indistinguishable from indiscriminate bombing,” Paul said.

“There is no way to use a 2,000-pound bomb discriminately in an urban environment.”

Challenge Airlines, and the Israeli military did not respond to request for comment.

“We work closely with all airport partners to ensure the safety of public, neighboring communities, and airport personnel,” said a spokesperson for the Port Authority of New York and New Jersey, which operates JFK Airport. “The federal government and commercial airlines have primary responsibility as to what is allowed to be shipped on aircraft. We are pre-empted under federal law from interfering with these activities.”

While the shipments of JDAMs and bomb bodies for BLU-109s did not include active munitions, previous shipments of weapons through JFK have included explosives, including 14 tons of nitrocellulose bound for Israel in May 2025.

The Intercept verified the data showing all three shipments of bunker-buster bomb bodies, and verified a portion of the data showing shipments of JDAM kits. Movement Research Unit, an investigative outlet whose prior work has uncovered shipments of drone tech to Israel and the transport of fighter jet parts by United Airlines onboard civilian passenger flights , shared the data on the condition that some specifics of its methods be withheld to prevent a crackdown on the availability of such data.

In response to the flow of weapons and materiel through JFK, the New York City chapter of the Democratic Socialists of America has been organizing a campaign to stop the flow of weapons to Israel through the airport.

“This is another example of a growing body of reporting that shows how civilian infrastructure is used for the genocide in Gaza,” said a DSA member named Henry, who asked to be identified without his last name in order prevent retaliation from his employer. “Civilian air travel should prioritize passengers, travelers, and the international community — not weapons — and no worker should be forced to serve the militarized supply chain.”

Most Read “Dead Man Walking”: Officials Say Hegseth Has to Go Nick Turse Haley Stevens Destroyed Her Political Career for Absolutely Nothing Eoin Higgins Pentagon Officials Float Names of Hegseth’s Replacement Nick Turse

Challenge Airlines shipped the bunker-buster bomb bodies on flights leaving JFK for Tel Aviv on March 12, April 30, and May 6, according to the data shared with The Intercept.

They shipped the guidance kits far more frequently, with 109 shipments leaving JFK for Tel Aviv between December 22, 2024, and June 7, 2026. Cargo documents indicate that most of the shipments were of JDAM kits designed for 2,000-pound MK-84 bombs but also included at least one shipment of kits for bunker-buster bombs.

In total, the airline shipped 175,884 pounds of BLU-109 casings and more than 5 million pounds of JDAM kits between December 22, 2024, and June 7, 2026, according to the data obtained by Movement Research Unit.

JFK Airport is the main export hub for such munitions flying by air to Israel, according to federal data: More than half of all Israel-bound air shipments of weapons that fit the government export category for bombs and missiles was sent abroad from JFK.

It was not immediately clear where the bunker buster and JDAM shipments originated, but sales of military hardware to Israel typically either come from deals between the Israeli and U.S. governments or direct commercial purchases under a special export license made by the Israeli military from private companies.

In the first two years of Israel’s war on Gaza, the U.S. spent $21.7 billion on military aid to Israel, according to a study by analyst William Hartung. That has included multiple shipments of 2,000-pound bombs like the BLU-109 and the MK-84, as well as JDAM kits to equip the weapons with GPS guidance.

The Biden administration in May 2024 halted the shipment of MK-84 2,000-pound bombs to Israel, citing the potential harm to civilians, but President Donald Trump resumed shipments of the heavy munitions within weeks of retaking the White House.

News of the shipments comes just over a month after the Associated Press revealed plans in the works for the U.S. to ink a vast $2.8 billion arms sale to Israel that would include thousands of 2,000-pound bombs.

The ongoing sale of such heavy weapons to Israel underscores the need for a federal solution, according to Rep. Delia Ramirez, D-Ill., who sponsored last year legislation dubbed the “Block the Bombs Act,” that would bar the U.S. from selling BLU-109s, JDAMs, and other munitions central to Israel’s war effort.

“It’s good that people are putting pressure locally, but ultimately it is Congress’s responsibility to make that happen.”

“It’s the only bill that prohibits these weapons transfers from happening, and the only bill that creates a comprehensive process of oversight,” Ramirez told The Intercept. “There’s been a big push, particularly in New York and around JFK, to block these transfers and it’s good that people are putting pressure locally, but ultimately it is Congress’s responsibility to make that happen.”

First introduced in May 2025, the bill has gathered more than 80 co-sponsors but has thus far languished in legislative limbo. With the House of Representatives soon to be under Democratic control, Ramirez said she plans to bring the bill to the floor next session.

IT’S EVEN WORSE THAN WE THOUGHT.

What we’re seeing right now from Donald Trump is a full-on authoritarian takeover of the U.S. government.

This is not hyperbole.

Court orders are being ignored. MAGA loyalists have been put in charge of the military and federal law enforcement agencies. The Department of Government Efficiency has stripped Congress of its power of the purse. News outlets that challenge Trump have been banished or put under investigation.

Yet far too many are still covering Trump’s assault on democracy like politics as usual, with flattering headlines describing Trump as “unconventional,” “testing the boundaries,” and “aggressively flexing power.”

The Intercept has long covered authoritarian governments, billionaire oligarchs, and backsliding democracies around the world. We understand the challenge we face in Trump and the vital importance of press freedom in defending democracy.

IT’S BEEN A DEVASTATING year for journalism — the worst in modern U.S. history.

We have a president with utter contempt for truth aggressively using the government’s full powers to dismantle the free press. Corporate news outlets have cowered, becoming accessories in Trump’s project to create a post-truth America. Right-wing billionaires have pounced, buying up media organizations and rebuilding the information environment to their liking.

In this most perilous moment for democracy, The Intercept is fighting back. But to do so effectively, we need to grow.

That’s where you come in. Will you help us expand our reporting capacity in time to hit the ground running in 2026?
