scraped.title: An Effective AI Pushback Has to Go Beyond the Local
scraped.description: The midterms made clear that Americans are angry about the headlong rush into artificial intelligence. We are blocked from needed federal action for now, but states and localities have options that can move us toward eventual national regulation.
scraped.h1: Jacobin
scraped.body_text:
Login

Get an introductory Jacobin subscription for just $20

The midterms made clear that Americans are angry about the headlong rush into artificial intelligence. We are blocked from needed federal action for now, but states and localities have options that can move us toward eventual national regulation.

States should force tech firms to bear the social costs of their speculative investments in data centers. (Jim West / UCG / Universal Images Group via Getty Images)

Our latest issue, “The New Empire,” is out now. Get this issue plus three more for just $20.

L ast week’s election returns embodied a broad, national, and bipartisan reaction against data centers. In forty-six of the forty-seven local referenda held across some thirteen states, voters rejected new data center construction. Public opposition reflects local concerns about water usage, grid sustainability, and noise pollution. This opposition is also bubbling up at a moment when most of the public distrust s artificial intelligence (AI) in general, when two-thirds of Americans hold negative views of AI firms and their close ties to the Trump administration, and when fears about AI rank high among Americans’ leading worries.

This confluence of AI-adjacent fears is no accident. Each anxious spark leaps from a different facet of a single Silicon Valley strategy for hyperscaling AI. If this strategy works, it would induce a dramatic decline in labor’s income share of income. If it fails, it would saddle the state with crushing mountains of debt.

Voters, to be sure, likely perceive this dilemma only weakly. Yet their vivid fears create a chance for the Left to articulate a comprehensive diagnosis of hyperscale AI’s manifold problems — one that not only affirms the public’s fears but also articulates a coherent response. And just as the Silicon Valley strategy runs on a logic of scale, so too an effectual pushback must escalate beyond the local.

G enerative AI is being developed by a small handful of firms. They are taking on massive amounts of debt to build computing power on which costly new tools can be offered at scale. Given the size of these investments, the firms are commercially viable only if they sell their wares at scale. This means either tapping hidden wellsprings of productivity growth ( unlikely ) or being used as a low-marginal-cost substitute for white-collar labor (more likely).

The ensuing debt-fueled displacement of white-collar labor, if successful, will induce a massive shift of income from labor to capital, as even the AI firms concede . The ruination of ecosystems and acceleration of the climate crisis are mere side effects. There is strong historical evidence of technology’s corrosive effect on the labor share: recent data from Europe suggests that AI, no less than other recent tech leaps, causes losses to labor and corresponding gains to capital. Worse, because most democracies tax capital at lower rates than labor, that shift will constrict the state, diminishing its fiscal capacity to cushion job losses and declining wages. In effect, hyperscale AI creates a distributional crisis and robs the state of tools to address it.

Of course, this strategy might not work. AI might not be transformative as its boosters claim. Markets may lose their nerve before profits can be reaped. But if the AI strategy isn’t successful, the leading firms now dominant in public equity markets (and hence our pensions and 401[k]s), will almost certainly demand a “rescue” akin to the 2008–9 federal financial-crisis interventions.

As of August, hyperscale AI firms had accrued more than $500 million in debt from private equity, banks, and institutional investors such as Blackrock and Pimco. If that debt sours, the repercussions of the crisis, as in 2008–9, would likely force the government’s hand. If that happens, a massive transfer of risk to public balance sheets will follow. This is capitalism as a “heads I win, tails you lose” proposition.

Whether or not it founders, hyperscale AI capitalism will cleave open immense lost opportunities for society at large. On one estimate , US AI investments will add up to some $10.3 trillion between 2025 and 2032, or an average of 3.63 percent of US gross domestic product per year. This is $10 trillion that will not and cannot be spend on maternal care, pre-K education, cancer treatment, environmental mitigation, or any other social programs and planetary reparative work we desperately need. It is, by any measure, a staggering divergence of investment away from areas of urgent moral priority.

No wonder, then, that the American public has such profound anxieties. The data center build-outs are simply the most apparent of the many economic, political, fiscal, and environmental crises that hyperscale AI is inducing.

W hat then might be an effectual response? Except in Harwood, North Dakota, voters have pushed back at a local level by denying construction permission, or in Perry, Ohio, demanding that firms post a bond as insurance against the risk of fiscal implosion. Localities’ responses are circumscribed, though, by their limited powers and their small geographic reach. Cities and counties can do little about the labor market effects or fiscal risk. Many environmental costs associated with new demands on the electric grid are out of their reach. Some cities such as Austin and San Antonio own and operate their own electrical utilities, giving them a lever that doesn’t exist elsewhere in the country. But these are exceptions. Solely local responses are usually tightly constrained.

Since the effects of hyperscale AI capitalism emerge at the national level, it would ideally be the federal government that drives a comprehensive response. Pessimism about the prospect of federal action is wise for now. After Tuesday’s election, Trump reiterated his belief that data centers are “gold . . . only foolish leadership will say NO.” His December 2025 executive order , barring states from regulating AI, remains in force, although the legal theories upon which it rests are flawed. Even if a Democratic-controlled House and Senate can overcome his veto, any resulting AI legislation will likely be weak thanks to the need to assemble supermajorities to ensure bills’ passage.

The difficulty of federal action, however, does not mean that progressives should give up addressing hyperscale AI capitalism. They still have ways to use both their control at the state level and at the regional level to highlight its costsand offer the beginnings of a commensurate response — indeed, one that might be fully nationalized in two years.

In January, Democrats will have “trifectas” in twenty-two states and hold the governor’s office in seven more (Kansas and Alaska are still not called as I write). This is a first platform for action. To date, states’ responses have been reactive and purely negative: New York’s and Oregon’s governors paused data center construction, while laws imposing moratoria have been introduced but not passed in sixteen states. Advocates of successful local ballot initiatives have indicated that they plan to turn to bans in their states.

Yet a pause is not a policy. It does nothing to communicate the complex and interconnected harms of hyperscale AI capitalism. So it leaves the field open for AI’s advocates to advance their tall tales of illimitable gain. Nor does it prevent the building of data centers elsewhere in the nation and so does nothing to rein in its fiscal and labor costs.

An alternate approach would be for states to force tech firms to not just account for the local effects of data centers but also recognize and take responsibility for all the social costs of their hyperscale strategy. It would seek to channel economic development into less costly, more decent forms. Bans, however, are a badly formed tool to this subtle end.

As a start, states could recognize their own complicity in hyperscale AI. In forty states, data centers benefit from exemptions from the sales and use taxes that would ordinarily accrue on building materials, machinery, and equipment. The nominal justification for such exemptions is the jobs new builds purportedly bring. But a data center at best tends to create only two or three hundred jobs, with no long-term effect on wages. Where a landlord like Equinix, Data Realty, or CyrusOne rents computing power to remote clients, even that meager gain goes unrealized.

States’ and localities’ ensuing revenue loss is hard to measure , because only some of the states with these tax exemptions report their fiscal effect. Texas, however, lost some $1 billion in FY2025; in 2024, Illinois lost $370 million; and Arizona lost $19 million. A simple first step is terminating all these tax exemptions on the ground that the local benefits from data centers have been illusory, following Maine’s example. That might also prompt states to reconsider more generally their blind pursuit of corporate investments through tax relief.

Having withdrawn their reckless subsidies, states should follow Perry, Ohio’s lead by forcing tech firms to bear the social costs of their speculative investments. New construction, for example, might be conditioned on bonds tied to the environmental and state-level labor market effects of their business models. Firms would first be required to report not only on expected environmental harms (including from increased energy demand) but also address whether a data center’s expected uses will displace human labor or otherwise have wage-suppressive effects (as a leading study has already found). It would then have to post bonds sufficient to pay for state investments to buffer those effects.

The law might impel an AI-funded guarantee fund to sustain state unemployment payouts and retraining costs generated by AI. States could also require that data center investments be backed by sufficient nondebt financing to mitigate any risk of catastrophic fiscal events. And even if data centers are not fully banned, states might simply target specific uses as verboten — say, the large-scale automation of American jobs. Firms that flout this would see their centers shut down.

At the same time, states need not act alone. An underappreciated part of the American constitutional order is groups of states’ latent authority to enter into binding “ compacts .” These are treaty-like agreements, often created without Congress’s approval, to coordinate regulation between a pool of states. Existing compacts address drivers’ licenses, insurance coverage, and medical practice. They allow states to set uniform standards and realize regulation at scale, even if the national government is AWOL.

Imagine Texas, Virginia, California, Pennsylvania, and New York forging an interstate compact on AI and data centers. No firm would be permitted to operate data centers in any state unless they agreed to meet certain environmental standards and avoid use cases that threatened serious job loss. The compacting states could require a common set of disclosures — not only about the data centers themselves but also about the fiscal and labor market risks associated with AI more generally, and perhaps about other AI-related harms.

Unlike simple bans, this arrangement is more likely to be politically self-sustaining. Firms would, in effect, have to document on an ongoing basis the knot of harms that flow from hyperscale AI — hence supplying the grounds for their own regulation. And they could not simply blame states for quashing economic growth. A race to the bottom as firms tried to pit states against each other would be more difficult.

It is true that hyperscale AI capitalists are likely to flee from compacting states. But notice that the creation of a robust compact would limit their flight options, at least within the United States. To see this, consider the political costs to a red state governor who welcomes fleeing data centers that decline to comply with environmental and labor market protections. Recall that some 89 percent of Americans oppose data center siting near them. Isn’t it likely that the governor will meet the same fate as other erstwhile champions of AI, such as outgoing Texas Governor Greg Abbott? Compacting to clarify AI’s harms makes it politically more difficult for noncompacting states to embrace the industry.

No doubt, these solutions are incomplete. But they offer a pathway for dealing with not just the local but also the national harms of hyperscale AI in a politically durable way. They not only signal clearly that voters’ concerns have been heard but also help build virtuous circles of disclosure, action, and revenue so the perils of hyperscale AI can be enduringly addressed — a groundwork that offers a foundation for national action when the time is right.

Aziz Huq is a professor of law at the University of Chicago Law School.

scraped.title: End the Private Health Insurance Tax: Pass Medicare for All
scraped.description: Make no mistake: the thousands of dollars that come out of your paycheck each year to pay for health insurance is a tax, just one paid to a private insurer rather than the federal government. Medicare for All would actually lower your taxes.
scraped.h1: Jacobin
scraped.body_text:
Login

Make no mistake: the thousands of dollars that come out of your paycheck each year to pay for health insurance is a tax, just one paid to a private insurer rather than the federal government. Medicare for All would actually lower your taxes.

We often overlook how much money comes out of our paychecks in the form of employer and employee health insurance premiums — effectively a tax paid to insurance companies. A single-payer system would be more efficient and lower your real tax burden. (Sarah Rice / Getty Images)

Our latest issue, “The New Empire,” is out now. Get this issue plus three more for just $20.

E very other Monday, I arrive at work bleary-eyed, still finishing my coffee, and settle into the workweek by reviewing my latest pay stub. I’m looking for miscounted hours, abnormal deductions — the sorts of mistakes that never happen but could.

This morning was different. I spent the weekend fixating on the sorry state of health insurance in this country, roused in large part by Democrats’ comprehensive midterm victory, including wins by supporters of Medicare for All like Troy Jackson and Abdul El-Sayed. I arrived at my desk alert and reviewed my pay stub, focusing specifically on health care contributions.

When we look at our pay stubs, employer and employee health insurance contributions combine into a number we numbly accept as we focus on our take-home pay. In my case, the biweekly total is $1,267. That adds up to about $33,000 over the year, higher than the average employer-sponsored family plan cost of $28,303 . Single-coverage plans average about $9,000, while workers buying on the marketplace pay upward of $7,500 annually ($12,000 in my home state of Alaska).

These figures represent real, consequential lost wages. And they get higher every year.

I have a stable union job with my local municipal government. My health insurance leaves a lot to be desired, often burdening my family with out-of-pocket costs (a reality brought home just last week during an emergency room visit for our daughter, who thankfully is fine). Still, it is better than what most American workers have. I am meant to feel lucky for it.

Look at the alternatives: I could have a lesser plan with higher deductibles and out-of-pocket limits. I could have no insurance at all, like roughly 10 percent of Americans. Or scarier still, I could be forced to pay taxes into a single-payer system that removes health care from the workplace and covers everyone equally.

But staring at a pay stub leaves us to wonder: What are health insurance premiums if not a tax? They’re compulsory; we can’t opt out. And even if we could, we would never expose ourselves to such catastrophic risk. The deduction is listed separately from federal taxes on the pay stub, but what makes it different?

The answer is who gets the money. Our health care premiums are nothing other than a compulsory tax paid to private insurance companies instead of the federal government. When included with our other taxes, they make the United States one of the highest-taxed countries in the world — higher even than the Nordic states .

The United States spends roughly 18 percent of its GDP on health care, double that of peer nations with universal health care systems. The oft-stated benefit of our system is that it saves us from taxes, but in fact it taxes us at a premium and sends the excess to insurers as profit. Worse, it burdens us with impossible out-of-pocket costs at our times of greatest need.

Our paychecks suffer from this waste. Rising premiums help keep our wages stuck as employers weigh insurance and wages against the same bottom line. Every dollar diverted to surging premiums is a dollar stolen from our wages and benefits. All the while, workers shoulder ever-increasing deductibles and contribution shares.

Y ou have heard, of course, that single-payer health insurance — Medicare for All — will cost trillions of dollars. It will raise your taxes. It will take away your hard-won and much-beloved employer-sponsored insurance.

It’s tempting to argue the obvious: yes, Medicare for All will raise your taxes, but the increase in your taxes will be significantly lower than your current premiums and out-of-pocket costs, which will disappear.

Looking at my pay stub, however, I don’t even want to concede that it will raise taxes. Again, payroll insurance contributions are a compulsory, unavoidable tax on your wages . Under Bernie Sanders’s Medicare for All proposal, my employer (a budget-strapped municipal government) would pay $260 per paycheck through a 7.5 percent payroll tax, and I would pay $94 via a 4 percent income tax after standard deductions. The combined total of $354 represents $913 in savings — $23,738 over a year.

Medicare for All will reconfigure your taxes, sure. But it won’t raise them. It will lower them.

The $24,000 newly freed from my paycheck would land on the bargaining table in negotiations over my union’s next contract. Some of this will go directly to wage increases. Some will go to benefits. Some will stay with the municipal government. For all future negotiations, though, we will not have to tackle the albatross of rising insurance premiums.

H ealth care is expensive, costing trillions per year no matter who pays. Currently, it’s paid for in a convoluted, wasteful scheme: private insurers act as payers using funds taken from our wages, while the government covers its share in Medicare and Medicaid. The rest is paid out-of-pocket by patients in times of need.

The effect is to chain us to our jobs, suppress our wages, and burden our negotiations.

We all know this is not what health insurance is for. Health insurance is meant to minimize risk, minimize costs, and mitigate catastrophes. This can only be accomplished with a single, government payer. A true tax should fund a public good to benefit society, not drain your wages to benefit profiteers.

With an overwhelming mandate and the policy still popular , Democrats ought to run a Medicare for All supporter in 2028 and make it their first priority in the new Congress. The policy will save up to a trillion dollars annually in overall spending. You can look at your pay stub to see where those savings will land.

Tim Higginbotham is a member of the Democratic Socialists of America in Anchorage, Alaska.

United Food and Commercial Workers Local 8–Golden State has been headed by one family since 1984. Reform candidates say union staff are using intimidation tactics to prevent a competitive election this year.

Eric Marcuz took a selfie at a truck stop with Jeff Berns, who he said had been following him for an hour at that point, starting at the union hall in Roseville, California. (At What Cost / Facebook)

Our latest issue, “The New Empire,” is out now. Get this issue plus three more for just $20.

I n a union that has been headed by one family with no competitive elections since 1984, a group of grocery workers is organizing for change. But last week, they say, union staff who back the incumbent administration went to outrageous lengths in an attempt to make sure there’s no election this year either.

On the afternoon of Monday, November 2, Eric Marcuz, a veteran Northern California Safeway worker, stopped at the union office to pick up blank petitions to get on the ballot in the union’s upcoming election. Marcuz is running for president on the At What Cost slate in the 23,000-member United Food and Commercial Workers (UFCW) Local 8–Golden State (8-GS), one of the largest locals in the union.

To get on the ballot, Marcuz and his slate-mates have to collect 443 petition signatures — 2 percent of the local’s active members — by mid-November. If they don’t get enough signatures, no election will be held.

After Marcuz picked up the petitions from the local’s Roseville office, he got in his car to drive three hours south to Fresno, to start collecting signatures with another candidate on his slate at a Save Mart store there. (The local spans a ten-hour stretch from Bakersfield up to the Oregon border.)

When Marcuz stopped for gas, he said he noticed that a black Dodge Ram pickup stopped as well. When he got back on the freeway, so did the truck.

At the next gas stop, Marcuz spoke to the man driving the truck. It was Jeff Berns, a staff representative for Local 8-GS. His brother, Mark, is also on staff at the union — and the local’s election chair, responsible for overseeing the election.

Marcuz asked Jeff Berns why he was following him. According to Marcuz, Berns said he wanted to make sure that all the members got the “accurate information” that Marcuz’s slate was going to “divide” the union. He said he was going to follow him the entire time Marcuz was out, all the way back to Marcuz’s house in Redding, several hours north. Marcuz jokingly asked him if he needed a place to stay. Berns said he didn’t — because he’d been staying a lot in the Redding area lately himself, which Marcuz said he thought was “creepy” because that’s where Marcuz lives with his family (and is not where Berns lives).

Berns would live up to his promise — following Marcuz for the next three hundred miles, through every stop, exit, and U-turn. He even followed him inside the Fresno Save Mart and camped out for an hour with another union rep while Marcuz ate dinner at a supporter’s house one hundred miles north in Modesto.

A t the gas station, Berns repeated the mantra, “Solidarity works!” That’s the motto of the incumbent president, Jacques Loveall, who is heading the Solidarity Works Team slate in this election.

Loveall was appointed to lead the union in 2004, when his father, Jack Loveall, stepped down. The elder Loveall had held the top office since 1984; when he retired he was one of the highest-paid union officers in the country, earning the equivalent of $1 million today. (The Contra Costa Times reported that he had a $28,000-a-year country club membership and “two pilots on staff to chauffeur him in a private jet.”) Neither father nor son has ever faced a competitive election in the local.

Back on the freeway, Marcuz called a Department of Labor agent whom he had already been in touch with. They had previously spoken about the local’s apparent attempt to cancel the election by merging with a mysterious organization called the Staffing Agencies Federated Employees, an entity that listed one of Loveall’s relatives as its president on its initial filing. The agent told him to report the intimidation to the election chair and tell him to get the rep to back off.

Marcuz then called Mark Berns, the election chair, who he said told him he would talk to staff about acting in a professional manner.

H owever, when Marcuz arrived at the Save Mart store in Fresno to begin collecting petition signatures, he and another slatemate, Mike Romero, said that three union reps were waiting for them, including Jeff Berns. One of the others was John Micheletti, a longtime Local 8 vice president. Far from being called off, they said, the intimidation had actually intensified.

Marcuz and Romero said the reps interfered with every conversation they attempted to have with workers about signing their nomination petition. The very first worker they engaged about signing, a longtime acquaintance of Romero’s, fled once a rep entered the conversation and became confrontational. The worker did not sign the petition.

“They were everywhere inside the store,” said Marcuz. At least one of the interactions was filmed on a phone.

Marcuz said that Berns told him, “I’m going to make sure everyone knows who you are and not to sign that.” And additionally, “We’re going to invalidate every single signature that you get.”

It is illegal for union staff and officers to campaign on union time. Berns said he was on vacation.

Romero, who has worked at Save Mart for thirty years, said, “This is the most I’ve seen of union staff in six months.” He said a fourth rep turned up after Marcuz left.

T hese tactics — following opposition candidates and invalidating signatures — have both been alleged by previous members of the local who attempted to challenge the Lovealls.

A Contra Costa Times article published in 2004 reported that supporters of Loveall’s father got members to rescind their signatures to keep dissident candidate Jack Nordby off the ballot in 1997. A book written by then Local 588 reform activist Doug Slaydon states that as many as 150 signatures were removed. (Local 588 merged with another local to form Local 8-GS in 2006 — postponing a potential competitive election that year.)

Nordby also alleged that he was tailed by a pickup truck while collecting ballot signatures, followed around by union reps in stores, and once chased in his car while driving his wife and two daughters to church.

The Contra Costa Times also reported allegations that Local 588 staffers staked out the home of a member of UFCW Local 1179 who had led a successful rank-and-file opposition campaign to an attempted merger of the two locals and “tailed him in union cars.” “In June 1994,” reported the Times , the member, Michael Ross-Smith, “was rear-ended in Walnut Creek by three UFCW 588 business agents following him too closely in a white 1993 Ford Thunderbird leased to the union, according to a traffic collision report from the Walnut Creek police department.”

M arcuz and Romero said they quickly realized that they wouldn’t be able to collect petition signatures with this level of interference. Marcuz’s next stop was going to be to drop off petition forms with a supporter at the Turlock Safeway, over an hour to the north, but he made plans to meet the supporter at their house in Modesto instead.

When Marcuz left the parking lot of the Fresno store, Romero said three vehicles followed him. Romero also realized that one of the reps had stayed behind, and he became worried that he would be followed as well. He drove around for a long time before going home, to make sure he wasn’t followed.

Marcuz, meanwhile, said that Berns and Micheletti followed him for ninety miles, all the way to Modesto. They stayed parked outside the house while Marcuz ate burritos with the supporter — finally leaving after an hour, after 8 p.m.

“It’s crazy that they would literally go two hours out of their way to make sure nobody else can talk to the employees,” Romero said.

Marcuz said he almost canceled his plans to stay alone in a hotel in Roseville overnight, worried he would be tailed there, and contemplated driving for four more hours home to Redding. In total, he estimates he was followed for seven hours, over a distance of three hundred miles.

S ection 610 of the Labor-Management Reporting and Disclosure Act (LMRDA) forbids the threat or use of force or violence to restrain, coerce, or intimidate union members from exercising their right to nominate candidates or to vote in union officer elections, while Section 401(e) bars “improper interference” in the rights of union members to run for and support candidates for local union office.

“It makes me think of everyone that has known there’s been a need for change in the past and has been scared away from pursuing it,” Marcuz said. While Marcuz and his slate are standing strong, he said, “this might work. They might intimidate and scare enough people out of participating.”

In the morning, Marcuz filed a police report with the Roseville Police Department alleging stalking and harassment, citing the time and distance he was followed and the behavior he encountered in the Fresno store.

Local 8 did not respond to requests for comment.

Petition signatures are due November 17, and ballots will be mailed November 21.

Lisa Xu is an organizer with Labor Notes .

They debate whether removing Hegseth would help bring the war in Iran to an end, why President Donald Trump bears ultimate responsibility for his administration's actions, and whether Congress will finally assert its authority over military decisions.

The conversation turns to Trump's decision to replace White House chief of staff Susie Wiles with Stephen Miller, and what the move signals about the administration's response to its crushing midterm defeat. scraped.title: Gina Hinojosa wants to freeze electricity rates in Texas. New Jersey shows why that won’t work.
scraped.description: New Jersey spent $500 million on ratepayer relief, but utility bills stayed high as supply and transmission costs persisted.
scraped.author: Tosin Akintola
scraped.h1: Gina Hinojosa Wants To Freeze Electricity Rates in Texas. New Jersey Shows Why That Won't Work.
scraped.body_text:
Log In

Create new account

Texas

Tosin Akintola | 11.9.2026 5:19 PM

When Democrat Gina Hinojosa is sworn in as Texas governor in January, one of her first acts, "within an hour of taking the oath of office," she recently told The Texas Tribune, will be to "declare a high-cost emergency in the state of Texas and issue an emergency executive order to: one, suspend the gas and diesel tax; and two, freeze electricity rates."

Hinojosa—who tied increases in property taxes and electricity bills to Republican Gov. Greg Abbott's policies— promised during her campaign that if elected, she would "direct the Public Utility Commission to freeze the rates residential customers pay until we have laws to ensure that data centers and other high-load users pay for themselves."

With Texans seeing a 3.3 percent increase in the average electricity price for residential customers between August 2025 and August 2026—roughly in line with the national increase—the state's electorate clearly found Hinojosa's pledge compelling. However, it's unclear if Hinojosa actually has the power to follow through on her campaign promise.

In Texas' decentralized market, retail providers, not regulators, set electricity prices. This means Hinojosa has very little authority over residential prices, and her order would not lower costs. But as Click2Houston.com points out, Hinojosa could still impact prices; she could use her influence over the state budget "to push lawmakers toward her priorities," including forcing data centers to pay more. Of course, this would do little to address the primary cause of nationwide electricity spikes: transmission and distribution charges.

Instead of Texas imposing price controls on the free market, Hinojosa could learn from the mistakes of New Jersey Gov. Mikie Sherrill, a fellow Democrat who has failed to meaningfully lower electricity prices in her state despite signing an executive order that declared a state of emergency and froze rate hikes by the state's utilities.

Sherrill realized that even if she froze rates, it wouldn't erase the factors driving higher electricity prices, such as the supply and transmission costs providers pay. In June, to offset the increases utilities typically pass on to customers, Sherrill signed off on a budget authorization that allocates $500 million to provide ratepayers short-term relief. Yet in October, a CBS News report found that even after the rate freeze, utility costs in the Garden State remained high, with one resident remarking her electricity bill had "nearly doubled."

In July, the consulting firm E3 released a report—commissioned by Sherrill for the New Jersey Board of Public Utilities—that found that changes to state policy mainly affect distribution, which is "roughly a quarter" of the charges on residents' electricity bills, and that "no single reform or modernization option" could be presented as a standalone fix.

It's not just New Jersey that has tried (and failed) to bring down utility costs by freezing electricity rates; last July Georgia's Public Service Commission unanimously approved an agreement to freeze base power rates for at least three years. A year after the freeze was implemented, the average electricity price for residential customers in Georgia rose by 2.3 percent . Meanwhile, in October, Virginia Democratic Gov. Abigail Spanberger called for a six-year freeze on residential electricity rates as a condition for approving the proposed $67 billion merger between utilities Dominion Energy and NextEra Energy.

Regardless of where it's proposed, a rate freeze is a superficial fix for a problem that requires less government thumb on the scale, not more.

At least one Democratic governor has declined to use rate freezes as a temporary panacea for rising energy costs. In a March appearance on CBS 2's " The Point ," New York Gov. Kathy Hochul was asked if she thought a "two-year moratorium or freeze on utility rates statewide" was "doable." She quickly rejected the idea, favoring an "all-of-the-above approach to find more sources of energy to help drive down [costs]."

What rate freezes like Hinojosa's miss is that states have little direct impact on electric prices. As the E3 report notes , "Most of a typical bill…is set in federal and regional markets with limited ability at the state level to influence those costs."

Still, that doesn't make the idea behind these policies—that government should interfere in the market—any less harmful.

Without the price signals they receive from electricity rates, utilities can't properly plan for upgrades, expansion, or future demand. Freezing electricity rates clearly polls well as policy, but it works better on the campaign trail than in practice.

scraped.title: S. Ct. Suspends District Court's Injunction Blocking Border Barrier Building
scraped.description: "There is no such thing as a 'constitutional' major-questions claim."
scraped.body_text:
Log In

Create new account

Mostly law professors | Sometimes contrarian | Often libertarian | Always independent

Major Questions Doctrine

"There is no such thing as a 'constitutional' major-questions claim."

Eugene Volokh | 11.9.2026 4:32 PM

From today's Supreme Court unsigned opinion in Mullin v. Friends of the Ruidosa Church (with Justice Jackson essentially dissenting):

Section 102 of the Illegal Immigration Reform and Immigrant Responsibility Act of 1996 (IIRIRA) grants the Secretary of Homeland Security broad authority to construct border barriers and roads "to deter illegal crossings in areas of high illegal entry into the United States." The same section expressly authorizes the Secretary "'to waive all legal requirements'" as "'necessary to ensure expeditious construction'" of those barriers and roads, and sharply limits judicial review of all claims arising from such waiver determinations. Specifically, the statute provides that "'[a] cause of action or claim may only be brought alleging a violation of the Constitution of the United States'" and courts "'shall not have jurisdiction'" over nonconstitutional claims. §102(c)(2)(A).

Earlier this year, the Secretary invoked Section 102's waiver authority to initiate a border-construction project at the U.S.–Mexico border, in a region that U.S. Customs and Border Protection has designated the "Big Bend Sector." The Secretary found that the Big Bend Sector "is an area of high illegal entry" requiring additional border barriers, and waived the application of a variety of environmental and conservation laws to facilitate expeditious construction.

Shortly thereafter, respondents—an individual river guide, an environmental nonprofit, and a nonprofit organization dedicated to preserving a historic church in Ruidosa, Texas—challenged those waiver determinations by filing suit in the U.S. District Court for the Western District of Texas. Respondents claimed, among other things, that the Secretary's waiver determinations "violat[ed] the major questions doctrine under the U.S. Constitution, Article I, Section 1." Although styled as constitutional, that claim simply alleged that the Secretary exceeded his statutory authority in issuing the waivers.

On October 2, 2026, the District Court entered a preliminary injunction blocking the Secretary's waivers and halting all associated construction. The District Court acknowledged that its jurisdiction was limited to constitutional claims. But it nonetheless concluded that respondents' "major questions doctrine claim" qualified because, in its view, the "major questions doctrine is a constitutional clear statement rule grounded in separation of powers." The court further held that respondents' "major questions doctrine claim" was likely to succeed on the merits because the Secretary lacked "'clear congressional authorization' to issue" the waivers. Because the Fifth Circuit lacks jurisdiction to hear this case, IIRIRA §102(c)(2)(C), the Solicitor General filed an application requesting either summary reversal or a stay of the District Court's preliminary injunction.

We grant the requested stay. The Government is exceedingly likely to prevail on its argument that the District Court lacked jurisdiction to adjudicate respondents' so-called major-questions-doctrine claim. However it is labeled, respondents' claim does not "'alleg[e] a violation of the Constitution of the United States,'" the only type of claim the statute permits district courts to adjudicate. IIRIRA §102(c)(2)(A). It alleges instead that the Secretary exceeded his statutory authority. And we have long recognized that "claims simply alleging" that the Executive Branch has exceeded its "statutory authority are not 'constitutional' claims." Dalton v. Specter (1994).

That conclusion does not change where, as here, a plaintiff invokes the major-questions doctrine. Many canons and rules of statutory interpretation reflect constitutional principles, including "constitutional avoidance, the clear-statement federalism rules, and the presumption against retroactivity." When courts invoke those canons, however, they do so in service of adjudicating statutory claims, not constitutional ones. The same is true when a court invokes "the major questions canon of statutory interpretation." There is no such thing as a "constitutional" major-questions claim….

Respondents claim that construction in the Big Bend Sector will diminish their ability to use and enjoy the area. But Congress's enactment of IIRIRA §102(c)—which permits the Secretary to waive the requirements of environmental-protection and other conservation laws—reflects a clear preference for expeditious border construction over the very harms respondents assert. And courts "of equity cannot, in their discretion, reject the balance that Congress has struck in a statute." The Government's interest therefore outweighs any aesthetic, recreational, and environmental harm alleged by respondents….

NEXT: The Butler Didn't Do It

Eugene Volokh is the Thomas M. Siebel Senior Fellow at the Hoover Institution at Stanford, and the Gary T. Schwartz Distinguished Professor of Law Emeritus and Distinguished Research Professor at UCLA School of Law. Naturally, his posts here (like the opinions of the other bloggers) are his own, and not endorsed by any institution. He is also the co-host of the Free Speech Unmuted podcast .

scraped.title: Iran War Day 255: Qatar’s PM to Meet Trump, Vance to Push for Deal
scraped.description: State of the Union: Trump says he’s “not looking to” restart the active phase of the war.
scraped.author: Jude Russo
scraped.body_text:
Qatar’s Prime Minister Mohammed bin Abdulrahman al-Thani will meet President Donald Trump and Vice President J.D. Vance in Washington Monday as the Gulf monarchy tries to close the gap between American and Iranian peace deal demands.

According to a Saturday report in the Guardian , Qatar has proposed that Iran allow UN inspectors into its nuclear sites in exchange for the U.S. lifting its naval blockade and unfreezing some of the Islamic Republic’s assets. Al-Thani spoke to Trump Friday about the new proposal. An Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesman said Monday that Iran remained committed to its obligations under the Nonproliferation Treaty, but could not honor them under current circumstances.

Diplomatic activity has intensified amid concerns that fighting will be renewed in the wake of last Tuesday’s American midterm elections. U.S. Central Command on Saturday announced “Task Force Iron Gate,” a staff devoted to stopping Iranian overland trade to complement the naval blockade in the Persian Gulf.

Both sides have expressed reluctance to return to the active phase of hostilities. Trump said in an interview with 60 Minutes that aired Sunday that he did not intend to renew military escalation against Iran. “I’m not looking to. I don’t think there's any reason to. I don’t think there’s any reason to,” he said. Iran’s President Masoud Pezeshkian said Monday that Supreme Leader Ayatollah Mojtaba Khamenei had given him a mandate to end the current “neither war nor peace” impasse with the U.S., including through diplomacy if possible.

In addition to Qatar, other countries are reportedly taking an active role in heading of further war. Turkey’s President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan urged Trump over the weekend not to escalate against Iran, according to a Monday comment from the Turkish intelligence chief İbrahim Kalın. Kalın also said that Vance and the Iranian Secretary of the Supreme National Security Council Mohsen Rezaei would travel to Qatar next week for negotiations. The Washington Post ’s David Ignatius claimed Friday that the Trump administration had reached out to China for help brokering an end to the war. The Chinese Foreign Ministry declined Monday to comment on the substance of that report, but asserted that the war is not in the best interest of both parties and the international community.

Energy markets responded positively at the prospects of a diplomatic settlement. Brent crude opened Monday at $97.63 and began tumbling. AAA reported further easing for consumers, with Monday’s national average prices per gallon coming down to $4.01 for regular gas and $6.17 for diesel.

Jude Russo is the managing editor of The American Conservative and a contributing editor of The New York Sun . He is a 2024–25 James Madison Fellow at Hillsdale College and was named one of the ISI Top 20 Under 30 for 2024.

scraped.title: Jeffries Backs Hegseth Impeachment
scraped.description: State of the Union: Rep. Hakeem Jeffries, likely the next Speaker of the House, is a “hard yes” on removing the defense secretary.
scraped.author: Luke Nicastro
scraped.body_text:
Rep. Hakeem Jeffries (D-NY), the top Democrat in the House of Representatives, said Sunday he supports a resolution to impeach Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth. “I’m a hard yes on the Hegseth resolution,” Jeffries told ABC in an interview. “The so-called secretary of defense has abused his power, undermined our national security, and engineered this reckless and costly war of choice in Iran, which has skyrocketed prices on the American people and made the country less safe.”

A measure to impeach Sec. Hegseth was introduced by Rep. Thomas Massie (R-KY) in September, but Speaker Mike Johnson (R-LA) recessed the House before the resolution could receive a vote. Rep. Massie is expected to reintroduce this resolution now that Congress is back in session, teeing up a vote later this week. If the measure passes the House, Sec. Hegseth could then be removed from office by a two-thirds vote in the Senate (an outcome most analysts consider extraordinarily unlikely).

Luke Nicastro is a senior editor at The American Conservative. Before joining the magazine, he spent nearly a decade working on defense and foreign policy in both government and industry, most recently as National Security Advisor to U.S. Senator Josh Hawley. He has also worked at the Congressional Research Service, the Department of the Navy, the National Defense University, and several defense contractors.

items.summary: The difficulty of divided government will make a return to Trump-hunting and lawfare tempting. The post Will Democrats Squander Their Midterms Mandate? appeared first on The American Conservative. Politics Will Democrats Squander Their Midterms Mandate? They didn’t just win Congress in a landslide. They landed a two-year j...

scraped.title: Will Democrats Squander Their Midterms Mandate?
scraped.description: The difficulty of divided government will make a return to Trump-hunting and lawfare tempting.
scraped.author: Andrew Day
scraped.body_text:
The difficulty of divided government will make a return to Trump-hunting and lawfare tempting.

I hope the Democrats understand what the results of the midterms really mean. They didn’t just win Congress in a landslide. They landed a two-year job interview with the American people, with the presidency in 2028 as the real prize if they do well, a chance to prove in hard policy terms they should be handed the White House. Or they could squander it beating up on the lame-duck President Donald Trump.

Democrats have clearly been facing restiveness from their base over failing to stand up to Trump. They are unlikely to cooperate with the administration. If a faction of Republican lawmakers turn on Trump, they may even be able to override a presidential veto and will possibly have the votes available to impeach and convict him, something they lacked in Trump’s first term. But probably not. So, how will they use the power they’ve just been handed by the American people?

Americans face higher prices after being promised economic relief. They want cheap gas as their birthright. Their healthcare bills aren’t getting any cheaper. They were promised an end to American wars of choice in the Middle East only to watch Trump launch the conflict in Iran. It appears voters either did really pretend Trump was on the ballot—and voted against him—or that they in a small way began to hold Congressional Republicans’ feet to the fire for letting so many bad things happen on their watch. There is no doubt the people spoke, the center held, the system worked, and all the pre-election noise about the end of democracy was just guff.

But Trump will be president for about another two years. He acts unilaterally and somewhere between boldly and erratically, so for better or worse, he can still pursue a blizzard of executive policy actions. The winning Dems won’t take office until January, and even 2027 for them will be bifurcated by the start of serious campaigning ahead of the 2028 presidential election. They don’t have much time. But to pass the test the American people have set before them—do something about the economy—it is unclear what they can accomplish.

Trump-appointed Republicans still control Treasury and Commerce, and the Fed will still do its business more or less free of political interference. People seem unclear about the actual status of tariffs after so much Trumpian fidgeting, never mind what the actual impact has been. ICE and its sister organization, Customs and Border Protection, are largely untouchable in the short run, as they are already funded for the balance of Trump’s term. There are no obvious Supreme Court vacancies coming. If you can’t control interest rates and thus inflation, and if you can’t slam the brakes on Trump in Iran and thereby lower gas prices, what can you do? What was the point of electing Democrats again?

If the practical side of the Democratic Party is stymied, it opens the door for the vengeful and radical left wing. Internal Democratic struggles, not legislation, will then probably dominate. Promoting narratives about Epstein, Elon Musk, the Arch and other Trumpian construction projects, and corruption will overrun getting real things done if progressives like AOC and El-Sayed rush into the gap while centrist Dems find themselves frustrated on the sidelines. It is hard not to see voter dissatisfaction with the Democrats grow even though they did so well in the midterms. The people showed up and voted, but they won’t get much of what they wanted.

None of this is helped by the apparent inability of the Democratic Party to boost viable presidential candidates. Polling shows the leading Democratic candidate at present is Kamala Harris with 34 percent support; she badly lost both past primaries and the general election. AOC, who has little support outside coastie progressives, is at 11 percent. New-blood governors like Andy Beshear and Josh Shapiro did not show enough support to even make the chart. Dems appear to have no strong successor with a national following, which only reinforces the impression of a party that can organize opposition but struggles to articulate a governing alternative.

Instead, the people will likely get more of what Democrats have specialized in throughout the Trump era: lawfare. Following that fateful night in 2016 when the world said goodbye to Hillary Clinton, the Democrats sought to first overthrow Trump in a deep state-assisted coup centered around Russiagate, then to destroy him politically via two impeachments, then during the Biden administration to bankrupt and/or jail him with New York prosecutions, civil suits, MeToo, and debanking, and more recently, by connecting Trump with supposed personal misconduct, hidden inside the Epstein Files, that is so vile even his base will walk away. Expect more of all that—food-fight impeachments and investigations over the controversy du jour —but the details don't really matter. Revenge, and dragging Trump through the mud hoping to have some of it rub off on Vance in the process, does.

The problem for the Democrats, of course, is that this strategy hasn’t worked to bring down Trump. Arguably, surviving them made Trump only stronger and Democrats weaker for having failed. Even as he was found guilty of multiple felonies for falsifying business records (this remains the only criminal conviction against Trump), he wound up getting no prison time, no probation, not even a fine, and no apparent political punishment from the voters. A civil case of sexual assault resulted in millions awarded to the victim, but even this case seemingly hasn’t much hampered the president politically. Much of the country yawned seeing how one city, New York, wedded to its liberal values and home to biased juries, could stir up a lot of smoke and fail to start a fire. The Biden administration and the pro-Biden FBI had the full Epstein files for years and evidently found inside them nothing to wield against Trump.

It seems likely that instead of following through on their promises to fix the country’s real problems, the Democrats will squander the opportunity and end up looking petty and overly focused on hurting Trump rather than helping Americans.

Peter Van Buren is the author of We Meant Well: How I Helped Lose the Battle for the Hearts and Minds of the Iraqi People , Hooper’s War: A Novel of WWII Japan , and Ghosts of Tom Joad: A Story of the 99 Percent .

scraped.title: Massie reintroduces articles of impeachment against Pete Hegseth
scraped.description: The Kentucky congressman may be leaving congress, but he wants to help clean house on his way out, starting with the defense secretary
scraped.h1: Massie reintroduces articles of impeachment against Pete Hegseth
scraped.body_text:
The Kentucky congressman may be leaving congress, but he wants to help clean house on his way out, starting with the defense secretary

Rep. Thomas Massie may not be returning to congress next year but he is determined to make the most of his last two months on Capitol Hill, starting with initiating impeachment proceedings against defense secretary Pete Hegseth, which he introduced on Monday.

In a live feed, the Kentucky Republican issued the impeachment articles on the floor of the US House of Representatives ahead of a scheduled press conference Monday afternoon.

It was not yet clear when a vote would take place but it will take place within the next two days under House rules. It will be the first major vote since Democrats’ landslide victory in the midterms last week. With vastly different dynamics today, there are better chances this could pass even with the current GOP majority, this time around.

“I suspect there are members who want to put some daylight between themselves and this war, between themselves and this administration,” Massie told reporters in a press conference on Capitol Hill following his floor speech, noting that if passed, the House could kick this to the new Democrat-controlled Senate in January.

Massie initially introduced the legislation in September, but Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) sent members home before the House could hold a vote, seemingly motivated by a desire to avoid what would have been a politically tricky vote for party leadership. Johnson has denied that he made the decision to avoid a vote on Hegseth's impeachment.

“I’ve seen some of my colleagues say @SecWar Hegseth has been effective and they agree with the war, so they’ll vote not to impeach,” Massie wrote on social media on Monday. “That’s not the question though. The question is whether he committed impeachable acts, and the answer is yes, eight times.”

Massie’s eight articles of impeachment accuse Hegseth of waging unlawful wars against Iran and Yemen, dismantling the DoD safeguards intended to protect civilians during a military conflict, and authorizing extrajudicial strikes against alleged drug-smuggling boats in the Caribbean and Eastern Pacific, among other offenses.

"I have never seen, in my entire lifetime, any Secretary of Defense that has more strongly earned an impeachment vote," charged (Ret.) Lt. Col. Daniel Davis, host of the Deep Dive podcast, tells RS. Drawing on the charges outlined in the articles Davis said, "(Hegseth) has been not merely an abject failure, but done outright harm to the Department of Defense, our troops, and American national security."

In September, Massie told Responsible Statecraft’s Kelley Vlahos that this was “the only legislative remedy that I could think of that might work” to bring about an end to the war in Iran.

During that interview, Massie acknowledged that targeting Hegseth rather than President Donald Trump was a question of political viability. He also said some of the articles of impeachment, namely the degradation of the "infrastructure" in place to minimize civilian casualties and the attempted suppression of Sen. Mark Kelly’s (D-Ariz.) free speech, were squarely on Hegseth.

“Peter Hegseth wins the award for most crimes committed,” Massie told RS in September.

While the impeachment vote likely would have been close back in September, last Tuesday’s wave election has further complicated the politics for the GOP. Republicans have less incentive to remain loyal to the administration, and those who lost re-election may skip lame-duck session votes entirely, lowering the number of votes needed to secure a majority.

“With the absences I expect from our side, I wouldn’t be at all surprised if it passed,” an anonymous House Republican told Politico. “Assuming Trump doesn’t extricate him first.”

The war in Iran was among the leading causes of the GOP’s crushing defeat at the polls, and Hegseth would make a convenient scapegoat. Though Trump has remained publicly supportive of the defense secretary, claiming he was only guilty of “winning two wars,” he also said on Sunday that Hegseth was one of the “guys that was most responsible ” for the war.

A Trump adviser recently told Axios that the defense secretary is on “ thin ice ” with the president, though they added that his removal was not imminent. Trump could be incentivized to remove and replace Hegseth before the new Congress is seated in January in order to avoid a potential nomination battle.

Massie says he would only withdraw his articles of impeachment if Hegseth resigned.

Since the congressman triggered his resolution, the Speaker of the House will have two days to bring it to a vote. If the House successfully impeaches Hegseth, two-thirds of the Senate would have to vote to convict him in order to remove the secretary from office. Reports today indicate that would be unlikely .

Dan DePetris, syndicated columnist and fellow at Defense Priorities, is concerned that without full-scale changes in the administration, a Hegseth impeachment would be “cosmetic.”

“Even if he’s impeached by the House and removed by the Senate — no sure thing given the congressional math — any successor won’t be an improvement if the lack of transparency persists and the same old policies on Iran and the Western Hemisphere continue,” DePetris told RS.

“What the Defense Department needs just as much as effective leadership is a worldview that doesn’t result in wars with murky objectives and unnecessary military adventures, like the boat strike campaign, that are geared more toward social media visuals than actually mitigating a problem."

scraped.title: Russia is courting African states. The US shouldn't overreact.
scraped.description: There is room for mutually beneficial results for Washington and Moscow's interests in the Global South
scraped.h1: Russia is courting African states. The US shouldn't overreact.
scraped.body_text:
There is room for mutually beneficial results for Washington and Moscow's interests in the Global South

As part of an effort to keep Russia on the radar of African countries still struggling from some of the negative externalities of Russia’s continuing war in Ukraine, Russian President Vladimir Putin hosted African leaders in Moscow last week for the third Russia-Africa summit .

Between October 28 and 29, Russian officials met with their African counterparts in high-level discussions covering a wide range of issues, primarily focused on continued security relations and opportunities for greater economic collaboration.

Of course, Russian engagement with Africa isn’t new. The Russian paramilitary group Africa Corps has around 2,500 fighters on the continent, where it has formed relations with a number of African governments to fight armed groups in exchange for payment, including through access to commodities. The paramilitary group, which has committed human rights abuses and has largely failed to stop the spread of the armed group violence , has caused a souring of Russian goodwill in Africa.

But in an increasingly geopolitically fractured world, African leaders are looking for any partner willing to offer strong terms, Russia included. Forty-eight African countries sent delegates to the summit, with 22 sending heads of state. Although this represented a decrease from the 43 heads of state who attended the first summit in 2019, it’s a notable increase from the 17 African heads of state who attended the previous summit in 2023 in St. Petersburg, when Russia’s invasion of Ukraine was still fresh on the minds of leaders across the Global South.

The U.S. should adopt a balanced response to Russia’s courting of African partners. Policymakers in Washington often view Russia as a necessarily nefarious actor in the Global South — a country whose actions are geared entirely towards usurping American interests wherever it goes. But Russia, like all countries, has its own economic and security objectives, many of which exist independent of its rivalry with the West.

Where Russia can serve as a productive partner to African states — especially as a mediator to resolve thorny conflicts or as a trade partner providing Africans grain and other goods that help improve food security — American interests could indeed be advanced.

The situation in Ethiopia offers an instructive example. Just as the summit was kicking off, news emerged that Russia had expedited the sale of 12 fighter jets to Ethiopia , which is fighting rebels in its northern states and is facing increasing tensions with its northern neighbor, Eritrea. Russia also agreed to send Ethiopia four defense batteries, which will arrive at a later date.

Despite the sale of this defense equipment, there might be an opening for Russia to flex its diplomatic muscle in the conflict. Eritrean President Isaias Afwerki , who attended the summit in Moscow, gave an interview on Russian television in which he expressed a willingness to allow Russia to negotiate solutions to the ongoing crisis brewing between the two neighbors. Ethiopia’s Abiy Ahmed , who also attended the summit, has previously expressed interest in having the Russians join other countries in mediating an end to the tensions with Eritrea. Russian officials have confirmed they’d be interested in mediating a peace agreement.

From the perspective of the United States, any potential end to tensions in the region would be beneficial to its interests, given the widespread economic investments and substantial geopolitical interests the United States has in the region. The U.S., therefore, ought to welcome the idea of Russia successfully lowering tensions in the Horn through diplomatic mediation.

Beyond security relations, the big news coming out of the summit was an effort by Russia to expand its economic connections to the continent.

Trade between Russia and Africa stood at an estimated $27 billion in 2025, far below the $40 billion Putin had established as his goal during the 2019 summit, but still a sizable increase from the $16.8 billion of trade between the two in 2019. This time around, the Russians set out a new goal of reaching $50 billion in trade with the continent in the “near future,” claiming that Russian companies are deeply interested in expanding the trade of grain and fertilizer to Africa. Last year, Russia exported over 18 million tons of grain to Africa, and its fertilizer shipments to the continent have increased from 1.5 million tons last year to 2.2 million tons so far this year.

Russia is a major energy exporter and is looking to expand this industry in a continent hungry for more diversified energy options. At the summit, agreements with at least six African countries were announced on nuclear energy, and the Russian state energy company Rosatom is in advanced talks with Egypt, Togo, Namibia, and Tanzania to build floating nuclear power plants off their coasts.

These energy agreements should signal to U.S. policymakers that Africa’s increasing interest in diversifying its energy mix is advancing at a rapid clip. If the United States hopes to seize on energy demand in Africa to export its own technologies to African consumers, it should move fast by incentivizing greater American investment in the continent’s energy through the levers of the Development Finance Corporation .

Russia’s interest in this region is not, as some suggest , simply performative; rather it is intended to solidify Moscow as a regional actor with the ability to advance political and security outcomes at odds with some of the objectives pursued by Western states. With few venues for projecting power directly across the continent, Russia’s ability to entrench itself as a regional player hinges on making compelling pitches to African partners.

Putin’s promise to African leaders to refrain from “neo-colonial exploitation” is a reference that is likely to be well received. Yet these overtures cannot replace the cost-benefit logic that any state would apply when evaluating prospects for bilateral cooperation.

Here, Russia’s prospects are mixed. On the one hand, economic, diplomatic, and political cooperation with Moscow has become a pillar of the multi-alignment strategies adopted by many African countries.

However, the global chaos wrought by the Ukraine war has put a damper on some venues for cooperation. Food and energy security issues have cast a long shadow over Russian engagement with Africa. Moscow agreed to the short-lived Black Sea Grain Initiative (also known as the Russia-Ukraine grain deal) from 2022 through the summer of 2023, which guaranteed shipping corridors extending from Ukraine’s Black Sea coastline, partly out of fear of being perceived as an obstacle to global food security. That concern has given way to a logic of escalation whereby both Moscow and Kyiv have assumed ever-greater risks to degrade each other’s infrastructure.

Moscow’s recent decision to impose a de facto blockade on all shipping from Ukraine’s logistically vital port city of Odessa generates upward pressure on food prices for African and other Global South countries already reeling from energy deficits and other sources of market instability generated by the Iran crisis. Moscow sought to address these concerns by shipping free grain to struggling economies and through targeted export deals with key customers such as Egypt, but such makeshift measures can hardly reverse the war’s harmful macroeconomic impacts.

Meaningful, sustained relief can only come through another grain deal, a partial ceasefire covering Black Sea shipping, or an end to the war, none of which seem likely in the short term.

Several African governments, precisely because they value their ability to pursue multi-vector policies, have expressed alarm over reports alleging the forcible recruitment of Africans into Russia’s armed forces. These allegations are credible enough to warrant direct intervention by Putin, who assured his Ghanaian counterpart John Mahama last week that there will be a ban on all recruitment of Ghanaian citizens into Russia’s military; an identical agreement was reached with Kenya .

But herein lies the strategic paradox that has become a defining theme of Russia-Africa ties: Moscow’s prosecution of the Ukraine war has generated powerful incentives for it to strengthen engagement with African and other non-Western states, yet the instability unleashed by that war imposes clear constraints on these relations that can be managed but never fully lifted while the fighting continues.

U.S. policymakers should keep these constraints in mind before overreacting to Russia's next maneuvers in Africa.

scraped.title: The vindication of Marjorie Taylor Greene
scraped.description: Trump called her crazy and a traitor when she was just telling the truth: That Americans saw his Iran war and arming Israel a betrayal of 'America First'
scraped.h1: The vindication of Marjorie Taylor Greene
scraped.body_text:
Trump called her crazy and a traitor when she was just telling the truth: That Americans saw his Iran war and arming Israel a betrayal of 'America First'

Ten weeks ago, Donald Trump called Marjorie Taylor Greene, his former ally and a former Georgia Republican congresswoman, a “LOSER.”

Greene shot back that Trump was a “neocon puppet for Israel.” Both of them do this a lot these days .

Last week, it was Republicans who were big losers in the midterm elections. The president might have been the biggest loser of them all.

Greene knew why.

“Look, if you're in the administration and you're ready to… run for president, you need to continue taking in the lessons that were sent by the American people on Tuesday, and it was really the same lesson that was sent in 2024,” she advised in a video post the day after the midterms .

Greene laid out what she considered core issues that led to the 2024 re-election of Trump, and then, as borne out in the exit polls and vote counts , the Democrats’ 2026 sweep.

“No more foreign wars, (Americans) don't support the war in Iran,” Greene said. “We don't want to fund foreign countries and foreign wars. We don't want to fund Israel , we don't want to fund killing children in Gaza.”

“And we want to put Americans first,” she added.

The deeply unpopular Iran war was at the center of why Republicans performed so poorly on Tuesday. Even before that, voters in both major parties were already souring on the U.S. backing of Israel and particularly the bloodshed in Gaza at the hands of the Israel Defence Forces, a policy that Trump has been fully invested in, as was President Joe Biden . This anger was particularly salient among younger voters and even most young Jewish-Americans .

Among Republicans, Greene was ahead of the curve on this.

In mid-2025, then-Rep. Greene, who the New York Times described at the time as “an avatar of MAGA politics on Capitol Hill,” became the first congressional Republican to call the Gaza crisis a “genocide.”

“It’s the most truthful and easiest thing to say that Oct. 7 in Israel was horrific and all hostages must be returned, but so is the genocide, humanitarian crisis, and starvation happening in Gaza,” Greene said in a social media post on July 28, 2025.

As her vocal opposition to the war grew, so did her criticism of foreign aid , which she saw as prioritizing Israel over U.S. interests. She also demanded the administration release the Epstein files, an original MAGA promise. It was then that Trump began machine-gunning MTG with new names: calling her “wacky ,” “ lunatic ,” and even “Marjorie Traitor Greene,” insisting that the once avid MAGAite had turned against him and his movement.

When she was elected to Congress in 2020, Greene was presented regularly by legacy media as merely the QAnon candidate , reportedly dabbling in rightwing conspiracy theories. In that same period, Trump called Greene “a future Republican star.”

Five years later, after she resigned from Congress, it was Trump who was calling Greene crazy. By then, the feeling was mutual.

Yet it was also Trump who went from promising no new wars on the campaign trail, often flanked by Greene , to later justifying his own war of choice by conjuring up questionable, but familiar, propaganda about Iran being weeks away from having a nuclear weapon and the U.S. having to end the war with Tehran after “ 47 years .”

In November 2025, Greene announced that she would not run for re-election, saying she refused to be a “battered wife,” seemingly referring to Trump’s reneging on his campaign promises combined with increased attacks on her personally. Trump had already vowed to back a primary challenger against her.

"I have too much self-respect and dignity, love my family way too much, and do not want my sweet district to have to endure a hurtful and hateful primary against me by the president we all fought for, only to fight and win my election while Republicans will likely lose the midterms," Greene explained a year ago.

Greene was in a similar position to that of her friend and fellow antiwar Republican ally , Rep. Thomas Massie (R-Ky.), who did run for re-election this year and was defeated in his Kentucky GOP primary in May by Trump-aligned, billionaire pro-Israel donors in the most expensive House primary race in U.S. history.

Greene never surrendered her antiwar, anti-genocide posture, and in fact has probably become more fierce since she decided not to seek re-election. Nor has she abandoned the America First brand that defined Trump’s 2016, 2020 and 2024 presidential campaigns, a message that some Democrats successfully capitalized on after Trump discarded it.

And Greene noticed.

When Zohran Mamdani, the self-described democratic socialist mayor of New York City, participated in a debate during his 2025 campaign, the candidates were asked if he or she would like to visit Israel. Popular rightwing populist Tucker Carlson remarked to Greene during an interview that Mamdani, “was the only person in the New York City mayor’s debate to say he wanted to focus on New York City.”

Carlson noted that unlike the other candidates, Mamdani said “I’m running New York. That’s my job.”

“He gave the right answer,” Greene responded. Carlson agreed. How prescient both were.

In late October, Greene said the best way the Trump administration could ensure a win for Democratic Michigan Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed over reliably hawkish Republican Mike Rogers would be to attack Iran again before the midterms.

It’s a stupid senseless war and America hates it,” she posted on X

“We also hate neocons,” Greene added. “This is not an endorsement, I’m not a Democrat, but I’m also not a neocon Republican.”

El-Sayed himself was asked in July about a potential crossover between his philosophy and Greene’s, known to many as just “MTG.”

“So I talked to a former congresswoman Marjorie Taylor Greene on this podcast in April and it's kind of remarkable how similar some of your positions are. Like, she also has condemned AIPAC's influence and politics, called for no more US taxpayer dollars to Israel, said that the cost of health insurance needs to go down,” Dasha Burns posited to El-Sayed on her POLITICO podcast, “The Conversation.”

“Do you think you could build this new coalition with people like MTG?” the Democrat was asked .

“When you ask me about why establishment elite Democrats are so worried about me? It's because there are a lot of people who listen to her who are going to vote for me in the general election,” he replied.

Many who once voted for Trump in 2024 went for Democrats in 2026.

Democrat El-Sayed handily defeated his Republican opponent last Tuesday by running his own version of an “America First” campaign. “And when it comes to the question of foreign policy, the difference is usually AIPAC money. And if we got that money out, maybe our political consensus would match our public consensus,” El-Sayed said of the formidable pro-Israel lobby .

Greene said after the election, “I think America spoke very loudly that we don't want politicians that are loyal to AIPAC and loyal to a foreign country.”

Marjorie Taylor Greene began her Washington career as the most devoted Trump loyalist, who would go to the wall for his America First message. She still does.

It was Trump who reversed course, leading so many in the same coalition that delivered him the election two years ago to now reject him and his latest iteration of the GOP.

“Marjorie is strong on everything and never gives up - a real WINNER!,” Trump wrote in 2020.

“We never changed, Trump did,” Greene wrote in August.

Donald Trump was right. Marjorie Taylor Greene never gave up.

But he did.
