scraped.title: SCOTUS Nukes Blockade On Trump's Border Wall Construction
scraped.description: On Monday, the Supreme Court ended a lower court blockade that sought to stop Trump's border wall construction along the U.S.-Mexico border.
scraped.author: Shawn Fleetwood
scraped.h1: SCOTUS Nukes Blockade On Trump’s Border Wall Construction
scraped.body_text:
‘The Government’s interest therefore outweighs any aesthetic, recreational, and environmental harm alleged by respondents.’

The U.S. Supreme Court agreed on Monday to end a lower court blockade that sought to stop President Trump’s border wall construction along the U.S.-Mexico border. Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson would have allowed the blockade to remain in place.

In its per curiam ruling , the high court granted an emergency application by the Trump administration to temporarily pause an Oct. 2 ruling by District Judge Kathleen Cardone. The Bush 43 appointee issued a preliminary injunction preventing the government from constructing border wall in the Big Bend region of Southwest Texas.

The case deals with a series of waivers that former and current Department of Homeland Security Secretaries Kristi Noem and Markwayne Mullin signed to set aside various conservation and environmental laws that blocked the wall in the Big Bend area, which includes the region’s national park. According to U.S. Solicitor General John Sauer, the secretaries made the decision in accordance with federal immigration law after determining that the Big Bend region “is an area of high illegal entry” that required construction.

Cardone argued in an Oct. 14 opinion explaining her injunction that the challengers are likely to prevail on their claims that the DHS secretaries lacked the legal authority to waive the contested laws under the major questions doctrine . That doctrine states that executive agencies cannot make regulatory decisions on issues of “vast ‘economic and political significance’” unless Congress specifically says so.

Sauer argued in the administration’s SCOTUS application that Congress “denied district courts jurisdiction to entertain” claims like those made in the case. The solicitor general further contended that challengers’ “major-questions claim borders on frivolous” and that Cardone “effectively rewrote [the law in question] to atextually limit the Secretary’s waiver authority to only areas of ‘ comparative[ly] ’ high illegal entry.”

In its Monday ruling, the Supreme Court found that the administration is “exceedingly likely to prevail on its argument” that Cardone did not have jurisdiction to adjudicate the challengers’ “so-called major-questions-doctrine claim.” The majority held that, regardless of how “it is labeled, respondents’ claim does not ‘“alleg[e] a violation of the Constitution of the United States,”’ the only type of claim the statute permits district courts to adjudicate.”

“It alleges instead that the Secretary exceeded his statutory authority. And we have long recognized that ‘claims simply alleging’ that the Executive Branch has exceeded its ‘statutory authority are not “constitutional” claims,’” the decision reads. “That conclusion does not change where, as here, a plaintiff invokes the major-questions doctrine.”

The high court went on to note that the other factors used to determine whether a stay is warranted also favor the government. This includes the administration’s demonstration that it will suffer irreparable harm if Cardone’s injunction is permitted to remain in place, as well as a showing that the “balance of the equities” tilts in its favor.

“Respondents claim that construction in the Big Bend Sector will diminish their ability to use and enjoy the area. But Congress’s enactment of [the Illegal Immigration Reform and Immigrant Responsibility Act] — which permits the Secretary to waive the requirements of environmental-protection and other conservation laws — reflects a clear preference for expeditious border construction over the very harms respondents assert,” the court ruled. “And courts ‘of equity cannot, in their discretion, reject the balance that Congress has struck in a statute.’ … The Government’s interest therefore outweighs any aesthetic, recreational, and environmental harm alleged by respondents.”

Justice Jackson did not provide a reason for her dissent.

According to Monday’s ruling, Cardone’s injunction “is stayed pending the filing and disposition of the Government’s petition for a writ of certiorari, if such writ is timely sought.” The Supreme Court’s pause will terminate if a petition to SCOTUS is denied by the high court or if SCOTUS agrees to consider the matter and issue a judgment on the merits of the case.

items.title: A Trump Amnesty Deal Would Betray Not Just His Voters But All Americans
items.summary: America's immigration laws are not something the Republican Party or Trump should trade away after a bad election.

scraped.title: A Trump Amnesty Deal Would Betray His Voters And All Americans
scraped.description: In a Sunday interview with CBS News' '60 Minutes,' Trump suggested an amnesty deal may be on the table with Democrats
scraped.author: Brianna Lyman
scraped.h1: A Trump Amnesty Deal Would Betray Not Just His Voters But All Americans
scraped.body_text:
America’s immigration laws are not something the Republican Party or Trump should trade away after a bad election.

At a July 2024 rally, then-candidate Donald Trump told a crowd of cheering supporters what he’d do on his first day back in office: “We will begin the largest deportation operation in the history of our country.” Days earlier, delegates at the Republican National Convention waved signs that read “Mass Deportations Now.”

Yet in a Sunday interview with CBS News’ 60 Minutes, Trump suggested an amnesty deal may be on the table with Democrats. Reflecting on the loss at the ballot box on Tuesday, Trump told Ross Douthat that his deportation policy might have been “too tough.”

“I think it might be too tough, yeah. And a lotta people would say that it’s great. But a lotta people think it’s too tough,” the president said.

Trump then pointed to frustration that some Americans have because they believe that illegal aliens working in hotels, landscaping, and other jobs should not have been deported and noted there are others who want illegals who have managed to evade the law for “10 or 15 years” to stay. When asked about working with Democrats on it, he said it was “actually doable.”

In short, the president who ran on mass deportations is once again floating amnesty. If his takeaway from Tuesday is that Republicans need to let more illegals stay, somebody ought to show him exit polls.

As bad as Tuesday was for Republicans, voters gave Republicans an edge on immigration, with an NBC News exit poll showing that 43 percent of voters said GOP “ is better able to handle immigration ” compared to 41 percent who said Democrats. Another poll showed that when asked how important immigration policies were in deciding who to vote for, 73 percent of voters said immigration was a “crucial or a major factor” and among those, Republicans won 51 percent to 47 percent.

Democrats’ own advertising suggests they knew how poorly a campaign against immigration enforcement would play outside their base. An Axios analysis finding that “ICE” was the third-most featured policy topic in Democrat primary ads for 2026 but that when it came to the general election, it was ranked 35th among policy issues talked about in Democrat ads.

But even if the polls showed Trump data that his enforcement policy was a problem to the voters who turned out (Republican turnout was lower than Democrats’, which means oversampling could be likely), Trump still owes Americans the enforcement he promised. Our immigration laws are not something the Republican Party or Trump should trade away after a bad election.

Yet now Trump is toying with backing away from the only thing voters seemingly agree that he and his party got right. While Trump hasn’t laid out what an amnesty deal would look like, Rep. Maria Elvira Salazar’s DIGNIDAD Act gives us a pretty good idea of what some Republicans are already willing to offer.

The DIGNIDAD Act would create a seven-year program for illegal aliens who evaded our laws before Dec. 31, 2020, to get to stay. Illegals with DUI or DWI convictions could stay, while other illegal aliens can have their deportation proceedings halted while applications are pending. Illegal aliens already deported can apply to return to the U.S. if they were deported but would have otherwise been eligible for this amnesty under the provisions of the bill.

Salazar pitched the legislation as a way for Republicans to retain Hispanic support and thereby keep winning elections. Yet eight of the bill’s co-sponsors lost their races anyway, while Salazar’s race is so close it’s going to a recount. Of course the other question that arises is who does Trump think he needs to appease with an amnesty deal?

For years Democrats and the left have waged an assassination prep campaign against Trump that sought to dehumanize and vilify him, desensitizing people to any violence directed toward him. And it worked — Trump has now survived multiple assassination attempts, and the left still calls him a “fascist,” “Hitler,” and a “threat to democracy.” Trump owes the very party that has contributed to his assassination attempts absolutely nothing — least of which is amnesty. He owes his base that delivered him the Oval Office everything — starting with remaining steadfast in his deportation efforts.

But the notion that illegal aliens who violated our sovereignty and social compact should be rewarded simply because they will pay back some taxes or want to work (thus displacing American workers by working for less) is an insult to all Americans. America’s borders and laws are not optional. When Republicans talk about amnesty for persons who have evaded the law longer than others because they’ve been here for a long time and work in regular jobs, the right falls into the left’s trap that empathy must override the rule of law. It’s emotional blackmail.

Republicans should recall how well buying into that emotional blackmail worked out for Republicans when they were seduced by the false promise that amnesty is compassionate. Ronald Reagan’s 1986 Immigration Reform and Control Act was sold to Americans as a one-time fix that would give amnesty to 3 million illegal aliens in exchange for long-lasting border security. If there was supposed to be an electoral payoff, consider Reagan’s home state. George H.W. Bush carried California in 1988 and Republicans haven’t carried it since. Reagan’s amnesty didn’t buy Republicans a meaningful advantage there, and if anything, it signaled to Democrats that with enough grandstanding, they could get their way.

In fact, Salazar admitted her legislation is the launchpad of eventual citizenship, and Trump himself understands that any amnesty leads to citizenship and, more crucially, voting. Beto O’Rourke and Rep. Maxwell Frost have already made clear their priorities involve giving illegal aliens a pathway to citizenship.

Trump himself knows this too, saying in a 2013 tweet that “Amnesty is suicide for Republicans. Not one of those 12 million who broke our laws will vote Republican. Obama is laughing at @GOP.”

Perhaps he should heed his own warning.

scraped.title: Freedom Caucus Demands GOP Pass Agenda Before Next Year
scraped.description: The Freedom Caucus demanded that GOP leadership fast-track passage of conservative priorities before Dems take control of Congress in January.
scraped.author: Shawn Fleetwood
scraped.h1: Freedom Caucus Demands GOP Leadership Pass ‘Unfinished’ Agenda Before Dems Take Congress
scraped.body_text:
‘Moreover, we request that we not leave town until we accomplish these objectives. Every one of us — including those leaving Congress on January 3rd — should be committed to finishing the job.’

The House Freedom Caucus demanded on Monday that GOP leadership fast-track several conservative priorities before Democrats take control of Congress in January.

“Some of us called for action after our first reconciliation package to continue to move to support the American people. Unfortunately, that agenda stalled, and now we will no longer have the majority in the next Congress. We respectfully request that we take action in the next 60 days to protect the citizens we represent,” the caucus’ board wrote in a letter to House Speaker Mike Johnson and Senate Majority Leader John Thune.

The coalition of conservative lawmakers laid out several policies it says the current Congress should advance before Democrats take over. This includes using the reconciliation process — which would require a majority vote in both chambers — to pass a package “to deal with debt, spending, and tax relief.”

The Freedom Caucus argued more specifically that this reconciliation measure should fund defense modernization “to stop Democrats from using it to leverage for expansion of the welfare state.” It also called to make available “significant tax relief for families — particularly for healthcare: Expansion of [ Health Savings Accounts ] in terms of both savings amount and use to drive down the price of healthcare for families, and codification of Short-Term Limited Duration Plans .”

The conservative lawmakers said that the GOP should cut federal spending by “at least” $1 trillion to “pay for all these items” and reduce the federal deficit.

Congressional Republicans should furthermore “[l]imit annual spending to current levels (for 3rd consecutive year) via a [continuing resolution] CR or Appropriations without policy riders that divide us or constrain the Administration’s ability to eliminate wasteful, fraudulent, and abusive government spending,” the letter reads. And we should “[o]ppose a year-end omnibus with poison pills.”

Outside of spending, the Freedom Caucus also called on Republican leaders to move forward with codifying President Trump’s “border security policies” and a ban on sanctuary cities into law. The body specifically referred to the Permanent Trump Secure Border Act and Shut Down Sanctuary Policies Act of 2026 , both of which cleared the House Judiciary Committee and are tailored at addressing such issues.

Other agenda items on the to-do list include passing permitting reform, a ban on stock trading for all branches of government, voter ID legislation, and confirming Trump’s remaining executive and judicial nominees in the Senate.

“Moreover, we request that we not leave town until we accomplish these objectives. Every one of us — including those leaving Congress on January 3rd — should be committed to finishing the job,” the letter concludes.

🚨BREAKING: House Freedom Caucus leadership just dropped a lame-duck roadmap for @SpeakerJohnson and @LeaderJohnThune . Strip Democrat leverage. Deliver real wins. Do it before the clock runs out. No leaving town until it’s done — let’s finish the job! pic.twitter.com/oHGnZwWi8A

A representative for Majority Leader Thune’s office told The Federalist that confirming Trump’s remaining executive and judicial nominees will be a “top priority” for Senate Republicans during the lame-duck session. The representative’s statement did not address whether the Senate will advance the policy items advocated for by the Freedom Caucus, however.

Speaker Johnson’s office did not respond to The Federalist’s request for comment by deadline on whether they plan to advance such policies during the lame-duck session.

Monday’s letter comes nearly a week after Republicans suffered tremendous losses in the 2026 midterms. In addition to the Iran war and its associated costs, a leading factor likely contributing to the drubbing was the GOP Congress’s (more specifically, the Senate GOP’s ) refusal to fulfill their 2024 promises to voters.

While Johnson announced his intention to step down as House GOP leader, Thune is preparing to seek the position of Senate minority leader in the next Congress. The quick rush for leadership elections has prompted pushback from (so far) roughly half a dozen Republican senators, who are calling for a delay to such contests given the party’s midterm losses.

Sen. Ron Johnson has sent the letter to Senate Republican Conference Chairman Tom Cotton calling for leadership elections to be delayed until Senate Republicans meet as a conference to discuss their "stunning defeat" in the midterms. The letter is signed by Johnson, Ted Budd,… pic.twitter.com/3YjJZve6mr

scraped.title: Why Won’t Boomers Grandparent?
scraped.description: Grandparents have more wealth and leisure than any generation before them, writes Arthur Brooks. So why are so many spending less time with their grandchildren?
scraped.author: Arthur Brooks
scraped.body_text:
“I don’t see the slums. I don’t see death and destruction. I don’t see murders. You don’t see a lot of children running around here, either.”

These are the words of a resident of The Villages, an enormous retirement community in Florida profiled in Lance Oppenheim’s excellent 2020 documentary, Some Kind of Heaven . The residents have moved into a culture deliberately distinct from ordinary intergenerational life. No one under 19 may live there permanently, and visiting children are generally limited to 30 days a year. The residents spend their days in leisure activities without distraction. Think of the philosophy behind Eat Pray Love — but for old people. “You’re not gonna be tomorrow the same age you are today,” says a resident. “So think about you. You come here to live.” Life in this ecosystem is pickleball, not grandparenting.

I found the documentary amusing. My wife, Ester, found it utterly befuddling. Why on earth would someone move thousands of miles away from their grandchildren?

scraped.title: Lame Duck Donald. Plus. . .
scraped.description: In today’s Front Page, Carrie McKean meets the voters who swung Texas, River Page on how normies won the middle, and Charles Lane says transgender ideology is still a losing issue.
scraped.author: The Free Press
scraped.body_text:
It’s Monday, November 9. This is The Front Page , your daily window into the world of The Free Press —and our take on the world at large. Today: Carrie McKean reports on the rural Texas voters who flipped the state. Charles Lane on why trans is still Democrats’ biggest loser. And much more.

But first: Is Trump doubling down?

With the Republican Party still reeling after last Tuesday’s results and amid a deluge of obituaries for Donald Trump’s political movement, one important question risks getting lost: How will the president govern for his final two years in office?

As he enters his lame-duck era, Trump is sending mixed messages. On the one hand, he has suggested that he would be open to compromise with Democrats on immigration, including in his first post-election sitdown interview , with 60 Minutes correspondent and Free Press columnist Ross Douthat . On the other, he has installed hard-line and loyal adviser Stephen Miller as his new chief of staff. Read Eli Lake on whether Trump will find a dealmaking groove, or double down.

The president’s biggest headache after last week’s vote is the same as it was before: the Iran war. In the days since the election, the conflict has been blamed—most prominently by Vice President J.D. Vance—for the Republicans’ poor performance. But how will the midterms change Trump’s strategy in the Middle East? The answer, according to Michael Doran , depends on whether the president agrees with his deputy’s postmortem. Vance didn’t just say that the Iran war was to blame for the defeat, but that America needs to “change our relationship to Israel.” Does Trump feel the same way? Read Michael’s column to understand the issue dividing the right after the midterms—and which side Trump will take.

—The Editors

Last week, Democrats across the country were hoping for a blue wave—and they got a tsunami. Among all the victories, none is more totemic than the wipeout of statewide GOP candidates in Texas. Progressives celebrating may be tempted to wear their Texas wins like a bluebonnet in their caps (in fact, you can purchase celebratory “ Blue Y’all ” shirts).

But despite their astonishing success up and down the ballot, Carrie McKean , who lives in rural Texas and reported from there extensively for The Free Press on everything from the fight over prayer in schools to ICE overreach —warns against reading too deeply into the results. She spoke to first-time Democrat voters and reports that what looks like a blue wave is more like a purple tornado. “I hope I never have to vote for a Democrat again,” said one.

What do the new Democratic stars from unlikely parts of the country have in common? River Page covered the rise of the likes of Kansas Senator-elect Adam Hamilton, and Sam Forstag, the Montana smoke jumper heading to Congress. Read his piece on how normies won the middle, what their success says about 2028, and why the key to maintaining Democratic dominance depends on “middle-aged white women who smoke.”

One further indicator of the moderate mood: the fate of ballot measures relating to transgender issues across the country. In states blue and red, almost without exception, voters gave a thumbs-up to the idea that sports should be organized by biological sex, and that gender transition surgery should not be performed on minors. Today, Charles Lane reviews these results, and what they mean.

NVIDIA CEO Jensen Huang is under intense scrutiny after admitting to an affair with an alleged Chinese spy. “I owe my family and all of you an apology,” Huang said in a letter to his employees. “There is no excuse for what I did. I am deeply sorry.”

The House is reportedly set to vote on the impeachment of Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth this week. The effort has been led by Republican Thomas Massie, and top Democrat Hakeem Jeffries said he’s a “hard yes” on ousting Hegseth.

President Trump announced in a Truth Social post this weekend that he offered UFC CEO Dana White the job of White House press secretary. White said he declined, and the president clarified Sunday that he was “only kidding” about the offer.

Former White House health aide Calley Means alleged that corporations and special interest groups heavily influenced policy during his tenure in an interview last week. His comments specifically targeted Susie Wiles and political adviser James Blair, adding to the divide between President Trump’s administration and the Make America Healthy Again movement.

items.summary: The EU blob is celebrating too soon For most of the past decade, the political blob in Europe has been struggling with two things it does not understand. One is Donald Trump. scraped.title: What the AI doomsters get wrong
scraped.author: Wolfgang Munchau
scraped.h1: What the AI doomsters get wrong The EU blob is celebrating too soon
scraped.body_text:
What will the Democrats do to Nvidia? (Credit: Justin Sullivan/Getty)

What will the Democrats do to Nvidia? (Credit: Justin Sullivan/Getty)

For most of the past decade, the political blob in Europe has been struggling with two things it does not understand. One is Donald Trump. The other is AI. Last week, Trump was battered in the midterms and AI-related stocks collapsed. What a wonderful day for the blob.

But that was last week. This week, Trump is back on his Truth Social sounding off about Democrat “sleazebags”, and the market is recovering. For the newspaper headlines were far more dramatic than the reality. The Nasdaq fell 4.8% — a correction, not a crash. The index is still up substantially over the past five years. A real tech crash would look very different.

Meanwhile, Europe still doesn’t get AI. The dollar and AI are what make America so powerful. The Europeans have a single currency, but no idea how to leverage it globally. And they are nowhere in the AI race. The gap between the US and China on one side and Europe on the other is massive and unbridgeable. The only important European high-tech company I can think of is the Dutch company ASML. It makes sophisticated machines which edge tiny pathways into integrated circuits of microchips. Further down that food chain are a couple of German companies that supply the precision optics. That’s good stuff. I raise my hat. Some of our old engineering skills do still count. But we Europeans are no longer at the center of the world; our old maps are out of date.

We have sidelined ourselves by enacting a raft of disastrous anti-tech regulation. The General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) might have started as an honest effort to protect people from abuse of their personal data, but it ended up a monster — a cookie monster. The legislation is a massive burden on small businesses in particular. And the AI Act has been an act of calamitous self-harm, preventing the formation of a viable AI industry here. Social networks are treated as criminal organizations that need to be censored by officially approved civil society organizations. We should have called it the Tech Business Destruction Act.

We can’t rule out the possibility that a Democrat-led Congress could usher in a Luddite phase by copying us — there are some Democrats who think like the Europeans. But I don’t think the party as a whole will go down this route. Bill Clinton, don’t forget, turned the Democrats into the party of financial capitalism. And both the Obama and Biden administrations supported US technology. My sense is that this new intake of Democratic lawmakers is different from the European centrist blob. Yes, they are certainly more cautious about data centers, which don’t provide many jobs and consume a lot of energy. But I have yet to see the rabid anti-tech vigilantes we have here.

In any case, there are limits to politics. We cannot un-invent AI, just as we could not un-invent the nuclear bomb. If a future US administration attempted to cripple Nvidia with ever stricter regulation, it would create a far bigger security threat than one posed by reports that Jensen Huang was dating a suspected Chinese spy. China is the reason America cannot just abandon AI as Europe has done.

Right now, the top Chinese AI companies are lagging behind OpenAI and Anthropic, but not by much. And these models can do mind-boggling things. I created my own AI-driven media app, by getting ChatGPT (which is brilliant at solving open math problems) to give detailed instructions to Claude (which excels at software). After a night of intense hackery, my agents and I created something that would otherwise have cost me a fortune in software development. The idea that AI is just another bubble is spread by people who have no idea what it does and how it works. Many of them live in Europe.

And many of them are economists. There are honorable exceptions, such as Luis Garicano, who recently wrote that physical AI is currently the most important thing that is happening in the world. But too many approach AI through that familiar history of speculative bubbles: right about the valuation and wrong about the revolution.

The economists Carmen Reinhart and Kenneth Rogoff wielded an enormous influence on our thinking about what constitutes a bubble with their 2008 book This Time is Different . The title refers to a comment that market optimists have been using since time immemorial to justify high stock market valuations. It is the belief that whatever the technology they happen to be invested in at the time is special. We saw it play out with the Railway Mania in the 1840s, then with cars, radios, even bicycles. And most recently with the dot-com bubble. Investors were not wrong about the technology as such. The internet was indeed a big deal. But they made stupid bets on the wrong companies — like internet cafés in Europe.

The financial economist Robert Shiller gave us a way to assess these bubbles. He developed a metric to gauge whether the stock market as a whole is overvalued: the Cyclically Adjusted Price-to-Earnings (CAPE) index. Think of it as a smarter version of standard measures like price-to-earnings ratios. Right now, Shiller’s CAPE stands at 40.7, close to the all-time peak of 44.2 reached during the dot-com bubble in late 1999.

By Yanis Varoufakis

Taking into account the work of Reinhart, Rogoff and Shiller, it would indeed be rational to bet that AI has pushed stock markets into bubble territory. But be careful. The idea that AI is indeed different is based on something very real. Something that conventional economic analysis has undervalued: this technology is going to transform the inner workings of our economy. And it’s happening already. AI has decimated the white-collar profession of the legal assistant. It is coming for many more. The author Nassim Nicholas Taleb predicted that all jobs that were invented this century are prone to the AI tsunami. I agree. The financial sector in particular. Similarly, our think tanks produce tomes of biased and predictable analysis. The profession of the newspaper columnist, one I happen to know a little about, is also on that list. If I open the Guardian or the Daily Telegraph , and look at the columns there, I know exactly what each columnist is going to say. For AI, predictable, biased and unoriginal journalism is low-hanging fruit. So is pretentious modern art. No wonder that the blob is so alarmed. They are on the list too.

AI is going to have a substantial and measurable impact on the productivity of the entire economy. An AI-assisted law office or newsroom will be able to achieve the same output with fewer people. The productivity effect is not in doubt. But what is in doubt is the timing. History shows that we are often too pessimistic about the impact of a technology and too optimistic about the timing. Ten years ago, the car-tech fanboys predicted we would all have self-driving cars by now. Forty years ago, sci-fi movies suggested we’d be in flying cars.

If investors get the timing wrong on AI, the market might crash. The tech may have killed the legal assistant but it could take a lot longer for it to see off the mortgage broker or the high-street solicitor. Investors won’t wait indefinitely for promised profits to materialize. That said, progress in AI-driven robotics is proceeding fast and may bring surprises.

What we are seeing right now is how volatile today’s stock markets have become. The crash in Alphabet’s shares, Google’s parent company, tells us at the very least that the positive AI story is not a uniform one. As the economist Hanno Lustig remarked, current AI stock valuations presume “a structural transformation of US capitalism favouring capital at the expense of labour”. And this is AI’s inherent promise: the replacement of labour by capital. Reinhart and Rogoff’s book may have helped us be more suspicious about financial valuations, but AI isn’t another investment fad. It is a technological revolution. Make no mistake: this time it really is different.

Wolfgang Münchau is the Director of Eurointelligence and an UnHerd columnist.

scraped.title: Why nobody stopped Russell Brand
scraped.author: Poppy Sowerby
scraped.h1: Nobody stopped Russell Brand The predator was Noughties TV gold
scraped.body_text:
“Brand belonged to a rougher, readier era of programming.” (Jeff J Mitchell/Getty)

“Brand belonged to a rougher, readier era of programming.” (Jeff J Mitchell/Getty)

It’s always the ones you most expect. That, at least, has been the conclusion online after the rape conviction of Russell Brand. Rather than admit that Brand’s conspicuous, hypersexual persona was a rather effective sleight of hand — one which successfully distracted production companies and audiences from his criminal private life for two decades — social media has spent the past week telling itself it can spot a wrong’un a mile off. So it is that long-buried clips of Brand making rape jokes on Channel 4 quiz shows have popped up on our timelines: see , these posts say, this is what a rapist looks like .

It’s a reaction I can understand. Watching back clips of Brand’s big-haired heyday, it is difficult to understand why nobody raised the alarm. There’s the recording of Brand offering to send his personal assistant to Jimmy Savile, naked; “Nothing wrong with that,” warbles the elder predator. There’s the clip of him on a talk show, bragging about convincing women to “trust me” by posing as gay — before “bang! Pregnant” . There’s the one where he jokes about dragging a woman “into a cubicle” to “show her my pubicles” (a similar account cropped up in court). This was a man whose recurring gag was being vulgar, boastful, libidinous and frightening. In isolation, these snippets are shocking — but lest we forget, these qualities were once the very foundations of late-night television. The rape jokes look stark in retrospect; in their context, they were seen as naughty asides in a comedy culture which loved nothing more. Half the joke was the ambiguity of whether Brand “meant it”.

It’s impossible to imagine perviness being a joke today, so squeaky-clean is our post-#MeToo mainstream comedy culture — but the recent past is a foreign country. The Noughties, the decade that produced Brand, was positively anarchic by today’s standards. Programs like Never Mind the Buzzcocks (fronted by Simon Amstell) and Big Brother’s Big Mouth (a reality-recap spinoff fronted by Brand) were so watchable because of their sweary, offensive, unpolished banter. Guests would drink heavily, hosts would tease relentlessly and a barrage of obscenities and fights would cap off the night. These shows were combustible by design: panelists’ flimsy egos were flambéed at every opportunity in a way that would give an on-set welfare officer a coronary today. In one memorable spat on Buzzcocks , Amstell goaded the mononymous singer Preston (remember him?) to storm off by reading out the most airheaded portions of his wife Chantelle’s autobiography.

By Poppy Sowerby

Producers today would cower from “platforming” anything quite so third-rail, or even slightly mean — which is why the BBC, ITV and Channel 4’s late-night offering is a revolving door of Rob Beckett, Romesh Ranganathan and whatever green-haired Goldsmiths graduate they can drag off the street. Late-night banter has been replaced by light-entertainment lols in Scottish castles. We are a million miles from the 2007 Brit Awards, hosted by Brand, in which he managed to crack jokes about the Queen’s “privates”, the friendly-fire death of a soldier in Iraq and the hanging of Saddam Hussein.

Brand belonged to a rougher, readier era of programming in which hosts functioned as ringmasters and made a spectacle of wrangling unpredictable stars. Something “happening” — a fracas, a sly joke, a flash of nudity — was precisely why we watched. After the watershed, moral instruction vanished. After Fiona Bruce had packed up her papers, a band of twenty-something brigands would saunter on set to deliver vulgar nightly sermons. Brand was the most vivid product of this culture — the most flamboyant bird of prey, and a breed now long extinct. Part of this week’s social-media cope is the insincere refrain that Brand was not just evil, but unentertaining — a more honest reckoning would acknowledge that his theatrical, voracious, quippy persona was in fact TV gold. His perviness was not incidental here; it was part of the act. Looking back at clips from Big Brother’s Big Mouth , audiences are delighted by the edginess of it all; they like the feeling of being shocked.

All this — gasps included — meant great ratings. In the 2000s and 2010s, British television was buoyed by a handful of charismatic but creepy men. In the years since, many of these men have been unmasked as various shades of problematic. There is David Walliams, the poor man’s Kenneth Williams, who was dropped by his publisher and lost a tie-in with Alton Towers after being accused of inappropriate behavior towards women (a claim he denies ). There’s Gregg Wallace, the cheeky-chappie-in-chief of the MasterChef kitchen who producers brought on as a working-class hero — only for him to be investigated for inappropriate behavior, sexual comments and bullying (allegations he denies). The list of shamed male TV favorites seems to grow by the month: what began with Savile became respectable newsreaders like Huw Edwards and lovable children’s entertainers like Rolf Harris. Understandably, the industry has swapped its riskiest constituents — late-night livewires — for focus-grouped fun like Sky’s Saturday Night Live UK , stocked with on-message TikTok comedians. Not only has this made comedy worse — it also won’t work.

Gutting schedules of rogues is no guarantee of moral perfection. Padding out panel shows with scarf-swaddled softbois is an understandable reflex for production companies keen to avoid the mistakes of Endemol, the one-time handler of Brand. Really, though, you cannot judge a man’s propensity to rape you based on whether he wears natty little Victorian waistcoats or piles up his hair like a Whitechapel harlot. Brand may stick out as an example of where instincts should have been trusted — but so much of modern masculinity has been defanged and made to feel “safe” that real wrong’uns are incredibly difficult to discern. Think of Neil Gaiman , whose alleged sadism (which he maintains was always consensual) was packaged in the disarming guise of a sensitive sex nerd. At a time when audiences — and especially women — are suspicious of swagger, it has never been more fashionable to don sheep’s clothing. If he were starting out today, Brand would pose as a nice boy. There is no better evidence for his slipperiness than his spiritual conversion, itself a flagrant attempt to retcon his rapey years as a period in the wilderness.

In the Noughties, sexual appetite and celebrity ego were extraordinary bringers of social capital. Today public horniness is reserved for a select group of heavily media-trained women — Sabrina Carpenter and Zara Larsson, for example, who seem only ever to dry-hump their way through pop sets. Meanwhile men are more likely to cry on television and tell entertainment correspondents all about their body-consciousness than crack jokes about shagging. In comics, the transformation is perhaps the most noticeable of all — they have gone from carte-blanche provocateurs to professional personalities, ones who must withstand the same purity tests on the issues du jour as all other celebs.

None of that will stop the Brands of the future. The sanitized stars British networks choose to replace the rogues of yore could be just as odious behind closed doors. Bad behavior seems to seep out of the woodwork of celebrity with such regularity that we have to assume there is something corrupting in fame itself.

Our reckoning over Russell Brand is due. It is right that we ask ourselves how we could have ignored, even praised, such a conspicuous sleazebag. But we shouldn’t delude ourselves about what a bad guy “looks like”. The truly disturbing thing is that Brand, like Savile, was an unusual example of someone who bore his badness as a sort of double-bluff. The plethora of old gods tumbling out of favor over the 2020s represents the whole spectrum from grandfatherly to grotesque — proof of how easily some men slip under the wrong’un radar. In the wake of Brand’s undoing, it is tempting yet fruitless to trawl through old footage of this particular prancing perve to make ourselves feel better about “missing” the truth. In the ultra-horny Noughties, salaciousness was standard fare; today we live in a paranoid purity culture which prefers its famous men to look as unthreatening as possible. But the mistake is to confuse the performance of a personality with the evidence of character. Television may well have changed the men it celebrates, but that doesn’t mean we have learned how to recognize the dangerous ones.

Poppy Sowerby is an UnHerd columnist.

scraped.title: Erdoğan’s paranoid finale
scraped.author: Andrew Finkel
scraped.h1: Erdoğan’s paranoid finale A succession war is coming
scraped.body_text:
“Turkey is already entering a post-Erdoğan era.” (Utku Ucrak/Anadolu /Getty)

“Turkey is already entering a post-Erdoğan era.” (Utku Ucrak/Anadolu /Getty)

Rip Van Winkle slept for only 20 years and missed the American Revolution. In November 2024, İlhan Sami Çomak emerged, blinking, after 30 years in a Turkish prison to a country that had similarly changed beyond all recognition. In 1994, he had been arrested for terrorism offenses that could only have been committed by traveling 1,000 miles in a single day — along a railway line which did not exist. A promising student from a village in eastern Turkey, Çomak discovered politics and a Kurdish identity at Istanbul University in the early Nineties. He was tempted, he says, but never recruited, by the armed Kurdistan Workers’ Party insurgency, then near its zenith. That did not prevent his arrest and confession, extracted after 19 days of torture, for two separate arson attacks at opposite ends of the country. The European Court of Human Rights declared his trial unlawful, but he served a full three decades.

The pre-smartphone Turkey that Çomak left behind had been dominated by a military determined to tame the religious populism of its politicians. The Instagram-crazed country he re-entered is dominated by the very politician the military failed to tame.

In 1994, Istanbul had half of its present population of 16 million, but was already growing, largely through migration from Anatolia, at the rate of one Newcastle a year. No politician understood that human tide better than Recep Tayyip Erdoğan — street hawker, semi-professional footballer, hard-boiled party boss — who, that year, elbowed his way through a crowded field to become mayor of Istanbul for the pro-Islamic Welfare Party. Erdoğan, too, would see the inside of a Turkish prison: four months in 1999 for reciting a poem at a rally.

By Andrew Finkel

But he and Çomak drew very different lessons from injustice. Çomak taught himself poetry, and the writings he smuggled out of his cell have won him international fame. Erdoğan learned that power punishes weakness, and that victimhood is a potent political tool. Donald Trump said that the only reason he attended July’s Nato summit in Ankara was out of respect for the strongman president who shares his skepticism of the Western alliance. And, even though Turkey was among the last of the G20 to ratify the Paris Agreement, Antalya is now hosting dozens of world leaders at the COP31 climate summit, Andy Burnham among them. But which Turkey will they be visiting? The “New Turkey” that a younger Erdoğan once promised, or merely a stale caricature of the ancien régime he set out to replace?

No longer in a cell, Çomak talks of the marvel of regaining an unobstructed view of the horizon, of being able to lose himself in a crowd. Erdoğan built a 1,150-room palace. That palace has become a monument to an epoch bearing his name. There is little question that Erdoğan’s Turkey has grown in prosperity and self-esteem. In the early aftermath of the Cold War, the country was desperate to join a European Union that didn’t want it, all while promoting a Turkic identity that might win influence (and the odd contract) in former Soviet Central Asia. Today, it is nothing if not confident. A republic founded over a century ago from the ashes of empire is again redefining its region.

Turkish diplomats once cited the country’s “difficult neighborhood” as a shackle on its ambitions, and as a reason to preserve the military’s role in civilian politics. Erdoğan’s great achievement has been to tame the generals and transfer their power to himself. His growing international influence has become a source of national pride but also a useful distraction from his own retreat from democratic accountability.

That neighborhood, though still difficult, has become a kind of portfolio: mediating between Russia and Ukraine, helping to see off the hostile Assad regime in Syria, even locking horns with Israel, albeit in a contest unlikely to draw blood. Turkey once boasted of having Nato’s second-largest army, though large cohorts of conscripts were kept busy whitewashing fences. Now it boasts of drones and a growing defense industry, driven in large part by Baykar, the company chaired by Erdoğan’s son-in-law.

Even so, Turkey has not entirely abandoned the dictum of the country’s founder, Mustafa Kemal Atatürk: “Peace at home, peace in the world”— a principle that translates as “don’t mess with me and I won’t mess with you”. Turkey has the industrial and scientific base to be a nuclear power but has so far refrained from pursuing one. In the summer, it joined Saudi Arabia and nuclear-armed Pakistan in a mutual defense pact. Yet even after Houthi missile strikes on Riyadh in October, the government seems happier selling arms than sending troops into harm’s way.

When Erdoğan came to national prominence, the great divides in Turkish politics were between Left and Right, civilian and military. Erdoğan exposed a deeper fissure in Turkish society: the resentment of newly urban, pious and provincial Turks towards a Western-facing secular elite. The founding republican settlement subordinated religion to the state. The bureaucracy, courts and universities saw themselves as guardians of secularism, and the generals saw themselves as guardians-in-chief. The ban on devout women wearing headscarves at university became one of the grievances upon which Erdoğan’s Justice and Development Party (AKP) was founded in 2001.

“Erdoğan’s style is very similar to Trump’s,” says Daron Acemoğlu, the Istanbul-born economist and Nobel laureate. “The secular establishment in Turkey made the same mistakes as the liberal establishment in the US or the UK, but without any of its liberalism.” He argues that it’s impossible to understand the AKP without understanding the contempt that the secular establishment has traditionally shown towards conservative provincials. “Erdoğan is good at propaganda, but when he said ‘in this country there are white Turks and black Turks’, that wasn’t just made up.”

The headscarf may have been the most visible grievance, but the deeper one lay in people’s wallets. Erdoğan, running for the Welfare Party, the movement from which the AKP would later emerge, was boosted into the mayoralty by a collapse of the currency in January 1994, followed by an inflation rate of over 100%. An even worse economic crisis brought his newly formed party to national office in 2002. By sticking to an IMF program negotiated by its predecessors, the new government nursed the economy back to health. For the first time, ordinary families could get a credit card, or a loan to buy a house. In 2019, the six minarets of a vast new mosque appeared on Istanbul’s Bosphorus skyline, but shopping malls, highways and sprawling public housing estates became equally prominent symbols of AKP rule.

Yet the machine that built this loyalty is running out of fuel. The liberalization that marked the start of AKP rule in 2002 has long since come unstuck or else has been corrupted. Arguably, the great accomplishment of post-war Turkish politicians was to oversee the mass movement of people from the countryside into the big cities. But that movement also created social fault lines which, a few generations later, are set to shift again. Today’s voters want more than neighborhood-level favors. They aspire to the good life and opportunities once enjoyed by the old urban elite. They also know that to be successful you need to have the right political connections. The A in AKP stands for adalet or “justice”. For a growing number, that letter has gone missing.

That Erdoğan’s AKP fared so badly in the 2024 local elections — coming second with some 35% of the national vote, failing to win back Istanbul and Ankara, and losing a string of other big cities — is a symptom of that disillusionment. Panic that it was losing control is the driving force accelerating the government’s slide into unfettered autocracy. Hence the response to the recent discovery of a Ponzi-like scheme that has left some £13 billion of savers’ money in limbo, was to arrest the messengers. Five journalists were charged over their coverage of a scandal that extended up the ladder to AKP higher-ups. Accused of spreading false information, two are still in custody, joining 23 other journalists behind bars on assorted charges. Yet the fallout of the scandal is proving harder to contain, undermining even further the integrity of the government and eroding individual saving after sharp losses in other financial markets.

And the government still can’t arrest the price of tomatoes. “How happy is the one who says ‘I am a Turk’,” runs another much-quoted Atatürk maxim. But the all-too-common conversation among today’s struggling middle-class parents, throttled by inflation of around 30%, is how to build a life for their children abroad.

While the reforms after the 2001 crisis opened up a new world of consumer credit and mortgages, a disastrous macroeconomic experiment, pairing low interest rates with high inflation, has now left those managing the economy with only one real option: muddling through. The notion that people could put up with the AKP’s brand of autocratic piety because at least it could manage the economy is long gone. The cliché among Istanbul’s chattering classes had always been that, no matter how bad the economy, the restaurants were always full. “They’re not full anymore,” says Ekin Şahin, whose family is in the trade. “People need a handful of reasons to eat out. No one goes out on a whim.”

Just as New York Times leader writers struggled to explain how Trump was elected not once but twice, a large segment of the Turkish population despairs at what it sees as the cognitive dissonance of fellow citizens who still believe Erdoğan is leading the country in the right direction. Increasingly, however, loyalist support is being whittled away. More than half the electorate declined to back Erdoğan in the first round of the 2023 presidential election, and the 2024 local elections confirmed the drift. As in Trump’s America, loyalty is not inexhaustible. The AKP once sold its campaign for Islamic rights as part of a process of democratization. Whether or not that was ever the case, few believe it any more.

Erdoğan has proceeded methodically, transferring an already powerful state apparatus into his own hands. As mayor, he learned how public contracts could be used to build a base. He defanged the military through the high-profile “Ergenekon” trials of senior officers that began in 2008. He also sidelined senior figures in his own party who still regarded him as primus inter pares rather than top dog. The Gezi Park protests of 2013, a vast spontaneous protest to stop a central Istanbul park being turned into a shopping mall, taught him another lesson; he set about systematically capturing not just the legacy media but newly powerful social media too. The attempted coup of 2016 provided an opportunity to move against vocal opponents. The popular Kurdish politician Selahattin Demirtaş was arrested — he remains in jail despite a ruling by the European Court of Human Rights — and the government set about dismantling a rival religious movement, and former ally, led by the exiled cleric Fethullah Gülen. A referendum in 2017 abolished the office of prime minister and completed the transfer of power to a virtually unchecked presidency.

Unlike Trump, Erdoğan has held sway for almost 25 years, long enough to fine-tune a system of censorship and repression. Control of the courts has allowed his government to upend the legal process and divide the opposition. This took on fresh momentum with the arrest in March 2025 of Ekrem İmamoğlu, the Republican People’s Party (CHP) mayor of Istanbul, days before he was to be anointed the opposition’s presidential candidate. He now faces charges across several indictments, including bribery, embezzlement, leading a criminal organization, espionage and insulting public officials, which together carry a notional sentence of some 2,400 years. Halk TV — a channel that supported the opposition — was put under the control of a court-appointed trustee as İmamoğlu’s defense in court was about to begin. There is now a long list of mayors and elected officials under threat. It remains to be seen whether the fate of his fellow mayors — over 30 are still in detention — will be raised by another great proponent of devolved government and former mayor, Andy Burnham at this week’s summit. The mayor of Antalya, the host city, is also in jail.

By Lily Lynch

One explanation for this mounting insecurity is that even paranoiacs have enemies. But while the ruling party may have scored substantial successes in its kulturkampf with the old republican elite, it may now be losing the war. It is not so much that the other side is winning as that Erdogan’s politics of confrontation is wearing thin. Turkish social media hums with clips of schoolchildren, some still in headscarves from after-school Qur’an classes, singing and dancing along to Manifest, a girl band who have just played Wembley Arena after their sentences for obscene behavior at an Istanbul concert were suspended. Survey after survey shows that while the overwhelming majority of Turks identify as Muslim, most agree with Atatürk that religion should be a private affair. Erdoğan set out to mold a pious generation, but young Turks would prefer a decent job.

The possibility, then, is that Turkey is already entering a post-Erdoğan era, even with him firmly in control. As the old sources of popular loyalty weaken, the struggle within the ruling establishment may be less about governing Turkey than about controlling what comes next. One sign of a brewing succession war is that the revolution is now devouring its own. Where repression was once reserved for the regime’s opponents, pro-government pundits and well-connected business cronies are discovering that they, too, can be picked up. Former AKP mayors have been arrested in municipal corruption probes, while the Ponzi scandal has put a former deputy minister and the fund’s AKP-connected chief executive behind bars. These cases look less like a purge than a scramble for position among factions in the presidency, the prosecution service, the security apparatus and the business world. If so, Erdoğan may stay in power long enough to see his own accomplishments unravel.

Where, then, will change come from? Çomak, having given the state 30 years, is not waiting to find out. “I have changed. Life has changed,” he says. “But it cannot be said that there has been any fundamental change in the mentality of power.” Çomak sees little option but to plow his own furrow, to keep writing, and to enjoy the solidarity of a literary community that supported him in prison. He repeats Nietzsche’s old saw that what does not kill you makes you stronger. “Perhaps everyone should spend a month or two in prison,” he adds. “Then they would understand better that there is no room for hopelessness. Just don’t stay as long as I did.”

Andrew Finkel has corresponded from Istanbul for both international media and the Turkish press for over 30 years.

scraped.description: ZeroHedge - On a long enough timeline, the survival rate for everyone drops to zero
scraped.author: Tyler Durden
scraped.h1: Could Laura Loomer's Ukrainegate Scandal Push Trump Into Punishing Zelensky
scraped.body_text:
Authored by Andrew Korybko via Andrew Korybko's Newsletter ,

He hates being made a fool out of like Zelensky might have tried doing by attempting to manipulate him via Loomer, and he's known to have a short temper, so there could be hell to pay if Trump suspects that Zelensky was one of her clients who paid her to post on X in a bid to influence him.

The Washington Post cited former Trump advisor Alex Bruesewitz and three anonymous sources to report that " Trump ally Loomer was paid thousands for political tweets, people familiar say ". While she denied that she's paid to post on social media, she admitted to being paid for research and consulting. She also suspiciously announced shortly after they contacted her about their story that she's taking a supposedly preplanned break from her show to focus on her personal life ahead of her wedding.

I've been going nonstop supporting President Trump @realDonaldTrump ever since he came down the golden escalator. As many of you know, I am chronically tuned in, online, and I am always working. I am a machine. Some days I work more than 18 hours. My work has been one of the... pic.twitter.com/5djlbA9tea

— Laura Loomer (@LauraLoomer) November 6, 2026

None of this in itself is too scandalous, but their report goes on to state their four sources "said she is an effective, if sometimes unpredictable, messenger and a key way of trying to get a line directly to Trump." For background, she's considered to be one of his closest advisors by dint of him deeming her among his most loyal allies, so she essentially betrayed Trump by functioning as an undeclared lobbyist knowing that her reportedly paid posts could influence him on her clients' behalf without him being aware of it .

While the Washington Post wrote that "One person who said they had paid Loomer to tweet on behalf of clients said she was deliberate in her work and would only tweet if she agreed with the position", this still raises questions due to her sway over the world's most powerful man. In particular, it prompts speculation about whether the Ukraine government or someone associated with it financially incentivized her to flip-flop from supporting Russia to supporting Ukraine .

Her summertime reversal coincided with what Zelensky described as Ukraine's 40-day "influence operation" aimed at coercing Russia into agreeing to a ceasefire without preconditions, so it's reasonable to wonder whether he also planned to influence Trump as part of his efforts, perhaps to pressure Putin . A potentially effective means to that end would be paying Loomer to flip-flop on the conflict, which she was already arguably considering doing for semi-personal reasons , due to her influence over Trump.

A congressional investigation will likely never be approved by the Democrats since they just captured control of both chambers during the midterms , but the FBI's Counterintelligence Division could still look into it, especially if Trump's Attorney General tasks them with doing so . After all, what Ukraine might have done under Zelensky's orders is try to influence the President of the United States' foreign policy by paying one of his top advisors for this purpose, which is indisputably a case of foreign meddling.

Loomer's Ukrainegate scandal could also land her behind bars if she functioned as an unregistered foreign agent in violation of the "Foreign Agents Registration Act", but its most meaningful consequence by far is that it could push Trump into punishing Zelensky . In particular, instead of pressuring Putin like Zelensky hoped that he'd do under Loomer's influence in the event that Ukraine paid her to flip-flop on the conflict, he could pressure Zelensky by curtailing arms, intelligence, and/or Starlink/Starshield .

One of the ways that Trump could rally his demoralized base after MAGA's midterm walloping is swiftly ending the Ukrainian Conflict , which could be achieved via the "creative coercion" of Europe and Ukraine that was recently proposed here , and Loomer's Ukrainegate scandal could motivate him to do so. He hates being made a fool out of like Zelensky might have tried doing by attempting to manipulate him via Loomer, and he's known to have a short temper, so there could be hell to pay if Trump suspects this .

scraped.title: "Pettiness Is A Thing": Top Democrat Says His Gayness Will Fuel Vicious Trump Investigations
scraped.description: ZeroHedge - On a long enough timeline, the survival rate for everyone drops to zero
scraped.author: Tyler Durden
scraped.h1: "Pettiness Is A Thing": Top Democrat Says His Gayness Will Fuel Vicious Trump Investigations
scraped.body_text:
Rep. Robert Garcia (D-Calif.), who takes over the House Oversight Committee when the new Congress convenes in January, told a crowd that Trump officials are still Democrat targets after leaving office, saying "maybe it's because I'm gay" but "pettiness is a thing." He spoke at Crooked Con , the Crooked Media event in Washington that also featured Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker and Rep. Ilhan Omar (D-Minn.).

"Just because you're Kimberly Guilfoyle, or you're Kristi Noem, or you're Pam Bondi, and you're no longer in office, that doesn't mean that we're still not interested in accountability for all of your crimes and grift," Garcia said. "We're not going to forget. Like, we can't forget about these folks that are causing harm, like, you know, I think it's like, maybe it's because I'm gay, but like, you know, like pettiness is a thing ." The crowd cheered and applauded.

"Maybe it's because I'm gay, but pettiness is a thing. We're not going to forget these crimes." - Rep. Robert Garcia on prosecuting Trump's administration pic.twitter.com/HhitypiGz4

— Crooked Media (@CrookedMedia) November 7, 2026

"Like, I am mad, you know," Garcia continued. "This is a moment in history where all the young people, in our families, in our classrooms, they have to know that what's happening now is wrong. To just move on does a disservice to the future of our country." He named no specific crimes. Trump fired Noem in March and Bondi in April.

The remarks came days after Democrats won control of Congress in Tuesday's midterms. On election night, Garcia issued a statement about "The Trump Crime Family" and told Republicans to "lawyer up." Attorney General Todd Blanche then declined to rule out prosecuting Democrats who investigate administration officials : asked on CNN's "State of the Union" on Sunday whether lawmakers could face charges, he said "yes, there could be," and added, "I would be very worried if I was a member on that committee," as we reported .

Blanche said Congress has constitutional oversight authority but that recent Democratic statements went beyond it. "That is not oversight. I welcome oversight," he said. He cited no criminal statute and did not say any investigation had begun. He also said the Justice Department would provide legal defense to officials facing congressional scrutiny, including incoming White House chief of staff Stephen Miller.

Trump had made the same charge the day before. In a Truth Social post on Saturday, he wrote: "The Democrats are going around threatening a lot of people, including the Attorney General of the United States, and others, with Impeachment and many other forms of punishment, even though they admit they have no reason to do so." He called it "extortion at the highest level," said Democrats were "threatening our Donors" with imprisonment, and accused Sen. Elissa Slotkin (D-Mich.) of saying she would "go after all young people that believe in Republican Values." He closed by writing that "I am ordering the Department of Justice to look into this criminal act, immediately!"

Garcia answered the threats of prosecution directly: "They can come after us however they want. We're not going to be intimidated." The Oversight Committee's plans take in alleged wrongdoing by the administration, the president's family and corporate allies .

scraped.title: On The 'Party Of Victims'
scraped.description: ZeroHedge - On a long enough timeline, the survival rate for everyone drops to zero
scraped.author: Tyler Durden
scraped.h1: On The 'Party Of Victims'
scraped.body_text:
Authored by James Howard Kunstler via Clusterfuck Nation ,

". . . history and even corruption itself have a way of normalizing the unbearable."

- Naomi Wolf on Substack

That 60-Minutes interview with the President Sunday night was a doozy : he allowed Ross Douthat (moonlighting from his New York Times column) to over-speak him so audaciously you had to wonder why Mr. Trump even bothered to show up. He barely levered a word in edgewise and looked rather glum in the process. Actually, you were watching an act of political ju-jitsu: the president pretending to take it like a whipped dog, so that his antagonists would think he was offering himself up for slaughter . They'd better think again (but watch, they won't).

Senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed at His Victory Celebration

Also on Sunday, Roger Stone wrote that Stephen Miller, the new chief of staff, was just promoted to "wartime consigliere." You are a little off, Roger. It's more like wartime field marshal. The president has gone to war against the treasonous Democratic Party, the Party of Victims. Now they know. And now you know. The positions on both sides have hardened-up. I'm dreaming of. . . a strange Christmas.

Pardon me for going out on a limb here. The Party of Victims has flat-out said it wants to see the president drawn, quartered, beheaded, pissed-on, and stuffed into an unmarked hole in the ground. Plus, anyone who ever worked for him or voted for him to be hurled into prison. There's your casus belli. The curse it is cast.

The Party of Victims has also announced its intentions to shred the Constitution via legal legerdemain for the purpose of making the USA a one-party state and, as such, subservient to governing entities outside the USA. Those entities reside mainly in and around the European Union, including the EU itself, the financial elites that it serves, and an international NGO galaxy of aggrieved "activists." These are commonly identified as the "Globalists." Note that this cabal is already under extreme stress on its home territory as the nations of Europe explode in violence. IOW, these Globalists are already losing and turning ever more desperate.

Discount any prattle coming out of the Party of Victims and their ancillaries in the news media about "our democracy." The phrase is a ruse, aimed at malware they have already installed in your brain, straight out of Rachel Maddow's pretty mouth. "Our democracy" is a phantom concept to disguise a political apparatus that only works for the Party of Victims. Also note: the Party of Victims wants to make victims of everybody outside their party. "Our democracy" actually means: we get to push you around and do our bidding. . . or else go off and die .

So, the Party of Victims has "won" the midterm election super-bigly. They crushed it. They are supreme. Everybody and his uncle voted for them overwhelmingly, in record numbers so stupefying they seem. . . a little supernatural. Yes, like they got an assist from somewhere, from someone - and probably not from the better angels of our nature , if you know what I mean. Somehow an extra 20-million ballots were cast this midterm over the previous midterm in 2022. But they were strangely distributed.

In the Texas gubernatorial, for instance, almost two million new voters showed up this year above the total voters in 2022 - 9.9-million over 8.1 million. Nationwide, Republican votes were nearly the same in 2026 as 2022, but those 20-million new votes went strictly to the Party of Victims. Gol-lee! Where did they come from? I think we're going to find out. Of course, to find out, you have to first inquire. Why would you inquire if the election was one hunnert percent above-board, fair-and-square? How dare you! That would be election denialisim, spurious, illegitimate, . . . tyrannical. . . verboten !

That is Party of Victims' well-advertised "red line," right there, the thing that triggers their thing, which is activist activism going active in the streets, protest marches, shrieking nose-rings, froggie costumes, raging inflamed transsexuals, POCs unchained, Boomer grandmas in a lather, all of them maybe busting up some storefronts, setting a few fires, mostly peaceful, you understand, except where they're not. Chicago is suddenly like Paris was in October. And the Party of Victims double-dares you to do something about it!

The president will do something about it, probably something that entails federalizing the national guard, or failing that, sending in regular army troops. It will probably require him to declare the Insurrection Act (10 U.S.C. §§ 251-255), which overrides the Posse Comitatus Act. No approval from Congress is required.

Anyway, the U.S. has operated under multiple overlapping national emergencies for decades (the oldest still-active one dates to the 1979 Iran hostage crisis). The 2018 Election Interference Emergency order (EO 13848) is one of them. It was renewed by the president in August 2026. Which is to say, the country is already under an emergency, this one pegged to foreign interference in our elections. It mandates an "assessment" of foreign interference by the Director of National Intelligence, and further action by the DOJ. It may not be enough. Effective executive action might require the declaration of a National Security Emergency in the event that substantial evidence of election fraud is discovered.

The "Our Democracy" NGOs scheming in the background of the midterm election want the Party of Victims to go medieval on the president. This is where their plan kicks in to nullify the president and turn over his executive powers to a panel of governors (Newsom, Pritzker, Hochul, etc.), who will then supposedly preside over a "restructuring" of the basic charter of the USA. Their chatter about this was recorded and distributed across the internet the past month, along with their written memos to the same effect. It's all out there. In short, this actually is an insurrection, and Mr. Trump will oblige himself to stop it, just as Abraham Lincoln had to oblige himself to put down the southern secession. And for the same reason, to save the Union.

You might have noticed that there is also a lot of background chatter on the web about "stocking up" on food and supplies. . . about possible interruptions of the internet, perhaps days or even weeks . . . about threats to the electric grid. Of course, it's alarming. It implies rather extreme and severe circumstances. But do you really know what might happen? This is serious. Pay attention. Maintain situational awareness. This could be a very strange Christmas indeed.

scraped.h1: U.S. SEEKS LONG-TERM MILITARY PRESENCE IN VENEZUELA AS TRUMP ADMINISTRATION EXPANDS ITS STRATEGIC FOOTPRINT IN THE AMERICAS
scraped.body_text:
Gateway Hispanic

Negotiations over a Status of Forces Agreement could give Washington a legal framework to deploy American military personnel in Venezuela, opening a new chapter in the country’s relationship with the United States.

RUBIO: US WILL ACT AGAINST THREATS TO FORCES AND SHIPPING Secretary of State Marco Rubio says the U.S. will continue to act defensively against threats to American forces in the region and commercial shipping, emphasizing the right to defend itself against imminent threats. For… https://t.co/Hp1heZ16VJ pic.twitter.com/A87QxGNimM

The Trump administration is negotiating a military agreement with Venezuela that could pave the way for a long-term American military presence Venezuela, according U.S. officials familiar with the discussions.

The negotiations are being led by the State Department under Secretary of State Marco Rubio and involve the government of interim Venezuelan President Delcy Rodríguez.

The proposed agreement, known as a Status of Forces Agreement (SOFA), would establish the legal framework governing the activities and status of American military personnel operating in Venezuela. It could facilitate joint training, military exercises, naval visits and humanitarian assistance, among other mutually agreed activities.

The number of personnel, their locations and the duration of any deployment would require further arrangements. A senior State Department official said discussions about permanent bases were “way, way down the road” and that no negotiations on establishing such bases were currently underway.

For years, the governments of Hugo Chávez and Nicolás Maduro maintained an adversarial relationship with the United States, while strengthening political, economic and military ties with countries including Russia, China and Iran.

That relationship changed dramatically following the January 3, 2026, American military operation that resulted in Maduro’s capture and transfer to the United States, where he faces criminal charges.

Delcy Rodríguez, who had served as Maduro’s vice president, subsequently assumed the interim presidency. Her government has since engaged with the Trump administration on security, economic cooperation and Venezuela’s political future.

The negotiations over a SOFA agreement demonstrate how military cooperation has become part of this new bilateral relationship.

Venezuela’s strategic importance extends well beyond its internal political crisis

The country occupies a significant geographical position in the Caribbean basin, with a long Atlantic-Caribbean coastline and land borders with Colombia, Brazil and Guyana. Its location offers potential advantages for maritime surveillance, intelligence gathering, logistical operations and regional security cooperation.

Washington has increasingly focused on dismantling criminal networks operating across South America and the Caribbean.

Venezuela’s border regions, particularly those shared with Colombia, have long been affected by the presence of armed groups, including the National Liberation Army (ELN), as well as drug-trafficking networks.

Recently, the NYT has also reported on U.S. intelligence assistance in a Venezuelan operation against an ELN camp in Apure.

A formal military agreement could make future cooperation more structured, allowing American and Venezuelan personnel to coordinate training, intelligence-related activities and security operations under agreed legal conditions.

Venezuela has historically maintained close relationships with Moscow, Beijing and Tehran. Those relationships have given Russia, China and Iran political, economic and strategic influence in a country located within the United States’ immediate regional sphere of interest.

A sustained American security relationship with Caracas would represent a significant geopolitical change.

It could reduce the opportunities available to Washington’s strategic competitors and give the United States a more direct role in regional security arrangements.

Trending: Netanyahu’s Crypto Plan to Bypass Sanctions Sparks Political Firestorm in Israel

Venezuela’s Caribbean coastline is particularly important for maritime surveillance and regional security.

A greater American military presence, if eventually authorized, could improve coordination against trafficking routes and strengthen cooperation with neighboring countries.

It could also affect the regional security calculations of Colombia, Guyana, Brazil and Caribbean nations.

In particular, Guyana’s territorial dispute with Venezuela over the Essequibo region remains an important consideration. Any expansion of foreign military activity in Venezuela would inevitably attract attention from neighboring governments.

One of the most important legal questions surrounding the negotiations is Article 13 of Venezuela’s Constitution.

The provision explicitly prohibits foreign military bases and installations serving military purposes on Venezuelan territory. It also states that the country’s geographical space constitutes a zone of peace.

This creates a potentially significant legal and political obstacle to any proposal involving permanent American military facilities.

Any arrangement involving facilities or a sustained deployment would raise questions about constitutional compliance, the authority of Venezuela’s interim government and the role of its national institutions.

Nevertheless, several questions remain unanswered:

1. Will the two governments formally sign the SOFA agreement?

2. What number of American military personnel, if any, will eventually operate in Venezuela?

3. Will cooperation be limited to training, exercises and naval visits, or expand into operational missions?

4. How will the agreement be reconciled with Article 13 of Venezuela’s Constitution?

5. What role will Venezuela’s military institutions and political opposition have in determining the country’s long-term security arrangements?

For Washington, Venezuela has become a potential security partner in a region where organized crime, drug trafficking, geopolitical competition and maritime security are increasingly interconnected.

This potential military agreement could reshape the balance of power in the Caribbean and South America. But, whether it also contributes to a stable, sovereign and democratic Venezuela will depend on the political and institutional arrangements that accompany it.

María Herrera Mellado es una abogada y analista política muy respetada. Licenciada en Derecho en EE.UU. y España, también tiene un doctorado en Ciencias Jurídicas y varios títulos de la Universidad de Granada (España), de la Universidad de Arizona y de la Florida International University. Con amplia experiencia en derecho internacional, asesoría en inversiones, representación en inmigración, y protección de la privacidad y lucha anticorrupción, ha asesorado a organizaciones y políticos europeos, estadounidenses e hispanoamericanos. Ha escrito sobre seguridad nacional e inmigración, protección de datos, derecho constitucional, consumo financiero y derecho bancario en revistas internacionales y coescribió libros publicados en Perú y Colombia. Es reconocida por su servicio comunitario en EE.UU. y es considerada una de las mujeres más influyentes de Florida. Es experta en varios idiomas y participa frecuentemente en debates en canales como Univisión, Fox, France 24, Telemundo y es la Editora Jefe de Gateway Hispanic.

Rubio immediately brought the discussion back to American interests.

“Duterte is not an American,” Rubio responded.

Rubio concluded:
