scraped.title: Outgoing Rep. Thomas Massie Introduces Articles of Impeachment Against SecWar Pete Hegseth › American Greatness
scraped.description: Rep. Thomas Massie (R-Ky.) formally introduced eight articles of impeachment against Secretary of War Pete Hegseth on Monday, forcing a House vote by Wednesday.
scraped.h1: Outgoing Rep. Thomas Massie Introduces Articles of Impeachment Against SecWar Pete Hegseth
scraped.body_text:
Rep. Thomas Massie (R-Ky.) formally introduced eight articles of impeachment against Secretary of War Pete Hegseth on Monday, forcing a House vote by Wednesday. The resolution accuses Hegseth of “high crimes and misdemeanors,” primarily for waging war in Iran without congressional authorization in violation of the War Powers Resolution of 1973.

Massie spoke on the House floor Monday for over an hour, outlining the eight articles:

• Article I: Waging the Iran war in violation of Section 2(c) of the 1973 War Powers Resolution. Massie alleged Hegseth directed U.S. forces into hostilities starting February 28, 2026, without a congressional declaration of war, statutory authorization, an attack on the United States, or an imminent threat, making the conflict unlawful from the start. • Article II: Continuing the Iran war in violation of Section 5(c) of the War Powers Resolution after both the House and Senate passed measures (including H. Con. Res. 86) directing the removal of U.S. forces. • Article III: Continuing hostilities in Iran past the War Powers Resolution’s 60-day clock (plus any 30-day withdrawal period). Massie charged that Hegseth treated these statutory deadlines as optional. • Article IV: Ignoring laws intended to minimize civilian casualties. This article cited operations in Iran, including a February 28 strike on the Shajareh Tayyebeh Elementary School that reports said killed more than 100 children. • Article V: Extrajudicial killings through unauthorized lethal military strikes on suspected drug-trafficking vessels in the Caribbean and eastern Pacific, replacing maritime law enforcement and resulting in at least 221 deaths. • Article VI: Retaliating against Sen. Mark Kelly (D-AZ) for a video in which the retired Navy officer told service members they could refuse illegal orders. Massie alleged Hegseth abused Pentagon authority by seeking to strip Kelly of rank and pension over constitutionally protected speech. • Article VII: Kidnapping a sovereign foreign leader. This referred to Hegseth’s role in Operation Absolute Resolve, the January 2026 raid that captured former Venezuelan leader Nicolás Maduro and his wife without, in Massie’s view, constitutional or legal authority. • Article VIII: Initiating unauthorized combat operations in Yemen (Operation Rough Rider, a 52-day bombing campaign) without congressional authorization or an imminent threat to the United States.

While all the Democrats and some Republicans will support impeachment, removal from office would require a two-thirds Senate vote, a threshold considered unlikely to be met

Massie, who lost his May primary and is retiring from Congress, first introduced the articles in September, but House Speaker Mike Johnson adjourned Congress to block a pre-midterm vote. Following the GOP’s sweeping midterm losses, Massie reintroduced the resolution to pressure President Trump to fire Hegseth before Democrats assume control of Congress in January.

When asked Monday about the impeachment push, Hegseth replied, “Oh, we’re not worried about that,” telling reporters that he will further address the issue at a press conference on Tuesday.

“We’re going to do a press conference tomorrow morning at the Pentagon on that very topic,” the secretary said. “So I’ll save my remarks for then.”

Secretary of State Marco Rubio defended Hegseth, Monday, saying the impeachment push is “unfair.”

“I think he’s done a great job, Rubio told a gaggle of reporters. “I’ve worked with him every single day and seen the professionalism. He’s very smart, he puts a lot of hours into this.”

“I think it’s unfair. I think Pete’s done a very good job, I really do,” Rubio insisted when pressed by another reporter.

“I see sides of him the media doesn’t see and members of Congress don’t see,” he added.

Rep. Derrick Van Orden (R-Wis.) stated on X that the military is experiencing its “highest morale in decades,” thanks to Hegseth’s leadership. He also credited Hegseth with prosecuting “some of the most extraordinary combat ops in the history of warfare,” and achieving “record recruiting.”

Taking aim at Massie, Van Orden added: “For some self-aggrandizing twit who never served in the military to try and impeach him is pathetic.”

Chief Pentagon spokesman Sean Parnell dismissed rumors last week that President Trump himself was ready to cut Hegseth loose.

“Secretary Hegseth will not back down or be deterred by politicians seeking to score partisan points or launch phony investigations where no wrongdoing exists,” Parnell told Fox News Digital. The Department of War has followed the law and our Secretary will continue to stand and fight every single day to support and defend the Constitution, lead our troops, and protect America.”

scraped.title: Jennifer Welch’s ‘I’ve Had It’ Podcast Loses Almost Every Sponsor After Ghoulish Anti-Charlie Kirk Clip › American Greatness
scraped.description: Over twenty sponsors have pulled support from the far-left “I’ve Had It” podcast after a disturbing clip of hosts Jennifer Welch and Angie Sullivan ghoulishly…
scraped.h1: Jennifer Welch’s ‘I’ve Had It’ Podcast Loses Almost Every Sponsor After Ghoulish Anti-Charlie Kirk Clip
scraped.body_text:
Over twenty sponsors have pulled support from the far-left “I’ve Had It” podcast after a disturbing clip of hosts Jennifer Welch and Angie Sullivan ghoulishly laughing at a vile comment about desecrating Charlie Kirk’s corpse went viral.

During their “Drinking MAGA Tears” episode on Thursday, the hosts read left-wing social media posts celebrating the results of the midterm election. One said something along the lines of “We’re digging up Charlie Kirk and doing it again.”

Welch and Sullivan laughed for an extended period—about 20 seconds— before peddling disinformation on the politics of Tyler Robinson, the accused shooter.

“No comment on that,” Welch chortled after regaining her composure.

“Other than he was shot by somebody who was super MAGA … family,” Sullivan sniggered, echoing the false accusation spewed by late night talk show host Jimmy Kimmel days after Kirk’s assassination in September 2025.

“He was shot by a MAGA person,” Welch agreed.

In truth, Robinson came from a conservative family but became a radicalized leftist at college.

On the day of the shooting, he justified the assassination as the only way to combat Kirk’s “hatred” in a text message to his furry boyfriend Lance “Luna” Twiggs.

“Some hate can’t be negotiated out,” Robinson said.

The viral clip of Welch and Sullivan laughing uncontrollably at the thought of digging up Charlie Kirk’s corpse drew widespread condemnation, prompting multiple advertisers, including Cash App and Chewy, to bail.

“We do not condone violence of any kind and we are no longer sponsors of this podcast,” Cash App said in a statement on Friday.

“We do not sponsor or support the ‘I’ve Had It’ podcast,” stated Chewy, a pet care company, on Saturday. “We unequivocally condemn violence in all forms. The comments made by the hosts do not reflect Chewy’s values or what we stand for as a company.”

The hosts on Saturday posted what is widely seen as an insincere “apology” on social media, calling the joke “insensitive,” and framing the political assassination of Charlie Kirk as merely “gun violence.”

“Whatever our political differences, there is nothing funny about gun violence,” the statement read.

Further goading conservatives, the hosts noted that they had made a donation to the Democrat-aligned anti-gun group “Everytown for Gun Safety.”

The fallout continued through the weekend, with several more companies dropping the show.

On Sunday’s podcast, Welch bitterly accused the “titty babies” at Turning Point USA of “spearheading” a cancel campaign against her podcast. She also disavowed her “apology,” saying it wasn’t meant for conservatives.

“That was for us,” she said. “Because somebody that I loved very much died from gun violence two years ago and I just didn’t feel good about that.”

TPUSA spokesman Andrew Kolvet, who denied coordinating the boycott, responded to Welch on the Charlie Kirk Show, Monday.

“Pro tip to Jennifer Welch. Apologies are for the people you hurt—they’re not for you, unless your a raging narcissist,” he said.

Kolvet also responded to the pair on X, stating: “Thanks for the video, but it’s not that hard. Just don’t legitimize political violence.”

You can blame me or Turning Point all you want, but we’re not the reason all your sponsors are fleeing. You are.

Your lack of remorse is the least surprising thing of all. I never once expected you to listen to me. But maybe, just maybe, you’ll listen to all the brands that no longer want to be associated with you.

As of Monday, twenty current sponsors had pulled all support from the podcast, according to Mary McDonald-Lewis, a conservative women’s rights activist promoting the cancellation campaign on X.

Those companies are Cash App, Chewy, Honeylove, Zenni Optical, Boll & Branch, Ethos, iRestore Laser, NOBL Travel, Lola Blankets, Zip Recruiter, Jones Road Beauty, Nutrafol, Ridge Wallet, Ethos, Ember Tech, Ladder, Casper, Momentous, and ASPCA Pet Insurance.

Multiple companies that have advertised in the past, including Cozy Earth, Hexclad, Branch Basic, Ro and Home Service USA, have indicated that they will no longer sponsor the show. The last ads those companies ran on the “I’ve Had It” podcast were reportedly months ago.

There are conflicting reports regarding One Quince, which may or may not have pulled support.

As of early Monday afternoon, the “I’ve Had It” podcast appeared to have only Article Modern and possibly One Quince as sponsors.

Update

Multiple X users have shared emails from One Quince stating that they have pulled their advertising so it appears that Article Modern is the lone holdout.

Δ

Debra Heine is a conservative Catholic mom of six and longtime political pundit. She has written for several conservative news websites over the years, including Breitbart and PJ Media.

scraped.h1: Gun Sales Expected to Surge After Democrats Regain Control of Congress
scraped.body_text:
Gun rights groups and retailers are projecting a surge in firearm sales after Democrats won control of both chambers of the U.S. House of Representatives and the Senate in last week’s midterm elections.

Citizens Committee for the Right to Keep and Bear Arms (CCRKBA) Chairman Alan Gottlieb is warning that gun control groups are heralding the wins and will be seeking new gun control legislation and restrictions.

CCRKBA PREDICTS GUN SALES SURGE AS ELECTION RESULTS THREATEN 2A

“We may be about to witness a surge in gun buying not seen since 2020.” —CCRKBA Chairman Alan Gottlieb

https://t.co/fY145lvCON https://t.co/Ca3HQObSuX

— CCRKBA (@CCRKBArms) November 5, 2026

Gottlieb said the threat of new gun control legislation isn’t limited to Congress and that Democrats also are set to push restrictions in states like Pennsylvania and Arizona.

In an interview Thursday, Gottlieb told The States:

Arizona’s gone from a you know a great gun right state right now to a very anti-gun state overnight. Pennsylvania, you know, that now the trifecta on the government controlled by the Democrats in Pennsylvania, many of which are anti gun and are gonna push all kinds of gun control measures.

States that previously enjoyed Republican protection of gun rights now may be facing state-level measures such as permit-to-purchase requirements, extended waiting periods, enhanced background checks, and restrictions on concealed carry permits, according to the Center Square .

Gottlieb noted that when there are big swings in politics towards gun control advocates getting in power, there’s also big sales surges of firearms. “In the couple of weeks leading up to the election, people, knowing and thinking that, you know, things were gonna flip, gun sales had a big spike and we’re seeing that continuation spike yesterday, today, and I think we’re gonna see it for months to come now.”

According to the National Shooting Sports Foundation , October 2026 saw 1,402,422 adjusted National Instant Criminal Background Check System (NICS) checks, marking a 7.9 percent increase compared to October 2025.

Federal Bureau of Investigations Firearm Background Checks statistics show more than 2.2 million NICS background checks across the country in October.

That’s up from 2 million in September, but the third highest month of 2026.

Gottlieb said one possible threat that gun owners could be facing from the newly-elected legislatures are what he characterized as workarounds:

I think on the anti-gun, the gun prohibition lobbies’ wish list, they start off of course with things like a permit to purchase so that you have to go through an extra hoop to be able to buy a firearm, extended waiting periods, extended background checks, different kinds of measures of where you where you can be able to take your firearm, more restrictions on concealed carry permits, be able to to get a permit to carry to for self-protection. Those are the things that they’re gonna start with pretty quickly, I think.

The new Congress will be seated Jan. 3, 2027.

scraped.body_text:
Jeffries is poised to become the first black speaker of the House in U.S. history — unless the DSA stops him.

House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.) lashed out against the Democratic Socialists of America and appeared to accuse them of racism.

The 56-year-old Jeffries will almost certainly become the speaker of the House unless enough Democrats oppose his elevation, and the far-left fringe has already signaled that they're arming up to do just that.

'We aren't doing this s**t. It's not about your race...'

He has previously faced opposition from forces aligned with New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani, also a Democratic Socialist, who threatened to mount a primary challenge aimed to unseat Jeffries.

Since Democrats swept the midterms, the feud between the far left of the party and the establishment has taken center stage.

When CNN asked Jeffries about a DSA crowd chanting that he was next to lose his seat, he pointed out the lack of diversity in the DSA.

"It was very interesting to me, as observed by others, that there was almost zero diversity in that crowd," he said.

His political operation has also referred to the DSA activists who oppose him as "team gentrification," according to CNN.

"If Team Gentrification wants a primary fight, our response will be forceful and unrelenting," his organization responded in June.

Mamdani backed off from that primary fight, but now the feud will help determine whether Jeffries becomes the speaker of the House or if a far-left extremist backed by the DSA beats him out.

Some Democrats are already fuming at the comment from Jeffries.

RELATED: Democratic Socialists will seek to RADICALLY upend the government in reported platform

"We aren't doing this s**t. It's not about your race, it's about you being beholden to corporate interests and opposed to the priorities of the voters who just handed you all this majority," responded Krystal Ball, a commentator and podcaster.

"Recall, Jeffries had to be dragged kicking and screaming to endorse Zohran at the last minute and [Sen. Chuck] Schumer (D-N.Y.) never did even though he was the Dem nominee and is one of the most popular figures in the party," she added.

Despite the DSA feud, Jeffries has the backing of former President Barack Obama, which will likely propel him into the speakership. If he is successful, Jeffries will become the first black speaker of the House in U.S. history.

scraped.title: Nvidia CEO admits to affair — as suspected lover is accused of smuggling banned chips to China-linked cutouts | Blaze Media
scraped.description: Several buyers of Nvidia's restricted products are accused of being shell corporations.
scraped.author: https://www.facebook.com/140738092630206
scraped.h1: Nvidia CEO admits to affair — as suspected lover is accused of smuggling banned chips to China-linked cutouts
scraped.body_text:
Several buyers of Nvidia's restricted products are accused of being shell corporations.

The story has as much worldwide implications as a typical James Bond movie, but unfortunately for those involved, this is real life.

While it's not uncommon for the United States government to declare Chinese companies are working for the country's ruling party, when Washington recently alleged that the head of a top data center company was causing information to be harvested by Beijing, it sparked a lot of complications.

'It is always dark for as long as it has been here.'

The situation escalated quickly as news broke purporting to substantiate the allegations. A Singapore-registered firm called Megaspeed bought 136,000 Nvidia GPUs over the course of 2025-2026, totaling around $2 billion, Tech Insider reported .

In 2023, Alice Huang — real name Huang Le, no relation to Jensen — was named managing director of Megaspeed. According to a New York Times report , Washington believes and alleges Huang Le has been passing information onto Chinese intelligence while also amassing the computer chips for her nation.

The report stated that American intelligence officials suspected that Huang Le was helping China evade American restrictions on its ability to acquire advanced chips and that she was providing information to China based on her direct personal access to Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang.

To make matters worse, in the wake of U.S. intelligence allegations that Huang was carrying on a "close relationship" with a female spy for China, he is now suspected of carrying on a significant romantic affair with Huang Le. Bowing to pressure, the CEO sent a company-wide email admitting to his infidelity but without naming names.

RELATED: Elon Musk's next target? America's self-entitled phone companies.

Sean Gallup/Getty Images

"I owe my family and all of you an apology. I was unfaithful to my wife. My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did. I am deeply sorry," Huang wrote.

"Regarding the national security concerns raised in news reports, Nvidia’s Board of Directors has initiated an independent investigation. I support the investigation and will cooperate fully," he wrote , per the Verge.

At the same time, the sales of Nvidia tech to Megaspeed and other companies have come under the microscope after reports have alleged that several of the companies in question are seemingly shell corporations or operating at suspiciously low capacity.

Two of the Nvidia buyers, New Matrix and Maginfra, were reported by Singaporean outlet the Business Times as being mostly vacant.

Maginfra had received a license to assemble Nvidia chips into AI servers earlier in 2026, but its office was found to be seemingly deserted when a NYT reporter visited it in September.

Same story goes for New Matrix , whose office also appeared uninhabited.

Both companies were approved to acquire Nvidia's H200 GPUs .

RELATED: Your smart home devices are vulnerable to cyberattack — protect yourself with these tips

Michael Nagle/Bloomberg/Getty Images

As for Megaspeed, its office was vacant, too, when the Straights Times paid them a visit in October. Located on the seventh floor of a Singapore office building called the Ocean Financial Centre, a tenant allegedly told a reporter that the office has always appeared to be unoccupied.

"It is always dark for as long as it has been here," the tenant in the building said while on her way to lunch. "I hardly see anyone visiting or in the office."

While Singapore police have confirmed publicly that it is investigating Megaspeed, the force has denied it is looking into Huang Le for having ties to mainland China.

"We would like to make clear that neither the Singapore government nor its officials said this. And there were no such investigations conducted in respect of Alice Huang," Singapore’s home affairs ministry said , per the South China Morning Post .

Like Blaze News? Bypass the censors, sign up for our newsletters, and get stories like this direct to your inbox. Sign up here !

Andrew Chapados

scraped.h1: Meet the new DSA members who make Bernie Sanders look conservative
scraped.body_text:
Pat Gray welcomes the new crop of democratic socialists headed to Congress.

The Democratic Socialists of America just scored major victories in New York, Colorado, Michigan, and Pennsylvania — and their newest congressional recruits aren't exactly hiding their radical ambitions.

“Now it’s time to meet some of your new DSA overlords,” BlazeTV host Pat Gray begins, before introducing Darializa Avila Chevalier, who has “consistently repeated anti-police rhetoric.”

“‘F you,’” she tweeted. ‘We’re going to defund and abolish police.’ ‘You don’t get to water down our movements,’ she said in June of 2020. Two days later, she repeated the call, and said that she supported 'no more police at all, ever,’” Gray explains.

“In another now-deleted post, she called then-candidate Joe Biden ‘a war criminal’ and the United States of America, where I don’t know, she lives, an ‘effing disgrace,’” he continues. “She also had some nice words for relationships between black and Arab men and white women. She wrote, ‘Black men and Arab men fetishizing ugly colonizer women should stop.’”

“She’s a U.S. congressman,” he adds.

Elected to the 1st Congressional District in Colorado is Melat Kiros.

“She is a 29-year-old immigrant from Ethiopia and another Democratic Socialist of America member. Easily won her district,” Gray says.

“She wants to abolish ICE,” he explains. “Universal child care and elder care, Medicare for All. And she wants to pass a federal trans bill of rights. Yes, let’s get them back into sports that they’ve been banned from. Let’s get them back into girls' locker rooms.”

“In another interview, she claimed socialism was more in line with the values of the Declaration of Independence than capitalism,” he continues.

“She also faced criticism over her comments on Israel and for saying that the 9/11 attacks were inevitable in the sense that we destabilized a lot of the Middle East, which led people to believe that another act of violence was the only response,” he adds.

Another member of the DSA, Donavan McKinney, “cruised to victory” for a Detroit-area congressional seat.

“He supports Medicare for All. Implementing the Green New Deal. Wouldn’t that be fun? Ending cash bail. Abolishing ICE, a government program to provide free housing to everyone,” Gray says.

He also “wants to use taxpayer dollars to fund all abortion and wants to, of course, give amnesty to illegal aliens.”

Pennsylvania’s third district winner, Chris Rabb, “wants to abolish ICE, create national grocery stores … wants to pass reparations for black people … implement the Green New Deal … invest in mental health responders, impeach President Trump, and abolish the death penalty.”

And last but not least, Claire Valdez, who won her election and will be representing parts of New York City.

“She made headlines during the campaign for promising to carry Mexico’s fight against imperialism to Congress,” Gray comments.

“Toss out that old America-first garbage. It’s Mexico-first for Claire,” he adds.

To enjoy more of Pat's biting analysis and signature wit as he restores common sense to a senseless world, subscribe to BlazeTV — the largest multi-platform network of voices who love America, defend the Constitution, and live the American dream.

BlazeTV Staff

items.title: Texas rechaza al aparato político republicano en unas elecciones de mitad de mandato históricas: ¿qué sigue?
items.summary: Millones de texanos y texanas rechazaron de manera contundente al aparato político republicano y dieron paso a una victoria demócrata arrolladora e histórica cuyas repercusiones trascenderán ampliamente las fronteras del estado.

scraped.title: Texas rechaza al aparato político republicano en unas elecciones...
scraped.description: Durante mucho tiempo, Texas ha sido considerado una de las joyas de la corona del dominio político republicano e incluso de la extrema derecha. Durant
scraped.author: Taylor Goel
scraped.h1: Texas rechaza al aparato político republicano en unas elecciones de mitad de mandato históricas: ¿qué sigue?
scraped.body_text:
Durante mucho tiempo, Texas ha sido considerado una de las joyas de la corona del dominio político republicano e incluso de la extrema derecha. Durante décadas, se ha tratado al estado como un territorio prácticamente imposible de conquistar para los demócratas: los republicanos controlaban los cargos de elección estatal y presentaban su dominio como un reflejo inevitable de la política texana. Las elecciones de mitad de mandato de este año han echado por tierra esa idea. Millones de texanos y texanas rechazaron de manera contundente al aparato político republicano y dieron paso a una victoria demócrata arrolladora e histórica cuyas repercusiones trascenderán ampliamente las fronteras del estado.

La demócrata Gina Hinojosa derrotó al gobernador republicano Greg Abbott, que buscaba la reelección, por aproximadamente siete puntos porcentuales, y puso fin a más de tres décadas de control republicano de la gobernación de Texas. Abbott, que había ganado las tres elecciones anteriores por márgenes de al menos diez puntos porcentuales, aspiraba a un cuarto mandato consecutivo – lo que lo habría convertido en el gobernador con más años en el cargo en la historia del estado.

James Talarico derrotó al republicano Ken Paxton por aproximadamente doce puntos porcentuales, convirtiéndose en el primer demócrata elegido al Senado de Estados Unidos por Texas desde 1988. Los demócratas también ganaron las otras principales contiendas estatales, incluida la de vicegobernador, en la que derrotaron al titular republicano Dan Patrick.

Estas victorias demócratas en Texas son históricas y reflejan un rechazo cada vez mayor al poder político establecido, a la clase multimillonaria y a las políticas crecientemente represivas que han caracterizado la era de Trump y que se han aplicado de buen grado en la política texana. Además, demuestran que el supuesto bastión republicano en Texas no es inamovible – incluso en lugares aparentemente muy conservadores existe la posibilidad de un futuro distinto cuando el pueblo se propone construirlo.

La pregunta ahora no es simplemente si Texas “se volvió azul”. Es si los millones de personas que se movilizaron contra la agenda republicana pueden construir un movimiento lo suficientemente poderoso como para exigir un cambio de fondo.

Un rechazo histórico a la agenda de Trump

Los resultados de las elecciones de mitad de mandato en Texas no pueden separarse del contexto político nacional. La clase trabajadora enfrenta el aumento de los precios de los alimentos y la vivienda, el estancamiento de los salarios y un futuro económico cada vez más precario. Mientras tanto, el gobierno de Trump ha redoblado su apuesta por políticas que convierten a los inmigrantes en chivos expiatorios, atacan a las personas LGBTQ, socavan la educación pública, buscan arrebatarnos nuestras libertades civiles y destinan enormes recursos a la guerra, la militarización y la represión.

En general, los republicanos han ofrecido pocas soluciones a estas crisis cada vez más graves. En cambio, han recurrido a las guerras culturales, a culpar de los problemas sociales a determinados grupos mediante discursos racistas, a la manipulación de los límites de los distritos electorales y a medidas cada vez más autoritarias en un intento desesperado por consolidar su poder.

Abbott y Paxton encarnaban esta agenda. Durante años, el gobierno de Abbott ha atacado los derechos reproductivos, impuesto restricciones a la educación pública y ampliado el aparato represivo del estado. Paxton se ha convertido en sinónimo de acusaciones de corrupción y de los intereses de la élite política adinerada. Ambos han sido figuras centrales de una administración que ha priorizado los ataques contra la clase trabajadora en lugar de abordar las condiciones que hacen cada vez más difícil su vida. En Texas, este rechazo también se extiende a la enorme influencia de multimillonarios como Elon Musk, cuya creciente presencia política y económica en el estado se ha convertido en un peligroso símbolo del poder que las personas adineradas ejercen sobre la vida y la seguridad públicas.

Texas es uno de los estados más ricos del país. Pero también es un lugar donde, como en tantos otros estados, millones de personas que producen esa riqueza tienen dificultades para pagar la vivienda, la atención médica, los alimentos y otras necesidades básicas – sin mencionar el aumento de los impuestos a la propiedad en Texas. Es imposible ignorar esta contradicción, y los resultados electorales expresan una frustración cada vez mayor ante esa realidad.

Los resultados también se han visto impulsados por la creciente ofensiva contra las comunidades inmigrantes. Texas ocupa un lugar central en el aparato de deportación del país. Encabeza la lista de estados por detenciones efectuadas por el Servicio de Control de Inmigración y Aduanas de Estados Unidos (United States Immigration and Customs Enforcement, ICE): una de cada cuatro, es decir, el 25 %, ocurre en Texas (el estado que le sigue es Florida, con alrededor del 11 %). En particular, el condado de Harris y el área metropolitana de Houston encabezan las estadísticas nacionales tanto de arrestos como de personas actualmente detenidas por ICE. Y pese a que el gobierno insiste en que ICE persigue a “delincuentes”, una proporción cada vez mayor de las personas detenidas y deportadas no tiene antecedentes penales.

Las redadas de ICE en Texas han afectado a muchas más personas que a las familias de quienes han sido detenidos – generan un clima de miedo que se extiende por todas nuestras comunidades. El asesinato de Ruben Ray Martinez, de 23 años, a manos de ICE en South Padre Island en marzo de 2025, el asesinato de Lorenzo Salgado Araujo en Houston en julio de 2026 y los disparos de ICE contra Wilber Rafael Garces Perez en Austin en octubre de 2026 han provocado indignación y movilizaciones tanto en comunidades inmigrantes como entre quienes no lo son.

El gobierno de Trump ha intentado utilizar la aplicación de las leyes migratorias para dividir a la clase trabajadora, culpando a los inmigrantes de la inseguridad económica mientras las corporaciones y los multimillonarios, que son quienes realmente se benefician de la explotación y el aumento de los costos, siguen acumulando riqueza. Pero la creciente oposición a ICE demuestra los límites de esa estrategia. Cada vez más personas reconocen que el problema no son los inmigrantes, sino el propio aparato político que intenta culparlos mientras no garantiza nuestras necesidades humanas más básicas.

El poder de la movilización de masas

Quizás uno de los aspectos más extraordinarios de estas elecciones fue el nivel de participación electoral. Más de 7,7 millones de personas votaron de manera anticipada en Texas, superando el récord anterior de unas elecciones de mitad de mandato, establecido en 2018. Más del 40 % del electorado registrado emitió su voto antes del día de las elecciones. Fue particularmente significativo el aumento de la participación de votantes negros y latinos. El voto anticipado se disparó en los condados de Hidalgo y Cameron, de población mayoritariamente latina, mientras que la participación de la población negra aumentó considerablemente, sobre todo en el área de Houston.

Esta movilización es especialmente importante si se tiene en cuenta la larga historia de supresión del voto en el estado y de los intentos por socavar el poder político de las comunidades racializadas. También ocurre en medio de agresivos esfuerzos republicanos por rediseñar los distritos electorales para concentrar el poder político y debilitar la influencia electoral de comunidades que históricamente han cuestionado el orden establecido.

La población negra ha desempeñado un papel central y decisivo como fuerza impulsora del cambio político en este país. Desde la Reconstrucción hasta la revolución por los derechos civiles, la movilización política negra ha obligado al establishment a ceder ante demandas que, de otro modo, habría ignorado. El aumento de la participación que vimos en Texas debe entenderse dentro de ese contexto histórico – como una negativa a aceptar que el rumbo político del estado está predeterminado y que las comunidades de la clase trabajadora carecen de poder real para cambiarlo.

Texas no es una excepción

La importancia de estos resultados va mucho más allá de Texas. Los demócratas lograron avances considerables en todo el sur del país y en otros bastiones tradicionalmente republicanos, incluidas victorias históricas en Georgia, Iowa, Ohio y Carolina del Sur.

En conjunto, estos resultados demuestran que el panorama político del país no es inmutable. Los estados que se han descartado por considerarlos permanentemente conservadores pueden, en realidad, convertirse en centros de grandes transformaciones políticas. La idea de un “territorio de Trump” inmutable invisibiliza a los millones de personas que viven en esos lugares y enfrentan las mismas condiciones económicas y políticas que la clase trabajadora en cualquier otra parte.

Texas siempre ha tenido una rica historia de lucha obrera, organización sindical y resistencia antirracista. La noción de que el estado es intrínsecamente conservador ha servido muchas veces para desalentar a quienes imaginan un futuro político distinto. Estas elecciones cuestionan esa suposición. Pero debemos tener cuidado de no confundir el rechazo al dominio republicano con un respaldo automático a toda la agenda del Partido Demócrata. Esa distinción es fundamental para comprender lo que viene.

Es hora de exigirles cuentas a los demócratas

Sin duda, el Partido Demócrata presentará estos resultados como prueba de que su estrategia electoral está funcionando. Pero ¿qué sucede ahora que los votantes han regresado a sus casas?

La historia nos da motivos de sobra para desconfiar de la “ola azul”. Una y otra vez, los demócratas han hecho campaña contra políticas republicanas profundamente impopulares y movilizado a la población con promesas de cambio, para luego volver a la política de siempre una vez que llegan al poder. Han absorbido la energía de los movimientos de masas, la han canalizado hacia campañas electorales y, al final, no han concretado los cambios fundamentales que la gente exigía.

Tomemos como ejemplo la política de control migratorio, que ha sido desarrollada y ampliada de manera continua por ambos partidos. Talarico ha comparado a ICE con una “policía secreta”, reflejando la profunda indignación que han generado sus operaciones cada vez más violentas. Sin embargo, no ha llegado a respaldar la abolición de la agencia – que es lo que realmente exige la mayoría de la población. Si ICE funciona como una fuerza represiva, ¿por qué debería el movimiento conformarse con reformas que mantienen intacta la institución y simplemente cambian el partido encargado de administrarla?

Lo mismo ocurre con el panorama político más amplio de Texas. Una victoria demócrata en la gobernación no revoca automáticamente las leyes y políticas aplicadas durante años de dominio republicano. Muchas están incorporadas en la legislación estatal y exigen un enfrentamiento directo con la estructura legislativa controlada por los republicanos que las creó y las ha mantenido. ¿Podemos confiar en que Hinojosa hará eso por su cuenta, sin la presión de las masas desde abajo?

Consideremos apenas algunos ejemplos:

Proyecto de Ley 4 del Senado de Texas (Texas Senate Bill 4): Aprobado en 2017, prohíbe a los gobiernos locales adoptar políticas que limiten su cooperación con las autoridades federales de control migratorio y exige que cumplan determinadas solicitudes de retención emitidas por ICE. Ha contribuido a institucionalizar la colaboración entre las fuerzas del orden locales y el aparato de deportación.

Proyecto de Ley 2127 de la Cámara de Representantes (House Bill 2127): Conocido comúnmente como la ley de la “Estrella de la Muerte” (Death Star), fue aprobado en 2023 y restringe severamente la capacidad de los gobiernos locales para establecer regulaciones en materia laboral, empresarial y de propiedad. Se diseñó, en gran medida, para socavar las protecciones locales que van más allá de lo autorizado por la legislatura estatal.

Proyecto de Ley 23 del Senado (Senate Bill 23): Aprobado en 2025, restringe aún más la capacidad de los gobiernos locales para reducir los fondos destinados a la policía, al exigir la aprobación del electorado para determinados recortes.

Si los demócratas realmente quieren representar a quienes se movilizaron para derrotar al aparato político republicano, deben responder por la derogación de estas medidas, el fin de la colaboración con ICE impuesta por el estado, la restitución de las facultades democráticas de los gobiernos locales, la protección de los derechos laborales, la ampliación de los derechos reproductivos y la asignación de recursos públicos a la vivienda, la atención médica, la educación y otros servicios esenciales.

Debemos construir un movimiento que vaya más allá de las urnas

Las victorias demócratas en Texas son importantes, pero no deben confundirse con una solución a los problemas que llevaron a millones de personas a votar. El Partido Demócrata tiene una larga trayectoria de hacer campaña contra los ataques republicanos, movilizar a las comunidades trabajadoras y prometer cambios, para luego retroceder cuando llega al poder y preservar los mismos sistemas que produjeron la crisis desde un principio.

La cuestión es si permitimos que nuestra energía se disipe después del día de las elecciones o si la utilizamos como base para construir un movimiento sostenido capaz de conquistar cambios materiales reales. Nada de esto sucederá simplemente porque los demócratas ganaron unas elecciones – la historia demuestra todo lo contrario. Harán falta organización y presión desde abajo: de trabajadores y trabajadoras, estudiantes, inmigrantes, comunidades negras, mujeres, personas LGBTQ y todas aquellas personas cuyos intereses chocan tan claramente con los de la clase multimillonaria y la élite política a su servicio.

Las elecciones en Texas han demostrado que millones de personas están dispuestas a movilizarse contra el orden establecido. La tarea ahora es construir algo que permita llevar esa lucha adelante, mucho más allá de las urnas – un movimiento independiente, multirracial y de la clase trabajadora que no limite su horizonte político a los demócratas o los republicanos.

El aparato político republicano ha sufrido un golpe histórico en Texas. Lo que ocurra después dependerá de que quienes hicieron posible esa derrota mantengan la presión.

items.title: University of Sheffield International College staff set to strike over falling wages and threatened job losses
items.summary: The long-running fight at the college demands that workers form a rank-and-file committee independent of the University and College Union.

scraped.title: University of Sheffield International College staff set to strike over falling wages and threatened job losses
scraped.description: The long-running fight at the college demands that workers form a rank-and-file committee independent of the University and College Union.
scraped.h1: Read more
scraped.body_text:
Teaching, administration and student support staff at the University of Sheffield International College (USIC) are to strike for five days from Tuesday, on November 10, 13, 16, 18 and 23.

USIC is run for profit by Study Group from a University of Sheffield building utilising the university’s branding. It prepares international students for master’s and bachelor’s degrees at the university, with courses costing up to £26,000 a year.

USIC’s University and College Union (UCU) branch voted overwhelmingly in mid-October to strike over management’s refusal to offer any pay rise since September 2023.

Under the Retail Prices Index measure, prices, including mortgage interest costs and structural housing expenses, have risen by 11.5 percent since September 2023. A static £35,000 salary is effectively worth just £31,376 today, and a worker would require £39,042 to match their 2023 standard of living.

In late October, Study Group issued 14 “At risk of Redundancy” notices to USIC staff—six student experience staff, six curriculum leaders and two heads of subject. In response the UCU branch entered a formal dispute over the planned redundancies. Study Group’s highest-paid directors receive up to £350,000 each in salary, bonuses and benefits, roughly the salaries of 10 to 14 full-time lecturers. Chief executive Ian Crichton took home more than £600,000 in 2024, including a bonus of over £195,000.

To cut costs further, Study Group intends to scrap its teaching hours workload agreement with staff. This aims to expand workloads without extra pay.

Study Group has never agreed to USIC workers’ repeated demands to include assessment and grading in their workload model. For part-time lecturers a more exploitative model exists, as management treats grading as unpaid work that staff must complete to fulfil their contracts or risk losing further opportunities. It has emerged that Study Group is attempting to pay new part-time staff an hourly rate beneath that paid to existing staff.

Study Group changed hands again in May, when Arete Education bought it. The previous owners, Bain Capital Credit and Intermediate Capital Group, had only taken control in 2025, buying the company from the private equity firm Ardian after a financial restructuring in which Study Group secured tens of millions of pounds in funding from them.

In its most recent accounts, from late 2025, Study Group UK Limited reported an operating profit of approximately £25 million–£30 million. The global parent company, SG Global Topco Limited, reported losses, mainly due to debt servicing.

These are not operational losses. It is the interest on this debt, run up under successive private equity owners, that produces the “short-term financial gaps” cited by Study Group management as the reason for austerity at USIC. Cuts to workers’ wages and jobs help pay the interest on the debt incurred to buy the business.

Arete is backed by Global University Systems, owner of multiple private higher education institutions, and Brightstar Capital Partners (BCP), a private equity firm. The two jointly own Arden University, after BCP bought a 50 percent stake in July 2025.

According to Companies House, Arden University Ltd recorded pre-tax profits of £87 million for the year ending May 2025.

The involvement of private equity in the form of BCP presages a huge shift in how Study Group operates, with enormous implications for workers’ pay and livelihoods. Arete says it is investing in AI-focused technology through Arden, and Study Group says the deal will bring “AI-enabled solutions and digital innovation.” This only points to a move away from physical colleges like USIC and towards online courses, educational technology and the widespread use of artificial intelligence.

BCP demands business costs be nailed to the floor. Resisting wage demands at USIC is integral to a strategy of standardising wages downwards across all the Study Group pathway centres. USIC salaries and hourly rates could be reduced to the lower rates advertised at other Study Group centres like Leeds, where the hourly rate is a measly £33.57 at most. This rate includes one hour of preparation for every hour of teaching, and the intensive grading and writing of comments on essays, exams, presentations and other assessments, which pushes the effective hourly rate towards the poverty-level minimum wage.

To combat BCP’s private equity playbook of wage and job cuts, the UCU offers only its now familiar intermittent one-day strikes, which add up in their entirety to a single working week. Such token action allows management to absorb the disruption, wait out the strike and return to its original position. This is what Study Group has done repeatedly since the first strike at USIC in 2022.

The UCU has a record at USIC of repeatedly suspending strikes on the flimsiest pretext, retreating from one negotiating position after another, leading to the imposition of pay cuts in 2022 and again in 2024. In 2025, a strike over compulsory redundancies was suspended after management merely swapped the threat for low-value voluntary severances and ill-fitting redeployments within Study Group.

The UCU is once again isolating the struggle in Sheffield from those across further and higher education, where college and university managements are cutting pay and destroying jobs by the hundreds and even thousands to meet the demands of the education “market.” UCU branches at more than a dozen universities, including Nottingham, Goldsmiths, Edinburgh, Glasgow Caledonian, Sussex and Exeter, are striking, balloting or in dispute over job cuts this term. An estimated 30,000 university jobs have gone nationally in the last three years.

Last month, the union ended its years-long dispute at the University of Sheffield, calling off 17 days of strikes due to begin on October 27 after members accepted a management offer. Sheffield UCU’s statement revealed that the agreement had not ended the threat of job losses: “We will continue to consult with members and offer spaces for discussion about how to continue to protect colleagues at risk of compulsory redundancy, as well as to fight the ongoing expansion of staff workload.”

The UCU bureaucracy has become the conduit through which job and pay cuts are imposed, legitimising the marketisation of higher education by ensuring educators and support staff do nothing that disturbs corporate-union relations.

Announcing on November 5 the USIC strikes, UCU leader Jo Grady said, “Strike action is a last resort for our members.” Grady does not call for a fight against all job losses. She asks only that management “remove the threat of compulsory redundancies and resolve the dispute, or face weeks of disruption.” Such rhetoric is the language of class compromise and abject surrender. Lifting that threat would allow management and union to sit down together to slash jobs behind the fig leaf of “voluntary” redundancies as happened at USIC in 2025.

USIC workers should take stock of where four years of struggle under the UCU’s leadership have left them. The value of salaries has fallen sharply while workloads have grown.

Educators and support workers must organise their own rank-and-file committee, democratically accountable to the membership, to take forward their fight. This will enable them to draw up their own demands not what is claimed “affordable” by Study Group’s billionaire private equity investors. No pay award should be subsidised by job cuts; these must be withdrawn. There must be full restoration of the wages lost over the past three years, for a demand of at least 12 percent.

There must be full oversight of negotiations, with no veto on strike action by UCU officials before the membership votes and decides it meets their demands. The schedule of strike action must be determined by those conducting the fight, who must reach out to co-workers across Study Group to build solidarity action and begin a counteroffensive against restructuring beyond one campus.

Study Group operates in more than 30 countries. Its workforce was slashed from 2,027 employees in 2022 to 1,704 in 2023, a reduction of 323 (16 percent) in just one year. Most strikingly, the number of teaching staff fell from 1,035 to 665, a reduction of 370 (36 percent). The fight against this profit-making company, which operates under the umbrella of the University of Sheffield, must therefore be extended into a broader struggle against the marketisation and privatisation of higher education.

This means challenging not simply individual attacks on pay and conditions, but the business model that places the reduction of labour costs and the extraction of profits ahead of the interests of educational staff and students.

scraped.title: Two syndicalists gut the 1926 General Strike of its political lessons—Part Three
scraped.description: Airy optimism about “the next surge” is cover for an anti-Marxist perspective, in this case syndicalism, foreclosing a principled and scientific answer to the strategic questions confronting the working class.
scraped.h1: Read more
scraped.body_text:
[ Part One ] [ Part Two ] [ Part Three ]

This is the third and concluding part of a series.

Today, the authors write that they “have not found a united and experienced vanguard. We’ve found small sparks, sometimes coordinated, often flaring out in isolation.” [ 1 ] What are the reasons for this situation and what must be done to change it? Readers will search in vain for an answer. Cant and Lee reply with loose gestures towards the future devoid of any political content.

They argue at one point: “if you keep going, the momentum swings. The mass of the class joins the vanguard and things start to move. You can never tell when that’s going to happen: it’s just a case of staying in the game and preparing for the next surge.” [ 2 ] Similarly, in the concluding paragraphs, “The one absolute lesson we take from 1926 is that as this vanguard begins to recompose itself, it should be aware that nothing in history is inevitable, neither victory nor defeat… We all make the world every day.” [ 3 ]

As always in politics, airy optimism about “the next surge” is cover for an anti-Marxist perspective, in this case syndicalism, foreclosing a principled and scientific answer to the strategic questions confronting the working class.

The Trotskyist movement represents nearly a century of struggle to answer those questions: to derive, defend and develop the ideas necessary to do precisely what Cant and Lee write must be done: “turn isolated workers into a united class force”. Without assimilating that history, itself based on all the preceding conquests of the socialist movement, a conscious proletarian vanguard cannot take shape.

Putting these lessons into practice is the essential task of the revolutionary party. But Cant and Lee view these fundamental Marxist conceptions as elitist. They refer disparagingly in their book to ideas “dreamt up by intellectuals external to the working class and preached to the workers as a master plan” or to “a distant leadership… entrusted with directing affairs”. [ 4 ] For them, what defines the vanguard “is the combination of organic leadership, workplace militancy, and articulation of the most advanced form of mass politics then available. They are the militant minority who turn single sparks into prairie fires. When the vanguard is advancing, even revolutionary parties have to run to keep up.” [ 5 ]

These are not new arguments. Their defeat was essential in the building of the Bolshevik Party which carried out the Russian Revolution of 1917 under Lenin and Trotsky’s leadership. Cant and Lee replicate almost word for word the arguments of the “Economists” and their defenders in Russia in the 1890s and early 1900s—a tendency Lenin labeled “tail-ism”.

The Economists wrote: “Just as human beings will reproduce in the old-fashioned way despite all the discoveries of natural science, so the birth of a new social order will come about, in the future too, mainly as a result of elemental outbursts, despite all the discoveries of social science and the increase in the number of conscious fighters”. They accused the group around Lenin of “having the incredible effrontery to impose upon the Party organisation solutions of tactical questions proposed by a group of emigrant writers more than fifteen years ago”.

Lenin answered in What is to be Done? :

Effrontery, indeed, and what an overestimation of the conscious element—first to resolve questions theoretically beforehand, and then to try to convince the organisation, the Party, and the masses of the correctness of this solution! How much better it would be to repeat the elements and, without “imposing” anything upon anybody, swing with every “turn”...

Rabocheye Dyelo [an Economist newspaper], however, not only follows this “tactics-as-process”, but elevates it to a principle, so that it would be more correct to describe its tendency not as opportunism, but as tail-ism (from the word tail). [ 6 ]

In another passage which reads as direct riposte to Cant and Lee, Lenin turns a phrase from his opponents against them, writing that revolutionaries “must and will make it our business to engage in this kind of ‘pushing on’ a hundred times more forcibly than we have done hitherto.” He adds that the “hideous phrase… cannot but rouse in the workers (at least in the workers who are as unenlightened as you yourselves) a sense of distrust towards all who bring them political knowledge and revolutionary experience from outside”. [ 7 ]

Leon Trotsky (1879-1940), was the co-leader of the 1917 Russian Revolution, socialist opponent of Joseph Stalin, founder of the Fourth International, and strategist of world socialist revolution.

Lenin was always among the first to recognise the initiative and innovations of the class, like the soviets in 1905. But he also understood that these depended in large measure on the prior work of organised Marxists, and that they were not sufficient to bring the class struggle to the point of the seizure of power and establishment of a workers’ state. The Russian working class overthrew Tsarism in February 1917, but it took the Bolshevik Party, guided by Lenin’s April Theses and Trotsky’s Theory of Permanent Revolution, to defeat the capitalist state, and fascistic counterrevolution.

A Bolshevik-type party is needed, Lenin first explained in theory then proved in practice. Firstly, to resist and overcome the influence of bourgeois ideology, which finds organised expression in the trade union bureaucracy; Cant and Lee write that “the labour aristocracy is highly organised” but draw no conclusions about the necessity of the vanguard to therefore be better organised. Secondly, to give the working class an all-sided, farsighted appreciation of its social position and political tasks.

This was the basis of the revolutionary party advocated by the first four congresses of the Third International, defended by Trotsky and the Left Opposition, and later the Fourth International. It was vindicated in the negative by the British General Strike.

The Future in Our Past , on the other hand, ties itself up in knots trying to reconcile its perspective with the experience of 1926. Cant and Lee note that, in the lead up to the General Strike, “Rather than providing independent leadership to the rest of the class, the vanguard watched and waited.” [ 8 ] As we have already seen, they point to the Communist Party as the force which could and should have rectified this situation. But their criticism that the CP “assumed councils of action would emerge as new centres of leadership” could just as well be turned back on the authors, who suggest no other course of action. [ 9 ]

Where this approach to politics ends up is made clear a few pages later, when readers are told of the Communist Party’s actions that “The most exasperating part of this failure is that it was foreseen in advance.” [ 10 ] They are then directed not to Trotsky, to whose analysis Cant and Lee are indebted for much that is correct in their book, but to J.T. Murphy—one of the CPGB’s leaders arrested in 1925 for seditious libel and incitement to mutiny.

The Future in Our Past cites Murphy’s 1922 comment on “Black Friday”, when the leaders of transport and rail unions broke their Triple Alliance with the miners by refusing to strike in solidarity:

We warned the masses to “Watch their Leaders.” We fostered the idea that the Triple Alliance would fail. But when it did fail the revolutionary movement was almost as demoralised as the union movement in general. We had not, to any great extent, considered or advised the masses what they could do in such an eventuality. Yet everything cried out for the preparation of a new centre of leadership in the organisations involved, to which the masses could gravitate as the leaders mined towards failure. [ 11 ]

Murphy in 1922 is selected over Trotsky in 1925, 1926, 1927 (and so on…) because he suits Cant and Lee’s political agenda: a leading member of the British Shop Stewards Movement, and later of the Red International of Labor Unions and the National Minority Movement, he serves as their model “organic” leader of the British vanguard. But an even halfway serious look at Murphy’s political biography demonstrates that militancy guarantees nothing, and “organic leadership” is a euphemism for leadership under the influence of the prevailing political pressures on the working class—in Murphy’s case, Stalinism.

A member of the CPGB until his resignation in 1932, he was described by Trotskyist leader James P. Cannon as “a wheel-horse of Stalin, not only in the British Party, but in the Comintern as well, and won many decorations for his part in the war against ‘Trotskyism’, loyally following the increasingly directly counterrevolutionary line of the Stalinist bureaucracy.” [ 12 ] He later supported the Hitler-Stalin pact and then spent part of the Second World War producing a friendly biography of the butcher of the October Revolution.

Murphy wrote the introduction to the 1925 book The Errors of Trotskyism , circulated in Britain to secure the allegiance of the CPGB to the Stalinist line. He concludes his miserable piece with the claim that: “The class political line of Comrade Trotsky, if applied by our Party as the leader of the proletariat of Britain, would mean and could mean nothing else but… the creation of dangerous illusions about their own strength amongst the proletariat.” [ 13 ] In this way, he played a critical role in destroying the revolutionary prospects in Britain. Whatever conclusions he drew from Black Friday were discarded.

The lesson here, contra Cant and Lee, is that we are not simply free to “make the world every day”. Questions of political orientation are objectively posed before the working class by the development of world capitalism and the class struggle. To name just a few of the most important today: the response to fascism, to imperialism, globalisation, the trade union bureaucracy, the national question and national separatism, and, still, to Stalinism. Failure to take a correct stand on these decisive world issues leads to catastrophe.

Only through the activity of a world revolutionary party can the working class find a correct orientation. This is especially the case in today’s highly complex globalised world, in the aftermath of the enormous and poorly understood struggles of the 21st century.

A socialist internationalist party must unify a working class numbering in the billions, carrying out every conceivable form of labour under virtually all conceivable conditions. It must win them to a programme of struggle against war; climate catastrophe; global unemployment, poverty and homelessness—and the profit and nation state system of capitalism which underlies them all. To do so it must overcome the influence of reformist and pseudo-socialist tendencies and the trade union bureaucracies in the working class, in large part by clarifying the historical experiences of the 20th and first quarter of the 21st centuries.

Cant and Lee write of the contemporary GMB and Community unions who “refused to ballot their members for strike action” over the closure of Tata Steel plants in the UK, “preferring to trust in negotiations,” and of Unite which “retracted its strike notice under pressure from the company”. At a demonstration in town, “none of the participants… seemed really to believe they could force the hand of giant multinational Tata Steel by marching past the shopping centre.” They write of the GMB’s “sweetheart scab partnership agreements with Deliveroo and Uber”. [ 14 ]

But The Future in Our Past provides no answers to the questions posed by these experiences: how to wage a struggle against transnational corporations, or in conditions of highly precarious employment, and, in all circumstances, against the anti-working-class apparatus in the trade unions. Even these challenges cannot be answered at the shallow level they are raised by Cant and Lee, let alone the decisive questions of war, recession, fascism and climate catastrophe that urgently confront the working class—which do not enter into their book.

A reader has no inkling from The Future in Our Past , for example, that events in Britain in 1926 were part of a chain of political disasters authored by the increasingly Stalinised international communist movement—such as the bloody defeat of the Chinese revolution in 1927 and culminating in the coming to power of Hitler in 1933—which left the working class chained to a bourgeoisie sliding rapidly to catastrophe. The tendency to war between British and US imperialism foreseen by Trotsky in Where is Britain Going? ultimately took shape in the Allied-Axis conflict of the Second World War just 13 years later — thanks above all to the rise of German fascism enabled by the Stalinists.

The International Committee of the Fourth International, the contemporary Trotskyist movement, has now analysed the early stages of the development of a third world war, bound up with a sharp turn to dictatorial, far-right forms of rule. This is driven by deep economic and social contradictions and taking the form of war to remake the world as if the Russian Revolution and the subsequent wave of anti-imperialist struggles it unleashed had never taken place. At the Congress of the Socialist Equality Party (US) this August, Chairman of the World Socialist Web Site David North explained:

If the war is, in its essence, the continuation of the century-long struggle of imperialism against the socialist revolution, then the fight against the war is, and can only be, the resumption of that revolution. It cannot take the form of the defense of any national state, nor of the restoration of a “rules-based order” that was itself an instrument of the counterrevolutionary project, nor of the pressure politics of the pseudo-left. It requires the independent political mobilization of the working class internationally on a program of socialist revolution. [ 15 ]

From this analysis, North and the ICFI draw the strategic conclusion that rank-and-file committees must be built not in the abstract, syndicalist way advocated by Cant and Lee but according to a definite political programme: as “organs through which workers formulate their demands, coordinate their actions across workplaces, industries and national borders, and break through the isolation imposed upon every struggle by the official apparatus”. They must be “organizing centers of an anti-bureaucratic insurgency” and “anticipatory forms of genuine workers’ democracy and workers’ power”. [ 16 ]

The growth of working-class struggles provides the essential basis for this programme of action. But, as North explained: “The radicalization of the working class, proceeding on every continent, poses the question of leadership; and the question of leadership is resolved in only one way—through the construction of the revolutionary party within the struggles of the working class itself.” [ 17 ]

We say bluntly, as Leon Trotsky did of Britain in 1926, that in the struggles of the working class today “there is not a ghost of such a leadership, and it is not to be expected that it can be conjured up out of the ground.” [ 18 ] That is because the lessons of the General Strike and other similarly decisive strategic experiences of the 20th century have been largely quarantined from the working class by Stalinism, social democracy, Pabloism and the petty-bourgeois politics of the pseudo-left.

The Trotskyist movement, the Fourth International, was founded to resolve this crisis of working-class leadership. Helping a new generation of revolutionary leaders to draw the necessary conclusions from the 1926 British General Strike is vital to this work.

Concluded.

scraped.body_text:
[ Part One ] [ Part Two ] [ Part Three ] [ Part Four ] [ Part Five ] [ Part Six ] [ Part Seven ]

This is the seventh part of a 10-part series responding to British-based historian Hakim Adi’s recently republished book, Pan-Africanism and Communism: The Communist International, Africa, and the Diaspora, 1919–1939.

Adi’s defence of the Sixth Congress rests in part on what followed. Discussing the “Third Period,” he argues that the Comintern’s analysis “seemed to have been confirmed” by the Great Depression, the rise of fascism and preparations for another world war. He concludes that the Comintern had been “perhaps not so far off the mark.” [ 1 ]

Hitler’s rise exposed the Sixth Congress’s catastrophic consequences. Adi never examines Hitler’s accession. This cannot be dismissed as falling outside the scope of a study devoted to the Comintern, Africa and Pan-Africanism. Germany posed the decisive test of the “Third Period” policy adopted after the Sixth Congress, and the 1933 catastrophe directly prepared the next major turn in Comintern policy: the counterrevolutionary Popular Front strategy, which Adi again defends.

The European events of 1933–38 are not a detour from the colonial question. They were the means through which the colonial struggles were subordinated to the diplomatic interests of the Soviet bureaucracy.

Examining Germany requires confronting the political consequences of the Sixth Congress, which enshrined the theory of “social fascism.” The theory treated Social Democratic parties not simply as reformist organisations defending capitalism, but as a variant of fascism. Cooperation with it, even against the Nazis, amounted to political capitulation. In Germany, this meant rejecting a united front of Communist and Social Democratic workers against Hitler.

While denouncing the Social Democratic leadership’s betrayals, Trotsky recognised that millions of workers still followed its organisations. They could not be won to revolutionary politics through denunciations alone. The Communist Party had to fight for a united front against fascism without surrendering its political independence. As Trotsky wrote in December 1931:

No common platform with the Social Democracy, or with the leaders of the German trade unions, no common publications, banners, placards! March separately, but strike together! Agree only how to strike, whom to strike, and when to strike!” [ 2 ]

The united front was a means of mobilising the working class against Hitler while breaking the influence of Social Democracy over millions of workers. Trotsky insisted that Communists must demonstrate “by deeds a complete readiness to make a bloc with the Social Democrats against the fascists”, explaining that “we must understand how to tear the workers away from their leaders in reality”. The struggle for the united front would enable Social Democratic workers to test their own organisations and leaders in practice, while exposing the disastrous consequences of the Stalinist theory of “social fascism”, which obstructed the unity of the working class in the face of the Nazi threat. [ 3 ]

Trotsky had already warned in September 1930, in The Turn in the Communist International and the Situation in Germany , that the Stalinist theory of “social fascism”, which equated Social Democracy with fascism, had become a “positive menace”. By obstructing common action between Communist and Social Democratic workers, this policy threatened to divide the working class in the face of Hitler’s advancing movement. Far from conceding political ground to reformism, the struggle for the united front was essential to winning millions of Social Democratic workers away from their leadership and towards revolutionary Marxism.

Leon Trotsky (1879-1940), was the co-leader of the 1917 Russian Revolution, socialist opponent of Joseph Stalin, founder of the Fourth International, and strategist of world socialist revolution.

The Stalinist leadership of the Comintern rejected Trotsky’s course. Hitler’s appointment as Chancellor in January 1933 became the decisive practical test of the Third Period. The Nazi victory had many causes, including the betrayals of Social Democracy and the backing of Hitler by the German ruling class. But the Comintern’s refusal to fight for a united front divided the two great organised battalions of the German working class, at the very moment when their combined mobilisation was most urgently required.

Within months the Communist Party, the largest in the world outside the Soviet Union, was suppressed, the trade unions destroyed and tens of thousands of socialist and communist militants incarcerated. Yet the Stalinist Comintern leadership refused to allow any serious international discussion of how the German working class had been defeated.

For Trotsky, this was decisive. Until 1933 the Left Opposition had fought for the reform and regeneration of the Comintern. After Germany, Trotsky concluded that an organisation which had allowed Hitler to seize power without a fight, and which had responded to such a historic catastrophe without correcting its leadership or programme, could no longer be reformed. In July 1933 he called for the building of a new, Fourth International.

Adi discusses none of this. Presenting the rise of Nazism as retrospective confirmation that the Sixth Congress had been “not so far off the mark”, he presents the Comintern’s subsequent abandonment of the Third Period and its adoption of the Popular Front strategy as a necessary response to the fascist threat. The German catastrophe, which connected these two diametrically opposed policies, is deliberately ignored.

The Stalinist response to Hitler’s victory was another abrupt turn. The Soviet bureaucracy sought diplomatic alliances against Nazi Germany, particularly with France and Britain, and the Communist International abandoned the rhetoric of “class against class”. At the Seventh Congress in 1935, it embraced the Popular Front: political alliances with supposedly “democratic” sections of the bourgeoisie. In the colonies, this meant abandoning colonial struggles in the name of fighting fascism.

Adi presents the change in favourable terms. He writes:

The demand for a united front of workers, and other sections of the people, against the growing threat of fascism, and therefore in practice a greater unity between Communists and a wide range of individuals and organisations was particularly evident in the popular front movements of Spain and in France... [ 4 ]

He continues:

This ‘new tactical orientation’, and the need for the broadest unity against the danger of fascism and war, was the main theme of the deliberations and resolutions of the Comintern’s Seventh Congress in 1935. In practice this resulted not only in a much greater emphasis on the need for a united front against fascism, but also on an anti-imperialist front in the colonial countries that could draw ‘the widest masses’ into a struggle not just for workers’ rights but also ‘against imperialist exploitation, against cruel enslavement, for the driving out of the imperialists, for the independence of the country.’ [ 5 ]

Adi spells out approvingly the class implications of this change: “It meant that in all countries the Communists had to concern themselves not just with the interests of the working class but in addition with those of the whole people”. [ 6 ]

France demonstrated what the Popular Front meant. The Popular Front’s 1936 electoral victory—an alliance of the Communist Party (PCF) with Léon Blum’s Socialists and the bourgeois Radical Party—was accompanied by an immense strike wave and widespread factory occupations. But the PCF worked to contain this movement within the framework of the Popular Front. The same logic was applied to the French colonies, where the PCF would soon instruct the colonial peoples that their liberation had to be postponed because French imperialism was now “democratic”.

Spain provided an even more decisive test. Franco’s military uprising in July 1936 against the Stalinist-backed Popular Front government unleashed a revolutionary mobilisation of workers and peasants, including factory seizures, land occupations and the formation of armed militias. The Stalinists insisted the struggle remain confined to defending the bourgeois Republic and opposed measures that threatened capitalist property or the alliance with republican bourgeois forces.

In service to this policy, Stalinists led the subsequent bloody suppression of revolutionary forces, killing revolutionaries and repressing opposition to the Popular Front. Stalinism had moved beyond policies that merely disoriented revolutionary struggles. In Spain, it became an active force in defending bourgeois state authority against them, including the murder of revolutionaries.

Trotsky’s call for a new International after the German catastrophe culminated in September 1938 with the founding of the Fourth International, defending the revolutionary internationalist heritage of the early Comintern against both the nationalist programme of “socialism in one country” and the successive Stalinist policies that had produced the German catastrophe and the Popular Front betrayals.

Its founding programme, the Transitional Programme , defined the epoch’s central problem as the crisis of revolutionary leadership. Germany, France and Spain showed the consequences of the counter-revolutionary programme imposed upon the working class by Stalinism.

The Transitional Programme rejected the Stalinist division of the revolution into distinct historical stages, in which national independence and bourgeois democracy had first to be completed under bourgeois leadership before the working class could fight for socialism. Trotsky insisted that “the struggle for the most elementary achievements of national independence and bourgeois democracy is combined with the socialist struggle against world imperialism”, and that democratic demands and the tasks of socialist revolution “are not divided into separate historical epochs in this struggle, but stem directly from one another.” The overthrow of the “imperialist yoke” and the agrarian revolution remained central tasks, but “it is imperative that in the struggle the masses outgrow” the democratic programme. The working class had to “oppose” itself “to the ‘national’ bourgeoisie”, fight for the leadership of the peasantry and establish its own organs of power. As Trotsky concluded, “Only they [the soviets] are capable of bringing the democratic revolution to a conclusion and likewise opening an era of socialist revolution.” [ 7 ]

The colonial consequences of the Stalinist turn were not long in coming. They were exposed in Ethiopia, where the Italian fascist invasion of 1935 — the event Adi cites as retrospective “confirmation” of the Third Period — radicalised a generation of African and Caribbean militants and revealed the full meaning of the Popular Front’s “anti-fascism” for the colonial world.

To be continued.

Op cit., p 57.

Leon Trotsky, “For a Workers’ United Front Against Fascism”, 8 December 1931. Available at: https://www.marxists.org/archive/trotsky/germany/1931/311208.htm

scraped.title: Upcoming Native Bidaské: Dean Dauphinais on Advocating for Native Veterans
scraped.description: On Veterans Day, Dean Dauphinais of the National American Indian Veterans joins Native Bidaské to discuss Native veteran advocacy, mental health and support for Native warriors.
scraped.author: Kristen Lilya
scraped.h1: Upcoming Native Bidaské: Dean Dauphinais on Advocating for Native Veterans
scraped.body_text:
Native News Online

This Veterans Day, November 11th, Native Bidaské host Levi Rickert sits down with Dean Dauphinais, the executive director of the National American Indian Veterans (NAIV) , for a conversation about the challenges facing Native veterans and the work being done to advocate for them.

The episode will examine how NAIV uses its status as a congressionally chartered Native American veterans service organization to advocate directly to Congress for legislation, funding and programs that address the needs of Native veterans.

Your contribution is appreciated.

Although Native Americans serve in the military at higher per capita rates than any other racial or ethnic group, Native veterans continue to face significant disparities, including disproportionately high rates of homelessness and suicide. Dauphinais will discuss how NAIV is working to address those challenges and strengthen the resources available to Native veterans.

A recent development came during the National Congress of American Indians (NCAI) gathering in Palm Springs, California, where NAIV successfully advanced three resolutions. The resolutions primarily focused on reinstating the Secretary of Veterans Affairs Tribal Advisory Committee, which would provide a direct channel for Native veteran advocates to communicate with VA leadership.

The discussion will also address NAIV’s efforts to expand its membership and regional leadership network. Dauphinais says building a stronger national presence is essential to increasing the organization’s ability to advocate effectively on behalf of Native veterans. Individual annual memberships are $25. Veterans interested in joining or learning more about the organization’s work can visit naivets.org .

The episode will also recognize the 251st birthday of the United States Marine Corps, observed Nov. 10, and reflect on the service and sacrifices of Native Americans in the armed forces. As Veterans Day provides an opportunity to recognize those who have served, Dauphinais has a message for fellow Native warriors: stay in the fight, lean on your battle buddies and never be too proud to ask for help.

Watch Native Bidaské on Wednesday, November 11th, at 12 p.m. ET on Facebook , YouTube , NativeNewsOnline.net , and TikTok .
