scraped.title: When Insurers Pulled Back 40 Years Ago, Tribes Built Their Own Solution
scraped.description: Forty years after Tribal leaders created AMERIND to address an insurance gap in Indian Country, the Tribally owned insurer continues to help Tribal governments protect homes, businesses, and community assets.
scraped.author: Kristen Lilya
scraped.h1: When Insurers Pulled Back 40 Years Ago, Tribes Built Their Own Solution
scraped.body_text:
Native News Online

Forty years ago, Tribal leaders faced a growing challenge. Traditional insurance carriers were pulling away from Indian housing programs, leaving Tribal nations with no affordable options to protect their homes and community assets.

Rather than wait for outside solutions, Tribal leaders built one themselves.

That decision led to the founding of AMERIND in 1986, the nation’s first and only 100% Tribally owned insurance carrier, which marks its 40th anniversary this year.

Four decades later, AMERIND continues to provide insurance, risk management, and educational resources designed specifically for Tribal governments, enterprises, and communities. Employees often describe that mission with a simple phrase: “Tribes Protecting Tribes.”

A Solution Born From Crisis

Tribal leaders founded AMERIND in 1986 after recognizing the need for insurance solutions tailored to Indian Country. At the time, Tribal housing struggled to secure affordable coverage.

“AMERIND was created to provide insurance protection for Tribal nations,” one employee said. “We want to provide sustainable and affordable insurance coverage.”

Unlike commercial insurers, Tribal leaders created AMERIND to provide affordable, sustainable insurance products and services for Indian Country.

As a Tribally owned insurance carrier, AMERIND says it helps keep insurance dollars circulating within Indian Country while providing coverage tailored specifically to Tribal communities.

That need remains as important today as it was 40 years ago.

Your contribution is appreciated.

As construction costs and disaster recovery expenses continue to rise, employees say affordable insurance plays a critical role in helping Tribal governments and families recover from unexpected losses.

Built for Indian Country

AMERIND’s ownership structure remains one of its defining characteristics. As the nation’s first and only 100% Tribally owned insurance carrier, the organization says it designs its products and services around the operational, governmental, and housing realities of Tribal nations.

Beyond insurance coverage, the organization emphasizes risk management and loss prevention to help Tribal governments and enterprises reduce risk before disasters occur and recover faster when they do.

Through its Protecting Tribal Families Fund, AMERIND also partners with organizations including the NNAHRA Foundation and the National American Indian Housing Council to support Native families and communities.

Expanding to Meet Tribal Needs

What began as an insurance solution for Tribal housing has expanded over four decades into broader coverage for Tribal governments, enterprises and communities.

Today, AMERIND provides property, general liability, and risk management solutions tailored specifically for Tribal governments and enterprises.

The organization says its programs recognize Tribal government and business structures while helping keep insurance dollars circulating within Indian Country.

Today, AMERIND serves more than 400 tribes, Tribal housing authorities, and Tribal designated housing entities through its Indian Housing Block Grant program.

Its services now extend beyond insurance to include loss prevention, risk management, and educational resources designed to help Tribal communities prepare for future challenges.

As its offerings have expanded to include Tribal Workers’ Compensation and specialized coverage for Tribal enterprises, the organization says its focus has remained the same: providing insurance and risk management solutions designed specifically for Indian Country.

Beyond Insurance

Insurance remains AMERIND’s core business, but the organization has expanded its focus to include risk management and prevention education for Tribal governments and enterprises.

Recently, AMERIND hosted a webinar highlighting federal grant opportunities available to tribes and Tribal organizations navigating changes in the federal funding landscape. Monica Braine, a project specialist at AMERIND, said a review of Grants.gov identified funding opportunities that remain available despite reductions in some federal programs.

The webinar reflects the organization’s broader approach of pairing insurance products with education and risk management resources.

Beyond webinars, AMERIND offers safety training, educational programming, and community outreach to help Tribal organizations strengthen long-term resilience.

Measuring Success

Employees say the organization measures its impact not by the policies it issues, but by how quickly families and Tribal communities recover after a disaster strikes.

“I think some of the impact that I’ve seen over the years is seeing the tragedies that have taken place and being able to see a family build their home back into a home just by having insurance,” one employee said.

Looking Forward

“I hope that our tribes see us as trusted partners and that we continue to be here as long as tribes need us,” one employee said.

Forty years after Tribal leaders created AMERIND in response to an insurance crisis, the organization says its mission remains unchanged: providing insurance and risk management solutions designed specifically for Indian Country. Looking ahead, AMERIND aims to continue serving as a Tribally owned partner focused on helping Tribal nations protect their people, property, and economic futures.

scraped.title: Deb Haaland's Mother's Love, Her Daughter's Tribute, and a Historic Victory
scraped.description: Overview: Deb Haaland’s historic election as governor and her child Somáh’s personal stories reveal the values behind her public service. Opinion Just moments after Deb Haaland’s name flashed across the television screens on Election Night, declaring her as the projected winner of New Mexico’s gubernatorial race, the standing-room-only crowd gathered in the ballroom of Route […]
scraped.author: Levi Rickert
scraped.h1: Deb Haaland’s Mother’s Love, Her Daughter’s Tribute, and a Historic Victory
scraped.body_text:
Native News Online

Deb Haaland’s historic election as governor and her child Somáh’s personal stories reveal the values behind her public service.

Just moments after Deb Haaland’s name flashed across the television screens on Election Night, declaring her as the projected winner of New Mexico’s gubernatorial race, the standing-room-only crowd gathered in the ballroom of Route 66 Casino Hotel erupted in cheers.

Moments later, the governor-elect entered the room, accompanied by family, friends, and campaign staff. The roar grew louder as supporters caught sight of the first Native American woman ever elected governor of a state making her way toward the stage. It was a moment filled with joy, pride, and the unmistakable weight of history.

There could hardly have been a more fitting place for such a historic celebration. Located on Laguna Pueblo about 20 miles west of downtown Albuquerque, the casino sits near the community where the governor-elect spent time as a young girl staying with her maternal grandparents. The land and its people were an important part of her childhood.

The diverse crowd brought together New Mexico’s political leadership and everyday supporters, all united in celebrating Haaland’s victory and the historic significance of her achievement.

The governor-elect’s only child, her daughter Somáh Haaland, introduced her to the jubilant crowd.

Your contribution is appreciated.

Somáh’s introduction, delivered on Nov. 3 during National Native American Heritage Month, offered more than a glimpse into her relationship with her now-famous mother. It also provided a deeply personal window into their lives and the experiences, challenges, and pride that shape what it means to be Native American in modern society.

“To anyone who ever referred to my mom as Auntie Deb, that makes me your cousin,” Somáh said. “Whether you are here in the room with us or listening from elsewhere, I would like to extend my deepest gratitude for your presence and for going on this journey with me and my family.”

Somáh described growing up with a single mother, who supplemented their bare-bones family budget with food stamps.

“A sitter was never in our budget, so she took me everywhere with her from the time I was a baby. I would ride shotgun in our red GMC van while we made salsa deliveries, or wait in the UNM Law School library for hours while she was in class,” Somáh said. “And whenever, whenever we came to a community gathering, my mom was always the first person there, and she wouldn’t even think of leaving until the floor was swept and the last dish was done. My mom taught me to make sacrifices without complaining.”

Somáh recounted a Christmas season when she was 16 years old, when there was little money for gifts or to repair the family car, which had broken down. Undeterred, her mom stayed up baking dozens of biscochitos, New Mexico’s traditional cookies, and then placed them in takeout containers. To deliver the homemade cookies, they borrowed a friend’s car. It was a true “Indian car” that would not go into reverse. On a couple of occasions, they had to ask for help backing it up so they could make their next delivery.

“We know that no one person has everything: knowledge, wealth, a car that goes in reverse or goes at all. But it is moments like this that taught me how things are meant to work by thinking of each other, showing up with love, and not being afraid to ask for help when we need it,” Somáh said. “What I remember most from that Christmas is the laughter, the snow, and the smell of biscochitos in the oven, and my mom’s commitment to making people feel loved.”

Somáh spoke about her mother’s love for the people of New Mexico.

“She has always shown me, through her actions, that love is the one plentiful resource that we are able to tap into under these conditions that have caused so many families like ours to struggle,” Somáh said.

“Because love heals, and although our circumstances have changed, her love for this beautiful state and its people has never wavered. From my perspective, some of her biggest accomplishments are not the elections she has won, but the joy and hope that she has instilled in others during the darkest of times,” she said.

Haaland was one of the first two Native American women elected to Congress and the first Native American to serve as a Cabinet secretary. Now, she is the first Native American woman elected governor of a U.S. state.

Somáh’s introduction, though, offered a way to understand Haaland beyond all of her historic firsts: through the work of raising a child, paying the bills and showing up for other people.

During Native American Heritage Month, Haaland’s election gives us reason for pride. Somáh’s stories give us something more to celebrate: the values we should expect from the people we elect to serve us.

Thayék gde nwéndëmen – we are all related.

Levi “Calm Before the Storm” Rickert (Prairie Band Potawatomi Nation) is the founder, publisher, and editor of Native News Online. Rickert was awarded the Best Column Award in the print/online category... More by Levi Rickert

scraped.title: Chiefs question motive behind Indian Act talks after meeting with Carney, premiers
scraped.description: First Nations chiefs say their meeting with the prime minister and premiers was overshadowed by talk of abolishing the Indian Act.
scraped.author: The Canadian Press
scraped.h1: Chiefs question motive behind Indian Act talks after meeting with Carney, premiers
scraped.body_text:
APTN News

Stories about First Nations, Métis and Inuit peoples

APTN News

Inside the room at the First Nations-First Ministers Meeting in Ottawa on Oct. 26. Photo: APTN.

First Nations chiefs who attended a closed-door meeting with Prime Minister Mark Carney and premiers last month say their concerns were overshadowed by Manitoba Premier Wab Kinew’s call for the abolition of the Indian Act.

One chief also criticized Carney’s tone as he responded to a comment about how the United States works with Indigenous people.

“We have to ask ourselves if this was a co-ordinated effort between Wab Kinew and the prime minister,” Treaty 8 First Nations Grand Chief Mercredi said of the talk about abolishing the Indian Act.

Chief Sheila North of Bunibonibee Cree Nation in northern Manitoba said it’s beginning to appear that way to her.

“I hope that wasn’t the case because that would mean they were disingenuous in what they wanted the outcomes [of the meeting] to be,” North said. “It was a complete waste of time if that’s the only outcome that they were hoping for.”

Chiefs gathered with Carney and most premiers in Ottawa in late October for their first meeting since the 2005 Kelowna Accord talks. First Nations leaders prepared for the meeting for months and even enlisted the help of former Indigenous Services deputy minister Gina Wilson to tailor their messages to government.

Chiefs said they wanted to use the gathering to discuss the federal government’s controversial major projects legislation, health services, policing and public safety and the Natural Resources Transfer Acts.

Those resource agreements were negotiated with the Prairie Provinces at a time when First Nations were barred by the Indian Act from hiring their own lawyers. Chiefs have said those agreements should be abolished or changed to ensure resource development projects meaningfully benefit their communities.

But the main topic to come out of the closed-door meeting was Kinew’s sudden call to abolish the Indian Act — something he acknowledged he didn’t consult on with chiefs beforehand.

The law, which dates from 1876, gives Ottawa sweeping power over First Nations communities and people, including the authority to decide who qualifies for status and what reserves can and can’t do. While there is a widespread consensus that the law is outdated and restrictive, there’s little agreement on what could or should replace it.

In an audio recording of the closed-door meeting obtained by The Canadian Press, Kinew referred to his own First Nations status card and said he would keep it until he dies or the Indian Act is abolished.

“The idea that we have a race-based identification in our country in 2026 is inconsistent, at the very least, with Canada being a leader for human rights and democracy around the world,” Kinew, who is Anishinaabe, told Carney, chiefs and premiers.

“Typically, prime ministers are around for about a decade. And if we don’t put it on the agenda for this prime minister, that means we’ll be back here in 2036 and I’ll still have my laminated plastic card …

“And to the chiefs who may be like, ‘He didn’t consult with us before he’s saying this,’ I just wanted to say I think this is consistent with what you’re bringing forward here.”

Kinew made similar remarks to media following the session.

In a closing press conference after the meeting with chiefs, Carney said he was “very open” to the idea of abolishing the Indian Act. He said it’s important that the call came from community members and not the federal government.

Assembly of First Nations National Chief Cindy Woodhouse Nepinak told The Canadian Press Kinew and Carney were the only ones at the meeting who brought up eradicating the Indian Act.

North said members of the Liberal Indigenous caucus told chiefs shortly after the meeting wrapped they didn’t believe Carney fully understood the comments he made about the Indian Act and that they would speak to the prime minister about clarifying his stance.

“I think they were a little bit caught off-guard, based on some of the reaction we got from them afterwards,” North said.

Carney did clarify his stance the next day, saying the Indian Act could be reformed instead of abolished.

In an emailed statement, a spokesperson for Indigenous Services Canada did not say if the relevant ministers were told in advance that the prime minister would be commenting on the Indian Act. The spokesperson said those ministers were in the meeting with chiefs when the Indian Act was raised.

North said it was inappropriate for Kinew to divert attention from the issues the chiefs wanted to talk about.

“He may be Anishinaabe, he may have a status card, but that was not his place as a sitting premier to be calling for that,” she said.

North said that when the controversial Natural Resources Transfer Acts were brought up during the meeting, Kinew left his seat and didn’t return until the subject had changed. The day prior, North said, Kinew told chiefs he wasn’t open to the idea of moving past those agreements.

The acts, known as NRTAs, signed in 1930, transferred control of Crown lands and the resources they hold to Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta. First Nations did not have a say in the negotiations that led to the agreements, nor were they allowed to hire legal representation to challenge them.

Chiefs, including former national chief Matthew Coon Come, have called for negotiations to change those agreements to something that better reflects their rights.

The Canadian Press asked Kinew’s office if he is open to revisiting the NRTAs and if he discussed the Indian Act with Carney before the meeting, and requested his response to the chiefs’ criticisms. His office said it would not be commenting further on the matter

In a statement sent to The Canadian Press, the federal Crown-Indigenous Relations Department said Carney has made it clear First Nations must have a direct stake in Canada’s economic future, and the NRTAs do not prevent the negotiation of new resource revenue sharing agreements.

Mercredi said that while conversations about moving away from the Indian Act aren’t new, it seemed “a little bit offside” to bring the topic up at a meeting when chiefs really wanted to discuss the NRTAs.

Mercredi also questioned the format of the meeting, saying Carney only responded to a handful of chiefs “when he wanted to respond.”

“There was no real discussion around the issues that we’re facing,” Mercredi said. “There was really no positive outcome when it came to this meeting.”

Another chief in the meeting took issue with the way Carney responded to their concerns.

Chief Rodger Redman of Standing Buffalo Dakota Nation in Saskatchewan said he told Carney in the meeting he thinks Indigenous people in the United States have a better relationship with their governments, and that they are generally left alone to govern their nations.

In a video of the interaction posted online, Carney asked if Redman was “seriously making that point.”

“Just look around this table. Imagine, imagine this in the United States, under a Democratic administration, a Republican administration. It doesn’t even enter their thinking to have this discussion,” Carney said, interrupting Redman’s remarks.

“It kind of got under his skin a bit and he went sideways on me,” Redman told The Canadian Press.

Redman said he thought it was a valid point to bring up, since the push to accelerate major project development in Canada — a push that some chiefs say threatens First Nations rights — is largely being driven by pressures in the Canada-U.S. trade relationship.

“How can you say that you’re being equal sitting at the table?” Redman told The Canadian Press. “What happened in that circus in Ottawa was just there for the photo ops. We weren’t there for the photo ops.”

In remarks to chiefs shortly after responding to Kinew’s comments, Carney said he “can’t sit here and hear that there will be no progress” on the issues chiefs brought forward.

“Part of a respectful dialogue is recognizing facts and where those facts fall short, and where there’s gaps. And, very importantly, where there are programs that don’t work and why they don’t work,” he said in the audio recording.

Story by Alessia Passafiume

Crystal Delvenne said sh...

scraped.title: Mother of Cassity Delvenne challenges authorities on her death
scraped.description: The mother of Cassity Delvenne is trying to force the authorities in Manitoba to come up with answers on how her daughter died.
scraped.author: Sav Jonsa
scraped.h1: Grieving mother livestreams private Manitoba police watchdog meeting to force transparency
scraped.body_text:
APTN News

Stories about First Nations, Métis and Inuit peoples

APTN News

Crystal Delvenne said 'there's no transparency' with how the Independent Investigation Unit of Manitoba decides which police-involved incidents to investigate. Photo: Sav Jonsa/The IJF.

A grieving mother is taking transparency into her own hands by livestreaming meetings with Manitoba’s police watchdog and justice minister over the lack of independent investigation into her daughter’s violent arrest and subsequent death.

Crystal Delvenne said she chose to livestream the meetings to Facebook because she’s “lost trust in these systems” over the last few months following the Independent Investigation Unit of Manitoba’s (IIU) refusal to investigate an arrest by the Brandon Police Service (BPS).

Crystal’s daughter Cassity told her police beat her during the June 12 arrest, leaving her with bruised ribs, bleeding ears and hearing loss.

Cassity was found dead in her apartment of an unknown cause nine days later. Police said Cassity’s death is unrelated to her arrest.

On Friday, BPS announced it concluded its investigation into her death, saying a “definitive cause of death has been determined,” but added it could not share it publicly due to privacy laws and out of respect for the family.

According to the family, nothing has been received at the time this story was published.

Still, Crystal has many questions regarding her daughter’s case and the IIU’s operations. She said the IJF’s reporting on the IIU’s transparency and low rate of charging police following its investigations into officer-involved deaths pushed her to get answers.

“[The IJF’s reporting] pushed me because I realized how the police aren’t taking accountability,” Crystal said.

“I want people to hear my questions and their answers firsthand, with a clear record of what’s said and what promises are made … I want transparency and accountability.”

The IIU is responsible for investigating all serious incidents involving every police service in Manitoba, including death, serious injury, and criminal allegations. It is currently led by acting civilian director Bruce Sychuk.

Crystal met with Sychuk on Oct. 19 and Justice Minister Matt Wiebe on Oct. 21.

Despite Crystal feeling the 90-minute meeting with Sychuk was “pointless” and “horrible,” she did learn that the IIU received dash cam footage from the police cruiser showing Cassity’s arrest — footage she alleges BPS originally told her did not exist.

She was left with the impression that her daughter didn’t necessarily attempt to “flee” the scene as BPS had publicly stated during a news conference, and that the IIU decided against investigating the arrest after an informal discussion with BPS and before receiving all the evidence.

Patrick Ritchot, a supporter of the Delvenne family, said that though they want justice for Cassity, their ultimate goal is policy change.

“The IIU is broken. The way that police forces are structured is broken,” he told the IJF.

“We would like to see some sort of policy change so that … if this injustice happens, the mothers and the family don’t have to sit here and investigate it themselves.”

What was said in the meeting with IIU

Cassity Delvenne, 24, was a nursing student and mother to a young daughter who was found dead in her Brandon, Man., apartment on June 21. She is a member of Shoal Lake 40 First Nation.

Over the weekend, BPS said in a news release that it concluded the investigation into Cassity’s death after receiving her toxicology, autopsy, and medical examiner’s reports. They said it was “non-suspicious in nature with no evidence of foul play.”

Crystal told the IJF she hasn’t been told the cause of death.

Nine days before Cassity’s death, BPS arrested her and charged her with impaired driving and resisting arrest.

A 45-second portion of the arrest captured on video by an unknown witness appears to show two officers hitting Cassity as she lay face down on the pavement.

Crystal says the witness sent her the footage six weeks after the arrest. Crystal then uploaded it to her Facebook account, where it has amassed more than 160,000 views since early September.

Here is a video of the arrest:

Crystal told the IJF her daughter was already handcuffed when the officers used force on her, adding that Cassity was a small woman who weighed around 110 pounds. She said Cassity also told her police used a taser on her.

Crystal told the IJF that it took “numerous” attempts to secure a meeting with Sychuk.

He met with Crystal last month to explain his decision not to investigate the circumstances around Cassity’s arrest. He said it was because her injuries did not meet the IIU’s serious injury mandate, nor is it in the public interest to investigate.

A supporter of the Delvenne family who was present livestreamed the meeting to Facebook on Crystal’s behalf, where it has garnered more than 2,000 views. Crystal told the IJF she wanted the meeting livestreamed because of negative experiences she’s had trying to get answers about what happened to her daughter. The IJF viewed the recording of the video.

The IJF reached out to Sychuk directly through his government email for comment on the meeting. He forwarded the questions to the provincial government.

The government’s media relations manager Glen Cassie scolded the IJF for contacting Sychuk directly.

“You know better,” Cassie said to the IJF. “Any future contact with provincial staff — do not email them directly.”

In an emailed statement, the province said Sychuk knew the meeting with Crystal was being recorded but did not know it would be livestreamed or posted to social media.

“The IIU is committed to open, honest dialogue with families and understands these can be difficult and emotional discussions,” the statement said.

During their meeting, Sychuk told Crystal he was first notified about Cassity’s arrest through an “informal discussion” with BPS that included photos related to the incident.

He told her that based on the information he received at that time, he decided it wasn’t in the IIU’s mandate to investigate because there was “no serious injury to this individual.”

He said BPS reached out to him again sometime later with a formal report that included more evidence, including dash cam footage from the police cruiser, civilian witness audio tapes and videos captured by Cassity and a witness.

Despite the new evidence, he again said it wasn’t in the IIU’s mandate to investigate because the use of force was “reasonable under the circumstances.”

“I’m not suggesting they didn’t punch her; the evidence was there. What I’m saying to you is that use of force was within the use of force continuum and causes me no concerns,” Sychuk said to Crystal during the meeting, according to the recording viewed by the IJF.

The province did not directly answer the IJF’s questions about how Sychuk determined reasonable force was used without an investigation.

During the meeting, Cassity’s grandmother Donna asked Sychuk why it was during an informal discussion with BPS that he originally decided not to investigate Cassity’s arrest. Sychuk replied that officers or police authorities sometimes reach out informally to check if an incident meets the IIU’s mandate.

It is not clear how long after Cassity’s arrest these discussions between the IIU and BPS took place.

Crystal questioned Sychuk on the existence of the police cruiser dash cam footage, as she said she was initially told by BPS that there was no camera on the police cruiser that night. The IJF asked BPS about this discrepancy but did not receive comment by deadline.

Sychuk agreed he was told something similar.

“Originally, that’s what I understood as well,” said Sychuk in the meeting, adding the police could have had technical difficulties that caused them to believe there was no footage. “There’s a difference between hiding [footage] and just not being aware that it had been available.”

“You don’t phone somebody and say there’s no video and then all of a sudden find it,” Crystal responded.

Sychuk also told Crystal during the meeting that the evidence BPS provided him showed Cassity “moved forward once she was placed under arrest,” which triggered the use of force interaction.

“But she didn’t run?” asked Crystal.

“Walk, run, skip, it doesn’t matter,” Sychuk replied.

“If you’re trying to evade the cops and take off, there’s a big difference if you’re trying to run,” Crystal responded.

During a September news conference , BPS chief Tyler Bates said Cassity “fled police to avoid apprehension” while he tried to correct the “false narrative and the misleading information” he said was being spread about the arrest.

“The truth matters and the details matter in assessing the appropriateness of the actions taken by police,” Bates told the media at the time.

Crystal asked Sychuk why Cassity’s injuries weren’t considered serious. She said they included bruised ribs, blood coming out of both of her ears and loss of hearing in one ear, a missing toenail and a chipped tooth. She said Cassity had to seek medical attention after the arrest, including getting X-rays done on her ribs because she had difficulty breathing up until her death.

Crystal also told Sychuk that her daughter said that she was “crying for medical attention in her cell” after the arrest but did not receive it.

The IIU’s website defines a serious injury as one that includes a fracture of various major bones, requires in-patient hospital admission due to internal injuries, burns, cuts or lacerations, the loss of any part of the body, vision or hearing and any injury caused by the discharge of a firearm.

Sychuk said if Crystal can bring him evidence of anything like the above, he would review Cassity’s file again and redetermine if it fits his mandate.

He said he would ask BPS about whether or not a taser was used.

“To the best of my knowledge, there wasn’t tasers,” said Sychuk. “If there’s evidence that they’ve hidden from me as you’re suggesting, I will ask for it and there’s serious consequences for doing that.”

Crystal also asked Sychuk if he would investigate the arrest as a matter in the public interest. The IIU’s website says the IIU can take on an investigation that doesn’t meet its mandate “when the civilian director considers it in the public interest to do so.”

Sychuk said Cassity’s case wasn’t in the public interest to investigate.

As for what constitutes a case of public interest, a provincial spokesperson said it “would generally be one where a further review of the events might lead to a change in something like a policy or officer training. This case did not meet that standard.”

Meeting with Manitoba justice

Two days later, Crystal invited Wiebe to Cassity’s sacred fire to discuss her meeting with Sychuk. She told Wiebe she felt the conversation “went in circles the whole time.”

This meeting was also livestreamed to Facebook by a supporter of the Delvenne family who was present. The IJF has viewed the recording.

Crystal told Wiebe that she no longer wants the IIU to investigate what happened to Cassity, even if they were mandated to do so.

“We want someone else looking at this. We don’t want that guy,” she said of Sychuk.

Crystal asked if Wiebe would consider assigning Cassity’s case to an outside agency for an investigation separate from the IIU and BPS, an option outlined in the Police Services Act .

He didn’t directly answer her. The IJF reached out to the province on this but did not hear back.

She also asked if Wiebe would arrange an independent review of the BPS.

“My understanding is that there are still some missing pieces to the ongoing investigation that they’re doing,” Wiebe responded. “So I think once we know some more of that information, I guess that’s when we can talk about the next steps.”

She told Wiebe that the BPS won’t talk to her or return her calls.

“I want them to give you as much information as possible,” Wiebe reassured her.

BPS told the IJF in a statement that it is in “regular contact with an intimate member of the family” and that an assigned family liaison is participating in the communications.

Crystal told the IJF that she thinks future IIU civilian directors should be elected by the public rather than appointed by government officials, and that the police watchdog should include grassroots community members for oversight.

She would like there to be clearer materials and resources available that explain the IIU’s process so families could better understand its decisions when it comes to choosing cases.

“There’s no transparency with this,” she said.

Crystal is now gathering donations for legal funds and plans to bring a lawsuit against BPS.

“No wonder why there’s so many families that quit — because it’s hard,” she told Wiebe, “But I’m not going anywhere.”

On Nov. 6, Premier Wab Kinew met with Crystal at Cassity’s sacred fire. The IJF reached out to the province for confirmation on what was discussed during the meeting but did not hear back before this story was published.

This story was produced by the Investigative Journalism Foundation, an independent, non-profit newsroom based in Canada.

Sav Jonsa is a Two-Spirit Michif with maternal roots in the Parisien family of St. Norbert, Winnipeg. They’re also English and Irish through their mother and Hungarian through their father. They are grateful to still be residing in the heart of the Red River Métis homeland, where their ancestors fought in the Victory of Frog Plain and the Red River Resistance. Jonsa is an award-winning reporter, and was a finalist for the JHR/CAJ Emerging Indigenous Journalist Award in 2024.

scraped.title: On the Outside: Is Manitoba contributing to its own crime problem?
scraped.description: APTN Investigates follows people who have been released by the correctional system to see how Manitoba supports them.
scraped.author: Tamara Pimentel
scraped.h1: On the Outside: Is Manitoba contributing to its own crime problem?
scraped.body_text:
APTN News

Stories about First Nations, Métis and Inuit peoples

APTN News

Otessa Lanceley waits at the Unicity bus stop in Winnipeg. It’s the first stop as you enter the city from the west.

This is where she is dropped off every time she gets released from the Women’s Correctional Centre in the nearby town of Headingley.

“I’ve been doing this my whole life,” she said, as she waits for the bus that will take her straight downtown.

“I’ve been in and out of jail every year since I was 12.”

Being left on the outskirts of the city, without a plan and with nothing more than a bus ticket and the clothes they were arrested in, is a common story for people exiting Manitoba’s provincial correctional system.

“There’s hardly no resources for somebody to grasp on to,” Lanceley said to APTN Investigates, “Especially if they’re only there for a little bit, they get dropped right back off to where they started.”

At a young age she was already caught in a cycle that would follow her into adulthood. Addictions and living on the streets would lead her to incarceration. With every release, she would end up back in Unicity, far away from resources in the inner city.

Indigenous women and girls are the fastest growing demographic in the prisons across Canada. In Manitoba’s correctional system alone, Indigenous people make up 80 per cent of inmates sentenced.

But according to a report filed by Manitoba’s Auditor General, Preparing Incarcerated Individuals for Transition from Custody , there isn’t enough being done to reduce recidivism and prepare incarcerated people for life on the outside.

The 2025 report found there is “little evidence of connecting inmates to outside resources.” As a result, release plans don’t effectively prepare inmates for release.

John Samson Fellows, a literacy instructor with the John Howard Society of Manitoba, teaches classes at the remand centre. He brought the report to his students, who came up with their own recommendations. He said housing and direct transportation to housing were at the top of their list.

“The report can’t really see the whole picture”, he said. “The people to consult on these issues are incarcerated and formerly incarcerated people.”

Despite many attempts to ask Manitoba’s justice minister about the report, Matt Wiebe never agreed to an on-camera interview.

Manitoba’s Auditor General, Tyson Shtykalo, said he’s unable to comment because the report is still undergoing a two-year follow-up process.

“Since this report has come out, conditions have gotten much worse,” Samson Fellows said. “The women that I teach are often three to a cell for 22 hours a day in remand. And it makes it incredibly difficult to accomplish what they’ve been told they need to accomplish, which is kind of restoration or rehabilitation.”

Kim Dimond, the director of Indigenous healing with the Inside Justice Project , advocates for people like Lanceley and offers supports when they leave corrections. But before that, she spent over 20 years working as a corrections officer and program worker. She met Lanceley inside the Manitoba Youth Centre in 2004.

“That environment, as an officer, was so toxic. It’s a miserable place for people,” she told APTN while holding a drum circle in her yard with Lanceley.

“Once you get out and you’ve had to experience that kind of desperate environment and then you’re back out here and you got to try again. But it’s the same old, same old. No one’s waiting out here for you to help you.”

Dimond said the most important part of reintegration is housing.

The Elizabeth Fry Society is trying to bridge that gap with a new transitional home in Winnipeg’s inner city that houses eight transitional beds and two emergency beds.

“Housing should actually be a core principle when people are being released. I think there should be a bigger connection between the institution and then reintegration into the community,” said Tasha Banfield, executive director at the Elizabeth Fry society of Manitoba.

The transitional home is in high demand. Banfield said it is always at full capacity. The emergency rooms are two of the few that are available in Winnipeg.

As Banfield showed APTN around the home, we met Sheila-Rae Nasekapow, a resident of one month. Having spent time in federal prison while recovering from an addiction, she now has a fresh start and is regaining custody of her kids.

“Having supports has not really been a big thing. I had to find them all myself,” she said while packing a bag for a visit with her children.

“Boredom is a big reason why people re-offend, you know. You need to, when you’re coming out of that environment, you need to have structure.”

Read More:

Our Relatives: Life on the Streets podcast

Prime minister announces $1B for housing, new hospital to ‘tackle’ homelessness in Winnipeg

Banfield said the home offers the structure that is needed, but can only accommodate 10 women.

“It’s scary when they’re being released. We have a lot of ladies that come out, and gender-diverse folks who say that if they didn’t have a place to go like Elizabeth Fry Society, they would be back on the street,” she said. “They’re usually released with no IDs, if there is a plan in place, are they able to successfully do the plan once they’re on their own in the community?”

It took Lanceley around 40 minutes to get to the inner city, where shelters and resources are located and where people that leave jail or prison often get stranded.

“Some people are just tenting outside, people don’t come from a good home life. Their families could be also in gangs or struggling with addiction so they don’t get the necessary help that they need and they’re trying to stay strong.”

Tamara is Métis from Winnipeg, Manitoba. She received a diploma in interactive media arts at Assiniboine Community College in Brandon and has worked as a videographer for CBC in Winnipeg and Iqaluit. Tamara was hired by APTN in 2016 as a camera/editor and is now a video journalist back in Winnipeg.

scraped.title: Attending the Arctic Circle Assembly as an Inuk Youth was transformative and inspiring
scraped.description: Frey Blake-Pijogge explains the kinship they found at the event in Iceland — as thousands of delegates discussed polar challenges from climate to defence, arts to geopolitics
scraped.author: Frey Blake-Pijogge, Local Journalism Initiative Reporter
scraped.h1: Attending the Arctic Circle Assembly as an Inuk Youth was transformative and inspiring
scraped.body_text:
Frey Blake-Pijogge explains the kinship they found at the event in Iceland — as thousands of delegates discussed polar challenges from climate to defence, arts to geopolitics

Frey Blake-Pijogge, Local Journalism Initiative Reporter

●

●

The shaking of hands and small smiles welcome me to Reykjavík, Iceland. So does the rain.

I meet the rest of the Arctic Indigenous Youth Cohort the evening before the annual Arctic Circle Assembly starts, all of us tired after journeying from our many time zones that tightly span the planet’s North.

On the streets downtown, people are buzzing. Reykjavík feels alive. And everywhere in the city of nearly 150,000, I see signs about the global assembly, held from Oct. 8-10.

Every October, the world’s northernmost capital city hosts the event , the largest annual gathering of its kind. Organizers say more than 2,500 people from 75 countries attended this year.

Over three days, participants take in the event’s more-than-200 sessions — including panel discussions, round tables, forums, and workshops, their topics ranging from climate change to Arctic sovereignty, military defence, arts, and more.

The Arctic Indigenous Youth Cohort program is run by the federal government’s Global Arctic Leadership Initiative .

The next morning, I arrive at Harpa Concert Hall and take in the ambiance of the crowd: the space is brimming with loud laughter and the steady, excited talking of delegates.

We meet in the designated Youth lounge — each of us bringing their own perspectives and skills from around the Arctic. Our cohort includes Indigenous Youth from “Canada,” the “U.S.,” Greenland, Norway, Finland, and Sweden.

The first day of the assembly goes by in a blur, as I’m jet-lagged and still getting used to the three-hour time change.

I attend sessions on the geopolitics of polar climate research ; one on why media coverage of the Arctic is the “ final frontier in public interest reporting ”; how the region today is seen through the eyes of Youth leaders; and short presentations by student researchers from fields of biology, law, language, children, and computer science.

All three days’ sessions are unique, yet echo similar themes.

It’s clear that Indigenous peoples are at the forefront of many of the international discussions.

“Indigenous peoples have so much richness to offer,” said the Inuit Circumpolar Council’s international chair Aluki Kotierk, former president of Nunavut Tunngavik. “I think states realize that.

“Many Indigenous peoples from the Arctic … have been very instrumental in Arctic diplomacy, and even globally.”

For the rest of the assembly, whether meeting people outside of panels or at the Youth lounge, I feel a huge sense of awe to see how us Inuit from all around Inuit Nunangat are at the forefront of these urgent global discussions.

Another thing I notice is how powerfully Inuit are showing up at the event — representing our culture through our voices, leadership and perspectives, adorned with our beaded earrings, our silapak (pull-over top), our furs, and our kakiniit (tattoos) and tunniit.

Throughout the assembly, I meet people who are Sámi, Iñupiaq, Métis, Inuvialuk, Gwich’in — and from many other nations.

They fill me with a powerful sense of shared kinship I’ve not experienced anywhere else, except with other Indigenous people.

Simply put, I hold this kinship very dear to my heart.

Across the three days of panels and discussions, I meet people from across the Arctic — panelists and participants alike — who I found all share similar values towards the present and future of the Arctic.

One core theme throughout the meetings is the environment — not only how it is being impacted by climate change, but also the predicted catastrophic collapse of the water current between the Atlantic and Arctic oceans.

The lands and waters that we hold so dear are facing the brunt of this rapidly worsening crisis, and each nation is deciding its own ways of adapting to meet this challenge head-on.

Our love for our lands and waters transcends states’ colonial borders. And the survival of all peoples is reaching a frightening tipping point.

“We will not be spectators to our own future,” Greenland’s foreign affairs minister Múte Inequnaaluk Bourup Egede, formerly the territory’s youngest-ever prime minister, told attendees.

“Our future will not be decided around us, it will be shaped with us — our future, our voice, our choice.”

Another topic that emerges again and again is culture and language, and how it’s so deeply connected to the lands and waters we live on.

I think about how my paternal grandma, Katie Pijogge, loved speaking Inuttitut with other fluent speakers. Her love for our culture and ways of life on the land were always so apparent in how she lived.

Arctic sovereignty and defence are also common subjects, as the polar region is being developed more and more rapidly — and increasingly at the heart of global superpowers’ military and economic ambitions.

“The Arctic is changing strategically, economically, and environmentally,” said Adm. Giuseppe Cavo Dragone, NATO’s Military Committee chair, in a keynote speech .

“This change is happening at an unprecedented pace … it is becoming a new frontier that creates additional room for geopolitical competition.”

Observing these discussions unfold among world leaders invokes questions about my own family: Could this be how it felt when my mother’s father, Sid Blake, lived through the Second World War as a child? Or how he watched all the rapid development of our pristine lands and waters over his lifetime into what we know today as “Labrador”? I wonder what he might think about his granddaughter attending such a high-profile international assembly alongside thousands of state, Indigenous, and academic leaders from across the North?

Every panel I’m able to attend — and there were too many difficult choices — sparks conversations with my fellow delegates outside in the hallways.

In fact, I think perhaps that is where the most meaningful discussions I was a part of actually occurred.

A highlight of my time at the Arctic Circle Assembly is discovering the backgrounds of the other 11 Youth participants who make up our Arctic Indigenous Youth Cohort.

Over our days together, I learn where they and their families are from, and hear stories of their parents, grandparents and Ancestors.

Somehow, all our journeys have converged to attend the same Arctic Indigenous Youth Cohort in Iceland last month.

Each of us in our cohort follows in the footsteps of our own ancestors — their stories, lives and perspectives from around the Arctic.

We made up just 12 individuals out of more than 2,500 attendees who journeyed to Reykjavík.

Another highlight I hold close to my heart is the music and dancing of an Inuit-soul group Pamyua , who blend Yup’ik and Cup’ik cultures and performed at the assembly’s closing night.

The band’s members hail from “Greenland,” “Alaska” and “Denmark.”

Their fun and upbeat music includes Inuit throat-singing, drumming, and dancing — and they will be on my list of favourite music groups for the rest of my life.

I met so many inspiring and powerful people from such a wide range of professions, expertise and experiences — Youth around my age who are leaders carrying entirely unique points of view.

For me, that is what made this huge assembly so incredibly memorable and unique: a massive gathering solely by and for Arctic people, devoted to the future of our beloved region.

Frey Blake-Pijogge, Local Journalism Initiative Reporter

Frey Blake-Pijogge is a journalist from Happy Valley-Goose Bay and is Inuk from Nunatsiavut.

And yet, I have hope for journalism because of the work we’re doing at IndigiNews.

At IndigiNews, we embody tâpwêwin — the Cree value of integrity and responsibility in truth-telling. We are committed to our independent, Indigenous-led newsroom rooted in community, accountability, and relationality. We believe storytelling is a sacred fire that connects our pasts, presents, and futures through the storytellers in our Storytelling Lodge . IndigiNews creates space for Indigenous journalists, storytellers, Knowledge Keepers, and communities to gather, learn, and share stories that matter.

As a registered charity, we are building a fire that allows our work not just to ignite but to thrive. Rather than relying on advertising or corporate acquisition, IndigiNews is sustained by people like you who believe Indigenous stories are important for the future of our communities.

Your support is making a real difference.

Our community of supporters, our Firekeepers , make it possible to grow our newsroom, publish award-winning journalism, train emerging Indigenous journalists through initiatives like the ReFocus Photojournalism Fellowship, and publish trustworthy stories that serve our communities across the country. Every story we publish helps fill in gaps left by mainstream media and ensures Indigenous perspectives are represented with care, accuracy and respect.

But there is still more work to do.

As the media landscape becomes more and more uncertain, community support is as necessary and essential as it’s ever been. Every new Firekeeper helps protect the independence of our newsroom and strengthens journalism that is accountable to our many and varied communities over corporations.

That’s why we’re inviting you to become a Firekeeper.

Firekeepers tend to and protect the sacred fire. Your monthly contributions directly support IndigiNews’s Storytelling Lodge, helps sustain our independent, Indigenous-led newsroom, and ensures future generations of Indigenous storytellers have the resources they need to do the work.

As a registered Canadian charity, all eligible donations receive a charitable tax receipt.

If you believe Indigenous stories matter, if you value independent journalism, and if you want to help build a strong future for Indigenous media, we invite you to join our circle of Firekeepers today.

Together, we can keep the fire burning.

— Eden Fineday, Publisher, IndigiNews

Matt Simmons

●

●

Twenty years ago, Haíɫzaqv community members raised λáλix̌sístala to help Youth reconnect with their language, songs, dances, culture and ceremony. Today, the first generation to grow up here is carrying that vision forward

Matt Simmons

●

●

Seeking truth when reporting in Indigenous communities sometimes means abandoning the idea of journalism as ‘observation at a distance’ — and embracing reciprocity

Every Firekeeper helps keep the sacred fire of Indigenous storytelling burning. Monthly gifts from readers like you allow us to report with independence, remain accountable to our communities, and invest in the next generation of Indigenous journalists.

scraped.description: Incumbent Eli Crane retains his seat as Arizona’s second congressional district representative to serve a third term
scraped.author: Daniel Herrera Carbajal
scraped.h1: Jonathan Nez falls short to become first Native American from Arizona in U.S. Congress
scraped.body_text:
ICT

Daniel Herrera Carbajal ICT

Republican incumbent Eli Crane will continue to represent Arizona’s second congressional district after narrowly beating former Navajo Nation president Jonathan Nez for a second time.

Indian Country's top stories from Native journalists. Free, every Thursday.

The Associated Press called the race for Crane, who had 49.7 percent of the vote compared to Nez’s 48.5 percent of the vote.

If Nez won, he would have been the first Native American from Arizona to serve in congress.

Donors made this story possible.

A $10 monthly donation keeps Native journalists on stories like this one.

The rematch between the candidates was close compared to 2024 where Crane had nearly 55 percent of the vote compared to just over 45 percent for Nez.

Arizona’s second congressional district is mainly rural. It covers more than half the state in land area, containing 14 tribal nations and nine counties. It has historically favored republican candidates.

This is a developing story, stay tuned to ICTnews.org for updates .

Daniel Herrera Carbajal is a Multimedia Journalist for the ICT Newscast and ictnews.org. Carbajal is based out of ICT Southwest headquarters in Phoenix, Arizona. More by Daniel Herrera Carbajal

items.summary: Certain provisions included in a bill the Senate is expected to vote on tonight could be detrimental to tribes seeking to protect their homelands and sacred sites The post Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act threatens tribal sovereignty, leaders warn appeared first on ICT. scraped.title: Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act threatens tribal sovereignty, leaders warn - ICT
scraped.description: Certain provisions included in a bill the Senate is expected to vote on tonight could be detrimental to tribes seeking to protect their homelands and sacred sites
scraped.author: Amelia Schafer
scraped.h1: Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act threatens tribal sovereignty, leaders warn
scraped.body_text:
ICT

Amelia Schafer ICT

A bipartisan bill aimed at improving energy costs and creating new jobs includes certain provisions tribal leaders warn would undermine tribal sovereignty and weaken federal protections.

The Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act or S. 5653 , aims to fast track the development of pipelines, energy projects and data centers on public lands by proposing changes to the regulatory process in place for granting and processing project permits.

Part of the fast tracking process would mean diminishing tribal nations’ ability to engage in meaningful consultation over projects involving their homelands and sacred or religious sites.

“It says that it’s addressing the affordability and jobs issue, but actually, it just means bigger infrastructure projects for the wealthy,” Jodi Archambault, Hunkpapa and Oglala Lakota and a policy analyst told ICT . “This bill guts many of the provisions in the Clean Water Act, in the Endangered Species Act, all throughout NEPA, the National Historic Preservation Act, it takes away the power of the tribes to care and protect the places that are very important to us.”

The senate is expected to vote on the bill Monday night.

Title III of the bill includes proposed changes to Section 106 of the National Historic Preservation Act. The proposed changes would strip tribes of their ability to voice concerns over project impacts on cultural and religious sites by allowing federal agencies to choose not to consult with tribes, a protection guaranteed under Section 106 of the National Historic Preservation Act.

Indian Country's top stories from Native journalists. Free, every Thursday.

Further, the proposed changes would limit a tribe’s options to seek legal action if a project does violate its rights.

The bill proposes shortening the review process timeline for projects and allowing agencies to only need to consider the impacts of mining activities on federal land even if a project covers state and private lands.

“It’s a very dangerous bill,” Archambault said. “It basically just speeds everything up and it locks everybody into place in a very short window of time. And so it again, this goes back to who profits from these big projects.”

While the bill proposes changes to landmark resolutions such as the Clean Water Act and The Endangered Species Act, some of the most concerning changes come from proposed changes to Section 106 of the National Historic Preservation Act, leaders said.

“These proposed changes violate treaty and trust obligations,” said Mark Macarro, President of the National Congress of American Indians during the organization’s annual conference on Oct. 19.

Section 106 has long served as a key protection for tribes in protecting lands not under their current jurisdiction, specifically for tribes who have been relocated from their homelands and no longer hold direct jurisdiction over sites.

Donors made this story possible.

A $10 monthly donation keeps Native journalists on stories like this one.

“This change is extremely disruptive and could literally be destructive,” Macarro, a citizen of the Pechanga Band of Indians, said. “In the end, the one thing that needs to be done at the moment, is that there needs to be a denial of this pending legislation draft that’s there right now.”

National environmental organizations, the Native American Rights Fund and National Congress of American Indians have all spoken out against the bill, warning if implemented, these changes could have dire environmental consequences.

Bill revisions on Saturday only addressed a small number of tribal leaders’ concerns, according to a Nov. 8 release from 11 tribal advocacy groups.

“Despite claims that the revised legislation responds to Tribal concerns, the proposed changes to Section 106 of the National Historic Preservation Act in Title III of BAAJA continue to fundamentally undermine Tribal sovereignty, weaken longstanding federal protections, fail to ensure meaningful government-to-government Tribal consultation, and threaten sacred sites and cultural resources,” the joint release said.

Representatives such as Rep. Melaine Stansbury (D- N.M.) and Rep. Sharice Davids (D-Kansas) and a citizen of the Ho-Chunk Nation, urged other Senators to join them in voting no on the bill and stand in solidarity with tribal leaders.

“There were changes made in response to some of the opposition that are just completely non-negotiable that would essentially take away the ability of tribes to define their cultural sites, [and] defend them in a court or law,” Stansbury said in a post Monday morning . “I appreciate that our colleagues are trying to get something big and historic done but it cannot be at the expense of our communities.”

Amelia Schafer is ICT's North Central Correspondent based in Milwaukee, Wisconsin. Schafer covers MMIP, Indian Gaming and business for ICT. She is of Wampanoag and Montauk-Brothertown Indian Nation descent.... More by Amelia Schafer

scraped.title: Canada honors sacrifices of Indigenous veterans - ICT
scraped.description: National Indigenous Veterans Day is celebrated on Nov. 8 each year in Canada
scraped.author: Miles Morrisseau
scraped.h1: Canada honors sacrifices of Indigenous veterans
scraped.body_text:
ICT

Miles Morrisseau ICT

ONTARIO, Canada — Dozens of people gathered at the cenotaph on the Chippewas of Kettle and Stony Point First Nation to honor and remember Indigenous veterans, a scene and sentiment shared across Canada in ceremonies Nov. 8 to mark National Indigenous Veterans Day.

The annual event began in 1994 to acknowledge the sacrifices made by First Nations, Métis and Inuit people who stood up for a country that did not always stand up for them.

Corporal Darcie Cameron of the 2 Military Police Regiment of the Canadian Forces Military Police Group in Ontario, is a member of the First Nation and is proud of Indigenous peoples’ history of service.

“What Indigenous Veteran’s Day means to me is just the importance of remembering what our peoples have done for us in this country even today, and back in the day they were in residential schools they were deprived of who they are, their language,” Cameron told ICT.

“I just think it is so important to honor them for the fact that everything that they went through and we still choose, they still choose, to honor Canada today.” she said. “It’s just beautiful to look back and see how many indigenous peoples wanted to serve Canada.”

According to Veterans Affairs Canada, over 12,000 Indigenous people from Canada served in World Wars I and II and the Korean Conflict, with 500 making the ultimate sacrifice, dying on the battlefield.

“It goes without saying that Indigenous Veterans have made invaluable contributions to the CAF (Canadian Armed Forces). They stood shoulder to shoulder with non-Indigenous members, demonstrating unwavering bravery and loyalty,” wrote Raquel Loth in a 2025 piece in The Maple Leaf , Canada’s military news .

“Yet, despite their service, many returned to a country that failed to honor them equally,” Loth wrote. “They were denied the same benefits, land grants, and reintegration support provided to non-Indigenous Veterans.”

Indian Country's top stories from Native journalists. Free, every Thursday.

Indigenous veterans were not welcome to Remembrance Day ceremonies in the years following World War II, and for decades their sacrifice was ignored despite personal sacrifices beyond the average Canadian soldier.

First Nations soldiers had to surrender their Indian status in order to sign up or they found upon their return that the Indian agent had removed them from membership. This was called “enfranchisement.”

Nevertheless, Indigenous peoples volunteered at a higher rate than other communities and contributed at the highest level. Cree soldiers served as code-talkers during the war, sharing strategy across enemy lines in a language that their foes could not decipher.

Tommy Prince, Brokenhead First Nation, was a residential school survivor who became one of the country’s most decorated soldiers after going behind enemy lines in southern France disguised as a local farmer to provide details of a German encampment. He was one of only three Canadians to be awarded the Military Medal from his home country and the Silver Star from the United States.

In addition to the international conflicts, Indigenous veterans from the Chippewas of Kettle and Stony Point were remembered for service during the American Civil War, the War of 1812 and during battles on the homefront to stand up for traditional lands. Among those honored was Dudley George, a land defender who was killed by the Ontario police on Sept. 6, 1995, following a raid on a peaceful occupation of the lands at Stony Point.

Donors made this story possible.

A $10 monthly donation keeps Native journalists on stories like this one.

The land had been taken by the Canadian government during World War II as a training ground under the promise that it would be returned after the war. It wasn’t. Following George’s sacrifice and the ongoing occupation, the land was finally returned in 2009.

The cenotaph in the community recognizes veterans across the generations.

“Today we acknowledge the challenges Indigenous veterans faced both during their service and upon their return home,’’ Chief Kim Bressette told those gathered.

“Despite these hardships they demonstrated remarkable strength, resilience and dedication,” Bressette said. “Their contributions are an important part of our shared history and must never be forgotten as we gather in remembrance we pay tribute not only to those who served in times of war conflict and peacekeeping missions but also to the families who supported them and carried the burdens of their absence.”

Wreaths were placed in honor of the many veterans from the community. Honor songs were offered by the local drum and prayers were shared by elders.

The Canadian Armed Forces released a statement to mark the day’s significance.

“On National Indigenous Veterans Day, we remember the First Nations, Inuit, and Métis Peoples who have fought for this land for generations, going back to the pre-Confederation era,” Lieutenant-General Michael C. Wright, Commander Canadian Army and Defence Team Co-Champion for Indigenous Peoples stated.

“We owe them a profound debt and have a duty to honour that legacy, not only through commemoration, but in the actions we take today to ensure those following in their footsteps continue to be seen, heard, and respected as part of the Defence Team,” Wright said.

The history of service continues today, with a new generation stepping up to follow in the footsteps of those who went before them. As for Cameron, she looks to her grandmother Carmel Cameron who served in Afghanistan and Iran.

“My own grandmother, she is an Indigenous veteran,” Cameron said with pride. “She served in many wars in the 2000s and she was just a really big inspiration to me and I love her with my entire heart. … I just want to make her proud.”

Miles Morrisseau, Métis, is a special correspondent for ICT based in the historic Métis Community of Grand Rapids, Manitoba, Canada. He reported as the national Native Affairs broadcaster for CBC Radio... More by Miles Morrisseau

scraped.title: Toukie Smith, trailblazing model and actress on '227', dies at 74
scraped.description: Toukie Smith, the trailblazing model who starred in shows such as "Miami Vice" and "227" has died. She was 74.
scraped.author: Brandon Caldwell
scraped.h1: Toukie Smith, trailblazing model and actress on ‘227’, dies at 74
scraped.body_text:
The famed model walked for numerous fashion houses in the 1970s before transitioning into acting. A longtime partner of Robert De Niro, she is survived by their twins, Airyn and Julian.

Toukie Smith, a model who walked runways for the likes of Chanel , Thierry Mugler and Hubert de Givenchy while starring alongside Marla Gibbs on the sitcom “ 227, ” has died. She was 74.

Her twins, Airyn and Julian, whom she shared with actor Robert De Niro, confirmed she died on Nov. 4 in a New York hospital after a “long, courageous battle” with multiple sclerosis, according to The Hollywood Reporter .

“I’ll always love you, Mom,” Airyn De Niro wrote in a brief tribute on Instagram.

A post shared by Airyn De Niro (@airyphim)

Born Doris A. Smith in 1952, Smith adopted the stage name “Toukie” from a childhood nickname her grandmother gave her after listening to a song “about a little red fire engine with lots of energy.”

“I’ve always had lots of energy,” she told the Los Angeles Times in a 1990 profile highlighting her career. At the time, she was planning an AIDS tribute to her brother, fashion designer Willi Smith, who died from complications of the disease at the age of 39 in 1987.

“Willi always had fun with fashion,” Smith said of her brother at the time. “He had a special energy and a love of keeping clothes from being too serious. He also totally designed for the masses.”

Her modeling career soon took off after she graduated from the Fashion Institute of Technology in 1972, as she landed on the pages of Ebony, Vogue, Cosmopolitan and Seventeen. In 1978, Bloomingdale’s named her its Model of the Year. However, she believed she was destined for more than fashion runways and transitioned into acting in the 1980s.

In 1987-88, she joined the cast of “Miami Vice” as Angie, a recurring character who served as the assistant to pop singer Caitlin Davies (Sheena Easton) in three episodes.

In 1989, she became a fixture on “227” opposite Marla Gibbs as Eva Rawley, an artist who moves into the Lexington Palace building where Gibbs’ Mary Jenkins served as the landlord. Although Eva managed the building for a spell, she and Gibbs would share screen time for the beloved comedy for two seasons before it wrapped in 1990.

Her filmography includes roles in 1991’s “Talkin’ Dirty After Dark,” opposite Martin Lawrence and John Witherspoon, and 1996’s “The Preacher’s Wife” opposite Denzel Washington, Whitney Houston and Courtney B. Vance.

Smith is the second notable member of the “227” cast to pass away this year. Hal Williams, who played the family patriarch, Lester Jenkins, died in July.

scraped.title: Dave Chappelle said he would test cancel culture. His Charlie Kirk joke may have done just that
scraped.description: The backlash over Chappelle's joke has revived scrutiny of Tony Hinchcliffe's similar joke about Floyd and the standards applied to comedians.
scraped.author: Kay Wicker
scraped.h1: Dave Chappelle said he would test cancel culture. His Charlie Kirk joke may have done just that
scraped.body_text:
The backlash over Chappelle's performance has revived scrutiny of Tony Hinchcliffe's similar joke about Floyd and the standards applied to comedians.

Just weeks after Charlie Kirk was shot and killed at Utah Valley University in October 2025, Dave Chappelle joked during an appearance at Saudi Arabia’s Riyadh Comedy Festival that discussing the slain right-wing commentator in America could get you canceled. Well, more than a year later, the comedian appears to have just tested the theory.

Over the weekend, during the New York stops of his “Karmageddon” tour at Madison Square Garden, Chappelle opened up about how he’s been feeling in the aftermath of Kirk’s death.

“I feel f— up saying this. It’s scary being a public speaker. Ever since that guy Charlie Kirk got murdered, and I shouldn’t say this publicly, but I feel better,” he told the crowd in footage circulating online .

He continued, “I know I shouldn’t say that, but it’s just a feeling. I didn’t ask to feel this way,” before joking about driving around in a good mood and suddenly remembering why.

Later, he added, “I’m sure Charlie Kirk is looking up at us right now, laughing so hard he can’t breathe.”

The latter joke may sound familiar to anyone who watched Netflix’s “The Roast of Kevin Hart” in May, when comedian Tony Hinchcliffe delivered a nearly identical punchline about George Floyd , who was murdered by Minneapolis police in 2020.

As the clips continue to circulate online, drawing backlash from Kirk’s widow, Erika Kirk, Elon Musk, Piers Morgan, and more, the controversy is reigniting a complex conversation about double standards in comedy and American culture and who has the right to make certain jokes.

Part of why Kirk’s supporters have been particularly incensed by Chappelle’s remarks is because Kirk actually publicly defended the comedian after he himself was attacked onstage in 2022. At the time, Kirk condemned Los Angeles County District Attorney George Gascón’s decision not to pursue felony charges against the man who rushed Chappelle during a performance at the Hollywood Bowl.

“By refusing to charge the armed maniac who attacked Dave Chappelle on stage, George Gascon is sending a clear message that public acts of political violence are justifiable—and even encouraged—against anyone who dares speak out against The Regime,” Kirk wrote in a post on X. “It’s Sinister & Un-American.”

In response to Chappelle, Morgan called the latest remarks “disgusting” and especially troubling given his own experience with violence. Meanwhile, Erika condemned comedians and commentators who treat political assassination as entertainment, without calling anyone out by name.

Now, it’s true that Hinchcliffe faced backlash of his own after his joke about Floyd. During the special, he of course also joked that Floyd was looking down from the afterlife, laughing so hard he couldn’t breathe, a direct reference to Floyd’s final pleas as a Minneapolis police officer knelt on his neck. While the joke drew widespread criticism, including from Floyd’s family, Hart defended Hinchcliffe’s right to make it.

At the same time, the somewhat relentless jokes about Floyd’s murder have also had consequences for his family. Following the roast, a spokesperson for the Gianna and George Floyd Foundation said Floyd’s daughter, Gianna, had experienced bullying at school in part because modern culture doesn’t take his death seriously.

Neither Floyd’s murder nor Kirk’s assassination is a laughing matter for their families. Yet the similarities between the two jokes invite an uncomfortable question about whether audiences are responding to the cruelty of the punchline itself or the identity of the person on the receiving end. And while appeals to stop making Floyd’s death a punchline have done little to stop the jokes, public commentary about Kirk has had serious consequences for people, including Karen Attiah, a former Washington Post opinion columnist who was fired in September 2025 after posting online about not wanting to publicly mourn Kirk following his death.

While she did not celebrate his killing or make light of it, the newspaper accused her of violating its social media policies and engaging in misconduct. An independent arbitrator ruled in August that the Post lacked sufficient cause to fire her and ordered her reinstatement with back pay. However, on Sunday, Nov. 8, Attiah announced that she had reached a settlement with the newspaper and would not be returning because she no longer felt confident she would have the freedom and institutional support necessary to do her work .

Chappelle, meanwhile, has spent much of his career testing the limits of what comedians can say on stage. However, it’s also worth noting that his latest remarks have reached audiences in a way he may not have intended. His Madison Square Garden performances were advertised as cellphone-free, yet here we have unauthorized recordings circulating online, separating the jokes from the rest of his routine.

The comedian has previously spoken about how Kirk’s assassination affected him, acknowledging in his December 2025 Netflix special, “The Unstoppable,” that the killing frightened him as someone who makes a living speaking publicly. Whether his latest jokes were intended as a commentary on the different reactions to Kirk’s and Floyd’s deaths remains unclear, but at least he did offer something of a fair warning.

“Right now in America, they say that if you talk about Charlie Kirk, you’ll get canceled,” he said in October 2025 during the Riyadh Comedy Festival. “I don’t know if that’s true, but I’m gonna find out.”

scraped.title: Wes Moore says Kamala Harris and Stacey Abrams 'ran so Keisha Lance Bottoms could fly'
scraped.description: Moore tells theGrio how Harris and Abrams paved the way for Keisha Lance Bottoms' historic election as America's first Black woman governor.
scraped.author: Gerren Keith Gaynor
scraped.h1: Wes Moore says Kamala Harris and Stacey Abrams ‘ran so Keisha Lance Bottoms could fly’
scraped.body_text:
The Maryland governor reflects on the Black women who paved the way for Bottoms' historic victory and why her leadership represents more than a political milestone.

Many are still celebrating the historic election of Keisha Lance Bottoms as Georgia’s next governor.

On Jan. 11, 2027, Bottoms will be sworn in as Georgia’s first African-American governor and will become the first Black woman in U.S. history to serve as a head of state.

Among those cheering on the historic achievement is Maryland Gov. Wes Moore —a close friend of Bottoms.

“I’m so excited that my friend is going to become a governor,” Moore told theGrio. However, the country’s once-lone Black governor said he said his excitement isn’t just because Bottoms is a “dear friend.

“It’s also the fact that she’s a really good public servant, and I think she’s going to be an outstanding governor,” said Moore, who was resoundingly re-elected in last Tuesday’s midterm election. Moore said he is confident in Gov.-elect Bottoms’ ability to address many of the critical issues he and other governors are working to resolve, such as ending child poverty and income inequality.

“If we can do that as a society, you will solve every other issue,” said Moore. “But we need to have leaders who are going to prioritize that, and that’s who Keisha Lance Bottoms is.”

As Bottoms looks ahead to becoming the 84th governor of Georgia and the Peach State’s first Black governor in its 249-year history as a formal state, Moore acknowledged that the historic moment would not be possible without the Black women who came before her at the top of an electoral ticket in Georgia: former U.S. Vice President Kamala Harris , who ran for president in 2024; and Stacey Abrams , who twice ran for governor in 2018 and 2022.

While Harris and Abrams were not successful in their respective campaigns, Moore told theGrio, “I think Stacey ran and Vice President Harris ran so that Keisha could fly,” adding, “I think Keisha understands that.”

Moore said he felt the same about his own historic election as Maryland’s first Black governor. He explained, “Doug Wilder [the first Black governor post-Reconstruction] and people like Deval Patrick [the first Black governor of Massachusetts] and people like [former Maryland gubernatorial candidates] Ben Jealous and Anthony Brown here in the state of Maryland, that they ran so I could fly.”

Reflecting on Bottoms’ historic election, which would not be possible without the civil rights history of the former Atlanta mayor’s hometown, Gov. Moore said, “I think there is an appreciation for all of the people who came before us that gave the opportunity for Keisha to be successful.”
