items.title: Meet the Black Organizers, Strategists, and Students Who Built the Midterm Blue Wave
items.summary: Midterm candidates got the headlines, but here's how some of the Black strategists, campus organizers and grassroots activists shaped the political landscape.Read more...

scraped.title: Meet the Black Organizers, Strategists, and Students Who Built the Midterm Blue Wave – The Root
scraped.h1: Meet the Black Organizers, Strategists, and Students Who Built the Midterm Blue Wave
scraped.body_text:
Black News, Opinions, Politics and Culture

Midterm candidates got the headlines, but here’s how some of the Black strategists, campus organizers and grassroots activists shaped the political landscape.

By

Phenix S Halley

Published

(L-R) Brooke Butler (Photo from DCCC), Damon Hewitt (Photo by Arturo Holmes/Getty Images for ESSENCE), LaTosha Brown (Photo by Leigh Vogel/Getty Images for Congressional Black Caucus Foundation)

The blue wave during last week’s midterms didn’t just happen. It was built by people working in the spotlight and plenty more working behind the scenes. We often think about Black leaders like Eric Holder and Stacey Abrams, but there are plenty more who have been doing the work for years that you probably haven’t heard of yet. When people talk about the 2026 wave, they’ll talk about the candidates and the election results. But there’s another story worth telling: the people who helped make it happen.

To view this video please enable JavaScript.

From Gerard Henderson and Waikinya J.S. Clanton to HBCU students across the South, they’ve all helped bring people together, build momentum and turn organizing into political action. Some opened doors, some raised resources, some knocked on doors, registered voters, and mobilized their communities. This is a look at the people and networks whose work helped make the wave possible.

At the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee (DSCC), Jessica Knight Henry helped lay the groundwork for competitive Senate campaigns through candidate recruitment, early investments, and strategic support. Her work helped give Southern Democrats the resources to compete before election season even heated up.

Mississippi, we’re feeling really good about tonight! Y’all have shown up and SHOWN OUT! Votes are still being counted in Lowndes and the Delta, and we’ve got 15,000+ affidavit ballots out. Buckle up, Mississippi. Change is coming, and we’re going to get this done! pic.twitter.com/cx8lq5JVjc

As campaign manager for Scott Colom’s Mississippi Senate race , Gerard Henderson helped build a serious statewide operation, coordinating on-the-ground strategy and turning a traditionally difficult contest into one of Mississippi’s most competitive races.

RELATED : How the GOP’s Redistricting Strategy Backfired in a Big Way During the Midterms

Behind Wisconsin Governor-elect David Crowley’s campaign, Garren Randolph, who previously worked on the Biden-Harris campaign , helped make every dollar and organizing effort count. From building coalitions to prioritizing voter outreach, he kept the campaign focused on turning Democratic support into actual votes.

From Georgia’s organizing movement to the Texas political landscape, Delilah Agho Otoghile has helped Democrats compete where it matters. Her field experience and strategic leadership have been instrumental in building coalitions and flipping key local races.

Long before Election Day, DeJuana Thompson was building the relationships that make turnout possible. Through Woke Vote, she helped redefine Southern organizing by connecting young Black voters, empowering communities, and making civic participation a sustained movement.

As executive director of Georgia’s Democratic Party , Felicia Blakely-Agostini helped keep the state’s political machinery moving. Her leadership strengthened the infrastructure, coordination, and organizational support needed to compete across Georgia.

As the director of Black Men Vote, Michael Bland made sure Black men were part of the conversation, pushing voter participation and political engagement.

Working at the DNC, Shelby Wiltz helped connect national Democratic resources with the state parties doing the work on the ground. Her role in coordination and frontline support helped keep campaigns connected and moving in the same direction.

As political director at the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee (DCCC), Brooke Butler helped shape where Democrats competed and where they invested. Her work expanding the Southern battlefield gave more attention and resources to districts that could help change the balance of power.

Remember when North Carolina Republicans voted to close early-voting sites at several HBCUs right before elections? Well, Adejoké Aladekere, a student at NCAT, helped turn student frustration into action by organizing young voters to march to the polls after voting stations closed.

On the campus of Jackson State University, another HBCU in Mississippi, Jakari Holland, founder of the Mississippi Access Project, brought a fresh Gen Z perspective to voting rights, empowering Mississippi students to get informed and engaged.

Back in Georgia, Helen Butler, the executive director of the Georgia Coalition for the People’s Agenda, continued her Georgia voting rights work, helping communities register and stay informed.

Took a second on the @bbc to talk about the AI safety legislation @JBPritzker signed last week pic.twitter.com/uiwpikP7GD

This DGA leadership team helped power Democratic gubernatorial campaigns across the South, bringing together funding, communications, and field strategy. Their work helped candidates build the statewide operations needed to compete in tough political terrain.

Waikinya J.S. Clanton understands that organizing can’t begin and end with an election. Through her work in Mississippi and the ANCHORED framework, she’s focused on building lasting community power, developing local leadership, and creating civic infrastructure that outlives campaign cycles.

Christina Cue has taken voter education and organizing beyond traditional campaign boundaries. Through OnCue Management, she’s helped coordinate multi-state outreach and turnout efforts, bringing the information, resources, and community connections needed to reach millions of Southern voters.

Since January 20th Democrats have been looking for ways to prove they are fighters who put everyday Americans first. That fight is NOT in a gerrymandering arms race in blue states, but here in Texas, by rallying the nation to pay attention & raising the funds for a quorum break. pic.twitter.com/g1pcxVbqUJ

While most campaigns focus on the easiest places to reach, Tayhlor Coleman takes the road less traveled. Living out of her van, Barb, she has registered thousands of voters in rural Texas communities that too often get overlooked.

These Black Voters Matter co-founders have helped make Southern voter turnout a movement of its own. From bus tours to local organizing grants, they’ve invested in the people and grassroots organizations doing the work where elections are won.

Quentin Turner focuses on the communities that traditional campaign budgets too often leave behind. His rural and non-metro organizing work helps bring overlooked precincts into the political conversation, proving that building a winning coalition means showing up everywhere.

Nsé Ufot helped transform how Southern communities organize, connect, and mobilize. Through her voting rights work and innovative relational organizing strategies, she helped build a model rooted in personal relationships, community trust, and the belief that lasting political power starts locally.

Ryan P. Haygood, the CEO of the Southern Poverty Law Center, brought civil rights leadership to the fight for democracy, voting access and racial justice.

Vote HBCU was one of several organizations that helped get younger generations to the ballot box. Vote HBCU registered more than 800 students within one month, reminding the nation that young Black voters have power.

Camille Wimbish is the national director of the Election Protection Coalition. She helped coordinate nationwide election protection efforts, making sure voters had support when they needed it.

The NAACP’s Chief of Field, Membership Growth and Unit Sustainability, Dominik Whitehead, helped lead a major voter mobilization effort, putting Black voters and political representation front and center.

This election cycle, The Root spoke to Anneshia Hardy , executive director of Alabama Values, who helped bring everyday voters into the conversation through grassroots organizing and community-centered advocacy.

Damon Hewitt, the president and executive director of the Lawyers’ Committee for Civil Rights Under Law, helped protect the vote, bringing legal resources and voter assistance to communities facing election barriers.

scraped.title: TV Shows, Movies to Watch After 'You Can See Everything'
scraped.h1: If You’re Having ‘You Can See Everything’ Withdrawals, Check Out These Movies and TV Shows Next
scraped.body_text:
Black News, Opinions, Politics and Culture

If you don’t know what to watch after getting your fill of “You Can See Everything,” these shows and movies might satisfy you in a similar fashion!

By

Shanelle Genai

Published

Screenshot: YouTube

Everybody loves a good hustle until the truth comes knocking. And if watching “You Can See Everything” has you questioning how much of what you see, hear, and believe is actually true and begging for more after the credits roll, we’ve got a few more shows and movies to add to your watchlist ASAP!

To view this video please enable JavaScript.

While some of these stories are inspired by real-life scandals, others are just really good scripted tales that feel a little too close to reality. Either way it goes, trust us when we say there’s plenty of money, mess, fraud, and foolery to keep you entertained and binging. Keep reading for more!

Naturally, we had to add the Hulu series “The Dropout” to this list. This is basically the same Theranos story of Elizabeth Holmes but told through an eight-episode mini-series. This show, starring Amanda Seyfried, really shows you the inner quirks, characteristics, and nuances that made Holmes the woman she is today and gives viewers an inside look at how she and her company crashed and burned.

Where to Stream: Hulu

Related: Why Black Folks Are Obsessed With the New Documentary, ‘You Can See Everything’

Speaking of crash and burn, the infamous Fyre Festival turned out to be perfect fodder for this documentary. In the same way that Holmes defrauded investors, the folks in charge of this 2017 festival also manipulated attendees to pay high prices for a mediocre, trash event. Check this one out!

Where to Stream: Netflix

Seeing Holmes’ failed attempt at starting a lucrative business definitely puts you in the mood to watch stories of other founders who couldn’t maintain their success, and lured people into what they were building under false pretenses and chaos.

Where to Stream: Hulu/Disney+

Celebrity vegan restaurateur Sarma Melngailis is the focus of this Netflix documentary. But sadly, it traces her New York restaurant empire as it takes a bizarre turn after she becomes involved with a mysterious man who makes too-good-to-be-true promises. What follows is a story of manipulation, bad financial decisions, and a relationship that spirals into an unbelievable criminal scandal.

Where to Stream: Netflix

Starring Octavia Spencer and Gabrielle Union, the first season of “Truth Be Told” follows a true-crime podcaster who reopens controversial criminal cases in search for answers that may have been overlooked the first time around. Much like “You Can See Everything,” the Apple TV+ series plays with perception, unreliable narrators, and the uncomfortable possibility that the truth isn’t always what it initially appears to be.

Where to Stream: Apple TV

Building on her popular podcast of the same name, comedian Laci Mosley takes viewers on a deep dive into some of the wildest scams, schemes, and con artists operating across the country. From Ponzi schemes to fake royalty and religious grifters, this series is perfect for anyone who loves watching the truth unravel behind a convincing hustle!

Where to Stream: Hulu/Freeform

This show will infuriate you, fair warning. In “I Care A Lot,” a professional guardian exploits the legal system by convincing courts to place elderly people under her care—right before draining their finances. It’s a truly twisted look at how someone can use a seemingly legitimate business to run a calculated scam, all while hiding behind a polished public image. That rings a bell, doesn’t it?

Where to Stream: Netflix

Starring Jennifer Lopez and Keke Palmer and more, “Hustlers” centers on a group of New York City strippers who devise an elaborate scheme to scam wealthy Wall Street clients out of thousands of dollars. Similar to Holmes’ quest, this movie raises questions about greed, survival, loyalty, and just how far people will go to get what they feel they’re owed.

Where to Stream: Hulu

Now this one might seem a little left of center, but hear us out! While “Snowfall” follows the rise of the crack cocaine epidemic, drug dealers, law enforcement, and the CIA members who played a role in it—similar to “You Can See Everything”—it explores the power structures, questionable motives, and sneaky decisions that allow people to build empires while leaving devastation in their wake.

Where to Stream: Hulu

( Author’s Note: This one is one of my favorite films) . In “The Wolf of Wall Street,” Leonardo DiCaprio stars as a stockbroker who builds a multimillion-dollar empire through shady business practices, financial fraud, and some seriously questionable decisions. It’s a wild look at Wall Street excess and what happens when making money and preserving your ego becomes more important than having a moral compass.

Where to Stream: Paramount +/ Prime Video (with an add-on)

Now you guys lowkey should’ve seen this one coming! “Inventing Anna” tells the infamous story of Anna Sorkin, a.k.a. Anna Delvey—the wannabe socialite who convinced New York’s wealthy elite that she was a German heiress with a fortune to her name. From luxury hotels to five-figure vacations, her elaborate grift is a fascinating look at how far a convincing lie can take someone before reality comes knocking.

Where to Stream: Netflix

In “The Girl From Plainville,” Elle Fanning stars as Michelle Carter, a woman at the center of a controversial case involving her boyfriend, Conrad Roy III, and the text messages that preceded his death by suicide. If you love questions of accountability, manipulation, and how much of someone’s story we can actually believe—this one should be right up your alley.

Where to Stream: Netflix

While this one is a scripted series as opposed to a documentary, “Dopesick” is still in the same vein as “You Can See Everything” because it exposes the dangerous consequences of corporate greed, powerful people, manipulating the truth, and a business built on a whole lot of deception in the pharmaceutical space.

Where to Stream: Hulu/Disney+

scraped.title: Chloe Bailey’s Christmas Music Video Sparks Backlash
scraped.h1: Why Fans Say Chloe Bailey’s New Christmas Music Video Belongs on the Naughty List
scraped.body_text:
Black News, Opinions, Politics and Culture

Critics have said Chloe Bailey’s choice to dress up like a child misses the mark of what makes a sexy holiday tune tasteful, like Eartha Kitt’s 1953 hit “Santa Baby.”

By

Samantha Chery

Published

US singer-songwriter Chloe Bailey attends the MTV Video Music Awards at the Peacock Theater in Los Angeles, California on September 27, 2026. (Photo by LISA O’CONNOR / AFP via Getty Images)

Chloe Bailey has found herself the subject of red-hot crossfire for green-lighting a sexy holiday-themed visualizer in which her outfits resemble a child Christmas character. Now, the Black internet is weighing in.

To view this video please enable JavaScript.

Viewers are pointing out what they called an unsettling juxtaposition in Bailey’s self-directed music video for “MRS CLAUS DONT HAVE 2 KNOW.” In the visual, she sings that her “cookie’s out for you, time to devour” because she’s “been a good girl all year”—all while clad in a velvety red Christmas cape, red hair bows, and Who-inspired hair and makeup. “Come give your sugar some spice / Don’t havе to say, it’s all right / Now watch me ride it all night,” she continues in the chorus.

Cheeky Christmas songs aren’t taboo . Eartha Kitt’s iconic song, “Santa Baby,” achieved commercial success when it was originally released in 1953. Generations later, it has been cemented as a Christmas classic despite its suggestive lyrics. So why the stark contrast in public reaction now? People defending Bailey have pointed out that Sabrina Carpenter hasn’t received nearly as much backlash for her recent innuendo-filled track “A Nonsense Christmas.”

While the premise of “MRS CLAUS DONT HAVE 2 KNOW” ignited widespread criticism online, even dedicated fans conceded that the art direction for Bailey’s latest music video missed the mark. Critics have taken the biggest issue with her apparent nod to Cindy Lou Who , the girl from “How the Grinch Stole Christmas!” who helped the Grinch’s heart grow during the holidays.

RELATED: Chloe Bailey Takes On the World While Defending Her Sister Halle From Pregnancy Rumors

On social media, viewers questioned why Bailey opted to dress as the innocent, underage character in the video instead of an adult Christmas character like Whoville bombshell Martha May Whovier. The rest of the video, which shows Bailey hugging a teddy bear and riding a small rocking horse, has further baffled people.

Ever since the Chloe x Halle singer embarked on her solo music career with the stage name Chlöe, she’s been unapologetic about sexual expression in her artistry. After her 2021 breakout hit “Have Mercy” topped Billboard’s Mainstream R&B/Hip-Hop Airplay chart, she’s seen success with similar songs like “Treat Me,” “Better Than She Can” and “Body Do.” Many of her fans argue that the frequent attacks she’s received for “trying too hard” or “doing too much” in her performances are unwarranted, and they’ve compared her energy and performance quality to a younger Beyoncé.

Despite the backlash, Bailey hasn’t let the controversy or critique deter her. She captioned a clip with her new song: “yknow you that 🐶 when you cause all this conversation.”

Singer Lizzo came to Bailey’s defense on Sunday, writing in an X post that “Chloë Bailey is giving us exactly what we need. She has endless artistic talent and is a lighting rod for our attention, like every mega star from any generations past. I hope she keeps creating and building a legacy that will have impact and value in our lives & in music culture.” That same day, Bailey replied to Lizzo on X: “thank you so much. i promise i will keep building!!! NEVA stopping.”

thank you so much. i promise i will keep building!!! NEVA stopping ✨ https://t.co/Oa0ynJdBy0

Bailey, 28, continues to promote her song with steamy Christmas-inspired photos even “Regina George would approve” of.

scraped.title: Katie Miller Walks Away from Podcast She Built After Leaving Elon Musk as Husband Stephen Miller Climbs to Power
scraped.description: An era has ended after a historic GOP defeat at the ballot box. Donald Trump suffered a major setback in the 2026 midterm elections that's affecting other
scraped.author: Yohance Kyles
scraped.h1: Katie Miller Walks Away from Podcast She Built After Leaving Elon Musk as Husband Stephen Miller Climbs to Power
scraped.body_text:
An era has ended after a historic GOP defeat at the ballot box.

Donald Trump suffered a major setback in the 2026 midterm elections that’s affecting other families in his inner circle. The Democratic Party won control of the House of Representatives and the Senate in nationwide landslides.

In the wake of those embarrassing losses, Trump decided to dump Susie Wiles as White House chief of staff. Trump appointed Stephen Miller to run White House operations and serve as the president’s gatekeeper.

Miller, 41, earned a promotion from deputy chief of staff, apparently impacting his spouse’s job as a media figure.

His wife, Katie Miller , spent the weekend playing defense for Trump’s inner circle. She proved that loyalty in the MAGA world can become a full-time job. But she made a career move that could change everything.

Trump Asked Stephen Miller’s Wife How She Liked Working with Elon Musk, and Her Answer Made Social Media Lose It

‘Oh, That’s Why You Said This’: Katie Miller’s Ex Before Marriage to Stephen Miller Comes Roaring Back After an Old Relationship Resurfaces

She made the shocking decision to shut down “The Katie Miller podcast.”

“I make every decision based on what’s best for my children and our family. With [Stephen] taking on this new role for President Trump, I’ve decided to stop recording new podcast episodes,” Katie, 35, tweeted on Nov. 8.

She said, “Nothing is more important than raising our four kids. While I’ve loved the podcast, the time commitment is too great, and now is the time to step away. I’ll be cheering President Trump and his team on from outside the administration.”

Launched in 2025, the podcast gave Trump allies a platform to promote his MAGA agenda.

Past guests include Vice President JD Vance , DOGE co-head Elon Musk, Secretary of State Marco Rubio, FBI Director Kash Patel, House Speaker Mike Johnson, and rapper Nicki Minaj.

The YouTube version of Katie’s podcast has racked up over 7.8 million views since July 2025. But some of the most recent episodes struggled to amass over 10,000 views.

Instead of sympathy over its end, Katie faced widespread ridicule online.

“I’m sure all 9 listeners are devastated,” one X user mockingly responded. A second poster jokingly wondered, “Awe, so sorry, is daddy making you quit? Did you embarrass the narcissistic sociopath?”

“Because NOBODY was watching is more like the truth! Riding on the coattails of your hubs never works!” exclaimed a critic of the Millers.

Other commenters zeroed in on Katie admitting she did not cast a ballot in this year’s election.

“I did not vote in Virginia because in Virginia when you vote, you dox your own address, and so I prefer my own safety and security over giving that up,” Miller explained while speaking with CBS News host Norah O’Donnell on election night.

One X user sarcastically wrote, “You didn’t even bother to f—g vote, but sure, you’re a patriot for pausing a podcast.” Another wondered, “No more recorded evidence, for files later?”

With her husband stepping into the role of Trump’s right-hand man, Katie has more time to handle political battles on social media.

The mother of four has already jumped in to defend Stephen against Democratic Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed of Illinois.

“[Trump] decides to hire the most broken man to continue to run the most dysfunctional White House that we’ve seen,” El-Sayed, 42, said about Miller’s new appointment on the “This Week” news program.

“I don’t know what Stephen Miller has actually contributed to our culture, our society, in any real way, except to make us more angry and stoke the worst kind of fear and vitriol,” he continued.

Katie clapped back, sharing a photograph of her husband playing with their children in front of a Teddy Roosevelt statue. The caption read , “Stephen has contributed far more to America at 41 than Abdul El-Sayed will in a lifetime.”

Stephen was not the only Trump ally Katie felt the need to shield from public criticism. “Saturday Night Live” also drew the wrath of the University of Florida graduate over a sketch mocking Musk, 55.

Comedian Jeremy Culhane played a fictional Musk in the “Weekend Update” segment. His character promoted a new feature for Musk’s Grok artificial intelligence assistant. The segment asked Grok to deliver an “epic vulgar roast” of the world’s richest man and father of 14 children.

“Elon Musk, you’re the worst thing South Africa has ever done. When you’re on TV, it feels like an episode of ‘Hate on the Spectrum.’ Maybe if you have 100 more kids, one of them will talk to you,” the AI voice responded.

Katie took offense to the joke. The cable news regular ran to X to call Musk a “devoted dad who prioritizes time with his kids.”

Furthermore, she complained that the ‘SNL’ bit was a “political hit job masquerading under the banner of comedy.” In another defense of Elon, she said, “In the end, the only people the Democrats will hurt are the American people.”

On Nov. 9, Katie took aim at Variety magazine for resharing a 2020 article about her and Stephen’s lives, “that starts when I was 13.”

Her podcast may be over, but she’s shown no sign of slowing down in defending her husband’s allies.

Katie may be stepping away from the microphone, but she clearly isn’t stepping away from MAGA’s defense squad.

With Stephen moving closer to Trump’s inner circle, she may have traded podcast drama for a full-time front-row seat to the political circus.

I make every decision based on what’s best for my children and our family. With @StephenM taking on this new role for President Trump, I’ve decided to stop recording new podcast episodes. Nothing is more important than raising our four kids. While I’ve loved the podcast, the…

We hope this story was worth your time. For over 14 years, Atlanta Black Star has stayed Black-owned and independently run. We didn't get here by waiting on ad budgets that were never built to prioritize us. Our readers did that.

Corporate support for Black media has always been thin. Outlets like ours get roughly 1% of the $170 billion spent on U.S. advertising each year, and that margin is shrinking further as advertisers walk back the DEI-linked commitments they made in 2020. That's the backdrop. It's not why we're asking.

The wider picture isn't any steadier. Newspaper ad revenue has fallen more than 80% since 2005, and local newsrooms are closing at a rate of roughly two a week nationwide. When outlets go under, it's rarely the ones built to center a Black perspective from the ground up that get to stick around.

We know a request for support isn't why you came here. But without readers choosing to fund this work directly, the depth of reporting we can do at home and abroad shrinks along with everyone else's. If you're not in a position to give, that doesn't change how much we value you as a reader.

If you are able to, a recurring contribution does more for us than a single one-time gift, because it lets us plan the next investigation instead of just the next invoice. It takes about 30 seconds, no long form, no account. Thank you for continuing to support independent journalism and freedom of the press.

Atlanta Black Star is a narrative company. We publish narratives intentionally and specifically to enlighten and transform the world.

Contact us: [email protected]

scraped.title: ‘We’ll See’: Chuck Schumer Faces Claims He Left Angie Nixon Behind Over Israel Stance After She Nearly Flipped Florida
scraped.description: Angie Nixon’s account of asking Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer for campaign help and receiving a noncommittal response is fueling criticism after
scraped.author: Nyamekye Daniel
scraped.h1: ‘We’ll See’: Chuck Schumer Faces Claims He Left Angie Nixon Behind Over Israel Stance After She Nearly Flipped Florida
scraped.body_text:
Angie Nixon ’s account of asking Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer for campaign help and receiving a noncommittal response is fueling criticism after her narrow Florida Senate loss, with critics questioning whether Democratic leaders failed to fully support the Black progressive.

Nixon described the conversation before the election. She told MS NOW that the Senate Democratic leader offered no firm commitment when she asked for help funding her race.

“When I did speak with Sen. Schumer on the phone, it was basically a ‘we will see,’” Nixon said during an appearance on “Clock It with Symone & Eugene.” “He’s going to look into it. That’s what was said, that he’s going to look into it.”

Asked whether national Democrats were doing enough, she gave a blunt assessment: “They could do a lot more.”

Nixon ultimately lost to Republican Sen. Ashley Moody by roughly three percentage points. Her performance far outpaced Democrats’ previous two Senate campaigns in Florida. It raised questions about whether stronger support could have helped close the gap.

Social media criticism links the party’s hesitation to Nixon’s support for Palestinian rights and opposition to aid for Israel. The commentary accuses Schumer of leaving her without the help she needed.

‘Mind Your Business!’: Nosy Neighbors Try to School Black Contractor on His Own Job and Get Unexpected Reality Check Carlee Russell Claims Hairstylist Who Took Payment Dispute Public Is Using Her Name to Boost Business, Left Her with Injuries

“This is basically the indictment that disqualifies Schumer from the majority leader position,” one critic wrote. “He has got to go!!! Shame on them! Ethics committee needs to investigate them both [Schumer and House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries] for accepting foreign money for their campaign, which is illegal by the way!” another person added.

The backlash comes as Schumer faces calls for new leadership from several incoming Democratic senators and activists critical of AIPAC’s influence. But those challenges reflect broader frustrations with the party’s direction.

Still, available reporting does not establish that her position on Israel drove his decisions. It also shows Schumer provided some support after the conversation Nixon described.

Punchbowl News reported Oct. 20 that Schumer was hosting a virtual fundraiser for Nixon. He had also contributed through his political action committee, met with her in Washington, and spoken with her ahead of the event.

That reporting undercuts claims that he never offered any help. It leaves unresolved whether the support matched the opportunity Nixon and her supporters believed existed. Moody outraised Nixon by around $3.2 million more, according to the most recent available figures.

Nixon offered her own explanations for the party’s reluctance during the MS NOW interview. She first pointed to her politics.

“I am a progressive Democrat, and I am very vocal about putting working-class families first. I am very vocal about progressive values,” she said. “So I think that may be the main issue.”

She also suggested that former Vice President Kamala Harris’ presidential defeat had made party leaders and donors more hesitant to back Black women.

“Folks are a little gun-shy because, unfortunately, Vice President [Kamala] Harris lost as a Black woman, and so people are being very hesitant in terms of funding Black women, especially in the South.”

The Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee pushed back on Nixon’s criticism.

“We are excited about opportunities to expand the map further and monitor all races closely, including Florida, where Angie Nixon is running an energetic campaign,” a spokesperson told MS NOW.

At the time, the committee had established a joint fundraising committee with Nixon’s campaign, and she had attended a fundraiser. The DSCC did not donate any money to Nixon’s campaign, according to The American Prospect.

A senior Democratic aide also disputed the suggestion that leaders were withholding support because Nixon was progressive. The aide pointed to investments in Michigan, where progressive Abdul El-Sayed was the Democratic Senate nominee.

The aide said improving Democratic prospects had expanded the number of races the party could contest, forcing difficult spending decisions with limited resources. Florida presented an expensive challenge in a state Republicans had increasingly dominated.

Nixon’s result nevertheless challenged expectations about how competitive a Democrat could be there.

Democrat Debbie Mucarsel-Powell lost her Florida Senate race by 13 points in 2024. Two years earlier, Val Demings lost by 16 points, WLRN reported . Nixon’s roughly three-point defeat marked a substantial improvement, though it does not establish that additional funding would have delivered a victory.

She had already made her differences with party leaders over Gaza clear. In 2023, Nixon introduced a Florida House ceasefire resolution that drew criticism within her own party, according to New York magazine.

Following her defeat, Nixon announced the Never Scared PAC to develop leaders and organize working people across Florida.

“We were never scared to take on the political establishment,” she said to WLRN, “and we’re not scared of the work ahead.”

The wider picture isn't any steadier. Newspaper ad revenue has fallen more than 80% since 2005, and local newsrooms are closing at a rate of roughly two a week nationwide. When outlets go under, it's rarely the ones built to center a Black perspective from the ground up that get to stick around.

scraped.title: 'Divorce In Black' Star Cory Hardrict Drops Cryptic Post About Peace and Privacy That Has Fans Wondering If There’s a New Woman in His Life
scraped.description: For Cory Hardrict, change and adjustment have been major themes in his life for the last few years. ​In 2022, his then-wife Tia Mowry announced they were
scraped.author: Danielle Jones
scraped.h1: ‘Divorce In Black’ Star Cory Hardrict Drops Cryptic Post About Peace and Privacy That Has Fans Wondering If There’s a New Woman in His Life
scraped.body_text:
For Cory Hardrict , change and adjustment have been major themes in his life for the last few years.

​In 2022, his then-wife Tia Mowry announced they were splitting after 14 years of marriage and two kids. Now they live apart and co-parent their 15-year-old son and 8-year-old daughter, Cree and Cairo Hardrict.

While the “Sister, Sister” star has been more vocal about her life’s evolution on social media, Hardrict has been more circumspect about his life after divorce.

​Though his Nov. 9 birthday post to himself was overall positive, some followers presumed he was subtly talking about his Mowry.

​The newly turned 47-year-old shared an image of himself wearing a pink fur coat, partially zipped down to show his bare chest.

‘Tia Come Look at This’: Cory Hardrict Debuts a Dramatic Glow Up That Has Fans Hoping His Ex Tia Mowry Spins the Block

‘Cory Must Be Having a Hard Time’: Tia Mowry Sets New Boundaries with Ex Cory Hardrict After Going Public with Her First Boyfriend Since Divorce Hardrict wore layered gold chains in the picture and had his hands placed in his pockets as he looked off to the side. Under the photo, he shared a message about growth.

​He began, “Another year of Life, a stronger purpose, a Heart full of gratitude.

Sometimes the loudest growth happens in silence. Life has taught me that not every road is easy, not every season makes sense, And somewhere between the falling and the rising, you discover who you truly are.”

​The actor added that “Privacy is power. I’ve learned to appreciate the quiet, protect my peace, and that growth doesn’t always need an audience.”

​Along with a gracious heart, Hardrict said he’s walking into this next year of life with “deeper faith” and a “strong sense of purpose.”

“I’m not walking into this new year trying to prove who I am. I’m walking into it becoming who God has called me to be,” he continued.

​Many fans kept up the positive spirit in the comments by not only wishing Hardrict a “Happy Birthday,” but also applauding his caption.

​However, some followers thought there was more to read between the lines, suspect ing his message was directed at Mowry.

​One fan who thought so said, “Basically what he’s saying is he’s allowing her to play herself which is exactly what she’s doing with that young punk she’s flaunting on the internet so when Corey pops up with his new woman, better not none of yall say [nothing].”

​Another person who took it upon themselves to shade Mowry said, “Happy birthday Cory. Great for moving in silence bc Tia out here rolling around on the ground like a look sick six graded.”

​But one person defended Mowry. One person typed, “Everything don’t have to be about Tia. He talking about his own personal growth. They’ve moved on so let’s move on with them folks… keep up.”

​After spending her first couple of years of divorce in solitude, Mowry introduced the world to her new man, Javon’e Williams, to the world in May.

She first hinted at a relationship by dropping a photo dump of herself and a man’s feet in February. She later said she was “in love” during an interview at the Essence Black Women in Hollywood in March.

​Paparazzi photos caught the couple walking hand in hand and sharing a kiss in Los Angeles in April. The next month, the actress shared her first post with Williams, who is an educator, artist, and about 12 years Mowry’s junior.

​Now they both occasionally post about each other online, sharing special moments. In her latest post with him, she smiled while lying in his arms. She captioned the post, “Black love.”

​The second fan who made fun of Mowry “rolling around on the ground” was referring to her Oct. 29 post where the words “Don’t fall for the younger guy. Me:” floated above her as she lay out in the grass, wearing a skirt and sweater.

​“Yall said stay grounded, here I am,” she wrote in the caption, hinting that she is happy in her relationship.

​As for Hardrict, he isn’t publicly in a relationship with anyone right now.

​Last year, when journalist Touré asked if he was dating , Hardrict said, “I believe dating is something that I would be open for. It just got to feel like I’m not chasing it; it’s kind of coming to me. And right now, it’s like I’m still trying to figure out who I am right now.”

Since their divorce was finalized in 2023, Mowry has also shared messages about growth and peace.

​She candidly admitted that after becoming an actress, a mom, and a wife, she realized she “didn’t actually know who [she] was underneath all of those roles.”

​Mowry said her rediscovery process included “therapy,” “neuroscience,” “meditation,” “prayer,” and “community.”

​In the end, she learned “that peace and joy are something you choose.”

A post shared by Cory Hardrict (@coryhardrict)

scraped.title: Rangers’ role must be built into biodiversity conservation commitments (commentary)
scraped.description: Environmental science and conservation news
scraped.author: Erik Hoffner
scraped.h1: Rangers’ role must be built into biodiversity conservation commitments (commentary)
scraped.body_text:
If you liked this story, share it with other people.

At the COP17 biodiversity summit in Yerevan, Armenia, conservation leaders from around the world gathered to conduct the first global review of progress toward the ambitious goals adopted in 2022 under the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework (KMGBF). Among them is Target 3 , a commitment to effectively and equitably conserving 30% of the planet’s land and waters by 2030 (30×30).

But achieving a shift in land and sea management on this scale will depend on something in conservation policy that has too often been overlooked: a large portion of the people responsible for actually making it happen — rangers. For years, the world has debated how much land to protect and how much money to invest in nature, while paying far less attention to the workforce needed to turn those commitments into results. Rangers play a central role in managing protected and conserved areas and delivering commitments on biodiversity, climate, and land degradation. Yet our latest research shows they remain largely absent from the policies and frameworks meant to guide this work.

Why rangers matter

Effective conservation requires people on the ground who can monitor ecosystems, manage protected and conserved areas, and ensure that rules governing their use are upheld. The International Ranger Federation defines a ranger as any person, regardless of title — wildlife warden, forest guard, game scout, marine ranger, park guard, and others — working in situ to safeguard nature and preserve cultural and historical heritage. Rangers work under many different governance systems and are not limited to government employees. They may serve national or local authorities, be members of Indigenous or local communities (IPLCs), or work for organizations responsible for conservation.

One global survey found that 36% of rangers are local people, employed within a 20-kilometer (12-mile) radius of where they live and drawn from local communities. From monitoring wildlife and restoring habitats to managing human-wildlife conflict and responding to climate-related threats, rangers perform a wide range of essential conservation duties that make them a critical workforce for the health of the planet. In many places, that work is carried out in partnership with IPLCs, including through locally determined rules and conservation practices.

Yet rangers face major challenges in carrying out their duties. Nearly half of rangers across Asia, Africa, and Latin America lack adequate equipment, training, and staffing. An average of two rangers die in the line of duty each week. Rangers face risks from confrontations with organized wildlife criminal networks, human-wildlife conflict, and natural disasters. Climate change adds to these pressures. Yet many still lack basic protection: only 47% have life or health insurance. This creates alarming instability at the foundation of global conservation.

Governments and donors are investing heavily in expanding protected and conserved areas while underinvesting in a portion of the people required to manage them. That imbalance puts conservation outcomes at risk.

Risk of paper parks

The key word in Target 3 is “effectively.” Conservation history offers an important lesson: designating protected and conserved areas does not automatically translate into conservation outcomes. Around the world, many sites are protected on paper but lack the staffing, resources, and management capacity needed to deliver effective conservation.

The success of 30×30 will depend not only on how many hectares we designate as protected and how many dollars we invest in them, but on how effectively those places are managed. And management depends on people. The three fundamental pillars of any enterprise are capital, space, and labor. By decoupling capital and space from labor, environmental governance risks proliferating poorly managed paper parks. Without sufficient staffing that is well trained, equipped, responsible, and accountable, even the best-designed conservation strategy will struggle to achieve its objectives.

The conservation community often describes biodiversity loss as a financing challenge. While funding undoubtedly matters, it is also a workforce challenge. Without the necessary people to manage these areas, those investments are at risk.

Missing piece

Despite being central to the success of biodiversity conservation, rangers have not been a major focus of policies and funding plans for biodiversity. One global estimate put annual global spending at around $24 billion, which is less than 40% of the roughly $68 billion needed each year to adequately manage the existing system. Rangers are not adequately recognized for their contributions to these policies and plans, or valued as a profession and an investment.

Our research — supported by the Universal Ranger Support Alliance (URSA), the International Ranger Federation (IRF), and others — highlights this critical gap. We reviewed 45 global and national conservation policy documents, including 21 National Biodiversity Strategies and Action Plans (NBSAPs). The disparity was stark: references to area appeared roughly 70 times more often than references to rangers, while finance appeared more than 80 times as often. Even in national biodiversity plans, where rangers received somewhat more attention, they remained far less visible than either finance or area.

The contrast is even clearer when conservation is compared with public health. In the World Health Organization and UNICEF’s “ Operational Framework for Primary Health Care ,” health workers — including nurses, midwives, doctors, and paramedics — are mentioned about 48 times as often as rangers are in the conservation documents we reviewed.

The conservation sector can learn from public health frameworks that routinely emphasize the importance of doctors, nurses, midwives, community health workers, and health care systems. Policymakers understand that hospitals alone do not save lives. Health outcomes depend on the people delivering services, but conservation frameworks do not currently apply the same logic. We celebrate protected and conserved areas, ambitious targets and innovative finance mechanisms, but we often overlook the workforce required to implement them.

Bringing the workforce back into policy

Addressing this “ranger blind spot” is essential to achieving global conservation goals, particularly the 30×30 target. Future policies governing protected and conserved areas (PCAs) must formally recognize the people responsible for managing them and ensure they have the staffing, resources, and institutional support to succeed.

The workforce must also be part of core negotiations for future conventions and targets, including innovative finance mechanisms such as carbon and biodiversity credits, which also fail to address it adequately. The same emphasis is needed at the national level, including in countries’ legal and constitutional frameworks and policies.

Equally important is the adoption of established standards for ranger training, professional conduct, pay, and working conditions. These should promote respect for human rights, equip rangers with the skills and support to do their jobs safely and effectively, and hold them accountable for their actions. They must also address gender inequality and extend appropriate recognition and protections to rangers employed by IPLCs and other nongovernmental organizations.

In the weeks following Yerevan and in preparation for the next meetings of the Convention on Biological Diversity, delegates should picture a gleaming new hospital with no doctors or nurses. Without the people needed to make it work, even the best-equipped hospital cannot deliver care.

The same is true of conservation. If rangers are not recognized in policy, they cannot be properly planned for or funded, and without them, even the most ambitious conservation targets will fall short.

Madhu Rao chairs the IUCN World Commission on Protected Areas (WCPA). Nik Sekhran formerly served as director for sustainable development at the UNDP and has more than 25 years of conservation and sustainable development experience across Africa, Asia, Oceania, and Latin America.

Citation:

Timmins, H. L., Churcher, J., Singh, R., Stolton, S., Acharya, K. P., Yadav, S. P., … Slade, J. (2026). The “ranger blindspot”: Global policy and implementation gaps. Ambio . doi: 10.1007/s13280-026-02496-7

scraped.description: Environmental science and conservation news
scraped.h1: Peruvian authorities seize more than 3,000 tarantulas from suspected European traffickers
scraped.body_text:
If you liked this story, share it with other people.

Peruvian customs agents and authorities from the National Forest and Wildlife Service (SERFOR) announced on Nov. 4, 2026, that they seized more than 3,000 tarantulas at the Jorge Chávez International Airport in Lima. The spiders were hidden inside socks put in luggage destined for Germany.

The alleged traffickers, two German citizens and a Polish national, include a “renowned tarantula researcher” who was not publicly identified, authorities said in a press release . They were reportedly detained by the Peruvian National Police’s environmental crimes unit and face criminal proceedings.

“Concealed in socks inside three suitcases, we found the tarantulas in different stages of life, from eggs and hatchlings to adults,” said Cora Suárez, a forest and wildlife control technician at SERFOR in a press release . “The traffickers made a meticulous selection to include different species, some of which have not yet been described by science.”

These arachnids, some vividly colored, were collected from the wild allegedly to be sold as exotic pets to collectors and for research. They came from across Peru, including Junín, Loreto, Cajamarca, Cusco and La Libertad, authorities said.

The seized spiders include members of the genus Pamphobeteus which includes some of the largest spiders in the world and are sold online for as much as 60 pounds ($80) each. Blue bird eaters ( Thrixopelma lagunas ), which can fetch 40 pounds ($53) online, were also confiscated along with several new-to-science spiders. Antikuna sp. was only described in 2021, and some species of Avicularia have not yet been scientifically described, according to Peruvian authorities.

The Bolivian blue leg bird eater ( Pamphobeteus antinous ), which was also seized, is listed as vulnerable to extinction on the list of threatened wildlife in Peru and is protected nationally. However, none of the seized species are internationally protected under CITES, the global wildlife treaty.

Authorities are still identifying the crawlies, and once that is complete, they will be housed in an “authorized breeding center,” the release said.

The seizure highlights a growing global trend in smuggling invertebrates from the wild for the exotic pet trade — from rare and protected ants to invasive cockroaches and venomous scorpions .

Current regulations in most countries, including the EU, allow for a smuggled species to be legally sold even if removing it from the wild broke national regulations in the native country — a loophole experts say must be closed.

“This is just another example of smuggling a non-CITES protected species, but caught in violation of national law in the country of origin,” Sandra Altherr told Mongabay. Altherr is from the German NGO Pro Wildlife , which documents such cases of “stolen wildlife” to Europe violating national regulations. “This is a pattern that we have observed again and again: If they were not seized they could have been legally imported to the EU, due to a legal gap . This means a lower legal risk for the smugglers but with high profit.”

Banner image: One of the seized tarantulas. Image courtesy of SERFOR.

scraped.title: Thick smog shrouds New Delhi after Diwali firecrackers add to seasonal pollution
scraped.description: Environmental science and conservation news
scraped.h1: Thick smog shrouds New Delhi after Diwali firecrackers add to seasonal pollution
scraped.body_text:
If you liked this story, share it with other people.

NEW DELHI (AP) — A thick blanket of smog shrouded India’s capital Monday after firecrackers lit up the skies over New Delhi during Diwali celebrations , compounding dangerously high pollution levels and intensifying the seasonal air pollution crisis that grips the city every year.

Despite restrictions on fireworks, residents in New Delhi celebrated the Hindu festival of lights with firecrackers on Sunday evening, releasing smoke and fine particulate matter into the atmosphere. The air quality index exceeded 350 in several parts of the capital on Monday morning, reaching the severe category and posing significant health risks.

Monitoring stations across the city recorded similarly alarming levels, while visibility deteriorated as a gray haze blanketed streets and high-rise buildings.

India’s Supreme Court in October had sought to limit Diwali pollution by restricting conventional firecrackers and allowing only approved “green firecrackers” under specified conditions for three-hour windows on Saturday and Sunday. The crackers produce fewer emissions but are not pollution-free. They still release particulate matter and other pollutants, adding to the city’s already hazardous air.

Isyad, a New Delhi resident who uses one name, said the worsening smog was taking a toll on his health.

“Because of the pollution there is irritation in the throat and itching in the eyes,” he said.

New Delhi and its metropolitan region, home to more than 30 million people, regularly rank among the world’s most polluted areas during winter. Pollution worsens as Diwali fireworks coincide with cooler weather and smoke from crop-residue fires in neighboring states of Punjab and Haryana.

After harvesting rice, farmers often burn leftover stalks to clear their fields for the next planting season. The smoke drifts toward New Delhi, adding to pollution from vehicles, industries, construction dust and other local sources.

The problem becomes particularly acute in late October and November, when cooler temperatures, low wind speeds and stagnant atmospheric conditions prevent pollutants from dispersing. The result is a thick haze that can linger over the capital and surrounding areas for days.

Authorities in New Delhi have implemented a set of measures to curb pollution, which include limits on construction activity and restrictions on diesel generators, while courts have sough restrictions on firecrackers. But the measures have not prevented the return of severe pollution each year.

Environmentalists say long-term solutions, such as cleaner energy and stricter controls on vehicle emissions, are needed to prevent the annual crisis.

Shweta Narayan, a public health expert at the Global Climate and Health Alliance, described the government’s response so far as “knee-jerk” and “temporary.”

“A lot of interventions happen only because the government is pressured or pushed in a corner to do something,” she said.

By Rishi Lekhi, Associated Press

scraped.title: Heat and high water: Floods pockmarked southern U.S. states during one of the hottest Octobers on record » Yale Climate Connections
scraped.description: The Four Corners area was especially hard hit by relentless rounds of heavy rain, while record-high tides sloshed onto coastlines in California and Florida.
scraped.author: Bob Henson
scraped.h1: Heat and high water: Floods pockmarked southern U.S. states during one of the hottest Octobers on record
scraped.body_text:
Yale Climate Connections

October 2026 was the fourth warmest in 132 years of recordkeeping for the contiguous 48 U.S. states, NOAA’s National Centers for Environmental Prediction reported on Monday . This was a microscopic cooldown at best in the wake of July, August, and September (plus March) all having set monthly U.S. heat records. The only warmer Octobers in U.S. history were in 1963, 2024, and 1947.

October’s U.S. warmth was remarkably uniform from coast to coast and from the Mexican to Canadian border, as shown in Fig. 1 above. Of the 48 contiguous states, all but two were warmer than average, and 32 of the 48 were “much above average”, meaning they ranked in the warmest 10% of all Octobers. No state had its warmest October, but Arkansas and Missouri saw their second-warmest October on record, and 12 other states were among the top five warmest.

Get news for people who love the planet. Sign up for our newsletters for the latest weather updates, tips, and inspiring stories

Although October wasn’t record-warm nationwide, the first 10 months of 2026 were the nation’s hottest Jan.-Oct. ever recorded. In fact, the 10-month average of 59.19°F was almost a full degree Fahrenheit warmer than the 58.34°F from Jan.-Oct. 2012. That’s a hefty margin for a nationally compiled long-term statistic like this.

Unless November and December are surprisingly chilly, 2026 appears destined to end up as the nation’s hottest year on record. This will happen if November and December together average at least 37°F – a threshold that’s been surpassed every year in this century except for 2013.

When pulled together for the nation as a whole, October wasn’t a standout month for precipitation: it came in as 51st-wettest across 132 years of data. However, Fig. 3 below suggests how much is hidden behind that number.

A total of 22 states were drier than average. Most dramatically, Mississippi had its 13th-driest October on record. Yet the overall extent of U.S. drought dropped notably in October. According to the U.S. Drought Monitor , the fraction of the contiguous U.S. covered by severe to exceptional drought decreased from around 31% on October 6 to around 23% on October 3.

Meanwhile, although just 11 states were wetter than average in October, these included most of the larger southwest and south-central states. Arizona, Colorado, Nevada, and Utah each had a top-ten-wettest October, as did Florida, largely due to torrential episodes of flooding rain that struck each state.

Colorado state climatologist Russ Schumacher referred to the Oct. 21-25 rains that struck normally arid regions such as the San Luis Valley as “ among the most extreme storms in state history ” and said the destruction has been “immense.” The Land Desk, a Substack feed that’s been covering the record Four Corners river crests extensively, noted one stark example : The Piedra River, a tributary of the San Juan River, hit streamflow rates more than twice as large as any others in data going back to 1964.

Among the region’s hardest-hit areas is the Navajo Nation, the largest sovereign tribal nation within U.S. borders. It covers most of northwest New Mexico and northeast Arizona, along with far southeast Utah, and includes some 173,000 residents. Multiple episodes of flood-inducing rainfall have hammered the region since mid-September, in many cases worsened by moisture carted inland from decaying hurricanes spawned by the Eastern Pacific’s record-busy tropical season. Many homes were damaged, and many roads remain mud-caked. In a TV interview , Navajo Nation President Buu Nygren said total damage will likely far exceed a $20 million fund established on October 30 to pay for road and home repairs and related equipment.

Disastrous flooding along the San Juan River in the Four Corners region. Here’s some of what I saw today in Shiprock, on the Navajo Nation in northwest New Mexico.

Another big problem in October was record- and near-record-high water levels along the coasts of southern California and Florida, driven by a mix of long-term warming and ocean expansion, persistent onshore winds, and astronomical “king tides” that are unusually large this autumn.

Among the landmarks set in October, as compiled by Jeff Masters:

Jeff Masters and Irene Sans contributed to this post.

items.title: Could skyscrapers be used as giant batteries?
items.summary: A startup wants to try it.

scraped.title: Could skyscrapers be used as giant batteries? » Yale Climate Connections
scraped.description: A startup wants to try it.
scraped.author: YCC Team
scraped.h1: Could skyscrapers be used as giant batteries?
scraped.body_text:
Yale Climate Connections

Transcript:

The architecture and engineering firm behind some of the world’s tallest skyscrapers has spun off a start-up that’s designing a new type of tall tower – one that stores energy like a giant battery.

Adam Semel is a partner at Skidmore, Owings & Merrill, which designed the Burj Khalifa and Willis Tower. And he’s co-founder and CEO of Ourea Energy .

He says Ourea’s design for the so-called GravityBank uses an approach called pumped hydropower.

A pumped hydro facility stores excess energy by using it to pump water from a low-elevation reservoir to a higher one.

Semel: “That difference in height allows us to use the power of gravity to do the work for us.”

When energy is needed, the water is released. It rushes down, spins a turbine, and generates electricity.

Typically, pumped hydro facilities are built in remote mountainous areas.

But Ourea plans to use the same approach in a tall tower with water tanks at the top and bottom. So it can be deployed almost anywhere – like near solar or wind farms or in cities where power demand is high.

Semel: “And more than 60% of the structure is actually empty, so we can start to think about putting other things in there.”

… like apartments, offices, or hotels.

So one day, these energy-storing towers could help shape city skylines.

Reporting credit: Ethan Freedman / ChavoBart Digital Media

scraped.title: Q&A: What is the Belém-Antalya mechanism for a ‘just transition’? - Carbon Brief
scraped.description: Carbon Brief looks at where the idea for the BAM came from, how it could support just transitions and what to expect from COP31
scraped.author: Molly Lempriere
scraped.h1: Q&A: What is the Belém-Antalya mechanism for a ‘just transition’?
scraped.body_text:
One of the key expected outcomes from the upcoming COP31 climate summit in Antalya, Turkey, is the launch of a “just transition mechanism”.

This follows years of calls from civil society to support a “ just transition ” as countries shift towards low-emissions energy systems and away from fossil fuels.

At the COP30 UN climate talks last year in the Brazilian city of Belém parties agreed to establish a “mechanism” to support this goal, called the “Belém-Antalya mechanism” (BAM).

Groups that have championed the BAM want it to act as a central hub on just transitions, providing support for workers and communities around the world.

However, the details of exactly what the much-touted BAM will consist of remain vague, with developed and developing countries disagreeing about its functions and purpose.

Disagreements continued at the UN climate talks in Bonn in June 2026, including on the crucial question of how the BAM will be financed.

Here, Carbon Brief looks at where the idea for the BAM came from, how it could support just transitions and what to expect from COP31.

A “ just transition ” is the idea that workers and communities should be supported in the shift to a low-carbon economy. It is a central principle behind the idea of climate justice .

Often, the term refers to those linked to the fossil-fuel industry, but it can also refer to transitions taking place in agriculture , heavy industry and various other sectors.

The concept originated in the 1980s, when US labour unions forged alliances with environmental justice groups. It has since become a key part of international climate discussions.

The preamble to the 2015 Paris Agreement includes a commitment to “tak[e] into account the imperatives of a just transition of the workforce and the creation of decent work and quality jobs in accordance with nationally defined development priorities”.

Bert De Wel , policy officer at the International Trade Union Confederation (ITUC), tells Carbon Brief:

“The labour movement is very happy with the wide audience and broad political support that the concept has received since its inception in the 1980s. The inclusion in the Paris Agreement, with the reference to the creation of decent work and quality jobs was a milestone for the movement. While other demands have been added…we continue to stress the labour dimension as being central to the concept.”

Three years after the creation of the Paris Agreement, at COP24 in the former coal-mining city of Katowice, the Polish presidency highlighted the issue of just transitions.

The need for carbon-cutting policies to ensure “a just transition of the workforce” that creates “decent work and quality jobs” was included in the “ Silesia declaration ”, issued by the presidency during the first week of COP24.

While the declaration was only signed by 50 countries – roughly a quarter of the parties at the summit – it was still “noted” in the final COP text .

This helped to drive momentum behind the idea, culminating in formal agreement at COP27 in Egypt to launch a “ work programme on just transition ” (JTWP).

De Wel says the establishment of the JTWP was a “major step forward” that allowed parties to “speak about just transition in more concrete terms”.

In the years since, negotiators have worked to flesh out the JTWP, with disagreements between parties about what its purpose should be.

Broadly, developed countries would like it to focus on domestic workforces, while some nations want a more global outlook, including support for transitions in developing countries.

The JTWP has proved a challenging negotiating space, with talks at the COP29 summit in 2024 closing without an agreement, in what one observer dubbed a “betrayal”.

However, despite these frustrations, parties at COP30 in Brazil agreed to establish a new institutional mechanism on just transitions, which has become widely known as the BAM. The move was hailed as a “ victory ” by civil society.

In the run-up to COP30, civil society began to push for the establishment of an “institutional arrangement” that would move work under the JTWP from talk into action.

(This was originally called the “Belém action mechanism” by civil society groups, who subsequently updated this to the “Belém-Antalya mechanism” following the outcome at COP30. However, in the JTWP text agreed at COP30 it is only described as a “mechanism”, sometimes also referred to as the “just transition mechanism”.)

Anabella Rosemberg , senior advisor on just transition at NGO umbrella group Climate Action Network (CAN) International, tells Carbon Brief:

“The idea of the mechanism emerged from the collaboration of civil society, trade unions, feminist groups, youth and Indigenous peoples in the UNFCCC.

“It was clear that the kind of activities being run under the JTWP – two dialogues a year and one ministerial – would not support the delivery of just-transition strategies on the ground, so a new approach was developed to get words into action.”

Following the inception of the idea, civil society did “tonnes of stuff to boost it up the agenda”, Dr Leon Sealey-Huggins , a senior campaigner at the charity War on Want , tells Carbon Brief.

This ranged from presenting demands and proposals to different constituents, organising joint letters and writing policy papers, all the way through to designing logos, creating memes and even a song .

These efforts ultimately paid off: during the Bonn climate negotiations in June 2025, one draft text included the idea for a new institutional arrangement. One of the options in the draft text was for a “toolbox, guidance framework, global platform, technical assistance network [or] mechanism”.

This inclusion was broadly welcomed as a “big win” for civil society groups, although parties acknowledged that more needed to be done to flesh out the idea.

Going into COP30, civil society groups continued to push the idea of creating a BAM, with protests, banners and badges visible around the venue.

Early in negotiations, the G77 and China – a large coalition of developing countries at UN climate talks – put forward their own proposal for a just transition “mechanism”. This, they suggested, could provide technical assistance, support international cooperation and help to foster partnerships in an effort to address implementation gaps.

Their proposal faced initial pushback from developed-country parties including Norway, the UK and others, who opposed it due to concerns that it would duplicate existing systems and require additional funding.

Developed countries also opposed the use of the term “ mechanism ”, with the EU suggesting an “action plan” as a potential alternative. Nevertheless, the creation of a “mechanism” was included in the final draft text on the JTWP.

This text was formally approved during the COP30 closing plenary to extended applause from many in the hall.

In a statement at the time, Chiara Martinelli, director at CAN Europe, welcomed the decision:

“Delivering BAM was a major civil society win. It creates a coordinated institutional home to drive forward progress on the just transition.”

The decision to develop the mechanism included a request for parties to work over the subsequent year – through to COP31 – on a plan to get things started.

According to civil society, the BAM could help tackle the fractured just-transition landscape by centralising resources and helping to overcome a number of barriers.

Speaking to Carbon Brief, Rosemberg says the just-transition space “lacks coordination and the right kind of support and is quite disconnected from climate action imperatives”. She adds:

“The BAM can play a role in bringing those [people] trying to make just transition happen together, identify gaps and barriers, foster cooperation and accelerate support.”

Civil society has put forward a number of proposals likely to inform the structure of the BAM. Most consist of a mechanism with three parts, which would encompass and expand upon the work that is currently being carried out under the JTWP.

One proposal by a coalition of five NGOs suggests the mechanism is formed of a steering body, a “knowledge arm” and an “implementation arm”.

The steering body would coordinate the work of the two arms of the BAM, including deciding the topics that should be discussed under the ongoing JTWP, which will continue to feature in climate negotiations. They suggest the body would recommend topics that require negotiation when “gaps that require political guidance are identified”.

Their proposal is illustrated in the infographic below, showing the steering body acting as a central hub for work within the BAM.

The final part of the BAM, the “implementation arm”, would act as a hub to enable and coordinate technical, financial and knowledge-based assistance for those pursuing a just transition.

Rosemberg says the vision of civil society is for work to go “beyond negotiators’ dialogues”. She says the BAM could enable the organisation of a “matchmaking platform” to provide support faster, as well as dedicated groups to identify and mobilise financial resources. She adds:

“Finally, through bottom-up identification of barriers, the BAM can also allow a discussion on enabling just transition that is informed by practitioners. The BAM can show that implementation does not necessarily mean taking issues outside of the UNFCCC.”

A separate proposal for the structure of the BAM from the Global Campaign to Demand Climate Justice (DCJ) – a separate coalition of NGOs – similarly proposes three elements. These would be: coordination and coherence; knowledge generation; and international cooperation and support.

Sealey-Huggins, who is affiliated with DCJ, notes:

“If it works in practice, what we’ll see is a cascade of just-transition policies implemented across countries, across sectors in a unifying, transformational moment for justice-centered climate action, and that will be the key to unlocking the transition that’s been missing so far.”

Another proposal for the BAM comes from the Grantham Institute at the London School of Economics. It suggests the three functions of the mechanism should be capacity-building, technical assistance and knowledge-sharing, but it recommends a dual-arm structure comprising a policy arm and an operational arm.

De Wel tells Carbon Brief that while there is “rather broad consensus on the functions”, parties are pushing in “very different directions” on how the BAM will be set up.

Within UN climate negotiations, some parties have raised concerns about the potential cost of the mechanism.

The push to launch the BAM comes at a time when the UNFCCC itself is facing a funding gap , following the US withdrawal . Several other parties have also delayed or reduced their contributions, in response to changes in domestic priorities.

This has led to the UNFCCC cancelling events and not filling vacated positions, as the organisation struggles to carry out its existing functions.

Membership

As such, some parties have expressed hesitancy about creating another mechanism under the remit of the UNFCCC, which also requires funding. However, proponents of the BAM argue that the costs of running it would be minimal .

Rosemberg tells Carbon Brief that the BAM represents “an opportunity to streamline and make efficient use of public resources”. She adds:

“The mechanism does not necessarily require the creation of a costly new institution. Instead, it can leverage existing climate-finance channels and philanthropy.”

She adds that a “similar body” to the potential mechanism, the Climate Technology Centre and Network , costs less than $10m a year. Rosemberg notes that this is “not an impossible amount to be found if there is political will to make just transition happen”.

De Wel notes that the mechanism will build on existing work inside the UNFCCC and out, including the International Labour Organization’s “ just transition policy gateway ”. He further emphasises that “we’re clearly not asking for a new [just-transition] fund, we want all climate finance to be just-transition proof”.

Alongside highlighting the potential efficiencies of the BAM design, many have argued that the potential benefits are well worth the cost of the new mechanism, with Sealey-Huggins telling Carbon Brief:

“The cost to the [BAM] secretariat pales in comparison to the potential benefit of the action.”

Despite the “victory” in Belém of agreeing to set up the new just-transition mechanism, climate negotiations in Bonn in June 2026 quickly hit sticking points.

While Bonn did ultimately agree on a “skeleton” draft text to send forward for further negotiations at COP31, many details still need to be agreed in Antalya for the BAM to start functioning.

De Wel cautions that a “swift approval of the agenda of COP31 allowing parties to start the negotiations” is “crucial”. He adds:

“We can’t lose any time, there is so much work that needs to be done on [just transition]. Then we need a constructive approach by the major country blocs. If one of them starts playing tactical games, then it will be lost.”

In a submission to the UNFCCC earlier this year, CAN called for a series of measures to get the BAM up and running. This includes calling for a decision to be made on a first face-to-face meeting of a “just-transition committee” – a core part of the mechanism in the group’s proposal – to be held in April 2027.

Ahead of COP31, negotiating groups such as the Alliance of Small Island States (AOSIS), the least developed countries (LDCs) and the African group expressed support for the mechanism and called for it to be focused on implementation.

The EU also supported the launch of the mechanism, but along with other parties cautioned that it should be complementary to the JTWP.

While no submissions opposed the creation of the mechanism, groups such as LDCs called for a focus on “means of implementation” – commonly understood as finance – highlighting it is likely to continue to be a key point of discussion in the upcoming summit.

Sealey-Huggins tells Carbon Brief what his “pie in the sky best-case scenario vision” for the outcome at COP31 would look like. He continues:

“G77 and China make the case again that the mechanism must be equally resourced. It must be well-designed. It must include people’s participation. It must address the barriers to implementation of just transition. It must facilitate the means of implementation. It must ensure justice at the very heart of climate action.

“And then it’s agreed and it’s implemented immediately. So this work begins straight after Antalya to start forming committees and other bodies that can undertake the implementation.”

However, Rosemberg cautions that there is still a “question mark [remaining over] the level of ambition of the [COP31] presidencies, who need to move from simply talking about establishing any [just-transition] mechanism to engaging parties, so that we get a mechanism that is fit for purpose”.

scraped.body_text:
