By Canary Media

Canary Media

This article is part of the series “Power Struggle: Building Clean Energy in Rural America.” Read more.

9 November 2026

CHRISTIANA , Tenn. — As sunlight fell between the gaps in flinty November clouds, I found myself impressed by the quietness of the lawn mowers in a Middle Tennessee solar field. Instead of the obnoxious roar of diesel engines, they just produced an occasional moo.

Six months ago, Tennessee’s largest solar developer, Silicon Ranch, channeled its nomenclature and brought cattle to this 3 . 25 -megawatt solar project. The 15 -member herd rotates among 15 paddocks marked out by simple electrical wire, munching Bermuda grass that grows in the shade of the panels, which sit on higher-than-usual steel piles. The cows seem amenable to the situation, judging by how plump they’ve become in that short time.

This is the first commercially viable utility-scale project combining solar and cattle farming in the U.S., according to Silicon Ranch (an earlier 2 -MW project from AES sought to prove the concept in Massachusetts’ community solar market). If the model takes off, it could boost revenues for farmers while producing more clean, cheap electricity in regions that don’t have a lot of wide-open, unused spaces to develop. And it might remedy a major obstacle to ongoing solar growth.

The U.S. builds more solar installations than any other form of power plant these days. But the industry’s upstart success story is colliding with a bulwark of local opposition from communities that don’t like the idea of this relatively new technology taking over their landscapes. One way around that conflict is to use the same land for solar power and agriculture.

The solar industry already has adopted sheep grazing as a mainstream approach to cutting grass at project sites, while supporting a secondary market for domestic meat. Researchers have also found that grasses and some crops grow better in the shade of photovoltaic panels than in an open field. But the burgeoning ​ “ agrivoltaics ” sector has almost entirely excluded one of the major pillars of American agriculture — cattle ranching — for the simple reason that rambunctious bovines could easily wreck the carefully calibrated solar panels.

“ If you’re designing a solar facility that is suitable for cattle grazing, it generally requires more specific and unique design,” said Terry Jennings, principal team leader for renewable energy at the Electric Power Research Institute, a nonprofit that studies the electricity sector. That ​ “ adds cost to the overall project, which is challenging for utilities or electric power companies.” But he noted that research on this topic is still pretty new, and a lot of uncertainty remains around ​ “ how cows really interact with the solar panels.”

To go mainstream, and help meet America’s soaring demand for electricity with more carbon-free generation, cattle-friendly solar needs to appeal to large-scale developers who rigorously maximize megawatt-hours generated per acre while minimizing cost.

In the countryside about 45 minutes southeast of its Nashville headquarters, Silicon Ranch has found that the commonly understood challenges for cattle grazing alongside solar were a little overblown.

“ I thought it would work — I just didn’t think it would work this well,” said Loran Shallenberger, a longtime farmer who now runs Silicon Ranch’s Regenerative Energy and Agrivoltaics division.

Shallenberger’s team designed a system to withstand the presence of cows at a minimal cost premium. Even for this first utility-scale installation, they held the cost of fortifying the arrays to just 3 % over the standard design, Shallenberger said, and nonetheless sold the power to local utility Middle Tennessee Electric for cheaper than the wholesale rates it was paying to the Tennessee Valley Authority.

As far as climate solutions go, this doesn’t deal with the immense greenhouse gas emissions that arise from cow burps and farts; many climate activists want to phase out commercial cattle entirely for that reason, or for animal welfare motivations. But as long as cattle production is widespread in the U.S., doubling-booking pastureland for solar production could produce more clean energy in a space-constrained world.

Clever innovations in solar rarely go anywhere. Entrepreneurs might drive a news cycle with ​ “ solar freakin’ roadways ” or solar roof tiles , but to succeed in this market requires ruthless efficiency and streamlined repeatability. Throwing a herd of cattle into the mix does not, at first glance, conform to that industrial mantra.

Shallenberger had ready answers for my journalistic skepticism.

On the hardware side, after studying the matter with a grant from the Department of Energy, Silicon Ranch resisted the urge to build towering solar supports, which would require even more steel underground to ensure stability. Instead, the company developed and patented a system dubbed CattleTracker : mildly elevated steel piles with customized controls for the tracker, supplied by NextPower.

Trackers typically rotate throughout the day to eke every last bit of electricity out of the sun’s arc. At the Christiana solar farm, the trackers in that active paddock go into ​ “ graze mode,” which limits their rotation from a maximum tilt of 60 degrees from the ground to 20 or 30 degrees — so the lower edges of the panels remain above the animals’ heads. At a regular solar farm, the low end of a fully tilted solar panel is 24 inches off the ground, but I could walk beneath the CattleTracker system with just a little ducking.

The cattle do their part to make this work.

Shallenberger bought a herd of Murray Greys , an Australian breed that ​ “ are widely regarded as having uniformly calm dispositions” — the kind of cattle you could grab a beer with. That docility makes them less inclined to damage solar equipment or charge at a technician who’s checking out the site. They helpfully don’t grow very tall, and they have ​ “ consistently good carcasses,” industry lingo for qualities like high meat-to-bone ratio and well-marbled steaks. Plus, Murray Greys can fatten up on grass alone, so they could be ready for market in 18 to 24 months without a stop at a feedlot.

I saw one specimen scratch its head against a steel pile, but none of the herd could reach the sensitive equipment. The concern is that if the cows hit the solar panels hard enough, they could cause microfractures that over time diminish electricity production. Shallenberger said that if he were building the site now, he’d drop the pile height by 6 or 12 inches, because it turned out to be a little overbuilt.

The nationwide cattle inventory has fallen to its lowest point in 75 years , as prolonged drought hits the vast arid ranchland of the Western states. Rising beef prices have incentivized ranchers in wetter parts of the country to get into the game. Tennessee, Shallenberger told me, is already one of the biggest cattle states east of the Mississippi.

Abundant local water sources aside, this was a particularly harsh summer in Tennessee.

“ If you’ve ever been out in a cattle ranch and there’s a single tree out in the middle of the pasture, they’re going to congregate around it for shade,” Silicon Ranch Chief Commercial Officer Matt Beasley said from his office in Nashville. Consequently, the cattle perform better under the shelter of solar arrays than in the open range, he noted.

The solar canopy also protects the grasses, keeping them green and dewy, even as nearby fields blanch and crisp in the sunlight. Shallanberger rotates the herd every few days, a key tenet of regenerative farming philosophy, so they munch on fresh grass while the rest of the field grows back. They move through all 15 paddocks in about 45 days; if the site relied on mechanical mowers, they’d trim every 45 days, too.

That cycle also keeps the grasses from shading the panels or messing with the machinery.

Vegetation management is one of the most significant costs for solar plant maintenance in the Southeast, Shallenberger said. In the first six months, the cattle took care of about 75 % of the mowing — he had to bring in conventional equipment for some woody weeds that the cattle don’t care for. Once the pasture is more established, the herd could handle up to 95 % of the site’s mowing needs.

“ The team had this anthem: It’s got to be good for the land, good for the animal, and good for the solar,” Beasley said. ​ “ If it’s not good for all three, we’re not doing it.”

CattleTracker does reduce solar production slightly, given the limited tilt on the small subset of panels in the active paddock. Silicon Ranch is happy to trade that loss for the drastic reduction in major operational costs. The herd doesn’t need the hands-on attention that sheep require; a camera watches to ensure they have enough water, and an attendant visits twice a week to move paddocks and perform a wellness check.

Cattle-friendly solar’s bucolic charm is undeniable, but its impact hinges on widespread adoption.

“ The hope is that it can be mainstream,” Shallenberger said. He pointed out that it doesn’t take more labor to open a paddock gate for 100 animals as opposed to 10 , so the operational cost savings should scale favorably for larger solar projects.

Silicon Ranch expanded its use of sheep for pruning solar fields after its executives got to know Will Harris , a leader in the regenerative farming movement whose land neighbors a Silicon Ranch project in southwest Georgia. The developer acquired 400 ewes in 2022 and has grown the herd to 5 , 000 through selective breeding. Silicon Ranch also partners with 14 sheep-farming families across six states for managed grazing.

“ In the back of our minds has always been, Can we replicate this with cattle?” said Beasley. Now, the team is scouring its development portfolio for sites to deploy CattleTracker. Silicon Ranch builds projects up to 300 MW , and hasn’t found any reason that cattle couldn’t graze at that scale.

“ It’s not too long down the road that you’ll be able to try a beef burger or a steak raised on Silicon Ranch land,” Beasley said.

The company’s agrarian activities play a strategic role beyond diversifying revenue streams. Local opposition to solar projects has become ​ “ the most existential threat to deploying solar projects in this country,” Beasley said. Wild theories about solar keep spreading on social media, and the popular revolt against AI data center construction can spill over to resisting the renewable energy source, even though rows of panels don’t come with the same downsides, like immense water use, inescapable droning noise, and fossil-fueled generator fumes.

Beasley said that approaching rural communities as an authentic agribusiness — one committed to long-term stewardship of the land it owns — helps address a lot of their concerns.

“ We’re not taking land out of ag production. In fact, most of the land that we’re buying wasn’t in ag production before, and we’re going to put it into ag production,” he said. ​ “ We’re going to raise grass-fed meats, and we’re going to hire local shepherds or partner with local farming families.”

The cows will release methane, making the site a bigger greenhouse gas emitter than it would be without the herd. But journalist Michael Grunwald, who literally wrote the book on how to feed the earth without exacerbating climate change, said the cattle-solar approach is a good example of the ​ “ sustainable intensification” that he wants to see more of.

“ This acre that was already making a lot of energy, now it’s also making some beef,” he explained. ​ “ Somewhere else you can take a beef acre and make it carbon storage or something.”

At scale, this dual use could produce much-needed food while easing pressure to convert other landscapes for cattle grazing. And half the ag land in the U.S. is dedicated to growing beef, Grunwald added. That leaves the hypothetical cattle-voltaics market plenty of room to grow.

scraped.description: A low-income Baltimore homeowner got help from a nonprofit to install electric appliances and a solar array. She’s very thankful for the “blessings.”
scraped.h1: After a gas furnace leak, this retiree went all-electric — for free
scraped.body_text:

Next Upcoming

By Canary Media

Canary Media

9 November 2026

A few years ago, a gas leak from Sherry Frazier’s furnace forced her and her daughter out of Frazier’s Baltimore home.

“ Oh, it was awful,” said Frazier, a retired educator who worked with students with disabilities in Baltimore public schools. ​ “ We had bad headaches and were kind of dizzy, wobbly on our feet.” Had they stayed any longer, she fears they would’ve ended up in the hospital.

But now, her home will never pose that danger again.

Frazier’s house has become an all-electric haven with solar panels pumping out power, thanks to an extensive retrofit coordinated by Baltimore-based Green & Healthy Homes Initiative ( GHHI ), a public health nonprofit that directly serves Baltimore and Providence, Rhode Island, and advises about 50 cities and 12 states.

“ I feel a lot safer in the home [and] my utility bill for heat and air conditioning is much lower,” Frazier said.

Frazier’s abode is among the thousands that GHHI has worked on in its efforts to ensure healthier living conditions for those who can’t repair, weatherize , or decarbonize their homes themselves. Fossil-fueled water heaters, furnaces, clothes dryers, and stoves emit toxic pollutants that pose health risks, including asthma, cancer , heart attacks, and carbon monoxide poisoning — the symptoms of which Frazier and her daughter experienced.

In addition to replacing these noxious appliances, GHHI first tackles any necessary underlying home repairs. The U.S. housing stock is the oldest it’s ever been — with a median age of 44 years — and older homes are most likely to harbor health and safety hazards, such as rotten roofs, mold, lead, and asbestos.

GHHI deals with all those problems. And in low-income homes that qualify for its services, the nonprofit covers the entire cost, tapping funding from local and federal sources, such as Maryland’s EmPOWER program and the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development’s Office of Lead Hazard Control and Healthy Housing, as well as private funding from philanthropic organizations and healthcare and utility companies.

GHHI was founded in Baltimore with the original goal of halting lead poisoning in children. But the organization learned ​ “ very quickly” that it needed ​ “ to think holistically about housing,” Ruth Ann Norton, GHHI ’s president and CEO , said in a July webinar .

“ We want to address the same things that we … originally saw in lead [pipes and paint], in carbon-emitting appliances and homes,” Norton added. ​ “ That is, the impairment that it causes for neurological development, for reproductive development, and for long-term health.”

Allow marketing cookies to load the newsletter signup form.

Frazier was referred to GHHI when she turned to a different nonprofit for aid to get a new fridge.

“ I just had no idea of the many blessings that I was about to receive,” Frazier said.

During an assessment in November 2022 , GHHI discovered Frazier’s home had a leaky roof, poor insulation, and other hazards besides those emitted by her gas appliances. By the end of March 2023 , the nonprofit had orchestrated a raft of improvements: Workers replaced the roof; installed carpet tread and handrails on the stairs as well as a shower seat; caulked air gaps; added fiberglass insulation to the attic; and swapped out every gas appliance with an electric one, upgrading the electrical panel to accommodate the switch. Among the electric devices new to Frazier — the heat pump system , induction stove , electric-resistance dryer, and heat-pump water heater — GHHI also put in a new fridge.

In July 2025 , GHHI added the pièce de clean energy résistance: a rooftop solar array. Altogether, the retrofit totaled about $ 73 , 200 , at no cost to Frazier.

“ I felt like it was a godsend,” she said. ​ “ I inquired about a refrigerator, and I wind up getting more done to my home than I ever dreamed.”

Since the overhaul, Frazier’s bills have gone down by hundreds of dollars annually, GHHI found. When she was still using gas in the year before the retrofit, they averaged about $ 230 per month. Electrification saved her $ 9 per month . And going solar has brought her bills down to around $ 170 per month as of May.

The road to lower energy bills had a big bump, though. In the biting winter of 2024 – 2025 , the second year Frazier had the heat pump, her costs were spiking up to about $ 600 and $ 700 in December and January, which puzzled the GHHI team.

But after checking out the appliance, GHHI quickly diagnosed the problem.

It turned out that Frazier had been putting a cover over the heat pump to protect it from snow, just as she had done with her old air-conditioning unit. That was preventing the heat pump from drawing in enough air to harvest heat, which was triggering much less energy-efficient electric-resistance backup heating.

Now, Frazier leaves the heat pump unencumbered year-round. ​ “ You’re never too old to learn new things,” she said.

Frazier has been raving about GHHI ’s retrofit program to friends and family, as well as patiently explaining the health reasons behind it.

“ I was really surprised that when I shared information with my friends who are seniors like myself, they were not aware of the dangers of gas,” Frazier said. ​ “ I make it my business to spread the word.”

scraped.title: Trump Calls Immigration Policy “Too Tough,” Then Promotes Stephen Miller
scraped.description: The new chief of staff has shaped some of Trump’s most draconian immigration policies, including family separation.
scraped.author: Shireen Akram-Boshar
scraped.h1: Trump Calls Immigration Policy “Too Tough,” Then Promotes Stephen Miller
scraped.body_text:
The new chief of staff has shaped some of Trump’s most draconian immigration policies, including family separation.

Support justice-driven, accurate and transparent news — make a quick donation to Truthout today!

In a “60 Minutes” interview that aired on Sunday evening , President Donald Trump admitted that Republicans’ massive defeats in the midterm elections resulted from widespread frustration with the war on Iran, as well as his immigration policies.

Reiterating that he “was not on the ballot” — as if to suggest that support would have been higher for him personally — Trump said that Americans “didn’t like the war” and “the fact that gasoline went up,” claiming he “had it down at a low” prior to launching the war. In Trump’s assessment, public opposition to his war on Iran is reducible to gasoline prices.

Trump also stated that Republicans’ massive losses during the midterm elections were due to “a great dislike, incredibly, for Israel” — characterizing growing opposition to the U.S.’s relationship with the genocidal state as mere “dislike.”

Trump then said that his immigration policies may have also affected the midterms, and that he may have been “too tough.”

“I think I got an A+ for closing up the border,” he said. “I get very high marks for getting the bad ones out. But I get hurt because we also took people that had good jobs, that created one violation, or breaking of the law, and that was that they came into the country illegally. And there’s a large group of people [that] think they should be allowed to stay.”

“So you think your deportation policy went too far?” asked CBS News ’s Ross Douthat.

“I think it might be too tough,” Trump replied.

In the interview, Trump acknowledged a central contradiction in his administration: that he is caught between the priorities of his far right base, who “would like everybody taken out” [of the country], and the general population, which rejects his brutal policies.

Shortly after his “60 Minutes” interview on Friday, Trump announced that he was promoting political advisor Stephen Miller to White House chief of staff — suggesting that he does not, in fact, plan to soften his approach to immigration enforcement. Miller is known as the hardline, white nationalist architect of Trump’s mass deportation policies, including his policy of family separation.

Over the past year of his administration, Trump has been forced to temper the most overt aspects of his immigration crackdown, after Immigration and Customs Enforcement’s (ICE) brutal “Operation Metro Surge” in the Twin Cities brought about widespread resistance, particularly after immigration agents killed Minneapolis residents Renee Good and Alex Pretti. As a result of widespread opposition, mass protests, and even a general strike in the Twin Cities, Trump replaced Department of Homeland Security (DHS) Secretary Kristi Noem with Markwayne Mullin, who promised that DHS operations would be less visible and stay out of the headlines.

While subsequent ICE operations have not been as brazen as that of Operation Metro Surge, the agency’s strategy has not fundamentally changed. In New York City in July and August, ICE’s “ Operation Rotten Apple ” resulted in the arrests of some 2,200 people — more than the amount detained by ICE during Operation Metro Surge earlier in the year. The New York City operation, however, managed to evade the same level of pushback, as ICE agents remained less visible, arriving in unmarked cars and detaining and disappearing people quickly, before resistance could emerge.

Trump also stated in the “60 Minutes” interview that he would work with Democrats on immigration. Indeed, his categorization of immigrants as either hard workers or “rough,” “drug dealers” and “killers” echoes rhetoric that has been key to both Republicans’ and Democrats’ approach to immigration since the 1980s — and to bipartisan “comprehensive immigration reform” policies that have increasingly ceded ground to the right.

While voters rejected Trump’s policies in the midterm elections, it is little surprise that Trump has offered to work with Democrats on immigration, as they do not represent an actual alternative to the criminalization, deportation, and precarity offered to undocumented immigrants and asylum seekers.

Meanwhile, the president’s promotion of Miller suggests that even as Trump’s own popularity falls, his aggressive deportation tactics are likely to continue.

scraped.body_text:
The alarming climate report was released on the opening day of the COP31 climate conference.

The alarming climate report was released on the opening day of the COP31 climate conference.

Support justice-driven, accurate and transparent news — make a quick donation to Truthout today!

The Earth is hurtling deeper into a climate emergency , with 2026 on track to be one of the four hottest years ever recorded, ocean temperatures and sea levels hitting record highs, and glacier melt accelerating at an alarming pace, according to a report released Monday by the World Meteorological Organization as the United Nations Climate Change Conference kicked off in Türkiye.

The WMO’s “ State of the Climate” report “shows that the past 12 years have individually been the warmest on record, with the past four years being the top four,” according to a summary of the 25-page publication.

WMO further noted that “the global average surface temperature for January – September 2026 was about 1.47°C above the preindustrial average,” or right on the brink of the 1.5°C of warming beyond which scientists say the risks of catastrophic and potentially irreversible climate impacts increase substantially.

2026 is on track to be one of 4 warmest years on record, marked by exceptional global temperatures, melting ice, rising sea levels, and a very strong El Niño that will unleash more heat & extreme weather into 2027.New WMO #StateOfClimate #COP31 Update↪️ https://bit.ly/stateofclimateCOP31pr

UN scientists said last month that the Paris Agreement’s goal of limiting warming to 1.5°C this century is no longer achievable without an overshoot.

The 1.47°C figure “is likely to rise through the end of the year because of the warming effect of El Niño, which has been intensifying since August and is expected to be the strongest on record by December,” the report’s summary states. El Niño is the warm phase of a pattern in the Pacific Ocean whose impact on disrupts weather, ecosystems, and economies.

According to WMO:

Earth’s energy imbalance is rising… The imbalance reached its highest level since monitoring began, as greenhouse gases trap unprecedented amounts of heat and upset the equilibrium between incoming energy from the sun and outgoing energy. The ocean absorbs 90% of this excess heat, and 2026 is on track to be the 10th successive year of record ocean warmth.

Sea level is the highest on record, and sea-surface temperatures hit monthly records during 2026. The long-term retreat of glaciers continuesv— the annual mass loss of ice in 2025 would have filled five Olympic pools every second of the year. Freshwater storage has been dwindling since 2014.

“Extreme weather has made headlines throughout 2026. Behind the headlines and the statistics in this report are people who suffered the loss of loved ones, threats to their health and safety, flooded homes, failed harvests, empty shelves, lack of water , and choking air,” WMO Secretary General Celeste Saulo said in the report.

“The past four years have been the warmest in the 177-year observational record, and the heat in the oceans is breaking records for the 10th year in a row,” she continued. “The ongoing El Niño is forecast to be one of the strongest on record, and the heat it releases from the ocean will continue to fuel high temperatures and extreme weather into 2027.”

“El Niño and indeed the state of the global climate in 2026 gives new meaning to the phrase off the charts,” Saulo added. “El Niño doesn’t add new heat to the planet. It releases heat from the ocean, which is the warmest ever measured. There is simply more heat available to release.”

Indeed, climate scientists are warning that the planet is closer than previously thought to tipping points leading to hellish feedback loops and a “hothouse Earth.”

United Nations Secretary-General António Guterres responded to the WMO report in a statement, saying: “We have entered a new age of climate extremes. A supersized El Niño is colliding with a planet already superheated by manmade climate change. Climate records keep falling. The human costs keep rising. And those least responsible are suffering first and worst.”

“Leaders must get serious by cutting emissions faster, accelerating a just transition from fossil fuels , and delivering the finance and protection vulnerable countries need,” he added.

The “State of the Climate” report was released on the first day of the UN summit, or COP31, in Antalya, Türkiye. Advocacy groups warned that world leaders must commit to phase out fossil fuels, finance a just transition to a post-carbon economy, and protect vulnerable populations from worsening climate harms.

“No country can confront this crisis alone. Those who have contributed least to global warming are often suffering the greatest harms. COP31 must deliver collective action that reflects this profound injustice,” Marta Schaaf, Amnesty International’s program director for climate, environmental and social justice , and corporate accountability, said Monday.

“ The world is not running out of climate warnings. It is running out of excuses,” she continued. “After more than 30 years of climate negotiations, governments can no longer hide behind promises of future action or avoid confronting their fossil fuel industry allies.”

“The climate crisis is not a failure of knowledge, but a failure of political courage,” Schaaf added. “It is time to break the stranglehold of corporate power over political decision-making and end the fossil fuel era before it ends us.”

Oil Change International global policy senior strategist Shady Khalil asserted that “we know what needs to happen. Governments must stop fossil fuel expansion, plan a fair phaseout of existing production, and invest public money in renewable energy and economic diversification.”

“Wealthy countries must move first and fastest and provide the finance needed to make this transition possible everywhere,” he added.

scraped.author: Ciudong Ng
scraped.h1: Aggression Against Iran Has Been Bipartisan. Will Midterm Results Change That?
scraped.body_text:
The US and Israel repeatedly subverted Iranian sovereignty, threatened nuclear war, and destabilized the Middle East.

Truthout is a vital news source and a living history of political struggle. If you think our work is valuable, support us with a donation of any size.

The Republican Party’s staggering losses in the November midterm elections have prompted speculation about the future of the U.S.-Israeli war against Iran, which is overwhelmingly unpopular with voters. Democratic leaders have portrayed President Donald Trump’s military offensive as an unconstitutional fiasco and an economic disaster driving inflation.

But their choreographed outrage conceals a long tradition of bipartisan support for aggression , which President Masoud Pezeshkian of Iran denounced in his UN address this September. For decades, the United States and Israel have referred to Iranians as terrorists, “but we are the victims of terrorists,” Pezeshkian underscored . His speech outlined a record of hypocrisy: U.S. and Israeli officials talk about peace, but plot to assassinate political leaders and negotiators . Most notably, both states command nuclear arsenals, yet impose debilitating sanctions on Iran’s atomic energy program.

As Pezeshkian emphasizes, the war is the latest episode in a turbulent history of energy and imperial assertion that contradicts U.S.-Israeli claims about proliferation risks and regional security. During the Cold War, Western powers shattered Iran’s democracy, before consolidating a brutal petromonarchy to guarantee access to its oil reserves. While undercutting Iranian energy sovereignty, they allowed Israel to become a nuclear-armed occupier, spreading dirty weapons and armed conflicts across the Middle East. This tangled history of oil and atoms is essential to understanding the war’s causes and contradictions, as two rogue states with thermonuclear weapons attack Iran under the pretext of nonproliferation.

Since the nineteenth century, Western powers have attempted to curb Iran’s sovereignty or seize its vast energy reserves. By 1914, Great Britain controlled its oil industry , after extorting concessions from the Iranian government. Over the following decades, the Anglo-Iranian Oil Company (AIOC) turned its refinery in the southwestern city of Abadan into the main energy supplier for the British Empire. Winston Churchill called the gushing wells “a prize from fairyland.” Yet AIOC officials warped Iran’s economic development by handpicking politicians and shamelessly exploiting workers. British personnel at Abadan lived in segregated splendor with swimming pools and servants, while local laborers inhabited parched slums.

After World War II, Iran attempted to improve its contract with the AIOC in order to raise government revenue and living standards. But company officials refused to compromise. In April 1951, Mohammad Mosaddegh became prime minister and initiated a series of ambitious reforms, which included nationalizing the oil industry .

Privately, the U.S. government lambasted the AIOC for behaving like a “typical nineteenth-century colonial exploiter,” while dealing “ineptly and disastrously” with Iran. Secretary of State Dean Acheson was scathing : “Never had so few lost so much so stupidly and so fast.” Nevertheless, U.S. leaders colluded with Britain to undermine nationalization. They feared that Mosaddegh’s policy set a destabilizing precedent , sapping British imperial power, upending the Cold War balance, and compromising Western control over strategic resources.

“I fought the fascists and Nazis,” one CIA adviser ruminated. “My lesson was that we were becoming just like them.”

Posing as a mediator, the State Department pressed Iranian leaders to make concessions, yet privately conceded that Britain’s demands were unreasonable. British negotiators advocated paying “lip service” to the principle of nationalization, while “keeping effective power … in our hands.” Ratcheting up pressure, the United States and Britain organized an oil embargo to suffocate Iran’s economy. Officials also bribed dozens of legislators , who physically assaulted Mosaddegh’s allies in parliament. And they launched a global propaganda campaign , pumping what one British operative called “a steady supply of suitable poison” into the press.

Mosaddegh held out until August 1953, when the CIA and British intelligence orchestrated a coup. From the shadows, foreign agents helped disloyal officers and paid rioters take Tehran, before assaulting the prime minister’s house. After a blistering shootout, Mosaddegh and his allies fled across his rooftop as his home dissolved into rubble. He would spend three years in solitary confinement and the rest of his life under house arrest.

Pressing their advantage, U.S. leaders broke Britain’s energy monopoly after the coup, securing the right to market 40 percent of Iranian oil. CIA Director Allen Dulles, whose law firm represented the AIOC , supervised a transition to unabashed authoritarian rule under Shah Mohammad Reza Pahlavi. The CIA bragged that it was “very active” in selecting parliamentary deputies, and the shah exclaimed to one American spymaster: “I owe my throne to God, my people, my army and to you!” Notoriously, U.S. agents helped establish the intelligence service, SAVAK, which tortured countless dissidents. “I fought the fascists and Nazis,” one CIA adviser ruminated . “My lesson was that we were becoming just like them.”

During the Mosaddegh administration, the United States and Britain portrayed Iran as a fanatical state tottering on disorder. Before international audiences, they fielded legal arguments opposing nationalization, claiming that Iranian leaders were hotheaded, breaking inviolable contracts, and flirting with communism. But the goal of U.S. and British stakeholders was always control: unfettered access to Iran’s bountiful oil and the suppression of demands for resource sovereignty across the Global South.

As Mosaddegh languished in prison, Israel launched a nuclear program that reflected the colonial double standards of Western energy policy. In July 1956, Egypt nationalized the Suez Canal, which French and British investors controlled. Outraged, Paris and London conspired with Tel Aviv to invade the Sinai Peninsula and retake the waterway. During secret talks, the diplomat Shimon Peres leveraged cooperation to secure French assistance for Israel’s atomic energy program. “I finalized,” Peres wrote in his memoirs , “an agreement for the building of a nuclear reactor at [the Israeli city of] Dimona.”

That October, the tripartite invasion of Egypt incensed both the Soviet Union and United States, which forced its Western allies to withdraw. Afterward, French Prime Minister Guy Mollet deepened his commitment to Israel’s nuclear program, portraying it as a consolation prize. “I owe them the bomb,” Mollet insisted . Within a decade, Western capital investment allowed Israel to join the nuclear club. Beersheba became a francophone enclave with 2,500 French citizens and Renault cars cruising its streets as guest workers constructed the Dimona plutonium plant.

Experts feared that the atom bomb would embolden Israeli aggression, undercut peace negotiations, and trigger a world war.

Meanwhile, both states exploited colonial Algeria as an arms range. Between 1960 and 1966, French authorities conducted nuclear tests in the Sahara, spreading radioactive fallout across North Africa while sharing their findings with Israeli observers and the Zionist state’s scientific establishment. The experiments spawned a toxic nightmare, reportedly poisoning 30,000 Algerians in 1962 alone.

Fearing nuclear weapons proliferation, U.S. President John F. Kennedy pressed Israeli leaders to accept inspections at Dimona. Yet Zionist activists succeeded in reducing them to a political charade. “I fought the strongest battle of my career to keep them from full inspection,” the lobbyist Abe Feinberg recalled . “I violently intervened … half a dozen times.” Under pressure, U.S. officials agreed to announce visits beforehand and forgo using their own testing equipment. Feinberg boasted that his political campaign turned inspections into “a scam job,” while secretly collecting funds for Israel’s nuclear weapons program from American Zionists.

In The Samson Option , journalist Seymour Hersh reveals that Israel went to extraordinary lengths to deceive inspectors. Before visits, the Israeli military covered paths and bunkers at Dimona with dirt and grass, relandscaping the complex to conceal its awesome scale. Officials also constructed a false control room with rigged computers, pretending to operate a modest 24-megawatt reactor. And an Israeli “cover up team” plugged information leaks . One member recalled scolding engineers who divulged secrets. “‘Listen, you mother-fucker, don’t answer that question,’” the official interjected in Hebrew. “The Americans would think I was translating.”

Privately, U.S. leaders suspected that Israel was building a bomb. Yet hostility toward the Arab powers, sympathy for Zionism, and electoral considerations encouraged them to tolerate its duplicity. Off the record, Kennedy was irate, confiding that Israeli “sons of bitches lie to me constantly about their nuclear capability.”

After acquiring nuclear capabilities, Tel Aviv invaded its Arab neighbors in June 1967, occupying the Sinai Peninsula, Gaza Strip, West Bank, and Golan Heights. Increasingly, the Pentagon regarded Israel as the world’s greatest proliferation threat . Experts feared that the atom bomb would embolden Israeli aggression, undercut peace negotiations, and trigger a world war. In his classic study, Israel and the Bomb , Avner Cohen unveiled a dangerous cycle , arguing that Washington boosted conventional arms shipments to reduce the appeal of nuclear weapons.

Anxieties peaked in 1968 when Secretary of Defense Clark Clifford sought Israel’s commitment to the Non-Proliferation Treaty in exchange for F-4 Phantom jets. After tense negotiations, the Israeli embassy again mobilized Feinberg to press President Lyndon B. Johnson’s hand. The maneuver worked. A tenacious lobbyist, Feinberg was also a major Democratic Party fundraiser with a direct line to Johnson, which he used to bypass the Pentagon.

“Clifford called Johnson and LBJ said, ‘Sell them anything they want,’” an aide to the senior U.S. negotiator claimed . He recalled that the secretary of defense was stunned, replying, “‘Mr. President, I don’t want to live in a world where the Israelis have nuclear weapons.’” Johnson simply told Clifford to not bother him anymore before hanging up.

Read together, the history of U.S. policy toward Iran and Israel offers surreal contrasts. Western empires crushed Mosaddegh’s attempt to achieve economic sovereignty, demolishing Iranian democracy in the process. Yet afterward, they helped Israel become a nuclear-armed occupier, while combating Arab nationalism. Repeatedly, they prioritized power over nonproliferation, opening a nuclear umbrella over the Middle East.

In October 1973, Clifford’s worst fears materialized, as Egypt and Syria launched a coordinated offensive to reclaim land that Israel had seized in 1967. Prime Minister Golda Meir’s government panicked, apparently mobilizing Israel’s nuclear arsenal. To calm Israel’s nerves, the U.S. government airlifted 22,318 tons of materiel to the Israeli military. According to Hersh’s reporting, Secretary of State Henry Kissinger told a colleague that Meir blackmailed him , implying that “if they didn’t get military equipment, and quickly, they might go nuclear.” As tempers flared, both Kissinger and Soviet leaders, who backed the Arab powers, engaged in nuclear brinkmanship , escalating the most dangerous standoff since the Cuban Missile Crisis.

Although averting Armageddon, American officials triggered an Arab energy embargo that boosted oil prices fourfold , upending the global economy and again elevating Iran’s strategic significance. Over the 1970s, the United States sold staggering quantities of high-tech weapons to the shah, in order to guarantee access to petroleum and “petrodollar recycling” — ensuring that oil-producing states reinvested the U.S. dollars flooding the region into Western banks and financial markets.

In particular, U.S. policymakers helped develop the monarch’s nuclear program, which became a symbol of his overbearing ego. The Massachusetts Institute of Technology established a special arrangement , which educated dozens of Iranian personnel and, consequently, helped raise the Atomic Energy Organization of Iran’s staff of scientists from 67 to 862 within three years. Pushing back, professors and students claimed that the agreement strengthened the shah’s “fascistic dictatorship” and organized a sit-in at the Nuclear Engineering Department in April 1975. One faculty member warned that MIT was potentially “training engineers to build bombs.”

Yet U.S. cooperation continued and was no outlier. Without exception, the European countries now spearheading sanctions against Tehran previously supported the shah’s drive for nuclear mastery, training scientists, building reactors , and selling sensitive technologies .

Until 1979, Israeli leaders also regarded Iran as an essential lifeline and helped build the shah’s military-industrial complex. At times, the monarchy was Israel’s sole oil supplier and a leading market for its defense exports. Revamping relations, Israeli military officers reportedly maintained regular contact with Iranian staff, and the shah helped them develop missiles capable of carrying nuclear warheads . Their relationship set a new pattern, as Israel helped authoritarian regimes build advanced weapons — including nuclear bombs — to secure hard currency. Prioritizing oil and petrodollars, Israeli leaders respected the shah’s ability to “stifle any resistance.” Any “change in this government will,” Ambassador Uri Lubrani stressed, “be to the detriment of our relations.”

Ultimately, U.S.-Israeli support for the shah backfired. In 1978, military and nuclear spending accelerated an economic crisis, which spiraled into a revolution. Israeli diplomats favored “extreme toughness” and “the establishment of a military regime” to crush protests . But it was too late: The shah fled Iran in January 1979. That same year, evidence emerged that Israel tested a nuclear bomb in the Atlantic, underscoring the failure and hypocrisy of U.S. nonproliferation policy.

In recent decades, American and Israeli officials have portrayed Iran as an existential menace bent on nuclear conquest. In 1992, Prime Minister Yitzhak Rabin warned that Iran was only years away from procuring a nuclear bomb, a claim his successors have repeated ever since. For Tel Aviv, demonizing the Iranian government served two purposes: It justified sending unrivaled levels of U.S. military aid to Israel and diverted attention from the occupation of Palestine.

Following the 2003 invasion of Iraq, President George W. Bush’s administration declared Iran a member of the “axis of evil,” labeling it a proliferation threat while preparing for war. Senior officials were “literally levitating off the ground in pure excitement,” the EU diplomat Alastair Crooke recounted . They boasted that “‘only the wimps … went to Baghdad,’” but “real men” would attack Iran. Over the following decade, U.S. and Israeli policymakers laundered false intelligence , manipulated the International Atomic Energy Agency, and spread unsubstantiated claims about an Iranian bomb program to promote regime change.

For Tel Aviv, demonizing the Iranian government justified sending unrivaled levels of U.S. military aid to Israel and diverted attention from the occupation of Palestine.

Upon taking office in 2009, President Barack Obama maintained pressure through sanctions and cyberattacks . He also tolerated Israel’s assassination program against Iranian nuclear experts; in one case, an undercover operative murdered a scientist in front of his infant daughter . Notoriously, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu took their propaganda campaign to the United Nations, where he brandished a poster of a cartoon explosive. Drawing a red line below the fuse, Netanyahu warned that Iran was approaching “the second stage of nuclear enrichment to make a bomb.”

To avert war, Obama concluded a nuclear agreement with Iran in 2015. But three years later, President Donald Trump arbitrarily scrapped the accord , initiating the latest wave of false accusations to justify unconditional support for Israel and a reinvigorated sanctions regime.

This February, U.S. and Israeli leaders finally launched a full-scale military offensive against Iran. With unintended irony, Trump has threatened to “annihilate the Islamic Republic” while insisting Iran threatens regional stability. Rehashing three-decade-old arguments, Netanyahu also asserts that the war is necessary to forestall disaster. “We have prevented Iran from carrying out a plan to annihilate us, and today they would have had … an atomic bomb to do so,” he informed a press summit .

That propaganda not only justifies the ongoing offensive but disfigures the historical record. Israel, not Iran, has thermonuclear weapons. The illegal offensive has killed thousands of civilians , upended the global economy, and undermined Republican dominance in Congress. The midterm election results represent a stinging repudiation of the war. But its implications remain unclear, as senior Democrats such as House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries have asserted that Iran is “a bad actor” that “must be aggressively confronted.”

Since the 1950s, U.S. and Israeli leaders have repeatedly subverted Iranian sovereignty, threatened nuclear war, and destabilized the Middle East. As under Mosaddegh, Iran once again confronts unapologetic Western aggression, while fighting the latest incarnation of its colonial past.

Donations are down for Truthout at a time when media is under immense pressure. Google’s AI search has driven our traffic down by 15 percent, Trump is arresting journalists, and many independent media organizations face heartbreaking cutbacks and closures.

At the same time, movement media is vital in the fight against Trump’s authoritarian reign. Our mandate to tell the truth, share strategies for resistance, and speak against fascism is ever more urgent in this deluge of political censorship and misinformation. Yet, we are struggling to meet our publishing costs when our work is so urgently needed.

We are fundraising right now for those basic operating expenses — we need $50,000 in the next 10 days. If you can support Truthout with a one-time or monthly donation, you will make a significant impact on our work. Anything you can do makes a difference.

scraped.title: COP31 is here. Will anyone finally say "fossil fuels"?
scraped.description: Three decades of climate talks have danced around the real problem. Turkey’s summit is the latest test.
scraped.author: Rachel Santarsiero
scraped.h1: COP31 Is Here. Will Anyone Finally Say “Fossil Fuels”?
scraped.body_text:
Participants arrive at the COP31 Blue Zone venue on the opening day of the United Nations Climate Change Conference, queuing to collect their accreditation passes and attending the opening ceremony, panel discussions, press conferences, workshops and other events in Antalya, Türkiye on November 9, 2026. Sandro Basili/Zuma

The world’s biggest climate conference kicked off today in Antalya, Turkey, a country known for growing political repression . Under an unusual compromise, Turkey is hosting, but Australia’s government will preside over negotiations among more than 190 nations seeking to address the climate crisis. And for the third year in a row, one problem underscores all the others: Why can’t anyone say “fossil fuels”?

For the next two weeks, delegates from all over the world—except, notably, the United States—will discuss their progress under the Paris Agreement, the international treaty they signed in 2015 (which Donald Trump has twice withdrawn the US from). Under that deal, countries committed to limiting global warming to well below 2 degrees Celsius above pre-industrial levels, and ideally to 1.5 degrees, by setting their own targets for cutting greenhouse gas emissions.

The timing couldn’t be more urgent. We’re in the middle of an El Niño season that has already smashed global temperature records and caused catastrophic flooding in Nepal . And last month, the United Nations warned that we’re on track to overshoot 1.5 degrees entirely. The urgency is real. So is the cynicism.

“UN climate summits have become all but synonymous with low expectations, long on rhetoric, short on action,” Covering Climate Now (CCN) reported , even though “an overwhelming majority of the world’s people, 80 to 89 percent of them, want their governments to ‘do more’ about the climate crisis.”

The annual Conference of the Parties, as COP is officially known, has been the backdrop to my entire life. I have vague middle-school memories of the 2009 Copenhagen summit, which ended in a weak, non-binding accord that left many observers deflated . As a college student in 2015, I remember the surge of possibility I felt when negotiators in Paris emerged with a deal described as “the best possible shot to save the one planet we’ve got.” As an adult, I joined the National Security Archive , where I interviewed dozens of former government officials, scientists, and advocates about all the ways we’ve gotten it wrong—and right—in our quest to save the planet.

Perhaps the most absurd part of this history is that for nearly 30 years—my entire life—international climate negotiations largely avoided naming the primary driver of the climate crisis: fossil fuels. It wasn’t until COP28 in Dubai in 2023 that a final agreement explicitly called for transitioning away from fossil fuels in energy systems, a step UN climate chief Simon Stiell called the “ beginning of the end ” of the fossil fuel era. But the deal crucially neglected to say how or when a phaseout would happen.

Last year was supposed to be different. Brazil hosted, which was a hopeful sign: In 1992, the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change was adopted at the Earth Summit in Rio de Janeiro , an inflection point that ushered in a new era of international cooperation on climate change. For the three years before that, the conference had been held in countries whose economies rely heavily on fossil fuels: Egypt, the United Arab Emirates, and Azerbaijan. But at COP30 in the Amazon city of Belém, delegates failed to make any new commitments on how they’d permanently ditch oil, gas, and coal.

It’s difficult to assess the long-term significance of any individual COP in its immediate aftermath. Copenhagen was considered a failure because negotiators failed to produce a global treaty to replace the 1997 Kyoto Protocol. But years later, observers credited it with having “killed off the top-down treaty-based approach” to climate change, as Joshua Busby, a public affairs professor and researcher at the Center for Climate & Security, pointed out in 2015.

In its place came the system of national pledges at the heart of the Paris Agreement. Those pledges, non-binding though they are, have had real impact. Renewable energy projects boomed. Energy demand growth slowed. Projected warming by the end of the century has dropped from about 3.6 degrees Celsius to 2.6 degrees.

Of course, 2.6 degrees Celsius is hardly a victory, and a gargantuan amount of work remains to avoid the most catastrophic climate scenarios, assuming all nations meaningfully pitch in. When President Trump refused to send a delegation to last year’s conference, former Secretary of State and Special Climate Envoy John Kerry told PBS that the absence of of leaders from the world’s second-biggest greenhouse gas emitter “defeats the fundamental purpose of these meetings” because “no one country can solve this problem by itself.”

Despite a handful of Democratic members of Congress attending this year’s summit, COP31 will be the second year in a row with a US delegation–sized hole in it. But plenty of other countries have woken up to the idea that we have to break up with fossil fuels, with over 60 nations coming together in April in Santa Marta, Colombia to discuss a fossil fuel phaseout outside formal COP negotiations.

A conference that fails to deliver the right language can still build momentum that changes what’s politically possible at the next one.

“We are a majority power that therefore can have confidence that we have a collective global community that really wants this to succeed, and that it isn’t too late,” Johan Rockström, director of the Potsdam Institute for Climate Impact Research, said at the close of an October webinar . “The window is still open, but rapidly shutting.”

scraped.title: Democrats finally lost their last state House seat in rural Kentucky
scraped.description: The party made big gains across the country—but suffered a loss in part of the Eastern Kentucky coalfields it had dominated for decades.
scraped.author: Satchel Walton
scraped.h1: Democrats Finally Lost Their Last State House Seat in Rural Kentucky
scraped.body_text:
The town of Pikeville is woven into the valleys of eastern Kentucky coal country of Pike County. Jahi Chikwendiu/The Washington Post/Getty

Eastern Kentucky Democrats used to brag that when the 1972 results came in, Richard Nixon had won nearly everywhere except for Massachusetts and Floyd County.

It’s been a long, long way down for Appalachian and rural Democrats since then. On Tuesday—as Dems made massive gains nearly everywhere in the country—they quietly lost the state House seat based in Floyd County, and with it, their very last rural representation in the Kentucky General Assembly. It won’t matter much for the political balance in the GOP-dominated legislature, but it is a telling bookend for one of the Democrats’ longest-lasting strongholds: counties like Floyd at the mountainous eastern end of the state, once reliant on coal mining and now beset by persistent poverty and population decline.

Democrats’ midterm results were a bonanza nationally and in other parts of the Bluegrass State, headlined by Zach Dembo’s decisive victory in a congressional seat that was considered safely Republican until recently. Downballot, they picked up seven seats in the Kentucky state House and two in the state Senate—all in suburban areas, mostly around Louisville.

But Republicans retained their so-called “super-duper majority” in both chambers, allowing them to easily override any vetoes issued by Democratic Gov. Andy Beshear. The GOP would have accomplished this regardless of the suburban results, for one reason: Even in a wave year, Democrats couldn’t win any of the more rural districts that cover most of the state.

In Floyd County, the incumbent Democrat didn’t run for re-election. Democrats’ nominee, Johnny Ray Turner, had deep experience, having previously served 20 years in the state Senate—some of it while simultaneously serving home detention and probation after pleading guilty to “not willfully” participating in a scandal involving “the distribution of campaign checks payable to various persons for the purpose of inducing them to vote for Johnny Ray Turner” in the 2000 election.

A brief aside: Back in 2020, Turner lost his state Senate seat to a similarly-named Republican, Johnnie Lloyd Turner. Neither Johnny Ray Turner nor Johnnie Lloyd Turner should be confused with former Sheriff John L. Turner of nearby Breathitt County, who was the ninth person to plead guilty or be convicted of vote-buying in a separate 2010 primary.

Some of the last legislation Democrat Turner sponsored before losing his state Senate seat to Republican Turner included a pro-life “born alive” bill and a measure to tweak regulations on cleaning up coal waste heaps. But even his long track record wasn’t enough to win more than 40 percent of the vote this year, even in a district that voted for Beshear three times in statewide elections.

Kentucky politicians have boasted of representing the whole breadth of the state, “from Paducah to Pikeville,” and Democrats (often conservative ones) used to rely on votes from some mountainous counties of Eastern Kentucky and farm-heavy areas of Western Kentucky. But as national forces came to dominate politics and Democrats elsewhere shifted left, the party has been eviscerated at both ends. US Senate candidate Charles Booker ran a progressive-populist campaign aimed at people “from the hood to the holler” and improved on his 2022 Senate performance, but he still lost 117 of Kentucky’s 120 counties.

Now, for the first time in history, the Kentucky Democrats in the next General Assembly will all hail from in and around Louisville, Lexington, and Frankfort, and from the suburbs of Cincinnati.

Beshear, whose personal popularity remains high, has long depended on support from Trump voters. But his rural successes have hardly boosted the rest of the party. Nearly all of his vetoes have been overridden, and he and Lieutenant Gov. Jacqueline Coleman are the only statewide elected Democrats. One Kentucky political commentator, reacting to last week’s results, wrote that Beshear “had an obligation to help rebuild his party at the legislative and local level, but he doesn’t seem to have done much of anything for it. Instead, he largely invested his political committee’s money in politicizing races for nonpartisan judgeships.”

In response to that criticism and questions from Mother Jones , Nat Turner, the director of communications for the Kentucky Democratic Party, defended the governor’s efforts, saying his endorsements and fundraising helped Dembo and the nine Democrats who flipped seats in the General Assembly.

“Governor Beshear is the leader of the Kentucky Democratic Party and is by far its largest fundraiser, raising over seven figures for the party this cycle,” Turner wrote. “With those resources, the party invested directly in mail and digital for state legislative candidates and was able to flip nine state legislative seats, including House and Senate leadership, and only lose one.”

Kentucky Republicans have spouted triumphalist rhetoric across their decades-long romp to victory in rural Kentucky. When Democrats’ very last rural state senator switched parties last year, Republicans called it “the final chapter of Democratic dominance in eastern Kentucky.” After Democrats lost their majority in the state House in 2016, GOP Congressman James Comer—who represents a sprawling district based in the western part of the state— joked that he wouldn’t make fun of them, lest he be indicted for abuse of a corpse.

Comer is widely expected to run for governor next year. He may face Coleman, or former Beshear adviser Rocky Adkins. When Adkins represented an Eastern Kentucky district in the state House, he cast pro-life and anti-gay marriage votes typical of rural Democrats at the time. But, facing a more liberal primary electorate next year, he has recently backpedaled , saying he and many Kentuckians have “evolved on those issues.” Coleman, too, once branded herself as a “pro-life compassionate Democrat” before gradually changing tune.

Tuesday was a surprisingly strong night for one Democrat from central Appalachia—Richard Ojeda, who ran staunchly populist campaigns for Congress in West Virginia in 2018 and 2020 and more recently called Rep. Virginia Foxx “Satan’s meemaw.” He won a US House seat in a huge upset, but it wasn’t in the mountains. Ojeda had moved to North Carolina and won a district anchored in rapidly growing areas between Greensboro, Fayetteville, and Chapel Hill.

Even on a strong night, neither Ojeda nor his party have much of a home in coalfields that Democrats once dominated.

scraped.title: Abortion laws treat “viability” as a bright line. It isn't.
scraped.description: Nevada and Virginia enshrined a right to abortion until fetal viability—but the standard leaves some of the most vulnerable patients behind.
scraped.author: Madison Pauly
scraped.h1: Abortion Laws Treat “Viability” as a Bright Line. It Isn’t.
scraped.body_text:
Andrea Levy

In 2021, Kate Dineen was standing in her kitchen in Boston when her doctor told her over Zoom that her son had experienced a catastrophic stroke in utero. There was only a 50 percent chance the baby would survive after birth, with zero chance of a healthy outcome. Dineen was devastated; she’d previously had a miscarriage and anxiously tracked pregnancy milestones. Still, the decision about what to do next was clear to her and her husband, she told me: “We felt motivated to protect our son from what would have been a life of suffering, however brief.”

But Dineen was 33 weeks pregnant, and when she asked her doctor about her options, she learned Massachusetts banned abortion after 24 weeks. That cutoff roughly corresponds with the “viability line,” or the point in pregnancy when the fetus has a good chance of surviving outside the uterus. There were exceptions if her own health was in danger, and for “lethal” fetal diagnoses, but the stroke didn’t qualify. Once the fetus reached “viability,” Dineen says, she became “an incubator in the eyes of the state.”

For decades, abortion opponents have slung around sensational terms like “late term” and “partial birth” in their efforts to block abortion outright. On its face, banning the procedure after fetal viability might appear like the moderate position—after all, people of all political stripes express discomfort with later abortions, and abortions after 20 weeks’ gestation are extremely rare. But viability is an imprecise term, more ambiguous than meets the eye, and one state recently opted to ditch it altogether.

Today, anything with the promise to live or succeed can be described as viable: a seed, a business plan, a political candidate. But the word originated as a descriptor for a baby. “Viable” entered the English lexicon in the 1820s, when Dr. Theodric Beck borrowed the term from French to describe the moment a fetus was “capable of living” and could therefore inherit a dead parent’s estate. Another doctor, R.E. Griffith, expanded on the idea in an essay titled “ Remarks on Feticide ,” arguing that in order to convict the mother of a dead newborn, courts must first establish that her child was “viable” at birth. To prove this, Griffith considered various techniques, including an old method of cutting out the lungs and placing them in water—reasoning that if they floated, the baby had likely drawn breath and was not just “a mere parasite of the mother.”

Even as medicine evolved in the ensuing 150 years, doctors’ use of viability as a metric of personhood held fast. Then, in Roe v. Wade , the Supreme Court seized on the concept as a compromise between abortion rights supporters and opponents, declaring a constitutional right to abortion nationwide—but only until fetal viability. States could ban abortion afterward, as long as they allowed exceptions to save the mother’s life.

“You don’t know the story until you are the story,” Sella remembers a patient telling her.

What determines viability, though? There was always something fraught about the court drawing a line at a stage that is, by nature, more a calculation of probability than a guarantee of survival. According to the American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists, the leading US professional association for OB-GYNs, fetal viability is based on internal and environmental factors: gestational age, sex, genetics, weight, the availability of neonatal care, and circumstances around delivery. “Even with all available factors considered, it still isn’t possible to definitively predict survival,” ACOG warns . Generally, viability is considered to be 23 to 25 weeks today—down from about 28 weeks in 1973—though babies born so early have only about a 50 percent chance of survival and often suffer long-lasting complications. Artificial uteruses could someday lead to even younger preemies.

Supreme Court Justice Samuel Alito zeroed in on these ambiguities when he voted to overturn Roe in 2022. “Is a fetus viable with a 10 percent chance of survival? 25 percent? 50 percent? Can such a judgment be made by a State?” he wrote , handing states the power to outlaw abortion at any point they wanted.

With more than a dozen states enacting near-total bans, factions of the pro-choice movement embraced viability in their efforts to safeguard dwindling rights. In the years since Roe was overturned, voters in four states have enshrined a right to abortion until viability into their state constitutions, with limited exceptions afterward—language designed to cover most patients while securing support from voters uneasy about abortion later in pregnancy. (In November, voters in Nevada and Virginia passed similar compromise initiatives.)

But other advocates argue that viability bans still allow the government to interfere in a decision that should remain between a patient and her doctor. In her 2025 memoir, Beyond Limits , Dr. Shelley Sella, the first female physician in the US to openly provide third-trimester abortions, says that by the time women came to her, they’d considered “all the factors relevant to their wellbeing and to their unborn child’s.” Her patients included domestic abuse survivors, women whose birth control failed, and, increasingly before she retired, those who sought abortions earlier in pregnancy but were prevented by state laws from obtaining them. “You don’t know the story until you are the story,” she remembers a patient telling her.

Dineen ultimately was able to terminate her pregnancy by traveling to Maryland, one of nine states where third-trimester abortions were legal. When she returned home, she started working with reproductive rights advocates to change the law in Massachusetts. First, in 2022, they broadened their state’s exception to include “grave” fetal diagnoses, but patients were still falling through the cracks . So this past summer, the legislature passed a new law eliminating the viability line entirely. Massachusetts now leaves the question of later abortions to the “professional judgment of the physician.”

“Pregnancy is complex, and there’s too much gray area to be governed by laws that are black and white,” says Dineen, now a mother of two. “It’s not about a specific fetal diagnosis, it’s not about the specific number of weeks, but it’s really about who gets to decide: Is it the patient and their doctor, or is it the letter of the law, the government?”
